Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation The work addresses targeted removal of factual knowledge from pretrained language models without full retraining. This matters to model developers handling privacy requests, unsafe or outdated facts, and data-governance obligations. Prior gradient-ascent and preference-based unlearning methods typically apply a uniform or model-confidence-derived forgetting signal, even though facts that occur frequently in pretraining are more deeply encoded and remain recoverable after apparent surface suppression. This creates a popularity gap: rare facts can be over-erased, damaging unrelated capability, while popular facts survive paraphrased or adversarial queries. The paper targets this asymmetry in entity-centric factual QA using an external popularity proxy rather than relying solely on the model's current token probabilities. Key Idea The central insight is that current model confidence is not a reliable measure of parametric encoding depth, so the forgetting signal should be conditioned on an external estimate of how widely a fact was represented in training data. AdaPop assigns popular facts β<1, causing their effective per-token gradient to remain or increase as token probability falls, while assigning rare facts β>1, causing forgetting pressure to self-limit. A dual-ascent retain controller complements this per-fact weighting by adapting the global retain penalty when retain loss drifts. The paper's most distinctive contribution is therefore the combination of external popularity-conditioned gradient dynamics with online retain-constraint control, rather than either component alone. Methodology The method receives a forget set of question–answer pairs with per-fact popularity scores and a separate retain set. For each answer token, it computes NLL ℓ_i,t and probability p_i,t=exp(−ℓ_i,t). It maps popularity s_i to β_i=clip(a s_i^(−b), 0.05, 2.0), using DUET-derived anchors β≈1.5 at s≈100 and β≈0.1 at s≈3,000, yielding a=58.7 and b=0.796. The stop-gradient forget weight is w_i,t=sg(p_i,t^β_i), and the loss is L_f=−mean(w_i,tℓ_i,t), optimized jointly with the retain NLL as L=L_f+αL_r. Because the weight is detached, the effective gradient scaling is p_i,t^(β_i−1): β>1 is self-limiting, β=1 recovers uniform effective weighting, and β<1 sustains pressure on low-probability tokens. The retain coefficient is α=α_0+λ, with α_0=0.5; after each epoch, the controller computes positive relative retain-loss drift δ_k against the epoch-1 reference and updates λ by projected ascent, λ←Π_[0,5](λ+0.1(δ_k−0.1)). Critical design decisions are the external proxy, the β=1.5/0.1 anchor choices, and epoch-level rather than batch-level dual updates. The proxy rationale is supported by corpus-frequency correlations, while the anchor values and controller hyperparameters remain partly heuristic; the paper reports sensitivity experiments but does not derive them from a fitted encoding-depth model. Key Results Experiments use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-7B-it, all adapted with LoRA rank 32 and LoRA scaling 64, on DUET and RWKU. At learning rate 10^−4, AdaPop's forget/retain ROUGE-L values are 0.043/0.959 and 0.078/0.972 on Llama, 0.056/0.950 and 0.016/0.855 on Qwen, and 0.023/0.976 and 0.034/0.948 on Gemma for DUET and RWKU respectively. Among stable methods, it has the lowest forget cosine similarity in all six cells and the lowest forget ROUGE-L in five of six; WGA is marginally lower on Llama/DUET surface ROUGE-L (0.036 versus 0.043). On DUET paraphrases, AdaPop obtains 0.045, 0.074, and 0.027 forget ROUGE-L for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, compared with WGA's 0.042, 0.104, and 0.050. On RWKU level-3 adversarial attacks, AdaPop obtains 0.262, 0.144, and 0.195 versus WGA's 0.396, 0.211, and 0.239. Model-averaged internal metrics show AdaPop with forget ΔLP of −160 on DUET and −23 on RWKU, ΔRank of +53,760 and +4,169, hidden-state cosine of 0.702 and 0.484, and KL divergence of 42.5 and 9.1; these indicate larger changes than WGA, whose DUET ΔRank is −3,714. General capability remains within 0.05 MMLU of the original checkpoint across models; HellaSwag is unchanged or improved on Llama and Qwen and drops from 0.64 to 0.62 on Gemma. The 2×2 ablation reports that without the controller, rare-fact retain ROUGE-L can fall to 0.769 versus at least 0.927 with dynamic α; at comparable popular-fact forgetting near 0.02, full AdaPop retains 0.724 versus 0.683 for controller-only weighting. A Wikidata score correlates with measured Pile-train frequency at Pearson 0.970 in log space and Spearman 0.839, while the LLM judge reaches 0.677 and 0.659; 100% label inversion still gives retain 0.92 and popular-fact forget ROUGE-L 0.05 in the reported stress test. On one A100, AdaPop takes 29.0 minutes versus 29.4 for WGA, 27.1 for GD, 23.4 for RMU, and 40.0 for NPO. GA and GD achieve near-zero forget scores only by causing generation and retain collapse, so excluding them from stable-method ranking is justified but makes the comparison dependent on a usability criterion. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The paper's genuine methodological contribution is the use of an external, fact-level popularity signal to set a power-law forgetting exponent and its combination with a dual-ascent retain controller; gradient ascent, loss reweighting, and primal-dual retain control are established ingredients, so the novelty is primarily their targeted composition for the popularity gap rather than a wholly new optimization framework. Rigor & Reproducibility The study evaluates three model families, two real-world benchmarks, eleven additional methods in the appendix, three random seeds for ROUGE-L, learning-rate sweeps, coefficient sensitivity, a 2×2 component ablation, proxy comparisons, label-noise stress tests, per-epoch dynamics, and internal metrics. Code is stated to be released at https://github.com/Anya-wUw/open-unlearning; data and model weights are not stated as newly released. The main baseline set includes GA, GD, NPO, and WGA, with broader comparisons in the appendix, but the evaluation uses a common learning rate and five-epoch protocol rather than clearly reporting equally extensive per-method hyperparameter optimization; this matters because several baselines are highly sensitive or collapse. Cosine similarity metrics are reported from a single seed, while only ROUGE-L has three-seed statistics; no confidence intervals or significance tests are given. The retain controller uses epoch-1 retain loss as its reference rather than the pre-unlearning checkpoint, which may absorb an initial shift and weakens the interpretation of the claimed retain constraint. The benchmarks and popularity proxies are closely related to the paper's motivating hypothesis, especially DUET's explicit popularity stratification, although RWKU provides a narrower external test. Hidden-state cosine, KL, and rank shifts are useful diagnostics but do not prove that the information is absent from all parameter subspaces or cannot be recovered through further fine-tuning. The authors report no formal convergence guarantee for the non-convex dual-ascent procedure. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: AdaPop runs with LoRA on commercially available hardware; the reported Llama/DUET run takes 29.0 minutes on one A100, and the popularity preprocessing costs approximately 12 minutes for 2,000 facts using Wikidata. Efficient: Per-step cost is approximately the same as WGA because the method reuses forward-pass probabilities and adds no extra pass, with only one retain evaluation and a two-scalar controller update per epoch; total cost relative to hand-tuned baselines is not fully established because the paper does not quantify hyperparameter-search budgets consistently. Effective: The evidence supports improved resistance to paraphrase and adversarial recovery over stable baselines while preserving MMLU and HellaSwag, but these are behavioral and representation proxies rather than a direct certification that the target knowledge has been removed. Scalable: The method is tested only on 7–8B models, small factual benchmarks, and LoRA adapters; behavior at 10×–100× scale, with larger forget sets, longer training, mixed domains, or full-parameter updates is not evaluated. The work delivers a reusable training implementation and code repository, but not a certified unlearning service, standalone production tool, or trained model artifact. Strengths - It identifies and directly targets a concrete failure mode—popular facts surviving unlearning—rather than optimizing only aggregate forget/retain scores. - The β analysis gives a clear mechanistic interpretation of the weighting: the β=1 crossover separates self-limiting from pressure-sustaining gradients, and the paper verifies the predicted tier-dependent learning-rate gap empirically. - The dual-ascent and popularity components receive a meaningful 2×2 ablation; the results show distinct failure modes when either component is removed instead of presenting only an end-to-end comparison. - Robustness testing goes beyond exact prompts, including held-out paraphrases, nine adversarial prompt manipulations, hidden-state changes, token-rank shifts, and proxy corruption. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge dependence on external popularity scores, limited coverage of Wikidata for procedural and creative knowledge, calibration requirements when a proxy has a different numerical range, and evaluation restricted to LoRA fine-tuning. They state that full fine-tuning was excluded because prior work found it difficult to stabilize, but they do not evaluate whether AdaPop changes that conclusion. They also acknowledge that proxy quality may limit gains outside entity-centric factual QA and suggest replacing popularity with domain-specific difficulty or harm-severity estimates. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper equates lower ROUGE-L, lower semantic cosine, hidden-state movement, and adversarial non-recovery with deeper erasure, but none tests whether the fact can be recovered by continued fine-tuning, access to neighboring prompts, model merging, checkpoint interpolation, or extraction attacks beyond the nine listed prompt manipulations. - The controller's constraint is measured relative to epoch 1 rather than the original checkpoint, and the reported claim that it keeps |δ_k|≤0.1 does not by itself establish preservation of the broader pretrained distribution. - The evaluation is dominated by entity-centric QA and uses a popularity-aware benchmark designed to expose the proposed effect; results on non-Wikidata knowledge, multi-hop facts, memorized text spans, code, procedures, personal data, or safety-sensitive content are absent. - The strongest numerical claims rely on comparisons among methods at a selected learning rate, while several baselines are known to require method-specific tuning and some are labeled unusable after collapse; a compute-matched Pareto comparison over independently optimized hyperparameters would make the ranking more decisive. - Internal metrics are averaged across models and have limited statistical reporting; cosine similarity is single-seed, and the paper does not provide per-example variance, uncertainty, or tests showing that representation changes predict resistance to unseen recovery attacks. - The method's claimed reduction in tuning burden is plausible but not rigorously quantified: the paper does not report the number and cost of baseline α or learning-rate trials needed to obtain each comparator's best stable point. Bottom Line AdaPop is a useful and technically coherent contribution for entity-centric factual LLM unlearning, with unusually strong robustness and component-ablation evidence, but its practical claims should be limited to LoRA-based 7–8B models and behavioral proxy evaluation until full-model, cross-domain, and recovery-after-retraining tests are provided.

#16 — Highly Innovative (78)

Do Language Models Consistently Encode the Current Year?

S van Adrichem, A Bhaskar, D Yang, C Potts, J Huang · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces associative and declarative probes for measuring how language models encode the current year, traces their internal mechanisms, and evaluates prompting, SFT, and weight editing as update methods. - Why it's important: A model can appear temporally aligned while retaining incompatible notions of time, creating risks for temporal reasoning, factual updating, safety behavior, and knowledge-cutoff management. - How it does it: It infers an associative year from the transition between past and present/future verb probabilities after prompts such as “In {year} there,” and compares it with directly generated years under declarative prompts, causal interventions, training-data analysis, and update experiments. - The good: Across 13 base models, the associative current year estimates the pre-training cutoff within 0.85 years on average, while mechanistic interventions identify a causal one-dimensional year-type subspace in OLMo2-7B. - The missing: The strongest mechanistic and training-dynamics evidence is concentrated in the OLMo2 family, and the paper does not establish that the proposed probes predict real temporal reasoning or behavior beyond highly controlled English prompts. - Read it or not: Researchers studying temporal knowledge, mechanistic interpretability, or model editing should read it for the distinction between robust pre-training associations and shallow post-training declarations; practitioners seeking a working method for refreshing model time should not expect a solution here.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (84) are strong because the associative/declarative distinction offers a genuinely informative formulation of temporal representation and model updating. Rigor (78) is supported by heterogeneous model coverage, alternative probes, causal interventions, training-stage analyses, controls, and update experiments, though the strongest mechanistic evidence remains concentrated in OLMo2 and lacks conventional multi-seed uncertainty. Completeness (82) and Resilience (76) benefit from explicit probe-relative limitations, but the central conclusion is not yet connected to downstream temporal reasoning or collateral damage from editing. Impact (58) is moderate because the work diagnoses a problem rather than delivering a reliable date-refreshing method. Problem & Motivation Language models must represent temporal context to answer time-dependent questions, interpret tense, and avoid confusing their knowledge cutoff with the actual date. Prior work largely evaluates temporal reasoning behavior or attempts to refresh models through prompting and fine-tuning without determining whether “the current year” is a single, coherent internal concept. The paper addresses the narrower representational gap between an implicitly expressed temporal association—whether a year should be described with past versus present/future tense—and an explicit answer to “what year is it?” It also asks whether either notion can be updated reliably, which matters for deployed systems whose knowledge cutoff or simulated date changes after training. Key Idea The core insight is that behavioral agreement on the current year does not imply representational agreement. The paper separates a pre-training-derived associative current year (ACY), read from the year at which verb-tense probabilities switch from past to present/future, from a post-training-derived declarative current year (DCY), read from explicit year generation. The ACY behaves like a factual year-to-tense association localized to a small causal subspace, whereas the DCY is prompt-dependent and lacks a stable causal pathway. This separation explains why interventions that update explicit date statements do not reliably update grammatical temporal behavior. Methodology The paper first defines ACY as the first year y for which the probability of past forms (was, were) falls below the probability of present/future forms (is, are, will) in prompts such as “In {year} there”; these five forms capture over 90% of next-token probability mass on average across the 13 main models. It also defines ACYM using year-month prompts and tests six alternative templates, twelve tense-before-year templates, and dictionary-derived verb sets. DCY is the average greedily decoded year across ten continuation prompts for base models or ten instruction prompts for SFT models. The experiments compare 13 base LMs, primarily spanning Pythia, GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, OLMo, Falcon, RedPajama, and Llama, and use OLMo2-1B and OLMo2-7B for detailed training-dynamics, data-distribution, causal, and editing analyses. The paper analyzes provenance by comparing ACY with reported or replicated perplexity-based cutoff estimates and with n-gram and sentence-level co-occurrence models constructed from OLMo2 stage-specific corpora. It analyzes mechanisms using distributed alignment search (DAS) under a causal abstraction Y → T, interchange interventions, random-subspace and randomly initialized controls, non-year entity controls, number-like controls, and attention/MLP knockouts. For DCY it uses attention and MLP knockouts over five-layer windows and four prompt families. Finally, it evaluates three update strategies on OLMo2-1B: year-shifted SFT, a system prompt specifying a target year, and low-rank editing with ROME for DCY or MEMIT for ACY. The paper introduces associative cross-entropy (ACE), which averages the cross-entropy between the model’s tense distribution and an ideal past-before-target/present-after-target distribution. The main design decisions—using verb tense as a scalable associative signal, separating base continuation prompts from post-trained instruction prompts, and evaluating update success over 351 target years from 1900 to 2250—are plausible and generally motivated, although the semantic validity of tense as a general current-year measure remains only partially established. Key Results Across 13 base models, ACY deviates from the stated pre-training cutoff by an average of 0.85 years, and ACYM by 0.75 years, compared with 2.71 years for the replicated or inherited WIKISPAN perplexity method. Individual deviations vary substantially: several models are within 0–12 months, while Falcon-RW-7B, RedPajama-7B-Base, and Llama models show errors of roughly 1–2 years; OLMo2-7B’s ACYM is a five-year outlier despite a one-year ACY error. In OLMo2, ACY shifts across the boundary between pre-training stages—OLMo2-1B from 2021 to 2023 and OLMo2-7B from 2022 to 2024—and remains comparatively stable within stages. Count-based n-gram and co-occurrence models track the LM tense distributions better than baselines, with cross-entropies as low as 0.34–0.36 for n-grams and 0.61–0.78 for co-occurrence models. DCY behaves differently. OLMo2 base checkpoints produce variable and often outdated explicit years: stage-1 and stage-2 DCYs range from 2011 to 2016 with confidence around 4.3–6.1%, whereas SFT models produce 2023 with zero prompt variance and roughly 52.5–60.0% confidence. Removing years from SFT data yields a coherent but shifted DCY of 2021; shifting all years in SFT data shifts DCY by the same offset with near-zero variance, supporting separate contributions from instruction following and year distribution. In updating experiments, system-prompt SFT reaches 94.6% exact DCY accuracy over 351 target years with mean error 0.45 years, but only 1.7% exact ACY accuracy. Across nine additional Gemma-3 and Qwen-3.5 models, DCY prompting reaches as high as 100%, while ACY prompting ranges from 0.3% to 53.3% and never approaches comparable reliability. Year-shifted SFT updates DCY accurately but moves ACY only near the original year; MEMIT shifts ACY to within six years for all eight tested targets but leaves DCY near 2022/2023. The DAS analysis on OLMo2-7B finds a one-dimensional year-type subspace from layers 4–22 at the final year token, with controls showing 0% IIA for a randomly initialized model, about 14% for random subspaces, and above 90% for early-layer interchanges with four-digit numbers in non-temporal contexts. These results support a structured number/year representation, but not necessarily a uniquely temporal or language-independent “current-year” representation. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the explicit separation and joint evaluation of associative and declarative current-year notions, together with evidence that they have different training origins, causal pathways, and update behavior; the probing and editing techniques themselves largely combine established causal-abstraction, DAS, ROME, MEMIT, SFT, and prompting methods. Rigor & Reproducibility The study includes meaningful robustness checks: alternative prompt structures and output-verb sets for ACY, tense-before-year controls, 13 base models for cutoff estimation, nine additional instruction-tuned models for prompting, stage-specific OLMo2 data comparisons, training checkpoints, random-subspace and random-model controls, non-year entity controls, and disjoint DAS training/evaluation pairs. It reports exact accuracies, mean errors, cross-entropies, prompt variance, confidence, and some standard deviations. The code repository is stated as https://github.com/Suzehva/current-year-in-lms, and the authors state that models and training data will be released; the supplied text does not provide a release URL or confirm that those artifacts are already available. The paper does not report conventional multiple-seed confidence intervals or statistical significance tests for most comparisons, and it does not quantify uncertainty in manually curated factual-recency annotations. The main ACY metric is also highly dependent on a hand-selected English prompt family and a threshold crossing, while the DCY metric depends on greedy decoding and a selected set of ten prompts. The comparison to perplexity uses inherited estimates for eight models and replicated estimates for five, which is reasonable but not a fully controlled contemporary baseline. Most importantly, the probes evaluate lexical probability behavior rather than downstream temporal reasoning, so the claim that the two notions are inconsistent should be interpreted as a claim about these operationalizations, not a complete account of temporal cognition. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The probes and prompting method can run on commercially available hardware, although reproducing training-checkpoint, SFT, and weight-editing experiments requires substantially more compute. Efficient: ACY measurement requires sweeping many years and token probabilities, while DCY requires only a small prompt set; the paper does not provide wall-clock, memory, or cost comparisons with alternative cutoff estimators. Effective: The evidence establishes reliable separation and update failure on the proposed probes, but does not show that ACY or DCY predicts performance on real temporal reasoning, factual recency, or safety tasks; indeed, the factual probes often fail to recover the cutoff. Scalable: Prompt-based ACY analysis scales across model families and tested target years, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger models, multilingual settings, longer temporal units, multimodal models, or deployment-scale update workflows. The work delivers research code and, according to the paper, planned model and data releases; it does not deliver a production date-refreshing tool or a method that successfully updates both notions. Strengths - The associative/declarative distinction is conceptually sharp and exposes a failure mode hidden by single-question evaluations of “current year.” - The ACY probe provides a surprisingly accurate, inexpensive proxy for pre-training cutoff across 13 heterogeneous base models, outperforming the reported perplexity proxy by average error. - The paper combines behavioral analysis with causal interventions, training-stage comparisons, corpus statistics, and update experiments rather than relying on correlations alone. - The update matrix is especially informative: prompting and SFT update explicit declarations but not grammatical associations, while ACY-specific MEMIT edits do not transfer to DCY, directly testing the practical consequence of the proposed distinction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly note that factual event probes cannot evaluate far-future years because future facts do not yet exist, require manual curation and grading, and are harder to scale than the tense-based ACY task. They also acknowledge that English lacks a clear morphological present/future distinction, so present and future forms are grouped, and that prompt structure affects interpretation. The paper notes that four-digit years may be split across tokens and that the year-type representation can generalize to number-like expressions outside temporal contexts. These limitations are confronted through alternative prompt templates and controls, although the broader implications for languages, tasks, and real temporal reasoning remain open. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The principal claim that LMs “do not have a consistent notion of the current year” is stronger than the evidence: the paper demonstrates inconsistency between two carefully designed probes, but does not test whether a shared latent variable emerges under broader behavioral, representational, or intervention-based definitions. - The mechanistic localization and modified-training experiments rely heavily on OLMo2-1B/7B; the larger-model generalization covers prompting only, so the causal and editing conclusions are not established across the Gemma and Qwen families. - There is no evaluation of downstream temporal reasoning, date arithmetic, chronological QA, calibrated knowledge-cutoff behavior, or harmful behaviors; therefore practical impact is inferred rather than measured. - The ACY may partly measure corpus-specific grammatical co-occurrence and tokenization artifacts rather than a model’s current-time representation. The number-like interchange results, including over 90% early-layer IIA for non-temporal four-digit numbers, reinforce this alternative interpretation and deserve a more direct disentanglement. - The target-year update range is synthetic and includes implausible years such as 2223; the paper does not test realistic post-cutoff updates involving new entities, facts, tense usage, or mixtures of dates, nor does it measure collateral damage from MEMIT, ROME, or SFT edits. - The use of different prompt formats for base and instruction-tuned models complicates direct comparisons between ACY/DCY development stages, and greedy decoding plus ten selected declarative prompts may understate output uncertainty and prompt sensitivity. Bottom Line This is a strong and useful empirical/mechanistic study for researchers investigating temporal representations and model editing, but its central conclusion should be read as probe-relative because it does not yet connect the ACY/DCY split to broad downstream temporal behavior or demonstrate a general solution for updating model time.

SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments (42 ▲ )

Bo Liu, Simon Yu, Yiding Jiang, Ao Qu, Andrew Zhao, Zichen Liu, Junsu Kim, Zijian Zhou, Seungone Kim, Tongzheng Ren, Mickel Liu, Hanfei Yu, Zhaorun Chen, Weiyan Shi, Paul Pu Liang, Luke Zettlemoyer, Yejin Choi, Natasha Jaques · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SPADE, a self-play reinforcement-learning framework in which one shared LLM learns both to generate executable Gym-style multi-turn environments and to solve them. - Why it's important: Fixed or frozen environment pools saturate as agents improve, limiting the supply of verifiable experience needed for continued reasoning and tool-use progress. - How it does it: SPADE trains the Environment Designer using the gap between the Reasoning Agent's hinted and unhinted returns, while grounding generation in sampled pretraining-corpus documents and an evolving memory of prior environments. - The good: On Qwen3-30B-A3B, SPADE raises the eight-benchmark games average from 50.2 to 58.3, exceeding the strongest retrained fixed-environment baseline by 5.3 points, and improves ACEBench-Agent by 13.9 points in tool use. - The missing: The paper does not establish that the gains persist at substantially larger training budgets or tested environment scales, and its tool-use comparisons rely substantially on results transcribed from papers with different models, data, harnesses, and benchmark versions. - Read it or not: Researchers working on LLM post-training, environment scaling, unsupervised environment design, or self-play should read it; readers seeking evidence of open-ended continual improvement beyond fixed benchmarks can treat the central claim as promising but not demonstrated.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents need large, diverse, verifiable interactive training distributions, but hand-built environments are expensive and frozen synthetic generators do not adapt as the learner improves. Existing self-play methods generally generate single-turn tasks or use heuristic difficulty, uncertainty, variance, or novelty signals, which can suffer from information-symmetry collapse, mode collapse, reward hacking, or generation of unsolvable challenges. The target problem is therefore adaptive environment design for general-purpose reasoning and multi-step tool use: environments should remain diverse, executable, solvable, and close to the agent's current learning frontier rather than becoming either mastered or impossible. Key Idea: The central insight is to make the environment generator a jointly trained player and reward it by hint-based regret: the difference between the same Reasoning Agent's success with a designer-provided privileged hint and without that hint. A large positive gap identifies an environment that is solvable when the relevant structure is exposed but not yet mastered unaided. Corpus grounding supplies external semantic breadth, while memory supplies difficulty-continuity and high-regret seeds. The code-as-environment representation is important operationally, but the frontier-targeting return gap is the paper's primary algorithmic idea. Methodology: SPADE uses one policy with role-specific prompts. In the Environment Designer phase, the policy samples a corpus passage and environment-memory records, emits a complete Python environment implementing reset()/step(), and emits a task-specific hint. Syntax, instantiation, reset, and probe-based execution checks filter invalid programs; tool-use environments additionally undergo deterministic solvability checks and an LLM screen. In the Reasoning Agent phase, the shared policy performs G=16 fresh rollouts without the hint and 16 with it, interacting through sequential actions; the task-completion reward is supplied by the generated verifier. For environment e, the basic designer signal is r_D(e)=mean[r_A(e|h)]−mean[r_A(e)], floored at zero during training, and blended with a difficulty-anchor reward weighted 0.4/0.6, targeting a 0.4–0.6 unhinted win-rate band. Both role trajectories update the shared policy with GRPO, using role-specific advantage normalization, delayed designer updates, truncated importance sampling for the resulting off-policy objective, asymmetric clipping (0.20/0.28), and KL regularization where configured. Games use 24 environments per rollout, six rotating cognitive skills with three active at a time, k=4 regeneration intervals, and 15,000 math/science corpus documents; tool-use environments use simulated function-calling APIs, three to five sequential user instructions, 15,000 code-corpus documents, and k=8. The major design choices are technically coherent but only partly isolated: the hint-regret signal is compared with an EMA learning-potential alternative, while corpus grounding, memory, and designer adaptation are separately ablated to varying degrees. Key Results: In the games setting, SPADE improves the untrained Qwen3 averages by +5.2 points at 4B (38.9 to 44.1), +5.7 at 8B (49.8 to 55.5), and +8.1 at 30B-A3B (50.2 to 58.3). At 30B-A3B, scores are AIME 2025 62.8, AIME 2026 74.4, GPQA-Diamond 75.8, LiveCodeBench-v6 Pass@1 47.3, and Reasoning-Gym win rates of 63.3/32.1/37.7/72.8 for math/algorithmic/cognition/logic. The strongest fixed-environment comparator, RLVE, reaches an average of 53.0, so the reported SPADE margin is 5.3 points; Fixed-env GRPO reaches 51.4. The strongest individual reported gains over RLVE occur on Reasoning-Gym Math (+7.5 points) and cognition (+6.8 points), although the table's main comparison is against each baseline per benchmark. In tool use, Qwen3-30B-A3B rises from 53.3 untrained to 61.1 after SPADE: BFCL v4 multi-turn 49.0 to 54.7 (+5.7), tau2-bench 49.0 to 52.6 (+3.6), and ACEBench-Agent 62.0 to 75.9 (+13.9). At 4B, BFCL improves by +10.3 and ACEBench-Agent by +8.9; at 8B, the corresponding gains are +6.4 and +9.0. The tool-use cross-system comparison is favorable on BFCL and ACEBench-Agent, but it is not a controlled head-to-head because reference scores come from different base models, training budgets, data, harnesses, benchmark versions, and user simulators. Qualitative and diagnostic measurements report 3,310 distinct accepted programs from 1,513 documents in the canonical 30B games run, learnable-band fraction rising from 0.16 to 0.31, Reasoning Agent win rate rising from 0.30 to 0.62, and corpus-grounded Vendi/n diversity of 0.68 versus 0.04 without corpus grounding. These measurements support adaptive difficulty and diversity, but they do not directly measure open-ended capability growth or real-world agent reliability. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the combination of an RL-trained, shared-parameter LLM Environment Designer, executable full-MDP generation, and hint-based regret as an online frontier signal; corpus grounding, replay memory, GRPO, Gym interfaces, and minimax-regret curriculum principles are established components, and the paper's theoretical result is an idealized adaptation of prior PAIRED-style reasoning rather than a new general optimality guarantee. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides substantial implementation detail, fixed hyperparameters, a 400-rollout training budget, three Qwen3 scales, a second Nemotron backbone check on Reasoning-Gym, component ablations, reward-signal ablations, training curves, and qualitative inspection of generated programs. The full code, run configurations, evaluation JSONs, and figure-generation scripts are stated to be released at https://github.com/spade-rl/spade; the project page is https://spade-rl.github.io. However, the evidence does not report multiple independent random seeds, error bars or confidence intervals for the principal benchmark scores, or statistical significance tests. The strongest ablations are informative but not perfectly factorial: the frozen self-play designer control also removes memory, and the GPT-5.5 control changes the designer model rather than isolating only the absence of RL updates. Checkpoint selection uses the best eight-benchmark suite average, which introduces evaluation-set selection pressure and weakens the interpretation of final scores. Generated-environment correctness is imperfect before sanitation: only 84.9% execute as emitted and 90.3% after stripping Markdown fences, with a reported 7.4% brace-escaping failure repaired by the pipeline; post-filter validity is 100%, but this makes the measured training distribution dependent on a sanitizer. The theoretical equilibrium result assumes sound generation, hints that attain the optimal unhinted value, and internalizability of hinted behavior; these are strong assumptions that do not hold for ordinary finite-sample LLM training, noisy hints, or imperfect verifiers. Tool-use benchmark comparisons are explicitly non-comparable in several respects, and generated environments are themselves produced from a corpus and fixed prompt template, so the claim of an unbounded environment space is conceptual rather than an empirical demonstration of unbounded growth. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the work trains and evaluates methods and releases a software implementation for generating and executing environments. - Practical: The approach uses commercially available 4B, 8B, and 30B-A3B language models and simulated Python environments, but the paper does not provide wall-clock cost, GPU type, total GPU-hours, or inference throughput, so practical deployment cost is not established. - Efficient: SPADE requires environment generation, hint generation, 16 hinted and 16 unhinted agent rollouts per environment, validation, and joint GRPO updates; relative compute and memory cost versus RLVE, fixed GRPO, or frozen-generator synthesis is not quantified. - Effective: Held-out scores improve across reasoning, code, procedural reasoning, and multi-turn tool-use benchmarks, with the largest tool-use gains on structurally similar stateful tasks; evidence remains proxy-based because generated environments are synthetic and no real API, terminal, web, or production deployment is evaluated. - Scalable: Results cover 4B–30B-A3B models and 400 rollout iterations, with one limited Nemotron transfer, but the paper does not test 10×–100× more environments, training steps, context, or model scale; it explicitly acknowledges that environment complexity is bounded by the designer's model and generation budget. The work delivers a reusable codebase and training/evaluation pipeline, but not a released large environment dataset or a production-grade environment service; generated artifacts can be regenerated from the released implementation. Strengths: - It addresses an important bottleneck—adaptive supply of verifiable experience—rather than only changing the solver architecture or inference-time harness. - Hint-based regret is a sensible mechanism for distinguishing learnable frontier tasks from mastered and impossible tasks, and the paper tests it against an EMA learning-potential alternative rather than presenting it only as intuition. - The executable reset()/step() abstraction supports both reasoning games and multi-turn simulated tool use, giving the method a clearer systems-level scope than task-only self-play approaches. - The ablations and diagnostics identify a nontrivial division of labor: corpus grounding maintains diversity (Vendi/n 0.68 versus 0.04 without it), while designer training increases difficulty and learnability; the reported late-training advantage over fixed environments is consistent with the proposed adaptation mechanism. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the designer's complexity is bounded by the base model's context and capabilities, that both roles still rely on a human-designed optimizer such as GRPO, and that hint-based regret has no formal guarantee of producing an optimal curriculum in the implemented setting. They also acknowledge that evaluation uses fixed benchmarks rather than a direct measure of open-ended reasoning growth. The paper confronts these limitations directly, but it does not quantify the compute burden implied by the designer's extra rollouts or establish robustness under much longer training. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper does not report independent-seed variance for the headline benchmark gains, which is especially important given noisy GRPO training, stochastic generated programs, and checkpoint selection. - The headline claim that designer adaptation itself drives the benefit is not cleanly isolated: the principal frozen self-play control removes both designer training and memory, while the GPT-5.5 control changes model identity and likely generation quality as well as adaptivity. - The method's verifier and environment code are generated by the same policy family that is being optimized, creating a risk that the agent learns quirks, exploitable reward functions, or artificial interaction conventions rather than transferable reasoning; the paper's LLM well-posedness rubric and smoke tests do not fully rule this out. - The paper claims arbitrary computable MDP expressivity, but actual generated programs are narrowly constrained by fixed prompts, corpus domains, Python templates, validation filters, and short 400-rollout runs; the results show diverse instances, not an empirically open-ended environment distribution. - Tool-use gains are strongest on ACEBench-Agent, whose stateful multi-step structure resembles the generated environments, while no evaluation uses real tools or unseen interaction protocols; this supports structural transfer but limits the practical generality of the claim. - Some qualitative claims about emergent curriculum and evidence-first behavior rely on selected transcripts and aggregate proxies; no blinded human assessment, behavioral intervention, or causal analysis establishes that the observed strategy changes are necessary for benchmark gains. Bottom Line: SPADE is a technically substantial and practically relevant advance over fixed environment synthesis, with credible but not yet fully controlled evidence that jointly training a corpus-grounded environment designer can sustain LLM post-training gains; it is worth reading for environment-scaling and self-play researchers, but its open-ended self-improvement claim remains ahead of its evaluation.

ChartProbe: A Diagnostic Study on Visual Reasoning through Perception, Grounding, and Simple Reasoning

M Khoshnoodi, SA Bargal · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ChartProbe, a programmatic diagnostic and skill-targeted fine-tuning framework that separates visual question answering into perception, grounding, and simple reasoning and measures their transfer to unseen complex-reasoning questions. - Why it's important: It challenges the common assumption that poor chart reasoning primarily reflects deficient multi-step reasoning, suggesting that improving visual evidence extraction can reduce errors without collecting complex reasoning traces. - How it does it: It generates exact probe questions from chart-rendering code or CLEVR scene graphs, fine-tunes VLMs on one or more atomic skills while withholding complex questions, and evaluates transfer across chart and non-chart domains. - The good: Across InternVL-3.5-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, and LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B, atomic-skill supervision improves held-out complex-reasoning accuracy, including gains as large as 27.6 percentage points for Qwen on unseen pie-chart questions. - The missing: The study does not compare against direct complex-reasoning supervision, so it does not establish that simple-skill training is more efficient or more effective than the standard intervention it is intended to replace. - Read it or not: Researchers studying multimodal reasoning, chart QA, or diagnostic evaluation should read it for the intervention-based decomposition and controlled transfer results, but practitioners seeking a validated replacement for reasoning fine-tuning will need stronger comparative evidence.

Problem & Motivation: Vision-language models often fail on chart questions involving comparisons, rankings, aggregation, and derived quantities, but aggregate accuracy does not reveal whether an error arises from reading visual structure, binding labels to visual elements, or computing over correctly recovered values. The paper targets chart QA and related visual reasoning settings in which perception, label-element grounding, and elementary computation are entangled. Its specific research gap is the lack of an intervention that isolates these skills and tests whether improving them transfers to complex reasoning without exposing the model to complex questions or reasoning traces. The motivation is diagnostic rather than application-specific: identifying the actual bottleneck before investing in chain-of-thought, reinforcement learning, or other reasoning-centered supervision. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat decomposition as a training intervention rather than merely an evaluation taxonomy: if a model's complex visual reasoning depends on upstream visual skills, then fine-tuning perception or grounding alone should improve held-out complex reasoning. ChartProbe operationalizes this by generating skill-specific questions from the same latent specification that renders each image, making the target answer exact while keeping the complex target questions out of training. The distinction between perception and grounding is particularly useful because a model may visually read an element correctly but bind it to the wrong category or label. Methodology: ChartProbe starts from ChartNet Python source code and CSV data for rendered single-series bar charts, or from CLEVR scene-graph JSON, and instantiates hand-authored templates into question-answer pairs. The chart template bank contains 26 schemas: 8 perception probes based on geometry without reading axis values, 9 grounding probes covering label-element binding, value lookup, and bounding boxes, and 9 simple-reasoning probes covering ranking, sums, means, differences, percentages, and closest-value comparisons. Training uses 1,000 bar charts, stratified by 3–5, 6–10, and 11–24 bars; evaluation uses disjoint sets of 500 bar charts, 500 pie charts, and 500 CLEVR scenes, plus 500 bar and 500 pie questions from independently authored ChartQA. Three open-weight VLMs are adapted with LoRA of rank 32 and alpha 64 on attention and MLP projections, while the vision encoder remains frozen. Five configurations train on perception (P), grounding (G), simple reasoning (SR), P+G, or P+G+SR, with no complex-reasoning examples; training runs for one epoch with fixed learning rates of 1e-4 for InternVL and LLaVA and 2e-4 for Qwen, and three random seeds. The paper does not state an explicit loss function beyond supervised fine-tuning. Critical design choices—the source-derived exact labels, exclusion of multi-series charts, and withholding of complex questions—are well aligned with causal attribution, although the hand-authored templates and synthetic rendering constrain what the intervention measures. Combined configurations confound skill coverage with training-set volume; a volume-matched ablation addresses this for InternVL only and shows P+G remains beneficial while the all-skill advantage partly disappears. Key Results: On held-out ChartNet complex-reasoning sets scored with RapidFuzz similarity, all three models generally improve after simple-skill supervision. InternVL rises from 24.0 to 36.7 on bar charts and from 26.0 to 40.9 on pie charts under perception-only training, and reaches 48.0 to 67.1 on CLEVR under grounding-only training. Qwen rises from 8.6 to 28.1 on bar charts and from 9.0 to 36.6 on pie charts with P+G, while CLEVR rises from 20.2 to 57.2; the largest reported gain is +37.0 points on Qwen CLEVR under P+G. LLaVA shows smaller chart gains and occasional regressions, but improves on CLEVR from 7.0 to 31.1 under grounding-only training. Atomic probes confirm large in-distribution skill improvements, including InternVL perception from 36.8 to 85.9 and grounding from 52.1 to 71.6 on bar charts, and Qwen perception from 15.2 to 57.4 under perception-only training. On independent ChartQA, every configuration improves both chart types for all models; perception-only training improves Qwen by 32.0 points on bar questions, while simple-reasoning training gives Qwen gains of 39.1 points on bar and 31.1 on pie questions. Chart-oriented reference models score 27.5/22.9 (bar/pie) for ChartGemma and 17.5/18.7 for Granite Vision 4.1, compared with 35.6/40.6 for all-skill InternVL, but these comparisons use smaller models and different training regimes. The results are striking but partly attributable to answer-format recovery: the qualitative traces show models changing from truncated or unparseable reasoning to scoreable answers, and RapidFuzz rewards surface-form similarity rather than independently verified semantic correctness. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the intervention-based use of exact, source-generated probes to train atomic visual skills while withholding complex-reasoning supervision and then test transfer; the underlying notions of visual perception, grounding, synthetic chart QA, LoRA fine-tuning, and programmatic supervision are established techniques recombined for this diagnostic question. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study reports three seeds for fine-tuned models, three inference repetitions for base models, fixed hyperparameters across skill configurations, disjoint evaluation sets, exact programmatic labels, and a volume-matched ablation. It also evaluates in-distribution bar charts, unseen pie charts, independently authored ChartQA, and non-chart CLEVR, which reduces the risk that the main result is solely a ChartNet template artifact. However, no error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or per-seed results are reported, and the volume-matched experiment covers only InternVL. The main evaluation uses RapidFuzz rather than exact or human-validated semantic scoring; this is especially consequential because several reported fixes repair truncated or verbose outputs rather than visual or reasoning content. The paper explicitly does not compare against direct complex-reasoning supervision, despite framing its result against that paradigm, and the chart-oriented reference models are not controlled head-to-head baselines. The authors state that ChartProbe is released, but no URL, repository, model weights, or precise release artifact is given in the supplied text. The synthetic source-based training data, fixed templates, frozen vision encoders, single-series charts, and small 1,000-chart training pool limit conclusions about natural images and larger-scale training. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: LoRA fine-tuning and inference run on four commercially available L40S GPUs, although the paper does not report the wall-clock time, adapter size, or whether the released probe generator supports ordinary user-provided charts. Efficient: The approach avoids complex-reasoning data and uses parameter-efficient LoRA, but efficiency relative to direct reasoning fine-tuning is explicitly not evaluated; combined configurations also use more examples. Effective: The evidence shows improved fuzzy answer scores on held-out ChartNet, ChartQA, and CLEVR, but it does not fully establish improved semantic visual reasoning because some gains recover formatting or truncation failures and the metric is not human-validated. Scalable: The experiments cover at most 1,000 training charts and 500 examples per evaluation slice, with chart complexity up to 24 bars; behavior at 10x–100x more data, multi-series or dense real-world charts, higher-resolution figures, and larger models is not tested. The work delivers a reusable diagnostic/data-generation framework and presumably released code, but the supplied paper text does not specify a verified software URL or a standalone trained model artifact. Strengths: - The source-derived supervision design cleanly eliminates annotation noise and makes the intended probe answer exact by construction, which is unusually well matched to causal skill isolation. - The intervention tests a stronger claim than ordinary probing: training perception, grounding, or simple reasoning without any complex target examples and measuring transfer to held-out complex questions. - The evaluation includes three meaningful distribution shifts—unseen pie geometry, independent human-authored ChartQA, and non-chart CLEVR—rather than relying only on synthetic in-distribution charts. - The paper reports negative and boundary cases, including cross-skill regressions under narrow supervision and LLaVA's near-zero chart perception, rather than presenting transfer as universal. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict the controlled setting to single-series bar and pie charts and CLEVR scenes, where exact source representations exist; they acknowledge that the templates do not directly generalize to natural images and that the trained skills correspond to the hand-authored template definitions. They note that combined configurations use more training data, that direct complex-reasoning supervision is not compared, and that no efficiency claim is made. They also acknowledge that the diagnosis is population-level rather than a per-example causal attribution, and that the work does not provide a mechanistic explanation for why upstream skills remain weak. These limitations are confronted directly, although they leave the practical scope substantially narrower than the broad conclusion that complex visual reasoning can improve without complex-reasoning supervision. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most important unaddressed issue is the absence of a controlled direct-supervision baseline: without matching data volume, compute, answer format, and fine-tuning budget against complex-reasoning training, the work shows transfer but not a superior intervention. The RapidFuzz metric and qualitative evidence indicate a substantial output-format component, so the paper should separately report semantic correctness, exact-match performance under robust normalization, and results after enforcing a structured answer format. The claim that each probe isolates one skill is not fully guaranteed: grounding value questions require perception and label binding, and supposedly geometry-only probes such as above-average visual judgments can impose nontrivial comparison demands. The CLEVR transfer result is informative but may reflect generic instruction-following or termination improvements rather than visual-skill transfer, especially because several qualitative fixes correct unparseable outputs. The study lacks significance estimates, per-seed variability, larger and current chart benchmarks such as ChartQAPro or CharXiv, multi-series and real-world chart stress tests, and experiments with unfrozen or stronger vision encoders. Finally, ChartGemma and Granite comparisons are too uncontrolled to support conclusions about chart specialization, and the paper does not provide enough release information to independently reproduce the claimed artifact from the supplied text. Bottom Line: ChartProbe offers a useful and reasonably convincing diagnostic insight—that upstream visual competence and answer commitment can bottleneck apparent reasoning—but its contribution is best viewed as a controlled empirical study and reusable probe framework, not yet as evidence that atomic-skill fine-tuning should replace direct complex-reasoning training in deployed VLMs.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a prompt-comment protocol that records the rationale and outcomes behind agentic coding instructions so future maintainers can prune redundant instructions without losing correctness. - Why it’s important: Growing context files consume prompt capacity and degrade instruction-following, while wholesale rewrites discard useful behavior and do not prevent regrowth. - How it does it: It models deletion as requiring recovery of latent rationale, measures age-dependent deletion hazards in Git histories, and gives maintainers a separate, executor-invisible comment channel containing failure lineage and outcomes. - The good: Across 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repositories, the study finds +226% lifetime growth and a declining deletion hazard, while informative comments reduce controlled-test excess size from +211.3% to +1.4% at 51 steps. - The missing: The causal experiment uses covers of only two or three instructions, one primary model family, artificial hidden constraints, and short horizons, leaving effectiveness at realistic prompt sizes and deployment conditions untested. - Read it or not: Researchers in agent memory, prompt engineering, and AI-assisted software engineering should read it for the measurement methodology and falsifiable maintenance hypothesis; practitioners should treat the protocol as promising but not deployment-validated.

Problem & Motivation: Agentic coding repositories use context files such as CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and copilot-instructions.md to specify persistent instructions for coding agents. Maintainers add rules after failures but rarely remove them because the original rationale, redundancy relationships, and evidence for an instruction’s usefulness disappear over time. This creates a maintenance problem distinct from ordinary instruction staleness: prompts accumulate constraints, consume context, and eventually impair instruction-following. Prior repository studies established file-level growth but did not track individual instructions or identify whether growth reflects changing requirements, fragile instructions disappearing early, or loss of rationale. The paper targets this gap for public GitHub repositories and for controlled agent-maintenance settings. Key Idea: The central insight is that prompt maintenance is an information-loss problem: adding an instruction is cheap, but safely deleting it may require evaluating exponentially many subsets because instructions can be redundant or interfering. If the rationale for an instruction is preserved at write time in a comment visible to maintainers but stripped before execution, later maintainers can use that provenance to identify failed or redundant rules and stabilize the prompt near a minimum cover. The paper calls the resulting accumulation process “catastrophic remembering,” the proposed inverse analogy to catastrophic forgetting. Methodology: The formal model represents a task as an objective plus an unobservable set of constraints, a prompt as a finite instruction set, and the target as the smallest instruction set achieving maximum expected constraint satisfaction. It assumes instructability, interference, redundancy, censored feedback, and stochastic outcomes. The analysis defines latent-rationale recoverability \(\rho(d,a)\), factors deletion hazard into recoverability and the probability that an instruction is excess, and argues that declining recoverability causes equilibrium prompt size to diverge. The empirical corpus is built by reconstructing all historical versions of 1,801 context files from 1,867 public GitHub repositories, segmenting clause-level imperatives, matching instructions across versions with exact, normalized, and fuzzy matching, and treating wholesale rewrites and sibling-file migrations as competing risks. The controlled experiment inverts IFEval: benchmark instructions become known minimum covers, verifiers remain hidden, and a maintainer repeatedly adds or deletes fixed instructions from censored feedback. The control receives no comments, the placebo receives uninformative comment-shaped text, and treatment receives frozen comments containing failure descriptions, recurrence counts, falsified approaches, and restoration lineage. A WildIFEval inversion seeds prompts with true instructions plus 16 distractors and evaluates instruction-following with an arm-blind LLM judge. Critical design choices include the 50% rewrite threshold, a comment-only maintainer channel with comments stripped from the executor, and feedback that names failure dimensions but not constraint identities or thresholds. The threshold and segmentation choices are only partially justified through validation and sensitivity checks; the controlled feedback regime was found by search, although the paper reports the search conditions and design failures. Key Results: In the repository corpus, the median final context file contains 39 instructions and the 90th percentile contains 131; 64.3% of multi-version repositories grow their instruction count versus 26.6% that shrink it, with a median net gain of seven instructions. Excluding mass rewrites, commits add a net average of 4.9 instructions; instruction count rises as much as 226% over a file’s normalized lifetime, while total prompt size rises 140% and mean instruction length only 10%. Wholesale rewrites account for 76.8% or 77.3% of instruction deaths depending on the reported filtering, reduce files to 59.5% of pre-rewrite size, and are followed by recovery to 91.5% within ten commits; post-rewrite growth is 4.9% per commit versus 4.1% before. The deletion log-hazard slope is -0.032 per commit with a repository-stratified 95% CI of [-0.047, -0.019]. A gamma-frailty analysis leaves a negative age slope after accounting for repository, file, and recurring-text heterogeneity; recurring text absorbs 30.8% of the slope but does not remove it. In the inverse-IFEval experiment, at 15 steps informative comments yield -5.8% excess size versus +60.4% for control and +53.2% for placebo, with comparable final satisfaction of 38.2%, 39.0%, and 40.3% respectively. At 51 steps, treatment yields +1.4% excess versus +211.3% control and +147.9% placebo, again with comparable satisfaction. By cover stratum, the control reaches +74.2% excess for two-instruction covers and +15.2% for three-instruction covers; treatment reaches -1.1% and -21.2%, respectively, but the three-instruction treatment sometimes prunes below the cover. With 16 WildIFEval distractors, control satisfaction falls from 65.6% to 41.5%, while informative comments raise treatment satisfaction from 50.4% to 62.0% over three rounds, an 11.6 percentage-point or 23.1% relative improvement. A second judge estimates a smaller 7.8-point gain, with the judge difference interval including zero. The strongest controlled results occur in settings with excess instructions; the paper reports no consistent gain when no distractors are present. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW FORMULATION, and a NEW METHOD for prompt maintenance, with an associated evaluation methodology; the comment mechanism itself adapts established software-engineering rationale comments and provenance practices rather than introducing an entirely new underlying concept. The genuinely new elements are instruction-level longitudinal measurement of agentic prompt growth, the imperfect-recall/catastrophic-remembering formulation, inversion of instruction-following benchmarks to make minimum-cover excess measurable, and a causal test of an executor-invisible rationale channel. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports large-scale repository data, repository-stratified bootstrap intervals, competing-risk treatment, matching validation, a frailty model, post-rewrite event studies, three IFEval world draws, placebo and content ablations, and a second-judge re-scoring of all 6,336 WildIFEval verdicts. It explicitly distinguishes the exploratory multi-author interaction from preregistered corpus gates and reports that the interaction coefficient is -0.0211 with z = -11.7, while acknowledging that author count only proxies for turnover. The matching procedure achieves 1.000 precision and 0.933 recall on 50 hand-annotated transitions, but that validation set is small relative to 299,440 transitions. The controlled experiment uses three seeds at 15 steps but only one seed for the 51-step result and several ablations; no multiple-model executor comparison or human ground-truth evaluation is provided. The WildIFEval outcome relies on LLM judges with 82.1% agreement and Cohen’s kappa 0.639, not verified labels. The study releases derived per-instruction tables and reconstruction code, but no repository URL or model weights is stated. Important reproducibility concerns include reimplementation of the 20 IFEval verifiers, a searched and highly constrained feedback regime, fixed Anthropic API models with undisclosed parameter counts, and evaluation on the same benchmark family used to construct the controlled worlds. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a prototype protocol and released analysis artifacts rather than a production tool. Practical: The corpus pipeline runs on CPU-only cloud containers with 8 vCPUs and 16 GiB RAM, and the comment protocol could be implemented in a text-file or coding-agent framework, but integration with deployed coding agents is not evaluated. Efficient: The canonical study consumed 49,680 model calls, 37.9 million tokens, and 45 model-hours; comments increase maintainer-input tokens from 7.0M to 9.9M, while executor-visible comments were shown to incur size without a correctness benefit. Effective: Evidence supports reduced excess size at roughly equal mechanically verified satisfaction and improved satisfaction under seeded WildIFEval distractors, but it does not establish better coding-task success, repository-level productivity, or safety in real agent deployments. Scalable: The repository analysis covers 1,867 projects, but the causal experiment tests only two- or three-instruction minimum covers, 15–51 rounds, and at most 16 distractors; behavior at median or 10×–100× larger prompt and constraint scales remains untested. The work delivers reconstruction code and derived datasets, but no stated end-user library, CLI, or integrated coding-agent implementation. Strengths: - Tracks individual instruction lifetimes rather than relying only on file size or line diffs, enabling deletion-hazard analysis and explicit treatment of rewording, rewrites, and migrations. - Uses a useful triangulation of observational corpus evidence, a formal recoverability model, and a controlled benchmark inversion with known minimum covers. - Includes a meaningful placebo condition and ablations showing that outcome-bearing rationale, rather than comment syntax or generic narrative, drives most of the pruning effect. - Confronts important failure modes, including treatment-induced empty prompts, executor-visible comment leakage, judge disagreement, matcher error, and the mismatch between small controlled covers and real context files. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the 50% rewrite threshold, migration censoring, instruction segmentation grammar, and small 50-transition matcher audit were not varied or fully validated at scale. They acknowledge that the controlled experiment uses only two- or three-instruction covers, a 15-step horizon for the main result, one maintainer/executor model, mechanically verifiable English constraints, and nearly free retention. The WildIFEval study uses 16 seeded distractors rather than growing prompts organically, scores prose constraints with LLM judges rather than ground truth, and does not test whether the ratchet persists at that scale. Scope is limited to public GitHub repositories and English context files; system prompts and skill files are not evaluated. The authors also acknowledge that comments are safe to write but deletion based on them can remove genuinely useful instructions, that the protocol emptied one prompt in eight, and that human review is needed for safety-relevant rules. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The causal experiment is deliberately constructed so comments provide unusually precise structured provenance and instructions cannot be reworded or annotated at the file level; this may overstate benefits relative to ordinary repository comments, commit messages, or imperfectly maintained rationale. - The central claim that imperfect recall is the unique explanation for repository growth is stronger than the observational design supports: declining hazard, frailty controls, and the author-count interaction are consistent with the hypothesis but do not rule out unmeasured selection, workflow, instruction-type, or repository-maturity effects. - The formal divergence result follows from strong assumptions about stationary constraints, constant additions, vanishing recoverability, and a hazard factorization; it is a model implication rather than an independently measured law of real prompt maintenance. - The paper lacks comparisons with practical alternatives such as LLM-based prompt compression, retrieval or eviction policies, version-control rationale extraction, rule deduplication, human pruning, or continual-learning-style rehearsal and regularization. - The long-horizon headline uses one seed, while the most realistic evaluation still has only four or five human-written constraints and one LLM judge; there is no end-to-end coding benchmark, repository task success measure, or human maintainer study. - The protocol can delete below the known minimum cover and causes measurable failures on emptied worlds, but the paper does not evaluate safeguards such as deletion floors, confidence thresholds, human approval workflows, or safety-class-specific retention policies. Bottom Line: This is a strong and unusually self-critical preprint for identifying and measuring a real prompt-maintenance phenomenon, but its practical recommendation remains a promising provenance design rather than a validated replacement for prompt compression, retrieval, or human review in production coding agents.

Large Discovery Models: Empirically-grounded Model-Based Open-Ended Search (49 ▲ )

Zhongwei Yu, Yan Song, Xue Yan, Anjie Liu, Xingyu Lu, Yihang Chen, Huichi Zhou, Siyuan Guo, Luoyang Sun, Sihan Chen, Xiangning Yu, Jun Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Large Discovery Models (LDMs), a recurrent search framework that combines an LLM-generated candidate reservoir with an online Gaussian-process surrogate and acquisition-guided inference-time search. - Why it's important: Scientific design often requires choosing a few evaluations from enormous, structured spaces when experiments are noisy, delayed, and expensive, making generation quality alone an inadequate decision signal. - How it does it: It exponentially tilts the LLM proposal distribution by a surrogate-derived acquisition value, repeatedly generating candidates, scoring them for predicted reward and epistemic uncertainty, evaluating selected designs, and updating the search state. - The good: Across code, antibody sequences, and molecular design, the reported LDM variants improve over the paper’s LLM-only and conventional BO baselines, with especially large gains on molecular hypervolume and the AutoResearch validation objective. - The missing: All primary evaluations use digital oracles and highly task-specific representations, kernels, and scaffolding; the paper does not establish performance in wet-lab discovery or demonstrate robustness at substantially larger experimental budgets. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-guided Bayesian optimization, autonomous scientific experimentation, or open-ended program search; skip it if you need validated biological or chemical discoveries rather than in-silico optimization evidence.

Novelty (82) is high because LDM explicitly treats the LLM as a dynamically changing candidate reservoir whose distribution is tilted by online acquisition values, rather than using it as an unreliable value estimator. Non-Obviousness (85) is also strong: the work cleanly separates discovery, exploration, and exploitation and supports the framing with mechanism-oriented ablations. Rigor (78) is substantial, with formal analysis, relevant BO and domain baselines, released code, repeated seeds for most studies, and multiple ablations, although headline AutoResearch comparisons and compute parity are less controlled. Completeness (75) and Resilience (72) reflect honest discussion of digital-oracle limitations, surrogate misspecification, domain-specific engineering, and missing wet-lab validation, but the broad discovery claims remain provisional. Impact (65) is meaningful through released implementations and benchmark integrations, though deployment and real scientific discovery are not demonstrated. The weighted empirical composite is 0.20*82 + 0.25*78 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*65 = 77.
