Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses sequential design under expensive black-box evaluation, where the system must generate structured candidates and decide which few to test in a vast or incompletely specified hypothesis space. Target users include researchers conducting neural-network architecture or training-program search, protein and antibody engineering, and molecular optimization. The motivating gap is the mismatch between LLM proposal likelihood or self-evaluation and externally measured scientific objectives, especially for out-of-distribution candidates, versus the complementary limitation of Bayesian optimization: calibrated uncertainty and budget-aware selection are available, but candidate generation and acquisition optimization are difficult in large discrete, semantic, or open-ended spaces. The paper distinguishes predictive uncertainty within the current surrogate support from search awareness—the ability to expose previously unreachable design families—and frames exploitation, exploration, and discovery as separate operations. This framing is explicitly restricted to search problems with a specified external evaluator and does not cover discovery for which the design space, objective, or evaluation process cannot yet be formulated. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat the LLM as an adaptive reservoir of structured candidates rather than as a value estimator, and to use an empirical acquisition function as the decision signal that reshapes this reservoir’s probability mass. Formally, the desired policy is a KL-regularized acquisition tilt, pi_t(x) proportional to p_theta,alpha(x | C_t) exp(eta a_t(x)); the LLM supplies coverage and semantic structure, while the GP supplies reward estimates and epistemic uncertainty. In the authors’ terminology, the LLM reservoir enables discovery, the uncertainty term enables exploration within reachable support, and the posterior mean enables exploitation. The mathematical KL-tilting construction itself is standard Gibbs variational optimization; the paper’s more specific contribution is its recurrent use with an LLM-induced, dynamically changing support and sequential empirical feedback. Methodology: At each round, LDM maintains an evaluated dataset D_t and a broader generation context C_t. It fits a Gaussian-process surrogate to observed rewards, using an RBF kernel for continuous AutoResearch parameters and a subsequence string kernel for antibody and molecule representations; posterior mean mu_t and standard deviation sigma_t feed EI, UCB, or EHVI acquisition functions. The LLM either directly generates complete programs, sequences, or SMILES, or indirectly specifies a parameterized search region from which an external sampler creates a larger candidate pool. The system scores the pool with the acquisition function, selects one or a batch using deterministic top-b selection or softmax/Gumbel-top-b sampling, evaluates the selected designs with a black-box oracle, appends observations to D_t and C_t, and repeats. In AutoResearch, reflection can revise the active program-feature parameterization after stagnation; in antibody design, policy-mode generation defines neighborhoods that are sampled externally; in molecular design, independent GPs and EHVI optimize docking and neural activity jointly. A second, slower loop distills acquisition-weighted candidate traces into a smaller proposer using weighted autoregressive SFT, optionally training on teacher-generated rationales describing exploitation, uncertainty, stagnation, constraints, or frontier expansion. Critical design decisions are the use of GP uncertainty rather than LLM confidence, the finite-pool approximation to the intractable tilted distribution, and the direct-versus-indirect candidate-generation split. The first is well motivated and ablated; the second is operationally necessary but its approximation quality is not rigorously measured; the third is empirically useful but requires domain-specific engineering and does not by itself establish a unified representation-independent method. Key Results: The study evaluates three digital-oracle settings. In AutoResearch, under a shared H100 five-minute training-run budget and a common starting val_bpb of 1.0069, the LLM-only baseline reaches 0.9767 after approximately 255 experiments, whereas the reported LDM trajectory reaches 0.9342 after 615 experiments, reducing val_bpb by 0.0727 versus 0.0301 for the baseline, or a 2.4x larger absolute reduction. A separate B200 run reaches 0.902291 in 59 runs, compared with 0.9264 and 0.9274 for two external leaderboard entries, but this comparison changes hardware and is not a controlled baseline experiment. In antibody CDRH3 design, five PDB targets are evaluated for 200 oracle calls each; policy-based LDM reaches mean final binding energies from -106.7 to -108.5 depending on selection rule, compared with -95.5 to -91.1 for pure LLM, -101.6 to -97.7 for TURBO, -93.8 to -89.1 for COMBO, and -110.1 to -107.7 for AntBO. Thus LDM is generally competitive with, but not consistently superior to, the domain-specialized AntBO baseline; policy-mode clearly outperforms direct generation. In KRAS G12D molecular optimization, over 80 evaluations, Direct-Softmax obtains hypervolume 27.325 +/- 5.475, ReaSyn-Softmax 21.707 +/- 3.676, MOBO 16.751 +/- 2.562, pure LLM 16.826 +/- 3.085, and random search 13.794 +/- 3.054. The paper reports this as a 62.4% improvement over LLM and 63.1% over MOBO, although the exact percentages depend on the displayed values and should be interpreted as oracle-benchmark gains rather than drug-discovery efficacy. Ablations show that larger proposal and acquisition-screening budgets help when scaled together, EI/UCB generally beat posterior-mean selection, and disabling dynamic discovery worsens the AutoResearch plateau. Fine-tuning with reasoning augmentation yields 0.9788 val_bpb on AutoResearch, molecular hypervolume 26.660 +/- 2.608 versus 16.489 +/- 5.867 for the untuned Qwen3.5-9B proposer, and task-level antibody transfer that matches the in-distribution model on four of five targets but fails on the narrow-optimum 1H0D_C target. Several comparisons have overlapping error intervals, and the strongest AutoResearch result is presented as a trajectory rather than a multi-seed aggregate. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely distinctive contribution is the explicit treatment of an LLM as a history-conditioned, dynamically evolving proposal reservoir whose candidate probability is tilted by an online uncertainty-aware BO acquisition, while the KL regularization, GP-UCB/EI/EHVI components, candidate-pool sampling, and supervised distillation are established techniques combined in a new open-ended-search setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides formal proofs for the Gibbs-optimal policy, a sampling lemma, and a regret decomposition, plus ablations for discovery removal, acquisition choice, proposal-pool size, acquisition bandwidth, temperatures, and reasoning augmentation. It reports standard deviations and usually uses five seeds for molecular, antibody, and many fine-tuning studies, but it does not provide significance tests, confidence intervals, or a consistent multi-seed protocol for the headline AutoResearch comparison. The code and benchmarks are stated to be available at https://github.com/yzailab/Large-Discovery-Models. Reproducibility is weakened by incomplete operational detail about prompts, model/API versions, search-state construction, candidate validity filtering, GP calibration, seed initialization, and the exact computational cost of inner-loop LLM generation. The main evaluations are all digital-oracle experiments: Absolut! simulation for antibody binding, docking plus a neural activity predictor for molecules, and a fixed training benchmark for code. The molecular task is especially vulnerable to proxy optimization because neither docking nor the neural activity score measures experimental binding, synthesis, toxicity, pharmacokinetics, or biological efficacy. Baselines are reasonably relevant, including AntBO, TURBO, COMBO, MOBO, random search, and LLM-only systems, but the paper does not establish parity in implementation, inner-loop compute, or tuning budget across all methods. The theoretical guarantee assumes globally calibrated GP-UCB, a metric and Holder regularity condition around the unknown optimum, and reservoir coverage quantities that are not estimated or verified empirically; consequently, it is more a conditional decomposition than a practical convergence guarantee for LLM-generated open-ended spaces. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a secondary SYSTEMS aspect because the authors release an implementation and benchmarks. Practical: the core loop can run on commercially available GPUs and standard oracle infrastructure, but high-budget candidate generation and AutoResearch experiments require substantial accelerator time, and wet-lab integration is not demonstrated. Efficient: LDM reduces expensive oracle calls relative to evaluating every generated candidate, but it adds repeated LLM inference, GP fitting, candidate validity checks, and acquisition scoring; exact GP updates scale cubically with the observation count, and the paper does not report end-to-end wall-clock, dollar, memory, or energy comparisons. Effective: the evidence shows improved optimization of the selected digital objectives over the tested baselines, but it does not show that the resulting molecules or antibodies have experimentally meaningful properties or that discovered code mechanisms generalize beyond the benchmark. Scalable: the method is tested at 80 molecular evaluations, 200 antibody evaluations per target, and hundreds of AutoResearch runs, while the paper itself acknowledges GP and context-scaling limits; behavior at 10x–100x larger experimental budgets or substantially broader design supports is not evaluated. The work delivers code and benchmark integrations, but no wet-lab dataset, trained general-purpose model weights, or independently validated scientific design artifact is reported as released. Strengths: - It identifies a real structural complementarity between generative proposal coverage and statistically grounded experimental allocation, rather than treating an LLM score as a substitute for uncertainty modeling. - The acquisition-tilted policy gives a simple common abstraction for direct generation, indirect search-region parameterization, single- and multi-objective acquisition, and batched candidate selection. - The experiments include mechanism-oriented ablations: mean-only selection, no-discovery support, candidate-pool scaling, acquisition bandwidth, and reasoning-free versus reasoning-augmented distillation, which provide evidence that gains are not solely attributable to adding an LLM. - The task-level transfer study is informative because it separates transferable acquisition behavior from domain-specific design knowledge; the failure on 1H0D_C usefully exposes that selection skill cannot replace in-domain candidate composition. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge cubic GP scaling with observation count, substantial LLM inference overhead from test-time candidate sampling, manual domain-specific kernels and feature representations, dependence on the LLM’s pretrained coverage, weak performance when the LLM has poor domain priors, omission of external “unknown knowns” such as databases and prior experiments, and the absence of wet-lab validation. They also mention surrogate misspecification and reward exploitation as risks. These limitations are confronted in the discussion and future-work section, although their practical severity is not quantified through cost or robustness experiments. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not experimentally validate GP uncertainty calibration, candidate-pool approximation fidelity, or the claimed relationship between discovery events and true coverage of the global design space. The dynamic-support formalization is under-specified: the LLM can define or revise the support, but the experiments use hand-designed feature schemas, reflection prompts, kernels, and domain-specific proposal mechanisms, so the claimed generality may rely heavily on hidden engineering. The headline comparisons do not consistently control total compute, and larger LDM inner budgets can make comparisons with LLM-only and BO baselines difficult to interpret as efficiency claims. The digital molecular objectives are surrogate benchmarks and may reward docking or predictor artifacts; the paper does not test synthesis validity, assay outcomes, scaffold novelty with deduplication protocols, or robustness to adversarial reward exploitation. The fine-tuning transfer results are promising but small: several use five seeds, the GP-hidden comparison uses only one seed for the proposed method, and some reported intervals overlap. The regret theorem’s discovery term is an exact decomposition plus a conditional bound rather than evidence that the LLM actually reduces reservoir coverage radius in an unknown-unknown space; the relevant coverage, metric, and calibration quantities are not measured. Finally, the work does not compare against stronger contemporary generative optimization, latent-space BO, evolutionary search, or domain-specific molecular and protein design systems under matched budgets. Bottom Line: This is a useful and technically coherent framework paper for LLM-guided model-based search, with credible in-silico evidence that explicit acquisition guidance can outperform LLM-only and basic BO pipelines, but its broad scientific-discovery claims should be treated as provisional until compute-matched comparisons, calibration and robustness analyses, larger-scale tests, and wet-lab validation are provided.

HumanTracker: Towards Comprehensive and Human-Aligned Motion Tracking Benchmark (15 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HumanTracker, a 153-hour categorized humanoid motion-tracking benchmark and HumanScore, a learned trajectory metric trained on 12,000 preference records to predict human judgments of rollout quality. - Why it's important: Existing pose-error metrics and small test suites can rank trackers favorably despite visible foot skating, mistimed contacts, instability, and failures during long-horizon or contact-rich motions. - How it does it: It feeds reference states and simulator-derived rollout, action, kinematic, contact, force, and velocity features into a masked temporal Transformer trained with Bradley–Terry and similarity losses on paired human preferences. - The good: HumanScore reaches 0.9083 preference alignment, compared with 0.8049 for MPJPE and 0.7882 for foot-contact accuracy, while retaining 0.8736–0.9383 bootstrap uncertainty bounds at the reported aggregate level. - The missing: The metric is validated only on one 29-DoF MuJoCo humanoid and rollouts from four trackers, with six expert annotators and no reported inter-annotator agreement or independent cross-embodiment, real-robot, or controller-family evaluation. - Read it or not: Humanoid-tracking researchers and benchmark designers should read it for the dataset protocol and contact-aware preference metric, but practitioners seeking evidence of hardware deployment or broad perceptual validity can defer until those evaluations exist.

Problem & Motivation: Humanoid teleoperation and whole-body imitation require evaluation that reflects whether a simulated rollout looks stable, natural, and physically plausible, not merely whether its per-frame joint poses are close to a reference. Mean joint or keypoint errors average away contact timing, support, foot skating, progressive drift, recovery behavior, and other trajectory-level artifacts. Existing evaluation also commonly relies on approximately 140 AMASS sequences and reports a single aggregate score, limiting coverage of asymmetric balance, rapid support changes, ground transitions, and other failure regimes. The target users are researchers developing physics-based humanoid trackers and controllers, who need controlled comparisons and category-level diagnosis across diverse contact conditions. Key Idea: Treat tracking quality as a human-preference prediction problem over synchronized rollout trajectories rather than as a manually designed pose or contact statistic. The central insight is that a short temporal history containing simulator contact dynamics and evolving kinematics can expose perceptual failures—such as sliding, jitter, drift, and unstable recovery—that any single frame or individual analytic diagnostic misses. Methodology: HumanTracker records optical motion from 24 professional performers, fits SMPL sequences, retargets them to a common humanoid with General Motion Retargeting, removes visually or physically implausible segments, and releases robot-space qpos trajectories, keypoints, velocities, contact labels, text descriptions, and four family labels: Daily, Highly Dynamic, Interaction, and Ground. The released data contains 24,995 trajectories, 27,480,590 frames, and approximately 152.67 hours, split 9:1 by source trajectory with related motions kept within one partition. For evaluation, each tracker receives the same retargeted reference, 29-DoF humanoid, MuJoCo entry point, 50-Hz rollout accounting, termination criteria, and metric implementation while retaining its native observations and action decoder. Episodes terminate when pelvis, ankle, or wrist vertical error exceeds 0.25 m, pelvis rotation error exceeds 1 rad, or state values become nonfinite; the protocol reports completion rate, joint-angle MPJPE, and additional velocity, keypoint, contact, acceleration, and jerk diagnostics. HumanScore training uses 6,000 original paired trajectory comparisons from GMT, Humanoid-GPT, SONIC, and TWIST2, bilaterally mirrored into 12,000 preference records involving 24,000 motions. Six doctoral humanoid-robotics researchers label each synchronized five-second pair as left better, right better, similar, or cannot compare; cannot-compare cases are excluded from optimization, while similar cases receive a symmetric equality loss. Each 250-frame trajectory window is represented by 539 features: 70 reference dimensions and 469 rollout dimensions covering robot state, actions and motor targets, contacts and forces, root motion, and 14 keypoint poses and velocities. A four-layer, eight-head, 256-dimensional bidirectional Transformer with masked mean pooling maps the sequence to an unbounded scalar reward. Strict pairs use the Bradley–Terry loss, `-log sigmoid(r_chosen-r_rejected)`, and similar pairs use the average of the two opposing preference losses. At inference, window rewards are sigmoid-normalized to [0,1], multiplied by 100, and averaged by valid frame count across the rollout. The important design decisions—using measured contact features, integrating up to five seconds of history, and splitting preferences by source motion—are empirically motivated, although the paper does not compare against learned linear or nonlinear feature-combination baselines. Key Results: On the held-out HumanTracker test split, Humanoid-GPT performs best on Daily with 94.4% completion, 0.046-rad MPJPE, and 54.7 HumanScore, and on Highly Dynamic with 86.9%, 0.047 rad, and 49.2. SONIC leads Interaction completion at 97.6% and Ground HumanScore at 26.5, while Humanoid-GPT obtains 97.2% and 0.070 rad on Interaction and 32.9% and 0.216 rad on Ground. GMT is substantially weaker, with 17.0%, 0.250 rad, and 2.4 on Daily and 0% completion on Ground; TWIST2 also has 0% Ground completion and 4.5 HumanScore. HumanScore agrees with strict human preferences at 0.9083 alignment, versus 0.8049 for MPJPE, 0.8404 for joint-velocity error, 0.8405 for keypoint-position MAE, 0.7882 for foot-contact accuracy, 0.6933 for average joint acceleration, and 0.7232 for jerk. A source-motion-clustered bootstrap gives HumanScore a 95% interval of 87.36%–93.83%, compared with 75.95%–84.76% for MPJPE. Removing the 20 contact-related input dimensions reduces alignment from 0.908 to 0.867 overall and from 0.879 to 0.759 on Ground; the kinematics-only variant reaches 0.878 overall. Restricting temporal context from one to five seconds increases alignment from 0.857 to 0.908. Adding future reference information slightly reduces alignment from 0.908 to 0.905. These results support the claim that contact state and temporal evolution matter, but they do not establish that HumanScore improves tracker behavior or transfers to physical robots. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and a limited NEW METHOD; the genuinely new elements are the large, contact-regime-organized humanoid-tracking benchmark and preference-trained evaluation metric, while the Transformer encoder, Bradley–Terry preference objective, and standard simulator diagnostics are established techniques applied to this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The work provides code at https://github.com/GalaxyGeneralRobotics/HumanTracker and a project page at https://dairuliu.github.io/humantracker, and reports model architecture, optimization settings, random seed, feature dimensions, data manifests, split construction, and file schemas. It uses motion-disjoint preference splits, balanced tracker pairings, randomized display order, family-balanced alignment reporting, and clustered bootstrap intervals. The contact-feature and temporal-context ablations identify meaningful components, but the ablation set is narrow: it does not test alternative temporal models, annotator aggregation methods, calibration, loss variants, or learned diagnostic composites. The preference labels come from six domain experts, with one primary judgment per pair and no repeated labels or reported inter-annotator agreement, so label noise and disagreement are not quantified. HumanScore training is based exclusively on rollouts from four trackers and the same benchmark motion distribution; its test split demonstrates generalization to unseen source motions, not to unseen embodiments, simulators, rendering conditions, or controller families. The four evaluated trackers are relevant contemporary systems, but the paper does not establish whether all implementations, training data, or evaluation assumptions are independently reproduced rather than taken from released checkpoints or authors' code. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a released benchmark and evaluation tool with empirical experiments, rather than a deployed robot system). * Practical: The evaluator and HumanScore can run on commercially available compute in MuJoCo, but the metric depends on simulator state, contact forces, and other privileged quantities that may not be available from real hardware. * Efficient: The paper specifies a 4-layer Transformer processing 250-frame, 539-dimensional windows but reports neither inference latency, memory use, nor comparison with the computational cost of conventional metrics. * Effective: Evidence shows substantially higher agreement with six experts than individual analytic diagnostics and reveals category-specific tracker differences, but it evaluates perceptual proxy alignment rather than downstream teleoperation quality, controller improvement, or real-world safety. * Scalable: The benchmark scales to 24,995 trajectories and 153 hours, but the paper tests only one 29-DoF embodiment, one MuJoCo setup, and four tracker families; behavior at 10×–100× larger data, additional embodiments, or real-robot rollout scale is not evaluated. The work delivers a reusable dataset, manifests, trajectory format, standardized evaluation entry point, and HumanScore implementation/checkpoint through the stated project and GitHub links; it does not demonstrate a hardware deployment or use HumanScore to train a tracker. Strengths: - The benchmark addresses a concrete evaluation bottleneck with 153 hours and 25,000 clips, substantially exceeding the approximately 140-sequence test suite identified by the authors and explicitly separating four contact and failure regimes. - The standardized protocol controls reference representation, robot model, rollout accounting, termination rules, and metric computation while preserving tracker-specific policy interfaces, improving comparability across systems. - HumanScore uses trajectory-level state, force, contact, and kinematic evidence rather than relying on a single hand-designed contact statistic; the controlled ablations show that measured contact features and multi-second context materially affect alignment, especially for Ground motions. - The preference evaluation includes balanced tracker pairings, motion-disjoint splits, family-stratified reporting, and clustered bootstrap intervals, which reduces several obvious distributional and leakage concerns. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that HumanScore generalizes only to unseen motions from the same robot, simulator, and controller distribution; its privileged simulator features may not be observable on hardware; each pair receives only one primary judgment without repeated independent labels; the comparison lacks broader fitted linear or nonlinear diagnostic composites; the benchmark has imbalanced families, particularly relatively few Ground clips; the experiments use one 29-DoF MuJoCo embodiment and no real robot; and directly optimizing HumanScore could produce reward-hacking behavior requiring regularization and independent human evaluation. They confront these boundaries directly and identify cross-embodiment, real-world, and reward-optimization evaluation as future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, annotator-wise consistency, confidence, or the fraction of strict, similar, and cannot-compare labels, making it difficult to assess the reliability and ambiguity of the supervision. It does not compare HumanScore with a learned or hand-tuned combination of the available diagnostics, despite claiming that preference learning captures information beyond rule-based measures. The preference dataset is generated only from four trackers, so HumanScore may learn tracker-specific artifacts or ranking priors and may fail on qualitatively different policies, failure modes, or intentional behaviors. The human judgments are based on rendered synchronized rollouts, whereas the model consumes privileged simulator features; viewpoint, rendering, and embodiment transfer are therefore untested. The benchmark's category labels and performer pool may not represent ordinary users, nonprofessional motion, varied body morphology, environmental interaction, or rare safety-critical contacts. Finally, the reported HumanScore values are not calibrated probabilities or validated against downstream task success, and no statistical test compares tracker rankings under HumanScore against human rankings beyond the metric-level bootstrap intervals. Bottom Line: This is a useful and reproducible benchmark contribution for simulated humanoid-tracking evaluation, with credible evidence that contact-aware temporal preference modeling outperforms individual kinematic diagnostics, but its practical significance remains limited until human-label reliability, independent learned baselines, cross-embodiment transfer, and real-robot validity are demonstrated.

DepTGL: A Parallel Framework for Memory-based TGNN Training with Adaptive Temporal Data Dependency Management

L Chen, Z Song, L Liu, Y Gu, Y Li, Y Zhang, L Cui, G Yu… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DepTGL, a distributed training framework for memory-based temporal graph neural networks that combines offline temporal-dependency replay, adaptive cache synchronization, and load-aware auxiliary-event pruning. - Why it's important: Continuous-time TGNN training is often limited by cross-worker temporal-state communication, synchronization barriers, and skew-induced stragglers, which can dominate training time even when the model and graph fit available hardware. - How it does it: DepTGL replaces many remote state requests with timestamp-ordered local replay inside synchronization windows, then uses gradient and batch-time EMAs to skip cache refreshes and prune auxiliary replay during unstable workload periods. - The good: Across six temporal graphs, two M-TGNN models, four baselines, and two hardware environments, it reports the lowest epoch time in every listed end-to-end comparison, including 4.39–7.32× speedups over Vanilla DDP for TGN in the main environment. - The missing: The paper does not establish that skipped refreshes and replay pruning preserve the same temporal-state semantics or convergence behavior, and it provides no reported error bars, multiple-seed results, or evaluation beyond three workers for its main scalability study. - Read it or not: Distributed temporal-graph-system researchers and practitioners should read it for its integrated communication/replay/load-control design, while readers seeking a formal correctness guarantee or evidence at cluster scale should treat it as preliminary.

Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (75) are strong because the paper integrates offline dependency replay, selective cache synchronization, and load-aware pruning around a coherent communication-versus-computation trade-off for distributed memory-based TGNNs. Rigor (68) benefits from six datasets, two models, two hardware environments, ablations, profiling, and memory measurements, but is reduced by preprint status, absent seed variation, omitted state-fidelity measurements, incomplete baseline coverage, and limited scaling to three workers. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses distributed training of continuous-time, memory-based TGNNs such as TGN and JODIE, in which node memories evolve recursively along timestamped events. A worker processing an event may need a remote node's state after a sequence of earlier events owned or processed elsewhere. Existing approaches either fetch or synchronize remote states frequently, materialize large remote histories, or use fixed execution policies; these choices create communication overhead, synchronization stalls, cache staleness, and severe imbalance when interaction streams are skewed. The specific gap is a unified mechanism that manages event-level temporal dependencies, remote-state freshness, and replay-induced load imbalance jointly rather than optimizing only caching, partitioning, dependency scheduling, or pipelining in isolation. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat remote temporal-state serving as a communication–computation trade-off: within a bounded synchronization window, construct worker-specific batches offline by replaying only the historical remote events needed to reconstruct later target-event states, then use selective boundary refreshes rather than refreshing every batch. This is combined with runtime heuristics that use optimization stability to reduce refreshes and worker-local execution-time anomalies to remove auxiliary replay, but the core conceptual contribution is replacing fine-grained remote temporal-state access with bounded, timestamp-ordered local reconstruction. Methodology: DepTGL first sorts the event stream by timestamp and partitions nodes by ownership across P workers. For each synchronization window of K batches, an offline backward dependency scan starts from each worker's source-assigned target events, builds a frontier of remote endpoints, and recursively inserts earlier events touching that frontier as deduplicated auxiliary replay events. It merges target and auxiliary events into worker-specific mixed batches and sorts each batch by timestamp. At window boundaries, the framework forms candidate refresh sets for remote base states. A gradient-aware controller maintains an EMA of batch gradient norms, g-bar_r = alpha g_r + (1-alpha) g-bar_(r-1), and skips a scheduled refresh when the latest gradient norm satisfies g_(r-1) < tau_g g-bar_(r-1); otherwise it refreshes the candidate remote states. A load-aware controller separately maintains a per-worker EMA of batch execution time and enters heavy-load mode when the previous batch exceeds tau_c times its EMA. In that mode it removes events whose source is not owned by the worker, treating them as pure auxiliary replay, while retaining all source-owned target events. The loss is an explicitly masked average of target-event losses, and final temporal states are synchronized before evaluation. Critical design decisions are the source-based ownership assignment, the window length K, and the two EMA threshold policies. The paper gives intuitive motivations and ablations for these decisions, but does not provide a correctness proof for the approximations or a principled method for choosing their thresholds. Key Results: On six public datasets—AskUbuntu (159.3K nodes, 964.4K events), MathOverflow (24.8K, 506.6K), Reddit (11.0K, 672.4K), MOOC (7.0K, 411.7K), lastfm (2.0K, 1.29M), and Wikipedia (9.2K, 157.5K)—DepTGL is evaluated with JODIE and TGN against Vanilla DDP, DisTGL, NeutronStream, and MemShare. In Env 1, using four RTX 2080 Ti machines and one Tesla P100, TGN speedups over Vanilla DDP range from 4.39× on Reddit to 7.32× on Wikipedia, with epoch times of 77.32s and 55.83s respectively versus 339.28s and 408.58s for Vanilla DDP. For JODIE, the reported speedups range from 5.25× to 21.15×, with 14.06× on AskUbuntu and 18.61× on Wikipedia. In Env 2, using eight RTX 4090 GPUs, TGN speedups range from 1.18× to 1.52× and JODIE speedups from 1.31× to 1.88×, indicating smaller but persistent gains when communication is faster. On the profiled AskUbuntu TGN run, DepTGL reduces synchronization count from 3,215 to 26.1, communication time from 487.64s to 7.57s, and communication share from 82.9% to 6.6%; its profiled total is 115.45s versus 588.09s for Vanilla DDP. In a memory-throughput comparison, DepTGL reaches 2,921 target events/s versus 466 for Vanilla DDP, while using 2.44GB peak GPU memory versus 2.44GB for Vanilla DDP and 3.10GB for Full Cache. With three workers, it reports 2,882.40 events/s on AskUbuntu and 2,928.71 on Reddit, corresponding to 42.08% and 40.98% scaling efficiency from the one-worker reference. Accuracy remains broadly comparable rather than uniformly superior: for Env 1 TGN, for example, lastfm improves from 0.7151/0.7198 AUC/AP under Vanilla DDP to 0.7908/0.8047, while AskUbuntu decreases from 0.7390/0.7944 to 0.7548/0.7997 only partly improves depending on metric; across the full table, some datasets and configurations show small losses. The reported 4.99× average speedup in the abstract is not independently reconstructible from the excerpt because the averaging procedure is not specified. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING that jointly adapting dependency replay, cache refresh, and replay pruning can substantially reduce distributed M-TGNN training time; the individual ingredients—caching, dependency-aware execution, EMA-based adaptation, and straggler mitigation—are standard families of techniques, while the proposed integration and its application to continuous-time memory-state reconstruction are the genuinely distinctive aspects. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations, a small hyperparameter sensitivity study, time breakdowns, memory measurements, and comparisons on six public datasets under two hardware environments. The ablation attributes substantial reductions to each stage: on Wikipedia, adding replay reduces epoch time from 408.58s to 103.02s; on AskUbuntu, adding adaptive synchronization reduces the incremental configuration from 437.85s to 137.81s; and on Reddit, adding pruning reduces time from 112.62s to 77.32s. However, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, repeated-seed results, or significance tests are reported. The authors state that code is publicly available at https://github.com/LFchen111/DepTGL and that the datasets are public, but the excerpt does not state whether model weights, preprocessing artifacts, exact partitioning scripts, or full configuration files are released. Baseline implementations use the authors' common runtime and reproduce key policies rather than necessarily using each system's official implementation, which improves control but can affect external validity. The evaluation omits several closely related systems listed in the related-work discussion, including Cascade, Sven, GNNFlow, and DistTGL in the main comparison, and does not report cache-state error, convergence curves, refresh-skip rates, pruning rates, or target-state divergence. Because the paper is marked arXiv:2608.16305v1 dated 17 August 2026, it should be treated as a preprint rather than a peer-reviewed result based on the supplied text. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile, because the paper implements and evaluates a distributed training framework rather than only presenting a formal model. Practical: The experiments run on commercially available NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, Tesla P100, and RTX 4090 GPUs, so the core system can run on accessible hardware, although deployment requirements for larger clusters and integration overhead are not stated. Efficient: In the reported Env 1 TGN AskUbuntu profile, DepTGL reduces communication from 487.64s to 7.57s and total profiled time from 588.09s to 115.45s, while its peak memory is 2.44GB, but it shifts work into offline dependency scanning, local replay, and runtime bookkeeping whose preprocessing and storage costs are not fully quantified. Effective: The evidence shows large epoch-time reductions while retaining broadly comparable link-prediction AUC/AP, but it establishes effectiveness only on a proxy task and does not directly measure temporal-state fidelity or convergence equivalence. Scalable: The method improves reported throughput from one to two and three workers, with 62.16%/42.08% efficiency on AskUbuntu and 71.87%/40.98% on Reddit, but the paper tests at most three workers in the explicit scaling experiment and provides no evidence at 10×–100× scale. The work delivers a reusable software artifact through the stated GitHub repository; it does not deliver a new dataset or a reusable formal proof technique. Strengths: - It identifies a system-specific bottleneck—remote temporal-state reconstruction and its auxiliary replay workload—that conventional static-GNN caching and partitioning abstractions do not capture. - The offline backward scan, mixed-batch replay, selective synchronization, and pruning mechanisms are integrated around a coherent communication-versus-computation trade-off rather than presented as unrelated optimizations. - The experimental evidence covers six temporal graphs, two memory-based TGNN architectures, four baseline policies, two substantially different GPU environments, memory use, time breakdowns, ablations, sensitivity, and limited multi-worker scaling. - The AskUbuntu profile directly supports the stated mechanism: synchronization count falls from 3,215 to 26.1 and communication share falls from 82.9% to 6.6%, while target-event throughput increases to 2,921 events/s without increasing peak GPU memory over Vanilla DDP. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly frame skipped synchronization and auxiliary replay pruning as controlled approximations that can reduce remote-cache freshness, and they state that a later refresh or final epoch-end synchronization realigns affected states. They also acknowledge through the sensitivity discussion that K, tau_g, and tau_c require balancing refresh frequency, replay overhead, cache freshness, and pruning aggressiveness. The paper does not state broader limitations concerning partitioning assumptions, preprocessing cost, cluster size, or convergence guarantees. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The claimed objective preservation is incomplete: masking preserves the set of target loss terms, but pruning auxiliary events and skipping refreshes can change the temporal states and predictions used to compute those target losses, so the paper does not prove preservation of the original training objective's gradients or semantics. The gradient-norm heuristic has no convergence or cache-error bound, and the analysis in Section VI is a cost accounting argument rather than a correctness theorem. The evaluation lacks multiple runs and variance reporting, omits direct measurements of state staleness and the fraction of skipped refreshes/pruned events, and does not isolate whether the large gains arise mainly from reducing synchronization frequency versus changing the execution semantics. Scalability evidence stops at three workers despite the framework's distributed-systems positioning; the Env 2 description says eight GPUs but the reported scaling table uses only one to three workers. The source-based node partitioning and source-assigned target policy may not generalize to arbitrary partitioning, and the offline dependency scan's preprocessing time, storage footprint, and behavior on much longer dependency chains are not reported. Several strong and closely related systems discussed in the paper are absent from the primary end-to-end comparison, limiting the strength of the claim relative to current alternatives. Bottom Line: DepTGL is a useful and plausibly high-impact systems contribution for distributed M-TGNN training, with unusually large measured communication reductions, but practitioners should validate state fidelity, preprocessing cost, and behavior beyond three workers before treating its speedups as deployment-ready.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OGR, an end-to-end generative recommender that directly produces ordered recommendation slates using recommendation-aware hierarchical semantic IDs, list-wise preference planning, pipelined SID decoding, and slate-level preference alignment. - Why it's important: Conventional retrieve–rank pipelines cannot recover items absent from the candidate pool and optimize generation, ranking, and slate utility in separate stages, while fully autoregressive slate generation is slow and poorly aligned with list-wise objectives. - How it does it: OGR combines TUSID semantic–collaborative item tokenization, a planner that models cross-position slate preferences, parallelizable position-wise SID decoding, and conservative reward-guided post-training. - The good: OGR improves effective-view NDCG@5 to 0.0633 on the industrial dataset and 0.1303 on KuaiRec, with reported relative gains of 48.2% and 27.2%, while delivering 2.43x–2.49x higher throughput than beam-decoded TIGER and OneRec. - The missing: The paper does not report dataset scale, confidence intervals or statistical significance for offline results, online traffic-volume details, or a controlled online ablation separating TUSID, GL2P, and SPA. - Read it or not: Researchers in generative and industrial slate recommendation should read it for the planner–decoder decomposition and deployment evidence, but readers seeking unbiased counterfactual slate optimization should treat the reward-alignment evidence cautiously.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses ordered slate recommendation for large-scale platforms such as short-video services, where the system must jointly select and order multiple items while accounting for inter-item dependencies and slate-level utility. Existing cascaded retrieval–ranking–reranking systems optimize only within retrieved candidates and can therefore miss relevant items; conventional generative recommenders avoid some candidate constraints but generally use next-token likelihood for individual item IDs, which does not directly optimize slate-level preference, ordering, diversity, or feedback-weighted utility. The paper targets the gap between end-to-end item generation and explicit list-wise slate optimization, while also addressing the difficulty of representing items with IDs that preserve both multimodal semantics and local collaborative structure. Key Idea: The central insight is to factor slate generation into a coarse, autoregressive preference plan over slate positions and independent intra-item SID decoding conditioned on each planned position. This allows the model to preserve cross-item dependencies through the planner while overlapping decoding across positions, reducing sequential dependency depth from O(KD) to O(K+D). TUSID supplies the item vocabulary by combining semantic and collaborative evidence before residual K-means quantization, and SPA adjusts the supervised policy using conservative, reward-calibrated slate preferences. Methodology: TUSID first encodes item image, audio, and text content with an MLLM and encodes Brand, Category, supply-side B-tags, and demand-side C-tags with a shared text encoder. Cross-attention uses the MLLM representation as query over the four attribute representations, and a learned sigmoid gate forms a residual semantic fusion, trained with a SASRec next-item loss plus a residual penalty, \(L_{fusion}=L_{rec}+\beta_{res}|B|^{-1}\sum_i\|g_i h_i^{attr}\|_2^2\). It then constructs distance-weighted local item co-occurrence vectors from positive-feedback training prefixes using a window of radius \(\omega=5\), compresses them with shared signed CountSketch hashing, applies signed-log transformation, normalization, and fixed random projection, and combines the result with normalized semantics through confidence-weighted concatenation. The collaborative weight is \(\alpha_i=\alpha_{col}\log(1+U_i)/(\log(1+U_i)+\tau)\), where \(U_i\) counts distinct supporting users; the unified vectors are quantized by four-level RQ-KMeans with 1,024 codes per level. OGR then encodes up to 128 historical SIDs with a Transformer history encoder, uses a two-layer causal Transformer planner to produce one preference representation per slate position, and uses a position-wise autoregressive SID decoder conditioned on that representation and the history. Training combines exposure-order SID loss and feedback-reordered SID loss, \(L_{sup}=L_{sid}^{eps}+\alpha L_{sid}^{fb}\), with \(\alpha=0.3\). SPA freezes the supervised model as a reference, evaluates non-duplicate logged exposure slates, standardizes primary feedback rewards and auxiliary diversity/novelty rewards within each user's slate set, suppresses auxiliary rewards when their direction conflicts with the primary reward, and optimizes a PPO-style clipped likelihood-ratio objective plus reference-policy KL and supervised replay. The main design choices—gated attribute residuals, confidence-weighted semantic–collaborative concatenation, and planner–decoder pipelining—are supported by ablations, although the paper gives limited theoretical or empirical justification for the fixed hyperparameters and reward weights. Key Results: On the industrial dataset, OGR reports effective-view Recall@5 of 0.0416 and NDCG@5 of 0.0633; on KuaiRec, it reports 0.1475 and 0.1303, respectively. It also reports industrial exposure-based Hit@5/Recall@5 of 0.2155/0.0511 and KuaiRec exposure-based Hit@5/Recall@5 of 0.5468/0.1393, with corresponding additional positive-feedback and exposure metrics in Table 1. The abstract claims relative NDCG@5 gains of 48.2% on the industrial data and 27.2% on the public data. Baselines include Caser, SASRec, BERT4Rec, PRM, Seq2Slate, TIGER, and OneRec; the generative baselines use comparable reported parameter sizes of 32 MB, but the paper does not establish that every baseline is tuned or matched equally in compute and decoding budget. TUSID reaches effective Recall@5/NDCG@5 of 0.148/0.130 on KuaiRec, versus 0.121/0.116 for RQ-KMeans and 0.129/0.115 for GNPR-SID. Removing the list-wise planner reduces industrial effective Recall@5/NDCG@5 from 0.0416/0.0633 to 0.0201/0.0359; removing SPA yields 0.0344/0.0419; removing conservative regularization yields 0.0227/0.0312. Inference experiments with slate size K=5 and SID depth D=4 report 2.43x and 2.49x throughput improvements over TIGER-Beam and OneRec-Beam, respectively, while the idealized critical-path reduction is 20/9≈2.22x. A one-week online A/B test using 3% of Kuaishou production traffic reports +1.120% Effective Views, +2.954% comments, +0.505% likes, and +1.255% forwards. The experiments use standard slate size and history length rather than stress-scale settings; the paper does not report the number of users, items, impressions, or total requests. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the integration of a list-wise preference planner with pipelined position-wise semantic-ID decoding and conservative, calibrated slate-level alignment; TUSID is a new semantic–collaborative SID construction variant, while its individual ingredients—cross-attention, gated fusion, CountSketch, RQ-KMeans, PPO-style clipping, KL regularization, and supervised replay—are established techniques combined for generative slate recommendation rather than fundamentally new primitives. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for semantic fusion, collaborative injection, confidence weighting, the list-wise planner, SPA, primary and auxiliary rewards, conservative regularization, and the two supervision orders. It states that offline results are means over five seeds (2025–2029), but reports no error bars, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The appendix specifies major hyperparameters, data leakage precautions for the collaborative sketches, reward weights, and the CountSketch construction, which improves reproducibility. However, the industrial dataset, full reward schema, multimodal encoders, and implementation are proprietary; no code, dataset, model weights, or repository URL is mentioned. A major methodological concern is that SPA does not actually evaluate newly generated or counterfactual slates: the appendix clarifies that its action sets consist only of logged exposure slates, with observed feedback assigned only to those slates. Consequently, the alignment stage is constrained by logged support and does not directly demonstrate optimization of rewards for generated slates. The offline evaluation also uses logged positive-feedback and exposure data, so it remains vulnerable to exposure bias and does not establish causal improvement. Baseline implementation and tuning details are insufficient to verify equal capacity, training data treatment, or inference-cost matching. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (with substantial empirical model evaluation), because the paper describes and evaluates a production-integrated recommender and reports an online A/B test. * Practical: The model runs on NVIDIA L20 GPUs in the reported experiments and was deployed to 3% of Kuaishou production traffic, demonstrating compatibility with commercially available hardware, although serving architecture and total resource requirements are not disclosed. * Efficient: The planner–decoder pipeline reduces idealized sequential depth from KD to K+D and measures 2.43x–2.49x throughput gains over beam-decoded generative baselines, but the comparison omits memory, end-to-end latency distributions, preprocessing/tokenization cost, and comparisons with non-generative production retrieval systems. * Effective: Offline metrics improve consistently over the listed baselines and the online test reports a +1.120% Effective View increase, but the reward-alignment evidence is based on logged exposure slates and therefore measures performance under limited logged support rather than unbiased counterfactual slate utility. * Scalable: The online test provides evidence at Kuaishou's production scale, but the paper does not report traffic volume, item-catalog size, model-serving fleet size, throughput under production load, or experiments with 10x–100x larger histories, slates, codebooks, or catalogs. The work delivers a production-evaluated recommender system and an implementable SID-construction and training pipeline, but it does not release a reusable software artifact, dataset, or trained model according to the paper. Strengths: - The planner–decoder decomposition addresses two coupled problems—slate-level dependency modeling and serial generative latency—with a concrete execution strategy and a measured throughput comparison. - TUSID separates semantic content, local collaborative structure, and evidence confidence rather than collapsing all signals into a single contrastive objective; its ablations show incremental gains from gated semantic fusion, CountSketch-based collaboration, concatenation, and confidence weighting. - The evaluation spans public and proprietary data, multiple sequential, reranking, and generative baselines, offline ablations, decoding-efficiency measurements, and an online A/B test. - The appendix explicitly corrects a potentially ambiguous description of candidate rollouts by stating that SPA uses logged exposure slates only, and it documents reward weights and leakage controls rather than presenting the alignment stage as unconstrained counterfactual reinforcement learning. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge confidentiality constraints that prevent disclosure of the full industrial reward schema. They also state that SPA uses exposure-only action sets and excludes newly generated or counterfactual slates from reward calibration. The paper does not provide a broader limitations section discussing exposure bias, catalog growth, cold-start performance measurements, diversity–engagement trade-offs, or online statistical uncertainty; these boundaries are therefore only partially confronted. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unacknowledged concern is the mismatch between the paper's motivation—optimizing generated slates beyond candidate constraints—and SPA's actual support, which is limited to logged exposure slates with observed rewards. The paper does not report dataset sizes, item-catalog coverage, the proportion of cold-start or long-tail items, online sample counts, confidence intervals, p-values, or experiment duration beyond one week. It lacks online ablations and comparisons against the incumbent system's individual components, making the source of the production lift unclear. The efficiency analysis focuses on sequential dependency depth and throughput against two generative baselines, but omits GPU memory, latency percentiles, preprocessing overhead, and strong industrial retrieval/ranking alternatives. The fixed reward weights and diversity definition may encode platform-specific preferences and are not validated through sensitivity analysis. Finally, claims that TUSID is collision-free and that OGR is candidate-unconstrained are only partially supported: the reported SID uniqueness metrics are dataset-specific, and generated SIDs still map through a finite learned vocabulary whose coverage and behavior for newly arriving items are not evaluated. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile systems paper for researchers and practitioners building generative slate recommenders because it combines a credible planner–decoder latency reduction with public-data ablations and production evidence, but its strongest claims about slate-level preference optimization remain limited by logged-slate reward support and incomplete statistical and serving-cost reporting.

CVE-Genie: An LLM-Based Multi- Agent Framework for Reproducing CVEs

S Ullah, P Balasubramanian, W Guo, A Burnett… · seclab.bu.edu · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CVE-Genie, an automated multi-agent pipeline that reconstructs vulnerable software environments, generates CVE-specific proof-of-concept exploits, creates verifiers, and stores reproducible CVE artifacts. - Why it's important: Security researchers lack large, diverse, dynamically executable vulnerability datasets, while manual reproduction requires substantial expertise and labor. - How it does it: It decomposes reproduction into source and context processing, environment building, exploit generation, and CTF-style verification, with specialized LLM developer/critic agents and feedback loops. - The good: On 841 publicly disclosed CVEs from June 2024 through May 2025, it produced 428 verified reproductions across 267 projects, 141 CWE types, and 22 languages, at an average reported cost of $2.77 per CVE. - The missing: The central correctness audit covers only 50 successful and 50 failed large-scale cases, and the paper does not establish independent validation of all 428 reproductions or compare against a strong end-to-end reproduction baseline. - Read it or not: Security-benchmark builders and researchers studying LLM agents should read it for its unusually broad artifact-producing evaluation; readers seeking evidence of reliable exploitation across unsupported platforms or at production scale should treat the claims cautiously.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (78) is strong at the system and benchmark level: CVE-Genie composes environment reconstruction, exploit generation, and verifier synthesis into a broad artifact-producing pipeline. Rigor (75) is supported by the 841-CVE evaluation, ablations, incomplete-context tests, cost accounting, public artifacts, and manual auditing, though only 50 successes were correctness-checked and there is no strong end-to-end baseline. Non-Obviousness (72) reflects the important insight that executable verifiers and critic loops can reject fabricated setups and weak exploits, but the component techniques are established. Completeness (72) and Resilience (68) are reduced by platform selection bias, heuristic success signals, unclear population-wide precision, and limited independent validation, while the authors do acknowledge many practical failures. Impact (82) is the strongest dimension because the released framework, VM snapshots, exploit scripts, verifiers, logs, and dataset can directly support security research. Problem & Motivation Software-security research needs vulnerability datasets containing accurate labels, vulnerable environments, executable proof-of-concepts, and validation procedures, but existing sources commonly provide only CVE descriptions or patch diffs. Manual reproduction is expensive—for example, prior work reportedly spent more than 3,600 hours reproducing 368 vulnerabilities—while synthetic, static-analysis-derived, patch-mined, and OSS-Fuzz datasets are limited by label noise, narrow vulnerability classes, stale software, or restricted language coverage. The target users are researchers evaluating vulnerability detection, fuzzing, automated repair, and AI security systems. The gap is an automated method that reconstructs real-world vulnerable projects and supplies both an exploit and a reliable, vulnerability-specific assessment procedure across heterogeneous projects and CWE categories. Key Idea The core insight is to treat CVE reproduction as a compositional, verified workflow rather than a single LLM task: separate context synthesis, environment reconstruction, exploit development, and verifier construction, then use critic agents and executable feedback to reject fabricated setups, mock projects, weak exploits, and unsound verification logic. The CTF-style verifier converts each CVE’s expected observable effect—such as a specific exception, sanitizer report, unauthorized state change, timeout, or memory threshold—into a machine-checkable success signal. Methodology The Processor retrieves affected source versions, CVE metadata, CWE information, patch diffs, advisories, and referenced PoCs, then uses a Knowledge Builder to distill them into a structured CVE knowledge base. The Builder uses a read-only Prerequisite Developer to inspect the repository and specify required services, important files, installation steps, and an expected final state; a Setup Developer then executes commands inside an isolated Ubuntu 22.04 QEMU/KVM VM with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM; a Setup Critic reviews logs for incomplete configuration, wrong versions, mock substitutes, or injected vulnerabilities. The Exploiter uses an Exploit Developer to reproduce an existing PoC or synthesize a Python exploit through tool interaction, followed by an Exploit Critic. The CTF Verifier Developer creates a three-stage verifier—pre-setup, immutable exploit execution, and post-execution success checking—while a Flag Checker executes it and a Verifier Critic reviews its logic; verifier generation receives up to five retries, whereas Builder and Exploiter feedback is limited to one iteration. The reported production configuration assigns o4-mini to knowledge building and Builder development, o3 to Builder criticism, Exploit development, and Verifier development/criticism, and o4-mini to Exploit criticism. The objective is operational correctness of the setup, exploit, and verifier rather than a learned loss function; no mathematical optimization objective is stated. The important design choices—modular decomposition, critic feedback, and structured context compression—are supported by ablations, although the model/prompt selection process relies partly on author manual scoring and small staged datasets. Key Results The main evaluation runs on 841 CVEs published from June 2024 through May 2025 with publicly available source code; the set covers 186 CWEs, 29 programming languages, and 440 open-source projects. Three iterative runs produced 481 successful setups, 442 successful exploit generations, and 428 final verifier-passing reproductions, or approximately 51% of the full set, spanning 267 projects, 141 CWE types, and 22 languages. The reported average cost is $2.77 per CVE; successful cases typically cost about $2 and take 18 minutes, while failed cases cost up to $4 and take 35 minutes on average, under a $5 and 45-minute per-CVE cap. Among 428 successes, approximately 46% reportedly had no prior PoC. In a 15-CVE architecture ablation, full CVE-Genie reproduced 15/15; removing the Knowledge Builder reduced this to 9/15, removing the Prerequisite Developer to 13/15, removing feedback loops to 5/15, removing critics to 8/15, and collapsing the system into one monolithic agent to 0/15. Under incomplete context, success was 10/15 without patches, 11/15 without advisories/PoCs, and 9/15 with only the CVE description. At the vulnerability-family level, reported success includes 79% for CWE-1333 ReDoS, 52% for SQL injection, 46% for XSS, 30% for use-after-free, and 0% for OS command injection without a PoC; authentication bypass reached 100% with a PoC but 36% without one. Manual auditing found all 50 sampled verifier-passing cases correct, but also 12 false negatives among sampled failures. The strongest evidence therefore concerns artifact generation under the selected environment and validation policy, not universal exploit correctness or platform-independent reproducibility. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is an end-to-end automated CVE-reproduction system that combines environment reconstruction, exploit generation, and CVE-specific verifier synthesis at substantially larger breadth than the cited prior systems; the individual ingredients—LLM code generation, ReAct tool use, multi-agent decomposition, self-critique, and CTF-style checking—are standard or adapted combinations rather than individually new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes component ablations, staged LLM selection, incomplete-context experiments, repeated runs, cost/runtime accounting, and a manually reviewed sample of 100 large-scale outcomes. It reports no error bars, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or multi-seed analysis beyond repeated nondeterministic runs; exact TPR/TNR values for critic selection are presented graphically rather than numerically. The 15-CVE ablation uses a deliberately easy, complete-context subset whose ideal performance is 15/15, limiting conclusions about architecture on difficult cases. The large-scale correctness audit samples only 50 passes and 50 failures, so the reported 428 successes are not independently validated exhaustively. Critics and manual evaluators are designed by the authors and may share the same assumptions as the pipeline, and heuristic checks based on time or memory thresholds can be hardware-sensitive. The source code, reproduced-CVE artifacts, agent logs, and visualization application are stated to be available at https://github.com/BUseclab/cve-genie, with experiment archives at https://osf.io/dcej4/; an extended version is linked at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.01835. The evaluation excludes CVEs without publicly accessible source code and is constrained to an offline Ubuntu VM, creating important selection and platform biases. The paper also does not provide a direct comparison with a current competing end-to-end reproduction system under matched compute and budget. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper builds and evaluates an executable software system that emits VM snapshots, exploit scripts, verifier scripts, metadata, and logs. - Practical: It runs on commercially available virtualized hardware using a single Ubuntu 22.04 VM with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM, but several targets require unavailable platforms, services, Docker images, external documentation, or hardware. - Efficient: The reported average cost is $2.77 and typical runtime is 18 minutes per CVE, but failed attempts consume up to $4 and 35 minutes on average, and the system depends on paid closed-source LLMs, so aggregate dataset-generation cost remains substantial. - Effective: It verifies 428/841 targets under its own generated success signals, with all 50 sampled passing cases judged correct; however, heuristic DoS checks are load-sensitive, 12 sampled failures were false negatives, and the evidence does not show that generated exploits transfer reliably beyond the constructed VM and verifier. - Scalable: The system was exercised on 841 CVEs, but it was capped at three runs, $5, and 45 minutes per CVE; the paper does not measure behavior at 10x–100x scale, concurrent execution, rate limits, model-service availability, or maintenance cost as CVE volume grows. The work delivers a reusable software framework, dataset of reproduced CVEs, VM snapshots, exploit and verifier scripts, interaction logs, and a visualization tool rather than stopping at a paper-only method. Strengths - It addresses a concrete infrastructure bottleneck and produces executable artifacts—environment, PoC, verifier, and logs—rather than only vulnerability labels or generated exploit text. - The 841-CVE study is substantially broader in projects, CWEs, and languages than the small manually curated benchmarks used by much prior LLM exploitation work. - The verifier design explicitly targets common LLM failure modes, including mock environments, wrong dependency versions, fabricated exploits, and spoofable output checks; the paper illustrates how critic feedback strengthens a weak verifier. - The ablation results identify feedback loops and modular decomposition as materially important: removing feedback reduces reproduction from 15/15 to 5/15, while a monolithic agent achieves 0/15 on the selected subset. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly report failures caused by the Ubuntu-only offline environment, Windows- and macOS-specific behavior, ASP.NET/IIS requirements, inaccessible documentation, unavailable Docker images, missing PoCs, binary build time, absent sanitizer signals, and vulnerability classes requiring stateful or high-level reasoning. They acknowledge that heuristic time and memory thresholds vary with hardware and system load, that critics prefer false negatives over false positives, and that 12 sampled failures were legitimate reproductions rejected because execution traces lacked sufficient proof. They also report poor performance for some categories, including use-after-free without PoCs and OS command injection without PoCs. These limitations are confronted in the failure analysis rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not establish the precision of the full 428-success population: auditing 50 passing cases supports a sample estimate but cannot rule out substantial unobserved false positives, especially because the generated verifier and critic are part of the same pipeline. - The baseline comparison is weak. The paper compares against a monolithic LLM ablation and summarizes prior systems, but does not run strong contemporary reproduction agents, human reproduction, fuzzers, or hybrid tools on the same 841-CVE set under matched budgets. - The architecture ablation is small and selected for consistent easy cases, while the most important claimed advantage concerns difficult, incomplete-context CVEs; component effects may differ substantially on the full distribution. - LLM and prompt selection risks overfitting: candidate models and prompts are selected using staged subsets, developer outputs are manually scored by the authors, and the same error categories inform critic prompts and correctness criteria. - “Verified exploit” often means triggering a local symptom rather than demonstrating security impact or exploitability in a realistic deployment. Crash, timeout, memory, and exception signals can be ambiguous, and the paper does not quantify semantic validity separately from signal triggering. - The source-code-availability filter, public-disclosure window, Linux/Ubuntu execution environment, and reliance on open-source projects limit generalization to proprietary software, embedded targets, cloud deployments, Windows/macOS systems, and vulnerabilities requiring complex infrastructure. - The reported cost excludes or does not clearly itemize VM provisioning, repository/API access, storage, manual auditing, failed setup infrastructure, and researcher time spent selecting models and validating outputs. Bottom Line CVE-Genie is a valuable and unusually broad benchmark-generation system whose public artifacts can materially benefit vulnerability-research tooling, but its strongest contribution is scalable candidate curation rather than established ground truth: practitioners should read and use it with independent validation, especially for non-crash and platform-specific vulnerabilities.

Training Leaves Traces: Centered Residual Signatures for Language Model Lineage Verification (16 ▲ )

Aman Singh Thakur, Rayan Khoury · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a data-free white-box lineage-verification score that compares centered residual-branch products in compatible neural-network checkpoints to determine whether they share weight ancestry. - Why it's important: Open-weight models are frequently fine-tuned, quantized, pruned, merged, or redistributed without reliable provenance records, creating supply-chain and attribution risks that hashes, metadata, and behavioral fingerprints do not address retroactively. - How it does it: It removes the generic identity-aligned component from each residual branch product, matches corresponding blocks with the Hungarian algorithm, and averages centered residual-signature cosine similarities calibrated against independently trained checkpoints. - The good: Across controlled MLP and approximately 30M-parameter GPT-2 benchmarks, the method reports AUROC 1.00 and remains at AUROC 1.00 under neuron permutation and reciprocal-rescaling laundering, while running 76x faster than Re-Basin+scale on GPT-2. - The missing: The evidence relies on very few independent training roots, synthetic or narrow language-model benchmarks, and limited real-world lineage cases, so the reported perfect discrimination does not establish reliable false-positive control across the broader open-model ecosystem or against stronger adaptive attacks. - Read it or not: Provenance, model-security, and neural-network fingerprinting researchers should read it for the centered residual-product construction and laundering experiments, but practitioners should treat it as a promising screening signal rather than ownership evidence.
