Problem & Motivation: The work addresses post-hoc verification of whether two compatible, open-weight checkpoints share weight-level ancestry when documentation is incomplete or untrusted. The target users are model distributors, auditors, security researchers, and organizations managing model supply chains. The specific gap is between methods that require unchanged parameters or trusted metadata, proactive watermarks, training records, probe data, or behavioral similarity, and the desired setting of symmetric, data-free, white-box verification after ordinary transformations such as fine-tuning, LoRA merging, pruning, quantization, and distillation. The task is deliberately limited to checkpoints with matching depth and hidden dimension and does not infer which checkpoint is the ancestor, ownership, or legal provenance. Key Idea: Trained residual branches develop a generic identity-aligned component in the product of their input and output projections, but independently trained models share that component, so it cannot itself establish ancestry. The central insight is to subtract the trace-derived identity component from each branch product and compare the remaining traceless geometry, which the paper treats as checkpoint-specific structure inherited through weight-preserving transformations. This separates a training-induced architectural signature from a lineage signal. The idea is nontrivial and supported by ablations, although the proposed gradient-coupling explanation remains explicitly a plausible mechanism rather than a proved causal account. Methodology: For each residual block, the method composes the linear maps in the residual branch, forming M_l = W_K ... W_1 while dropping nonlinearities; examples include W_2W_1 for transformer MLPs, W_downW_up for SwiGLU, W_3W_2W_1 for ResNet bottlenecks, and analogous attention products. It decomposes M_l into an identity-aligned term, tr(M_l)I/d, and a traceless remainder R_l = M_l - tr(M_l)I/d, then normalizes vec(R_l) to obtain a unit signature phi_l. For checkpoints A and B, it computes pairwise signature cosines G_ij, gates them using trace concentration, and solves a Hungarian assignment maximizing total similarity. The final symmetric score is L(A,B) = (1/L) sum_l <phi_l^A, phi^B_pi(l)>. Verification compares this score with a reference-specific empirical null formed from independently trained models and declares RELATED when the score exceeds the maximum null score. Critical design decisions are (1) centering away the identity component, which is justified by an ablation showing unrelated similarity falling from 0.019 to 0.0004 in one GPT-2 evaluation; (2) using architecture-aware products, which is necessary because incomplete products can destroy the signal; and (3) using algebraic invariance rather than explicit hidden-unit alignment, which yields robustness to permutations and reciprocal rescaling and lowers computational cost. The method costs O(Ld^2h) for products, O(L^2d^2) for signature similarities, and O(L^3) for assignment, but its reliance on matching architecture and appropriate factorization is substantial. Key Results: On a controlled depth-16 MLP benchmark with 52 pairs, including 30 related and 22 unrelated pairs, the method achieved AUROC 1.00 and Gap-Z +53.0. On a GPT-2 benchmark consisting of approximately 30M-parameter, six-layer models trained on TinyStories, it achieved AUROC 1.00 and Gap-Z +31.0 over 45 pairs; weight cosine and aligned Frobenius also achieved AUROC 1.00, while singular-value distance fell to 0.73, CKA to 0.86, and IPGuard to 0.91. In the expanded GPT-2 results, quantized and LoRA descendants had mean scores of 0.999 and 0.998, fine-tuned descendants 0.980, and 30-70% pruned descendants 0.937; the minimum descendant score was 0.855 versus a maximum non-descendant score of 0.004. In function-preserving laundering, the method retained AUROC 1.00 for permutation, mild and strong rescaling, combined permutation-rescaling, and subsequent fine-tuning on the MLP benchmark; Re-Basin+scale also retained AUROC 1.00 but required 0.8 ms versus 0.4 ms for the method on MLP and 387.9 ms versus 5.1 ms on GPT-2, a reported 76x speedup. On four public 7B-scale families, permutation laundering changed the proposed score by less than 10^-7 while reducing weight-cosine signal by roughly 93-95%. In the LLaMA-2-7B case study, LLaMA-2-chat and Vicuna scored 0.995 and 0.996, CodeLlama scored 0.336, and seven purportedly independent architectural clones scored between -5e-5 and 4e-4. Projection pairing reached 100% on the canonical MLP path across six language-model families, but alternative SwiGLU paths achieved only 68% on Qwen2.5 and 84% on DeepSeek-R1. Transfer experiments reported pairing AUCs of 1.00 for ViT, 0.85 for Whisper, and 0.96 for ResNet, but these are transfer of the structural signal rather than full lineage-verification evaluations. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM, NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the formulation of symmetric, data-free weight-lineage verification using centered traceless residual-branch products and the associated null-calibrated score; residual trace concentration and Hungarian matching are partly inherited from prior observations or standard algorithms, while the broader evaluation combines established transformations and baselines in a new provenance setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes centering, initialization, skip-connection, gradient-shuffling, synthetic-update, architecture-factorization, laundering, and partial-overlap experiments. It reports fixed deterministic seeds and detailed benchmark construction, but does not report conventional error bars, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or multiple independently repeated full benchmark runs beyond deterministic seed variants. The central evaluations use only two roots for the 52-pair MLP benchmark, three independent roots for the expanded MLP set, and eight GPT-2 roots split into calibration, development, and test, making the effective sample size far smaller than the number of pairs. The authors acknowledge this and use AUROC rather than strong false-positive claims, but the headline perfect scores remain vulnerable to root-level dependence and benchmark-specific construction. The LLaMA-2 study uses seven independent architectural clones and three documented descendants, which is useful but still a small and potentially nonrepresentative sample. Code, configurations, baseline implementations, per-pair score JSON files, and plotting scripts are stated to be released upon acceptance; no repository URL or currently available artifact is provided. The evaluation includes several relevant baselines, including Re-Basin+scale, but does not establish performance against a broad set of adaptive provenance-removal attacks or large-scale, naturally occurring checkpoint families. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL): Practical: The experiments ran on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB VRAM, so the method is implementable on commercially available hardware for the tested model sizes, although memory and runtime at 7B-scale full-checkpoint comparison are not directly reported. Efficient: It uses matrix products and assignment rather than repeated neuron alignment; on GPT-2 it took 5.1 ms per pair versus 387.9 ms for Re-Basin+scale, but no end-to-end cost is given for full 7B models or large checkpoint collections. Effective: The controlled evidence strongly separates tested descendants from independent and distilled models, including pruning, quantization, LoRA, and laundering, but it measures a constructed ancestry classification task rather than legal provenance or ownership. Scalable: Pairing transfer reaches GPT-2 sizes from 124M to 1.5B and public examples include 7B models, but the lineage benchmark itself uses approximately 30M-parameter GPT-2 models and does not test 10x-100x larger comparisons, multi-hop trees, heterogeneous architectures, or massive checkpoint repositories. The work delivers a prospective software artifact consisting of code and evaluation assets if released as stated; at the time represented by this arXiv v1 preprint, no public URL or released package is identified. Strengths: - The centered decomposition addresses a concrete confound: trace concentration alone gives AUROC 0.417, whereas removing the shared identity component produces a lineage signal. - The algebraic invariance to hidden-unit permutations and reciprocal rescaling is directly matched to realistic reparameterization-based laundering and avoids the expensive alignment search required by Re-Basin-style methods. - The evaluation distinguishes weight ancestry from behavioral similarity through independently initialized distilled students, rather than treating similar outputs as evidence of shared parameters. - The paper investigates partial layer grafts and linear merges, obtaining Spearman correlations of +0.96 with the planted overlap, which is more informative than binary clean-case classification alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the method to white-box access, compatible residual architectures, and matching depth and hidden dimension. It is symmetric and therefore cannot infer descent direction, reconstruct multi-hop family trees, or identify exactly which blocks were inherited under partial grafts or merges. The score weakens under aggressive transformations, reaching 0.58 at 85% MLP sparsity and 0.336 for CodeLlama relative to LLaMA-2. Orthogonal residual-stream rotations can destroy the centered signature in architectures where such transformations are function-preserving, although the authors argue learned LayerNorm or RMSNorm scales generally obstruct this attack. Calibration requires independently trained models from the same architecture, and the authors acknowledge that effective sample sizes are small and that broader architecture and ecosystem coverage remains untested. They also state that the score is not a legal determination of provenance, ownership, or wrongdoing. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unresolved issue is external validity: nearly perfect AUROC is obtained on small, author-constructed benchmarks with related and unrelated checkpoints generated from a few roots, so the method's false-positive behavior under many training datasets, optimizer choices, seeds, vendors, and common pretraining pipelines is not established. The null calibration protocol is operationally underspecified for deployments where only a handful of independent roots exist, and the maximum-null threshold can provide weak or unstable false-positive guarantees when roots are not exchangeable. The paper does not evaluate strong adaptive attacks beyond a limited gradient-based suppression experiment, including retraining, block replacement, low-rank obfuscation, quantization schemes, sparsity patterns, orthogonal transformations combined with normalization changes, or deliberate signature transplantation. The public LLaMA-2 validation uses documented relationships and architectural clones but does not independently verify ground truth or test near-neighbor models that share data, initialization, intermediate checkpoints, or partial training trajectories without direct weight inheritance. The paper also does not report full memory, I/O, and runtime at 7B or larger scale, nor confidence intervals for the public-case scores. Finally, the use of branch products that drop nonlinearities is empirically motivated but lacks a general theorem explaining when the resulting signature is preserved under all claimed post-training operations, especially for gated architectures whose alternative path pairing accuracy is only 68-84%. Bottom Line: This is a technically interesting and well-targeted provenance signal with unusually strong laundering experiments and a clear computational advantage, but its evidence supports a useful screening tool for compatible residual checkpoints—not yet a reliable general-purpose provenance verifier or ownership certificate.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Apodex Discovery, the TRACES benchmark of executable real-world environments and HDS6 process verification for evaluating complete tool-using solver systems on extended, verifiable investigations. - Why it's important: Existing language-model benchmarks largely evaluate fixed answers, while consequential scientific and engineering work requires sustained interaction with tools, hidden outcomes, intermediate checks, and iterative correction. - How it does it: It binds a foundation model and harness to a fixed environment–task–episode interface, records the full trajectory, separately scores final artifacts against hidden outcomes and process quality across Tools, Repair, Alternatives, Coherence, Evidence, and Scope, and can return outcome-blind repair notes. - The good: The benchmark operationalizes a meaningful distinction between a correct-looking answer and an auditable investigation, with 17 executable environments, 218 episodes, hidden verifiers, anti-leakage gates, and measured repair gains across 434 deficient trajectories. - The missing: The strongest causal claims about HDS6-driven repair remain unsupported by a matched no-repair control, and the process verifier relies on agentic model judges whose validity, inter-rater reliability, and robustness to strategic behavior are not established sufficiently. - Read it or not: Researchers building scientific or long-horizon agents should read it for the benchmark and evaluation design; readers seeking evidence of autonomous scientific discovery should be cautious because most demonstrations use retrospective proxy tasks rather than prospective discoveries or wet-lab outcomes.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the gap between answer-centric benchmarks and real-world discovery or engineering investigations in which the objective is open-ended, the state changes as the system acts, evidence arrives through tools, and definitive ground truth may be delayed or unavailable. The intended users are researchers and organizations evaluating AI systems for biomedicine, clinical translation, data curation, model training, scientific computing, and related industrial workflows. Prior interactive benchmarks such as SWE-bench, WebArena, OSWorld, and MLAgentBench provide executable environments but usually reduce evaluation to a narrowly defined task and terminal success signal; static benchmarks provide no state, external action, or recovery from intermediate failure. Apodex attempts to close this gap by making problem formulation, tool access, intermediate verification, trajectory recording, process assessment, and repair part of the benchmark rather than leaving them to an ad hoc agent scaffold. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat the complete solver–environment episode, rather than the foundation model or final answer, as the unit of evaluation. A fixed episode contract isolates the solver from hidden ground truth while exposing only declared data, tools, budgets, and feedback; the final submission is evaluated through an outcome channel, while the action–observation trajectory is independently evaluated through HDS6. This permits diagnosis and comparison of model, harness, agent-loop, tool-use, and feedback effects, and supports process-based evaluation when outcome labels are sparse or delayed. The idea is conceptually strong, but the environment–task–episode abstraction and trajectory-based process scoring combine several existing ideas from interactive agents, process supervision, verifiable rewards, and LLM judging rather than establishing an entirely new learning paradigm. Methodology: The authors first survey 561 industries across 16 sectors, select 10 domains, collect 423 candidate problems, and publish 20 registry problems after screening for technical fit, value, commercial access, verifiability, runnable instances, and closed-loop improvement potential. A problem manifest specifies the objective, decomposition, success criteria, hidden verifier, permitted data and tools, resource budgets, and anti-gaming rules. Each task is instantiated as multiple episodes with instance-specific data, seeds, budgets, and hidden outcomes. During execution, a solver consisting of a foundation model, harness, tools, memory, and control policy interacts with an isolated environment through actions and observations; the trajectory records calls, parameters, errors, resource charges, workspace state, and submissions. Outcome verification scores final and load-bearing intermediate artifacts against hidden labels or measurable proxies, normalizing results between a trivial floor and a known ceiling and applying hard leakage/contamination gates. Process verification uses HDS6, six capabilities—Tools, Repair, Alternatives, Coherence, Evidence, and Scope—implemented through 25 task-specific 0/1/2 subrubrics plus a load-bearing-step analysis that builds a dependency graph and independently re-solves influential steps. An agentic judge proposes scores with cited trajectory evidence, a second judge argues an alternative score, and a third arbitrates disagreements; the process judge is intended to be blind to outcome, solver identity, and private chain-of-thought. Repair notes identify deficient rubric bands and faulty steps without revealing ground truth, after which the system reruns the task. Critical design decisions include hidden outcome isolation, fixed interfaces for attribution, and separation of process from outcome channels; the paper motivates these choices well, but does not fully validate whether the judges measure transferable process competence rather than observable reporting style or whether normalized ceilings remain comparable across heterogeneous tasks. Key Results: The initial release contains 17 executable environments spanning 218 episodes, although the paper also reports a broader registry of 20 selected problems and 423 candidates; only two environments support the full verification–repair loop. In AAV capsid design, Apodex-1.1 obtains 0.904 mean out-of-distribution AUROC for viability versus CAP-PLM at 0.878, 0.635 tropism correlation versus Fit4Function at 0.622, 0.649 structure score versus AlphaFold 3 with symmetry expansion at 0.605, and 0.180 generative-design score versus 0.109 for AAVGen, 0.116 for AAVDiff, and 0.110 for ALICE. However, it is not the best solver on these tables: Kimi-k3 reaches 0.755 mean over AAV Tasks 1–3, Claude Opus-5 0.752, GLM-5.2 0.747, Claude Opus-4.8 0.741, and Apodex-1.1 0.729; Opus models refuse the generative task under biosafety policies. The reported “7%” advantage over published task-level references therefore reflects a selected comparison against task-specific published methods, not superiority over all evaluated model–harness configurations. On the 100-pair public drug-repurposing development set, adding the biomedical environment raises GPT-5.5 from 53.78 ± 3.22 to 56.30 ± 1.56 normalized points and GPT-5.6-sol from 54.21 ± 2.20 to 61.81 ± 3.92, based on three runs; categorical accuracy increases by 2.67 and 4.33 percentage points, respectively. In seven diagnostic LLM-engineering environments, balanced mean scores across four model-agnostic harnesses are 0.595 for GPT-5.6-sol, 0.573 for Opus-4.8, 0.553 for Kimi-k3, 0.516 for GLM-5.2, 0.478 for DeepSeek-v4-pro, and 0.459 for Apodex-1.0, showing substantial remaining failure rates and strong model–harness interaction. HDS6 correlates positively but imperfectly with outcome: pooled Spearman ρ is 0.51 over 409 trajectories, with 0.24 for AAV, 0.47 for clinical trials, 0.46 for data-for-LLMs, and 0.65 for training-and-systems tasks. For deficient trajectories with aggregate HDS6 below 3, repaired reruns improve outcome by 0.155 on average over 434 cases; 204 improve, 144 are unchanged, and 86 decline. Effects vary from +0.365 in solution verification and +0.360 in AAV viability to −0.077 in pretraining-data filtering. The paper reports only descriptive ablation effects for skill and verifier guidance, including +0.196 and +0.327 for GPT-5.6-sol on two selected tasks, because most instances receive one run and conditions are not fully controlled. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION are defensible classifications: the paper packages real-world problem scouting, executable environment contracts, hidden outcome verification, trajectory-level HDS6 scoring, and repair into TRACES and reports cross-domain solver studies; the individual ingredients—interactive environments, agent scaffolds, process supervision, LLM critics, hidden tests, and self-refinement—are established, so the genuine novelty lies in their integration around long-horizon, reality-facing tasks and in the proposed six-dimensional process taxonomy rather than in a wholly new algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is an arXiv preprint, version 1 dated 11 August 2026, not a peer-reviewed publication. It reports extensive task and harness matrices, explicit data splits, temporal and sequence-similarity controls for AAV, hidden labels, isolation, hard anti-contamination gates, resource budgets, and some repeat statistics; the DRR comparison reports mean ± sample standard deviation over three runs, and the AAV appendix gives detailed instance sizes such as 139,268 training and 133,433 test variants for one viability setting, 73,089 training and 6,032 held-out tropism peptides, 12 post-cutoff capsids for loop/assembly evaluation, and 100-query budgets for design. Ablations vary harness, model, initial skill guidance, and verifier guidance, but they are often underpowered: many cells use one run per instance, several results are affected by refusals, harness bugs, timeouts, submission failures, and hard gates, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for most comparisons. HDS6’s judge procedure includes multi-agent adjudication and citation re-grounding, but the paper does not report human agreement, judge calibration against expert labels, inter-rater reliability, judge-model sensitivity, or resistance to trajectory gaming. The repair study lacks a matched rerun without a repair note, so +0.155 cannot be attributed causally to diagnosis-based repair rather than rerun variance, additional stochasticity, or changed prompting. TRACES is stated to be available at https://discovery.apodex.com, but the parsed paper does not establish the availability of source code, environment implementations, hidden evaluation data, model weights, full verifier prompts, or a reproducible release version. Several evaluations use authors’ own environments, baselines, or reproductions, and the process verifier and some outcome components are model-generated or internally defined, creating risks of benchmark-specific optimization and evaluator bias. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL—the paper builds and evaluates a benchmark and complete solver systems rather than presenting a theorem. Practical: The LLM-agent and software-engineering environments can in principle run on commercially available compute, but the paper does not provide a complete costed deployment recipe and several biomedical tasks depend on proprietary, specialized, or computationally expensive services. Efficient: The framework explicitly meters time, tool calls, compute, data access, and experimental queries, but it does not give a unified cost or latency comparison against alternatives; repair adds another full solver run and can trade accuracy against efficiency, as illustrated by the pretraining-data case. Effective: The evidence shows measurable gains on retrospective proxies—AAV prediction/design metrics, clinical-outcome forecasting, code and data-engineering tasks—and process/outcome correlations, but it does not demonstrate a confirmed new therapeutic, validated AAV candidate in wet lab or humans, or a prospective discovery outcome. Scalable: The authors claim applicability to hundreds of high-value problems and delayed-outcome discovery challenges, but experiments cover only 17 environments and 218 episodes, with many tasks small or benchmark-local; no 10×–100× scale test of episode count, trajectory length, tool concurrency, judge cost, hidden-verifier maintenance, or prospective evidence latency is reported. The work delivers a benchmark/environment platform and associated harnesses, with the public release claimed at discovery.apodex.com; it does not deliver a generally trained heavy-duty solver or a reusable formal proof technique. Strengths: - The fixed environment–task–episode interface is a useful systems abstraction for separating model, harness, tool, budget, and feedback effects, and the paper provides unusually explicit treatment of hidden state, resource accounting, intermediate artifacts, and anti-gaming gates. - The benchmark targets scientifically and operationally meaningful tasks rather than only synthetic prompts, including AAV sequence design, clinical-trial reporting, drug repurposing, data curation, training recipes, numerical-kernel alignment, and verifier construction. - HDS6 makes process dimensions such as evidence grounding, scope control, alternative hypotheses, and repair visible even when terminal success is sparse; the clinical safety-table and corpus-size examples show how a process diagnosis can identify errors that a scalar outcome score cannot localize. - The paper is candid about several weaknesses, including incomplete coverage, model refusals, harness asymmetry, descriptive rather than causal ablations, and imperfect process–outcome alignment, and it publishes full harness–model matrices rather than only selected headline results. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that TRACES currently covers only 17 executable environments and 218 episodes, a subset of the 20 selected problems and 423-problem registry, with only two environments supporting the full verification–repair loop. They acknowledge that HDS6 alignment with outcome scores needs improvement and requires broader validation. They also note asymmetric harness coverage, packaged harnesses that cannot be compared across models, model–harness interaction, one-run-per-instance variance in mechanism ablations, submission and infrastructure failures, refusal behavior, and the absence of a matched no-repair control. They present the AAV and DRR findings as early evidence and distinguish retrospective evaluation from prospective discovery challenges, but the prospective challenge has not yet produced a reported external experimental outcome. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper does not establish that HDS6 is valid beyond its own task-specific rubrics and model-based judges; expert annotation, judge agreement, calibration, adversarial trajectory tests, and comparisons with simpler process metrics are missing. - The headline repair improvement is confounded by rerun variance because every deficient trajectory receives repair but no matched same-budget rerun without a repair note; the decline rate of 86/434 also needs statistical treatment and analysis by task, trajectory length, and diagnosis type. - The benchmark’s hidden verifiers and normalization ceilings may encode strong assumptions about what counts as a valuable discovery, and several “real-world” outcomes are retrospective proxies such as held-out assay fitness, clinical-stage tiers, or internal reference scores rather than real-world impact. - The comparison to published state of the art is not consistently apples-to-apples: Apodex-1.1 is inferior to several evaluated frontier model–harness systems on aggregate AAV Tasks 1–3, while published baselines use different implementation and resource assumptions; the paper should report matched compute, tool access, training data, and statistical uncertainty. - The environment and harness release is not documented sufficiently for independent reproduction in the paper: exact code, prompts, verifier implementations, hidden-data construction, judge versions, seeds, cost, and dependency versions are not specified in the parsed text. - The 561-industry scouting process is largely expert-driven and its scoring reliability, reviewer agreement, selection bias, and relationship to actual downstream value are not evaluated; commercial-access criteria may favor the authors’ deployment perspective. - The framework’s safety properties are underdeveloped for biomedical and industrial tasks: the paper measures biosafety refusals as benchmark outcomes but does not provide a systematic analysis of harmful capabilities, misuse pathways, or safeguards for deployment beyond isolated environment constraints. Bottom Line: This is a useful and technically substantive benchmark-and-evaluation report for researchers studying long-horizon scientific agents, but its strongest contribution is the infrastructure and measurement proposal—not evidence that current systems conduct genuine autonomous discovery—and its process-verification and repair claims require controlled, independently validated experiments before supporting top-tier claims about reliability.

CoRun: Padding is Simple and Efficient for Deterministic LLM Inference

S Zhao, J Yang, Q Chen, J Hu, J Zheng, G Chen… · arxiv.org · inference optimize llm faster inference throughput - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CoRUN, a scheduling-based deterministic LLM inference system that isolates variable-shape prefill, pads decode to a fixed maximum-concurrency shape, and preserves optimized position-invariant kernels. - Why it's important: Deterministic token generation is needed for reproducible evaluation, debugging, and reinforcement-learning rollouts, but existing batch-invariant kernels can reduce throughput by up to 74%. - How it does it: CoRUN controls execution shapes rather than making every kernel batch-invariant, combining singleton prefill, fixed-shape CUDA-Graph decode, selective deterministic reductions, disabled decode-time Split-KV, and request-bound RNG state. - The good: On Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3, and Hy3, CoRUN passes the reported determinism test and improves throughput over batch-invariant vLLM by 15–324%, with average TTFT and TPOT reductions of 51.8% and 48.6%. - The missing: The determinism evaluation covers only 32 prompts per model, at one batch size, one seed, and at most 8 generated tokens, leaving long-horizon and broader arrival-order validation insufficiently tested. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on reproducible LLM evaluation, RL rollouts, or high-concurrency serving; skip it for low-concurrency interactive serving, where the fixed padding and serialized prefill can be counterproductive.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) reflect the useful distinction between batch invariance and position invariance and the execution-shape contract that exploits it. Rigor (70) is credible through the formal conditional argument, operator ablations, multiple large models, and workload studies, but is reduced by the very narrow determinism test and lack of repeated-run and cross-stack validation. Completeness (80) is strengthened by explicit measurements of padding and prefill costs, while Resilience (70) is limited by untested kernel assumptions and absent direct comparisons with competing deterministic systems. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM inference can produce different token sequences for the same prompt, seed, and sampling parameters because dynamic batching changes GPU kernel tiling and floating-point reduction order. The problem affects model comparison, debugging, reproducibility, and training–inference consistency in reinforcement learning. Existing deterministic stacks address it with batch-invariant kernels whose reduction trees remain fixed across batch shapes, but this prevents shape-specific optimizations such as Split-K and Split-KV and can substantially increase latency. The paper targets the narrower setting in which outputs must be invariant to co-runners, batch positions, and arrival order while hardware, software, model, numerical format, and tensor-parallel configuration remain fixed. Key Idea: Full batch invariance is stronger than necessary when kernels are position-invariant: for a fixed execution shape, a request produces the same result regardless of its batch slot. CoRUN therefore makes the execution shape repeatable for each stage—by running each prefill alone and padding every decode iteration to a fixed maximum size—so optimized kernels can retain shape-specific tiling without allowing co-runners to alter a request's arithmetic. The central insight is execution-shape control as an alternative to universally batch-invariant kernels. Methodology: CoRUN wraps vLLM 0.25.0 without introducing a separate model-execution path. During prefill, its scheduler selects one request at a time, temporarily hides other running and waiting requests, and restores them after the ordinary vLLM scheduler creates a singleton prefill; chunked prefill for long prompts remains ordered and request-local. During decode, it sets the maximum concurrency to 256 and captures one CUDA Graph for 256 query tokens, padding inactive slots with masked tokens. It disables decode-time Split-KV because attention partitioning can otherwise depend on the ragged batch, while retaining standard position-invariant implementations for MatMul, RMSNorm, Softmax, and other operators; it uses fixed-tree collectives for reductions that are not position-invariant. The sampler also receives a fixed-size padded input and binds multinomial RNG state to requests rather than batch slots. The determinism argument defines a contract over co-runners, positions, and arrival orders and proves it by induction: isolated prefill establishes equal initial states, fixed-shape decode plus position-invariant kernels preserves equal logits and KV states, and request-bound RNG preserves equal sampling decisions. The key design decisions are technically plausible and mostly justified by operator-level measurements, but the paper does not independently verify every kernel, backend, or model configuration beyond relying on stated verification and the reported test harness. Key Results: CoRUN is evaluated on Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3, and Hy3 using 300 requests per workload from BurstGPT production traces, Blazedit code-editing workloads, and four synthetic input/output-length configurations. Against standard nondeterministic vLLM and vLLM batch-invariant execution, CoRUN improves throughput over the batch-invariant baseline by 15–324% and more than doubles aggregate throughput for every evaluated model; the paper does not provide all underlying numerical values in text, but the plotted totals are approximately 3,200–3,900 tokens/s for CoRUN versus roughly 1,100–1,700 tokens/s for batch-invariant execution, depending on model. On Qwen3-235B-A22B, one decode step with batch size 32 and variable context lengths takes 19.4 ms with standard kernels, 88.4 ms with batch-invariant kernels, and 32.6 ms with CoRUN. Relative to batch-invariant execution, mean TTFT falls by 51.8% and mean TPOT by 48.6% across six workloads. On a BurstGPT run with Qwen3-235B-A22B, standard vLLM finishes prefill in about 20 seconds and decode in 37 seconds, batch-invariant execution takes about 40 and 124 seconds, and CoRUN performs no decode during its first approximately 30 seconds because it serializes prefill, after which its peak decode throughput reaches 83% of standard vLLM. Disabling Split-KV costs 15–41% with variable prompt lengths and 1–9% with similar lengths. Padding is harmful at low utilization: with one active request, CoRUN throughput decreases approximately inversely with padding size and falls below batch-invariant execution when the padding size exceeds 64. CoRUN exceeds standard vLLM for one DeepSeek-V3 workload because separating prefill and decode enables CUDA-Graph execution that mixed batches prevent. The determinism test checks 32 prompts per model, temperature 0.6, seed 42, and up to 8 output tokens; all prompts match token sequences and sampled-token log probabilities between isolated and batched runs. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the distinction between batch invariance and position invariance and the associated end-to-end execution-shape contract are the main conceptual contributions, while the implementation combines known scheduling, padding, CUDA Graph, deterministic collective, and request-local RNG mechanisms in a new deterministic-serving design; it is not a new model, dataset, or fundamental GPU kernel algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a useful formal contract and an induction argument, operator-level latency comparisons, an end-to-end ablation separating decode padding, disabled Split-KV, and isolated prefill, evaluations across three large models and multiple workload shapes, and a concurrency sweep. However, the proof is conditional on the asserted position-invariance or batch-invariance of every exercised kernel and on request-local isolation; these properties are not established through a complete independently reproducible kernel audit. The determinism experiment is narrow—32 prompts per model, batch size 1 versus 32, one seed, temperature, and short eight-token generations—and does not report multiple seeds, long-generation divergence rates, statistical confidence intervals, or tests across repeated process launches, different CUDA versions, hardware, tensor-parallel configurations, or more varied batch sizes and arrival traces. Throughput results appear to use single configurations and do not report error bars or repeated-run variance. Baselines include standard vLLM and vLLM batch-invariant execution, but the comparison does not experimentally include competing verified-speculation systems such as LLM-42 or MarginGate, despite discussing them. The paper does not state that code, data, model weights, or a reproducibility package has been released, and no repository URL is provided. The results are therefore credible for the tested vLLM/model stack but do not establish broad cross-stack determinism or universal superiority. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the paper implements and evaluates a serving-system wrapper around vLLM. - Practical: The system runs on commercially available CUDA-capable hardware in an existing vLLM stack, but the paper does not specify GPU models, hardware counts, memory usage, or deployment cost. - Efficient: CoRUN avoids the large kernel overhead of batch-invariant execution and uses CUDA Graph replay, but pays for singleton prefill, disabled decode-time Split-KV, and padded decode; its one-request experiment shows throughput can fall below batch-invariant execution when padding exceeds 64 slots. - Effective: It achieves exact token and sampled-log-probability agreement in the reported short determinism suite and substantially improves throughput over batch-invariant vLLM, but it is evaluated primarily on the determinism proxy of sequence equality rather than directly measuring downstream evaluation reproducibility or reinforcement-learning training quality. - Scalable: Throughput increases with tested concurrency up to 256 on Hy3/Blazedit, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger concurrency, distributed deployments, changing maximum-concurrency settings, or workloads whose active set remains sparse; it explicitly identifies fixed maximum concurrency as a limitation. The work delivers an implemented vLLM scheduling wrapper and configuration, but the paper does not state that the implementation is publicly released; it does not deliver a new dataset, model, or reusable standalone library. Strengths: - The batch-invariance versus position-invariance distinction isolates a meaningful systems-level source of unnecessary determinism overhead and gives the design a clear technical rationale. - The stage-specific treatment is well matched to LLM execution: singleton prefill avoids global prompt padding while fixed-shape decode enables CUDA Graph replay and position-invariant kernels. - The paper measures the principal costs rather than reporting only aggregate throughput: it identifies MatMul and attention as dominant batch-invariance overheads, quantifies Split-KV and prefill-isolation penalties, and exposes low-utilization padding behavior. - The evaluation spans three substantially different large models, production-like and code-editing workloads, synthetic length controls, latency distributions, concurrency, and an end-to-end determinism check. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict the determinism contract to a fixed hardware architecture, software stack, numerical format, model, and tensor-parallel degree; they do not claim cross-hardware or cross-configuration reproducibility. They acknowledge that isolated prefill is CoRUN's largest overhead, that fixed decode padding is inefficient when concurrency is low, and that a fixed maximum concurrency is poorly suited to variable-rate online serving. They position CoRUN mainly for high-concurrency offline evaluation and RL rollout rather than sparse interactive traffic, and identify hybrid batch-invariant prefill or prefill–decode disaggregation as future work. These limitations are confronted directly and supported by ablations, although their implications for broader deployment are not fully quantified. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The strongest determinism claim is broader than the evidence: the reported test covers only 32 prompts, batch sizes 1 and 32, one seed, and eight output tokens, so it does not establish invariance over long autoregressive runs, arbitrary arrival orders, repeated scheduler perturbations, or all supported batch compositions. - The proof assumes the relevant kernels are position-invariant and that request-local metadata and collectives cannot introduce cross-request effects, but the paper does not provide a systematic per-kernel verification methodology, source-level evidence, or tests across CUDA, driver, GPU, and backend versions. - The throughput comparison omits direct experimental comparisons with LLM-42 and MarginGate, which may offer a more relevant alternative for mixed deterministic/nondeterministic traffic; the paper instead presents its own limited measurements of LLM-42 using Qwen3 models and a ShareGPT workload. - The evaluation does not report GPU hardware, number of GPUs, power or cost efficiency, memory overhead, scheduler overhead, or confidence intervals, making absolute performance and reproducibility difficult to assess. - The design's fixed maximum-concurrency choice is evaluated mainly at 256 and is not compared against adaptive padding sizes, multiple CUDA-Graph capture sizes, or a policy that changes the target shape with load. - The stated benefit for RL rollout is not measured on an RL pipeline: the paper does not demonstrate reduced training–inference mismatch, improved policy-training stability, or end-task reproducibility. Bottom Line: CoRUN is a technically coherent and practically relevant systems contribution for all-deterministic, high-concurrency offline LLM workloads, but its narrow determinism validation and lack of direct comparison with verified-speculation alternatives prevent the paper from establishing that it is the general best solution.

SemaPLC: A Project-Grounded, Verification-Gated Agent Harness for PLC Code Generation (111 ▲ )

Yanlun Tu, Huacan Wang, Ziyue Zhou, Jie Zhou, Ningyan Zhu, Ge Chen, Wangyi Chen, Tengfei Zhou, Yifan Zhou, Dasheng Yang, Xiaofeng Mou, Hui Zhang, Yi Xu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SEMAPLC, an open-source agent harness that generates PLC Structured Text within task or project context and accepts an implementation only after logged specification, compilation, and live-runtime checks pass. - Why it's important: PLC logic must integrate with existing industrial projects and satisfy timing-, state-, interlock-, and fault-dependent behavior, which compilation and static checks alone can miss. - How it does it: The harness grounds generation in the target project, feeds diagnostics and runtime traces back into a repair loop, and invalidates all prior verdicts whenever the code changes. - The good: Across seven models, SEMAPLC reaches a 72.6% mean strict verified-pass rate on 117 function tasks and a 52.2 mean dynamic-behavior score on 65 project tasks, versus at most 31.4 for the baselines. - The missing: Dynamic evaluation uses at most six benchmark-derived scenarios per task, so the results do not establish correctness under unseen operating conditions, broader plant states, or safety-critical deployment. - Read it or not: PLC-generation researchers and industrial-code-agent designers should read it for the runtime-centered evaluation and verification-gating design; readers seeking evidence of production deployment or general safety guarantees can skip it for now.

Problem & Motivation PLC code-generation systems have mainly been evaluated on isolated program organization units, compiler success, manually inspected outputs, or limited execution demonstrations. Industrial users instead need generated logic to fit an existing IEC 61131-3 project, reuse its variables and function blocks, preserve interfaces and initialization conventions, compile as an integrated program, and behave correctly over scan cycles and temporal fault conditions. Static or formal checks can miss wrong priorities, timer behavior, reset handling, dead outputs, and interlock violations; the paper targets the gap between syntactically or statically acceptable code and code that actually executes the intended control behavior. The affected domain is industrial automation, including factory lines, power plants, water treatment, and process plants. Key Idea The central idea is to make externally logged verification—not the language model's confidence or completion decision—the authority that determines delivery. Project grounding supplies the relevant existing structure, while a verification gate requires evidence from specification auditing, compilation, and runtime execution; any edit invalidates every previous result and forces rechecking. The individual tools are conventional, and the main conceptual contribution is their binding completion discipline plus benchmark-scale measurement of runtime behavior. Methodology SEMAPLC receives a natural-language requirement and either a local POU interface or an existing Structured Text project. It first grounds the context by retrieving project structure, declarations, interfaces, function blocks, and conventions, then loads generic PLC skills covering IEC 61131-3 practices, function-block patterns, timers, counters, safety, and architecture. A model-agnostic event-driven agent plans and generates or edits the candidate. The harness then runs three verification layers: a specification audit checks named signals and devices, boundaries, priorities, interlocks, coverage, and scan-cycle semantics; compilation checks syntax, types, symbols, interfaces, and integrated build diagnostics; and runtime validation builds and deploys a test copy, injects derived inputs, samples variables or traces, and compares outputs with requirement assertions or hidden-reference golden traces. Failed checks produce diagnostic feedback for repair, with at most two repair rounds per check and a global interaction budget. The completion rule requires valid machine-readable verdicts corroborated by tool logs; edits clear all verdicts, and the delivered file must hash-match the successfully compiled artifact. Function-track correctness is defined as a held-out judge satisfying at least 80% of requirement-derived model-checking properties, with inconclusive checks counted as failures. Project-track metrics are integrated compilation, static assertion satisfaction, and dynamic trace agreement. The project-grounding and external-verification choices are directly motivated by the target failure modes; the two-repair limit and interaction budget are operationally clear but receive limited justification, and the specification audit remains partly dependent on procedural skill documents and model interpretation. Key Results On the 117-task function track, SEMAPLC obtains the highest strict verified-pass rate for all seven backbones: 72.6% mean, compared with 63.9% for Agents4PLC, 62.4% for AutoPLC, and 30.2% for LLM4PLC. It reaches 82.1% with GPT-5.5 versus 79.5% for Agents4PLC, and its weakest model achieves 67.5%, above every baseline mean. Against the same backbone without the harness, the full system improves every model by 8.5 to 33.3 percentage points, from a 55.3% bare mean to 72.6%; the cross-model spread contracts from 37.6 to 14.6 points. On the 65-task project-context track, SEMAPLC averages 89.4% integrated compilation, 81.6 static behavior, and 52.2 dynamic behavior, compared with baseline means of 58.7–81.5, 71.7–75.7, and 22.4–31.4, respectively. It leads dynamic behavior for all seven models, but its GPT-5.5 advantage over Agents4PLC is only 65.4 versus 63.6, and it does not lead static behavior for that model. A DeepSeek-V4-Flash ablation increases dynamic behavior from 23.1 with generation alone to 30.3 with specification checks, 43.7 with compilation, and 54.1 with runtime validation; mean tokens and requests rise from 34,000 and 8.9 per task to 129,000 and 47.8. Formal verification is incomplete for timing constructs: all 174 properties in 32 timer-bearing programs receive inconclusive verdicts in the reported PLCverif/nuXmv pipeline. The runtime score remains substantially below the static score even for SEMAPLC, indicating that the tested generation problem remains unresolved rather than saturated. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and evaluation formulation: the genuinely new element is the verification-gated, edit-invalidating delivery protocol coupled with project-grounded PLC generation and benchmark-scale live-runtime evaluation; the agent loop, retrieval of project context, compiler feedback, tool use, and iterative repair are standard components adapted and integrated for PLC control logic. Rigor & Reproducibility The evaluation uses identical 117-task function data after a documented PLC-engineer audit repaired defects in 43 tasks, and a separate 65-task project corpus spanning ten industrial plants. It evaluates seven backbone models and compares LLM4PLC, AutoPLC, Agents4PLC, a bare SEMAPLC configuration, and the full harness under held-out judging. The paper includes a cumulative verification-layer ablation, an outcome decomposition over 3,590 scenario-port checks, interaction-cost measurements, a case study, oracle audits, leakage checks, and explicit separation between information seen during generation and hidden scoring artifacts. It reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and the layer ablation is restricted to one model. Static project assertions are derived from corpus runtime tests and retained only when the hidden reference satisfies them; this avoids direct answer exposure but creates a reference-dependent oracle and may reward structural resemblance rather than semantic equivalence. Dynamic scenarios are derived from the requirement and benchmark infrastructure, while scoring traces come from hidden references; because both scenario sources share the requirement, generation-time and evaluation-time coverage can overlap. The paper is an arXiv v1 preprint dated 19 August 2026, and the authors state that SEMAPLC is open-sourced at https://github.com/midea-ai/SemaPLC. The text does not state whether all model prompts, endpoint versions, run logs, trained weights, hardware details, or complete benchmark licensing arrangements are released. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems artifact. Practical: The harness uses commercially available PLC tooling and a live runtime through MCP/CLI tools, but the paper does not specify the required PLC hardware, runtime vendor compatibility, or safety certification needed for plant deployment. Efficient: Function-track wall-clock time is lower than Agents4PLC, 71 versus 454 seconds per task, but project-track time is comparable, 347 versus 344 seconds, while SEMAPLC uses 34.1 versus 6.9 model requests and up to 129,000 tokens per task in the full DeepSeek-V4-Flash ablation. Effective: The evidence shows improvements on compilation, static assertions, and bounded runtime trace agreement, with a 52.2 versus at most 31.4 dynamic-score advantage, but it measures proxy scenarios rather than full operational correctness or safety. Scalable: The harness is evaluated on 117 isolated tasks and 65 tasks across ten plants, not at 10x–100x larger projects, longer traces, more PLC vendors, or more complex multi-section integrations; scalability beyond the tested corpus is not demonstrated. The work delivers an open-source software harness, MCP server, CLI tools, procedural skills, and evaluation infrastructure, but not a production-ready end-to-end PLC development environment. Strengths - It identifies and measures a meaningful deployment gap: methods with similar static scores have sharply different runtime scores, with baseline dynamic means spanning 22.4–31.4 and SEMAPLC reaching 52.2. - The completion protocol provides a concrete delivery-integrity property: reported passes are tied to logged tool outcomes and exact delivered bytes, while edits invalidate stale evidence. - The two-track design separates isolated POU reliability from project integration and runtime behavior, and the repaired function oracle addresses known benchmark defects rather than silently relying on a flawed released evaluation. - The ablation connects verification layers to both outcome and cost: compilation provides a +13.4 dynamic-score increment and runtime validation a further +10.4 on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, while the full loop raises requests from 8.9 to 47.8 per project task. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that dynamic scoring uses a bounded scenario set derived from hidden-reference benchmark infrastructure, so behavior under unseen conditions is unmeasured. They also acknowledge that SEMAPLC's advantage narrows on the strongest model; on GPT-5.5 its dynamic lead over Agents4PLC is only 1.8 points, and it trails baselines on static behavior. They note that formal verification is inconclusive for timer-bearing programs in their pipeline and propose extending validation to process simulation and an end-to-end development environment. These limitations are stated directly, although the discussion does not quantify broader plant coverage, hardware/vendor portability, or safety-critical failure consequences. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The principal dynamic metric is reference-trace agreement on up to six scenarios per task, not exhaustive behavioral correctness; the paper does not test adversarial, randomized, long-horizon, concurrent, initialization, recovery, or unseen operating regimes. - The project static oracle is reference-filtered and largely extracted from existing runtime tests, with only 1–20 assertions per task; this may underrepresent valid implementations and leave untested requirements invisible. - No error bars, statistical tests, independent repeated runs, or per-task paired significance analysis are reported, so the stability of several-point differences—especially the 1.8-point GPT-5.5 dynamic margin—is unclear. - The main component ablation is single-model and cumulative, so interactions among grounding, skills, specification review, repair policy, and gate enforcement are not isolated; the bare-versus-full comparison also conflates all harness components. - Baseline comparability is imperfect because published systems are run at their published iteration budgets and Agents4PLC is reimplemented, while SEMAPLC has a different tool and interaction budget; the paper does not provide enough prompt, configuration, endpoint, hardware, or cost detail to reproduce the comparison exactly. - The study does not evaluate safety certification, human review burden, deployment rollback, malicious or misleading requirements, tool failures, PLC communication faults, or behavior on proprietary vendor dialects and larger projects. Claims about industrial reliability therefore exceed the demonstrated benchmark scope if interpreted as production readiness. Bottom Line This is worth reading for its concrete verification-gating protocol and unusually relevant runtime evaluation of PLC code agents, but its evidence supports improved bounded-benchmark reliability—not general PLC correctness, safety, or production-scale deployment—and should be read alongside work testing broader scenarios and vendor environments.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents often repeat environment setup mistakes, tool-use errors, debugging loops, and verification failures even when prior executions contain the needed procedure. Existing skill evaluations mostly ask whether injecting a skill improves final task success, which cannot distinguish benefits from procedural guidance, factual knowledge, outcome labeling, retrieval, or downstream invocation. The problem primarily affects tool-using and software-engineering agents operating over multi-step terminal environments, where procedural details and execution constraints are frequent failure points. The paper targets the gap between aggregate skill utility and mechanism-level understanding, including why the same skill can improve one task but harm another. Key Idea: A skill helps mainly by converting noisy execution traces into a compact procedural anchor—an ordered sequence of actions, checks, and failure mitigations—rather than by injecting missing domain facts. The paper’s central conceptual move is to treat skill use as a lifecycle involving representation, construction, transfer, retrieval, invocation, adaptation, and verification; this explains why distilled skills outperform verbose workflow traces in some settings while also introducing misapplication and applicability failures. Methodology: The study runs four controlled investigations. For RQ1, it collects successful and failed trajectories from Terminal-Bench 2.0, SkillsBench, and Terminal-Bench-Pro, constructs six fixed-budget source mixtures from 5 successful/0 failed through 0 successful/5 failed trajectories, and compares Raw, Workflow Memory, and Skill conditions on matched tasks. Workflow Memory appends cleaned procedural traces, whereas Skill distills the same traces into a standardized SKILL.md containing applicability conditions, preconditions, ordered steps, failure modes, recovery instructions, and verification criteria. For RQ2, it removes explicit success/failure annotations during skill construction while preserving the underlying trajectories. For RQ3, it constructs artifacts with Codex plus GPT-5.3-Codex and evaluates them with Gemini CLI plus Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview. For RQ4, it creates candidate pools of sizes 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 containing benchmark-ground-truth skills plus random, semantically similar, or dissimilar distractors; it evaluates Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B ranking, explicit agent selection, and independent full-pool execution. The mechanism analysis normalizes 8,135 trial records, samples 240 trajectories for open coding, derives 238 valid labels and 12 canonical modes, and applies an LLM judge to 528 raw/workflow/skill triples. Key design decisions—holding source trajectories fixed between Workflow Memory and Skill, separating offline retrieval from execution, and using paired triples—are well aligned with causal attribution, although the design still depends on generated skills, model behavior, and LLM-based labels whose validity is not exhaustively established. Key Results: Across 528 matched triples, Raw succeeds on 312/528 trials (59.1%), Workflow Memory on 295/528 (55.9%), and Skill on 327/528 (61.9%). Skill versus Workflow Memory improves by 6.06 percentage points, with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of [+0.76, +11.36]; Skill versus Raw improves by 2.84 points with an interval of [−2.27, +7.95]. In the 26-task compact-baseline study, Skill reaches 79.2% (103/130), compared with 62.3% for Workflow Memory, 59.2% for a workflow-derived test-first template, 50.0% for Raw, and 47.7% for an instruction-derived short plan. On the matched 83-task token analysis, Skill achieves 69.6% success with 521.5K total tokens per task versus 64.1% and 555.7K for Raw; Workflow Memory is cheaper at 426.2K tokens but reaches 64.8%. Mechanism labels classify 65.7% of skill effects as procedural anchoring and 4.5% as explicit knowledge injection. Skill reduces execution-layer/verification failures from 37.3% for Raw to 23.5%, including environment/infrastructure failures from 5.3% to 0.2%, output-format mismatches from 7.4% to 3.2%, and background-service failures from 2.7% to 0.8%; however, algorithmic logic errors remain 7.4% versus 8.3% for Raw, and static verification without runtime remains 11.7% versus 12.5%. Skill-specific misapplication or ignored guidance rises to 10.0%, compared with 0.8% for Raw, while Workflow Memory has 10.6% timeout/budget-exhaustion cases. In retrieval, averaged execution-time precision falls from 29.6% at pool size 5 to 3.3% at size 100, while downstream success changes only from 36.4% to 39.3%; offline embedding top-1 precision falls from 88.3% to 76.9%, and explicit selection from 70.0% to 63.7%. Similar distractors are especially damaging offline: embedding precision falls from 70.5% at pool size 5 to 53.4% at 100. The results support a separation between exact skill identification and task success, but the paper does not show that retrieval interventions improve end-to-end success. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; NEW FORMULATION; NEW EVALUATION METHODOLOGY. The genuinely new contribution is the controlled, contrastive decomposition of skill utility into procedural anchoring, execution robustness, invocation failures, outcome-label dependence, framework transfer, and retrieval/use mismatch; the underlying skill-file format, LLM-based distillation, embedding retrieval, and terminal-agent benchmarks are largely existing components combined for this analysis. Rigor & Reproducibility: The strongest rigor choices are matched source trajectories, fixed task and trial conditions, paired raw/workflow/skill comparisons, explicit no-hint ablations, independent retrieval arms, and bootstrap intervals for paired success deltas. The taxonomy pipeline includes human grounding checks for all 238 retained raw labels across 714 trajectory-label checks and reports 95.8% exact agreement with Cohen’s kappa of 0.952 for taxonomy aggregation. However, the full paired-triple labeling remains LLM-assisted rather than exhaustively human-coded, and one representative trial per task/setting/arm is selected for the main taxonomy analysis despite repeated executions. The paper reports no multiple-seed aggregate results or significance tests beyond bootstrap intervals, and the outcome-label ablation shows large model- and benchmark-specific variation, including cases where no-hint skills outperform normal skills. Some skill-arm token metadata are incomplete. The study uses current-looking but proprietary or preview models, changes from GPT-5.3-Codex to GPT-5.4 for RQ4, and explicitly restricts cross-RQ comparisons. Code, data, model weights, or a public repository URL are not stated; the paper mentions released artifacts for some retrieval statistics but gives no accessible URL in the provided text. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL—the paper evaluates agent methods and execution traces rather than delivering a deployed infrastructure system. * Practical: The evaluated terminal-agent configurations run in Docker with commercially accessible model APIs and therefore appear runnable on commercially available hardware, although API availability and proprietary model access are prerequisites. * Efficient: Skill uses 521.5K total tokens per task on the 83-task matched intersection, less than Raw at 555.7K but more than Workflow Memory at 426.2K; runtime, GPU/CPU cost, storage overhead, and skill-generation cost are not fully reported. * Effective: The evidence shows a modest aggregate advantage over Raw and a 6.06-point advantage over Workflow Memory, with especially large gains on selected tasks, but the effect is benchmark- and mixture-dependent and does not consistently improve all task classes or repair algorithmic and verification failures. * Scalable: Retrieval tests reach candidate pools of 100 skills, where actual-use precision collapses to 0.7–8.1% depending on model and distractor regime, but the study does not test 10×–100× larger pools, longer-lived skill libraries, continual updates, or multi-session deployment. The work delivers a standardized SKILL.md construction protocol, a 12-mode analysis taxonomy, controlled evaluation procedures, and analyzed trajectory/results artifacts; it does not clearly deliver a reusable library, CLI, deployed skill router, trained model, or publicly accessible dataset/repository. Strengths: - The comparison between Skill and Workflow Memory uses the same underlying trajectories, making the +6.06-point difference more informative than a comparison against Raw alone. - The procedural-anchoring interpretation is supported by both aggregate outcomes and concrete failure-mode shifts: skills sharply reduce environment, service-lifecycle, shell, and output-format failures while leaving deeper algorithmic failures largely intact. - The separation of offline retrieval quality from execution-time skill access and downstream success exposes a non-obvious result: exact ground-truth invocation is neither necessary nor sufficient for task completion. - The paired trajectory methodology and evidence-quote validation make qualitative mechanism claims more inspectable than typical success-only skill evaluations, even though the final labels remain largely LLM-generated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the evaluation focuses on terminal- and tool-using benchmarks and does not cover long-horizon web interaction or open-ended collaboration. They acknowledge the limited number of agent-model configurations and caution that findings may not generalize to other scaffolds, model families, or model versions. They also acknowledge that the taxonomy is induced from a stratified sample covering approximately 3% of normalized records, so rare behavioral modes may be underrepresented. The appendix additionally notes incomplete skill-arm token metadata, LLM-assisted full-dataset labeling, and deterministic selection of one representative trial per paired task-setting record. These limitations are confronted directly rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not fully disentangle the effect of the SKILL.md format from the skill-generation prompt, document length, content selection, and placement in the execution environment; the compact baselines partly address this but do not match skill content or generation budget. Workflow Memory is described as cleaned traces, yet the cleaning procedure and its information loss are not characterized sufficiently to rule out an unfavorable baseline. The source tasks are selected to have balanced successful and failed trajectories, which may induce survivorship or selection bias and limits conclusions about naturally occurring experience pools. The taxonomy’s high agreement measures consistency with an induced taxonomy, not whether its causal labels correctly explain why a trajectory succeeded. Retrieval uses benchmark-provided ground-truth skill identifiers, whose validity as the sole relevance target is not independently tested; useful related skills are counted as false positives by definition. The study reports limited evidence on variance across repeated trials, per-task statistical uncertainty, skill-generation quality, document size, prompt/context consumption during actual execution, or adversarially misleading skills. Finally, claims about reliable self-evolving agents extend beyond the tested one-shot construction and evaluation protocol, which does not measure continual skill revision, contradiction handling, deletion, or long-term library maintenance. Bottom Line: This is a useful empirical analysis for researchers studying agent memory because it shows that skills primarily stabilize procedures and introduces a credible vocabulary for their failure modes, but its causal and generality claims remain too narrow to support deployment decisions without broader models, tasks, human-coded trajectories, and end-to-end retrieval interventions.
