Problem & Motivation Knowledge graphs built by different organizations assign different identifiers, schemas, labels, and relation structures to the same real-world entities and concepts, making it difficult to consolidate information across DBpedia, Wikidata, enterprise graphs, and wiki-derived graphs. Entity alignment must identify equivalent instances, while full KG alignment additionally requires class and property correspondences. Existing embedding- and transformer-based methods can require training data or substantial computation and often provide limited explanations; lexical rule systems can be brittle, and the prior Tiered Iterative Matching (TIM) architecture requires a manually specified matcher order, runs bootstrap matchers only once, and assumes a fixed vocabulary of label relations. The practical gap is an unsupervised, explainable alignment procedure that can adapt matcher ordering to the evolving alignment and operate without predefined naming predicates. Key Idea The core insight is to treat matcher ordering as a state-dependent selection problem rather than a fixed pipeline. At each iteration, SECEA exposes the most restrictive matcher in every category that can produce at least one currently admissible match, scores each category by the coherence of its proposed set with the existing alignment and with 1-to-1/type constraints, and commits only the most coherent category's valid matches. This combines conservative within-category progression with adaptive across-category scheduling; the individual matching rules are largely extensions or reorganizations of ideas already used in TIM and traditional KG matching. Methodology SECEA begins by aligning elements with identical IRIs. It then iterates two phases: (1) a match-proposal phase that queries matcher categories from restrictive to permissive until each category yields a potentially addable match, and (2) a match-selection phase that chooses the proposal set with the lowest combined ratio of alignment violations, internal non-1-to-1 conflicts, and type mismatches, adding only valid pairs. The framework contains seven categories: unique identical-label matching; equivalent-triple matching; unique equivalent-triple matching; joint label/equivalent-triple matching; literal TF-IDF matching; instance-evidence-based class matching; and a class-constrained label matcher for instances. It dynamically identifies candidate label relations by retaining datatype properties with at least 95% unique tail values and coverage of at least 10% of entities. It maintains counts of full and partial triple equivalences as new alignments are added. Hyperparameters include label-match thresholds over possible numbers of unique labels, triple-equivalence thresholds below 20, TF-IDF candidate fractions from 0.2 to 9.8, and class-evidence ratios from 1.0 down to 0.4. The principal design decisions—dynamic category selection, injectivity/coverage-based label discovery, and strict rejection of ambiguous 1-to-1 proposals—are motivated plausibly, but the paper does not establish that the chosen 95%, 10%, 20, or 0.4 thresholds are robust across domains, nor does it isolate the value of each matcher category. Key Results On the five OAEI KG-track pairs, SECEA reports average class F-measure 0.98, compared with 0.95 for TIM and at most 0.84 for the other listed systems; it is best on four pairs and second on one. Its average property F-measure is 0.99, compared with 0.97 for TIM and FLORA, with scores from 0.95 to 1.00. For instance alignment, SECEA reaches average F-measure 0.89, above TIM's 0.88 but below DOGMA's 0.90 and FLORA's 0.94; the authors note that the OAEI instance reference mapping contains known duplicate-entity and disambiguation errors. On OpenEA-15K, SECEA obtains Hits@1 of 0.929 for EN-FR, 0.957 for EN-DE, and 0.699 for DE-W, ranking first on the first two and second on DE-W behind MIKG at 0.724. On OpenEA-100K, it obtains Hits@1 of 0.867, 0.906, and 0.600 for EN-FR, EN-DE, and DE-W, respectively, beating TIM at 0.818, 0.878, and 0.307 and ranking below MIKG on DE-W. SECEA matches only 60.8% of DE-W entities but reports 98.8% correctness among its produced matches. The comparison set includes recent neural systems and OAEI 2025 systems, although the evaluation is not fully apples-to-apples: SECEA produces only 1-to-1 matches and treats Hits@5 and MRR as equal to Hits@1, whereas embedding systems rank all candidates. Experiments use 15K and 100K entity benchmarks and OAEI graphs containing up to 210,996 instances, 700 properties, and 283 classes; reported runtimes are under 8 minutes for OpenEA and under 15 minutes for OAEI on a 48-core, 192-GB CPU virtual machine. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the state-dependent, coherence-based selection of rule-based matcher categories and automatic discovery of label relations within an explainable alignment framework; the individual matching signals, 1-to-1 filtering, triple-equivalence reasoning, and TF-IDF component are standard or closely related to TIM and prior matching systems. Rigor & Reproducibility The evaluation covers both entity alignment and class/property/instance KG alignment, uses OpenEA V1 15K and 100K datasets plus five OAEI KG pairs, and includes seven alternative matcher-selection strategies. The strategy ablation shows that the default combined-violation criterion achieves OAEI class/property/instance averages of 0.98/0.99/0.89 and OpenEA-15K/100K Hits@1 averages of 0.862/0.791, while selecting the largest proposal set drops OpenEA-100K average Hits@1 to 0.717. However, the authors explicitly omit ablations of individual matcher categories because TIM reportedly studied similar categories; this prevents attributing gains over TIM to dynamic ordering rather than implementation or preprocessing differences. No error bars, multiple runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; the deterministic algorithm is run once. The code and reproduction instructions are stated to be available at https://github.com/dice-group/SECEA, but no model weights or new dataset are released. Potential evaluation concerns include non-equivalent ranking metrics, reliance on imperfect OAEI instance gold mappings, hand-selected preprocessing such as adding an IRI relation for OAEI but not OpenEA, and no independent stress test beyond 100K entities. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a released software implementation rather than a deployed production system. * Practical: The reported implementation runs on commercially available CPU hardware and does not require GPUs, learned embeddings, or training data, although the 192-GB memory environment may exceed the resources of smaller deployments. * Efficient: The authors report under 8 minutes on OpenEA and under 15 minutes on OAEI using 48 CPU cores, but they do not provide memory measurements, asymptotic complexity, single-core results, or a controlled comparison of runtime against competing methods. * Effective: The evidence shows strong exact-alignment benchmark performance for classes and properties and competitive instance Hits@1/F-measure, but it measures benchmark correspondences rather than downstream integration, RAG, or fact-verification improvements. * Scalable: The method is tested up to 100,000 entities per KG and OAEI graphs with 210,996 instances, but claims about million- or web-scale use are not experimentally validated; the reported triple-equivalence and candidate-pair operations could become costly at 10x–100x scale. The work delivers a reusable open-source alignment tool at https://github.com/dice-group/SECEA; it does not introduce a new dataset, trained model, or formal proof technique. Strengths - The dynamic matcher-selection mechanism directly addresses a concrete weakness of TIM—manual matcher ordering—while retaining rule-level explanations for both proposed matches and selection decisions. - The framework performs well across distinct alignment targets: it improves over TIM on class alignment, property alignment, and most OpenEA entity-alignment settings, rather than optimizing only one metric or one element type. - The evaluation includes 15K and 100K OpenEA settings and reports competitive results without supervision, GPU computation, or learned parameters, making the low-resource operating point credible. - Automatic label-relation discovery removes dependence on a fixed list such as rdfs:label, which is a useful robustness improvement for heterogeneous RDF schemas. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that SECEA handles only equivalence relations and does not compute subclass or subproperty correspondences. They note that some class and property matchers require already matched instances, which can reduce performance when instance data is absent. They also identify the absence of a mechanism for removing earlier low-confidence matches when later evidence supports conflicting pairs, and propose self-correction and LLM-based matchers as future work. They acknowledge inaccuracies in the OAEI instance reference alignment and discuss their effects on measured performance. These limitations are confronted explicitly, although the discussion does not quantify their impact through targeted experiments. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not compare against a controlled TIM variant with identical preprocessing and matcher sets but randomized or alternative orders, so the gain attributable specifically to dynamic ordering is not isolated. - It omits an ablation of matcher categories and of the automatic label-relation discovery rule, leaving unclear whether the framework's performance depends primarily on one existing signal such as identical labels or triple equivalence. - The selection score is based on internal coherence with the current alignment, which can reinforce early false positives; the paper offers no adversarial, noisy, low-overlap, schema-mismatch, or initialization-sensitivity evaluation. - Runtime claims lack complexity analysis, memory profiling, scaling curves, and comparisons under matched hardware, so the assertion of million-scale scalability remains unsupported. - The OpenEA comparison uses Hits@1 for SECEA while neural systems receive ranked-candidate Hits@5 and MRR, and the paper's special treatment of unmatched entities is not evaluated with precision/recall or coverage as primary metrics. This makes headline comparisons difficult to interpret. - The method assumes 1-to-1 alignments and exact or near-exact lexical evidence, limiting applicability to many-to-one mappings, multilingual semantic equivalence, noisy literals, and ontologies whose classes lack instances. Bottom Line SECEA is worth reading as a practical and reproducible advance over fixed-order rule-based KG alignment, especially for explainable class and property matching, but its novelty and superiority claims should be moderated until component-level ablations, fairer coverage-aware metrics, and genuine large-scale robustness tests are provided.

Problem & Motivation: Temporal question answering requires both flexible interpretation of diverse temporal language and exact selection among time-indexed facts. Existing prompt-based and neuro-symbolic approaches often allow an LLM to perform the decisive interval, containment, ordering, or answer-generation step, which introduces probabilistic errors that are difficult to verify. Strict rule systems provide reproducibility but fail on non-boundary-aligned intervals, time-valued anchors, heterogeneous date formats, and paraphrased temporal operators. The target domain is zero-shot QA over structured or semi-structured temporal facts, particularly questions involving exact or inexact intervals, point-time containment, and predecessor/successor selection. Key Idea: The central insight is to make temporal reasoning an executable interface rather than a free-form generation problem: an LLM may normalize difficult language into a constrained, answer-free intent, but only a deterministic automaton can select evidence and emit the answer. The paper's substantive contribution is therefore the explicit separation between semantic uncertainty at the interface and deterministic temporal policy execution, rather than the use of finite-state notation itself. Methodology: STAIR first canonicalizes context statements into facts of the form `(subject, relation, object, start, end)`, using deterministic parsers for recognizable formats and a constrained LLM symbolic parser for other statements; malformed or temporally invalid records are rejected, and duplicate normalized facts are merged while retaining provenance. A rule-first query parser attempts to produce an executable intent. If it fails, a hard-structure detector routes cases involving non-exact intervals, time-valued anchors, unresolved date formats, or otherwise unsupported forms to an answer-free semantic adapter. The adapter produces a structured intent with a type such as `interval`, `point`, `before_anchor`, `after_anchor`, `first`, or `last`, temporal arguments, target subject/relation, anchor typing, and a policy such as `exact`, `overlap`, `immediate`, or `latest_start`; it cannot output an answer. Programmatic validation checks schema compatibility, date validity, target-key recoverability, supported operators, and answer leakage, with constrained fact or intent repair followed by revalidation. The Temporal Automaton Selector is a guarded extended finite-state machine whose stages validate facts, validate the intent, bind a subject-relation chain, apply a temporal policy, and aggregate the selected object spans. Exact intervals require matching start and end boundaries; non-exact intervals select facts with maximum positive overlap; point queries use closed-interval containment; before/after queries select the nearest predecessor or successor relative to an entity or time anchor; and first/last select the earliest/latest state. Empty or multiply distinct answer sets trigger typed failure. Only after repair and deterministic reselection fail does STAIR invoke a four-stage LLM fallback for symbolic representation, inference, checking, and final answer generation. The main design decisions—rule-first routing, answer-free semantic adaptation, and direct answer emission—are well motivated by the stated reliability goal and supported by ablations, although the paper does not fully establish that the particular policy inventory captures dataset semantics without benchmark-specific assumptions. Key Results: On TimeQA-Easy, TimeQA-Hard, TempReason-L2, and TempReason-L3, STAIR obtains average EM/F1 of 88.18/89.41 with Qwen2.5-7B, 91.01/92.18 with Qwen3-8B, 90.46/92.25 with Qwen3-14B, and 91.46/92.48 with GPT-4o-mini. Relative to the published NeSTR rows, average F1 gains are 12.71, 4.08, 3.45, and 2.78 points, respectively; EM improves by 17.08, 8.21, 5.96, and 6.26 points. STAIR improves EM in all 16 model-dataset configurations and F1 in 15, with the one F1 decrease occurring for Qwen3-14B on TimeQA-Hard, where F1 changes from 87.30 to 86.59 while EM rises from 82.20 to 84.18. Gains are largest on TempReason-L2 and L3, at 9.48 and 9.62 average F1 points over NeSTR, and smaller on TimeQA-Easy and Hard, at 1.89 and 3.08 points according to the paper's dataset-level analysis. On the Qwen2.5-7B TimeQA-Hard category analysis, STAIR improves F1 by 8.20 points for non-exact intervals, 9.28 for point-time queries, 6.93 for time-anchor-before, and 4.56 for time-anchor-after. Rule-only execution resolves 76.91% of TimeQA-Easy, 27.65% of TimeQA-Hard, 76.91% of TempReason-L2, and 91.46% of TempReason-L3. On a restricted, converted CronQuestions subset of 13,096 of the official 30,000 test examples, STAIR improves EM from 72.00 to 88.42 and F1 from 81.03 to 87.63 over NeSTR. Efficiency is favorable on easy and regular datasets: for Qwen2.5-7B, wall-clock time falls from 2.66 to 0.82 seconds on TimeQA-Easy and from 3.90 to 0.31 seconds on TempReason-L3, but TimeQA-Hard becomes slower, 3.13 to 3.61 seconds, with calls increasing from 1.00 to 2.12. These results are standard-scale benchmark experiments, not stress tests at production or 10x–100x scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper contributes a constrained answer-free semantic interface coupled to guarded deterministic temporal execution and shows that this division improves exact selection and reduces model dependence, while the underlying ingredients—symbolic parsing, programmatic execution, finite-state control, and LLM prompting—are established techniques combined for temporal QA rather than a fundamentally new reasoning formalism. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper evaluates complete test splits for four main benchmarks and reports three independent runs for STAIR, with standard deviations in the appendix; the reported run-to-run variation is small, such as average F1 standard deviations of 0.02 for Qwen2.5-7B and 0.06 for GPT-4o-mini. It includes interface ablations, executor ablations, routing coverage, category-level diagnostics, fallback rates, and an explicit failure case. On TimeQA-Hard, adding the semantic adapter raises F1 from 72.75 to 80.91 and reduces final fallback from 72.35% to 37.00%; removing max-overlap reduces F1 from 81.20 to 80.26, removing time-anchor typing reduces it to 80.19, and removing deterministic answer construction in the executor ablation reduces F1 by 4.47 points for GPT-4o-mini and 12.54 for Qwen2.5-7B. However, the primary comparison relies heavily on published NeSTR and TISER numbers, while the authors' NeSTR reproduction is described mainly as a consistency check and does not fully replace a matched rerun across all reported settings. No code, dataset release, model-weight release, or public repository URL is mentioned. The CronQuestions transfer evaluation is not a complete test-set evaluation: it excludes 14,308 unsupported examples and 2,596 type-supported examples lacking the required head annotation, and therefore measures only a converter-defined operator-supported subset. The use of LLM-assisted fact canonicalization and semantic adaptation also means that the deterministic executor's reliability depends on upstream probabilistic parsing; the paper reports adapter and fallback rates but does not provide adapter accuracy, intent-level precision/recall, calibration, confidence intervals over individual categories, or significance tests. The policy inventory and conversion procedure are closely aligned with the evaluated operators, creating a potential benchmark-interface selection effect that is not fully quantified. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile—the paper implements and evaluates a runnable QA system with a deterministic executor and LLM components. Practical: The reported experiments run on commercially available hardware, specifically an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with PyTorch, although deployment still requires access to one or more LLM backends and the paper does not describe a packaged library or service interface. Efficient: Rule-only cases substantially reduce calls and output tokens, but difficult TimeQA-Hard cases increase calls from 1.00 to 2.12 and latency from 3.13 to 3.61 seconds; no memory measurements, monetary API costs, or comparison against a fully deterministic parser are reported. Effective: The benchmark evidence shows improved EM/F1 on the tested temporal QA tasks, especially point containment and ordered before/after selection, but it does not establish correctness on broader temporal semantics, real-world noisy data, or unsupported operators. Scalable: The paper tests standard benchmark instances and a 13,096-example filtered CronQuestions subset, but provides no 10x–100x scale experiment, throughput curve, long-context evaluation, or analysis of how canonicalization and fallback costs grow with context size. The work describes a software-style system and formal execution specification, but no reusable artifact URL or release is stated. Strengths: - The parser/executor boundary is technically concrete: the adapter cannot emit answers, and the automaton exposes selected facts, activated policies, guard outcomes, and provenance for its deterministic path. - The method addresses two distinct temporal failure modes with explicit policies—maximum-overlap interval selection and nearest predecessor/successor selection—rather than treating all temporal questions as generic text generation. - The ablations isolate meaningful mechanisms: semantic adaptation produces the major TimeQA-Hard gain, deterministic answer emission materially reduces aggregation errors, and removing adjacency harms entity-anchored reasoning. - The authors report an important operational trade-off instead of claiming uniformly lower cost: STAIR is faster on structurally regular datasets but slower on the difficult TimeQA-Hard split because adaptation and repair add calls. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly states that unsupported phenomena include highly implicit event ordering, duration comparisons, negation, nested constraints, multi-hop temporal composition, and queries outside the predefined policy inventory. It acknowledges that canonicalization may fail, interval boundaries may yield multiple plausible candidates, adapter outputs may fail validation, and the final fallback sacrifices the guard-level procedural traces of the deterministic path. It also explicitly limits the CronQuestions result to the successfully converted operator-supported subset rather than the complete test set. The appendix directly documents a year-boundary/month-query failure in which the system returns Great Northern Railway instead of Westinghouse Electric Corporation for “in Feb 1908,” and proposes boundary-uncertain states as a possible extension. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not adequately quantify the reliability of the LLM-produced canonical facts and intents, even though these are upstream of every deterministic guarantee; a wrong fact or wrong policy can produce a traceable but incorrect answer. The fallback is substantial in the cases where semantic adaptation matters: it reaches 20.50% overall on TimeQA-Hard, 76.12% for time-anchor-after questions, and the paper does not report accuracy separately for deterministic, repaired, and fallback routes. The strongest baselines are not consistently rerun under identical conditions: NeSTR and TISER values are largely taken from prior work, and the four-stage fallback is modified for STAIR while NeSTR remains unmodified. The restricted CronQuestions conversion removes more than half of the official test set and is tailored to STAIR's supported forward/inverse timeline construction, so the transfer result cannot support broad cross-source generalization. The deterministic interval and closed-boundary semantics also encode assumptions about dataset annotation conventions; the documented month/year boundary error demonstrates that “deterministic” does not mean semantically correct when temporal granularity is underspecified. Finally, the paper does not test robustness to noisy extraction, overlapping concurrent states, ambiguous natural-language anchors, longer contexts, or unseen temporal operators, and it does not state whether code or prompts will be released. Bottom Line: This is a useful and empirically credible systems paper for researchers working on interpretable temporal QA, with strong benchmark gains and a well-isolated parser/executor design, but its practical and novelty claims should be discounted until the authors evaluate stronger matched baselines, quantify upstream parsing errors and route-specific accuracy, and release the implementation.

StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a \$15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling (129 ▲ )

Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, Zhangyang Atlas Wang, Kai Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces StateM, a YAML-configured, CLI-operated runtime that uses durable execution states, phase-local context, checked transitions, recovery rules, and versioned procedural practices to improve long-horizon agents without changing model weights. - Why it's important: Long-running agents can possess the capabilities needed for individual steps yet fail the completed task because they lose state, skip required procedures, or terminate before producing verifiable results; improving the harness may therefore be cheaper than scaling the model. - How it does it: StateM externalizes workflow state into a shared runbook and gates phase transitions with persistence hooks, executable or semantic checks, recovery paths, and stop-hook controls while leaving the agent’s open-ended reasoning loop intact. - The good: On Terminal-Bench 2.1, GPT-5.5 xhigh rises from an 83.1% public reference to 92.1%, while a frozen GPT-5.5-developed profile reaches 95.28% raw accuracy with GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh across 424 of 445 trials. - The missing: The paper does not isolate the generic StateM runtime from the heavily benchmark-adapted runbook and lacks component-level ablations showing whether states, checks, hooks, stop controls, or accumulated practices cause the gains. - Read it or not: Agent-runtime and evaluation researchers should read it for its concrete transfer hierarchy and cost analysis, but should treat the headline leaderboard result as preliminary because it is an unmerged, pre-adjudication public submission with possible reward-hacking cases.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses reliability in long-horizon command-line and workflow agents, where a model may solve local subtasks but fail the overall job because mutable state becomes ambiguous, plans and completion criteria are diluted by long tool traces, required procedures are not reactivated across runs, or the agent stops before independently verifiable completion. The affected domains include software engineering, service deployment, data and business workflows, and other tool-mediated tasks with irreversible side effects or multiple dependent phases. Existing general-purpose CLI agents typically expose plans, checklists, memories, and hooks as fragmented or advisory controls, while conventional graph or finite-state orchestrators can enforce transitions but may decompose reasoning into externally authored nodes and reduce agent autonomy. The paper targets the gap between these regimes: a control layer that is persistent and enforceable at consequential phase boundaries, yet remains visible and editable to both the agent and the human user. Key Idea The central insight is to treat a coarse workflow state as both a refreshed context boundary and an enforceable contract boundary. Entering a state reactivates phase-relevant instructions and durable progress; leaving it requires checks, evidence, or approval before the runtime commits the transition. This design also turns the runbook into procedural memory: selected postmortem lessons become versioned prompts, checks, routing rules, or recovery procedures that can be reapplied on later executions. The paper’s broader claim is that useful transfer is hierarchical: exact procedural profiles can transfer between nearby model versions, while only runtime structure and harness-development principles may transfer across providers or task families. Methodology StateM defines a runbook as a directed state machine B = (S, s0, ST, E, Φ), where states represent coarse phases, edges define permitted transitions, and Φ specifies prompts, entry and exit hooks, transfer checks, and local artifacts. A typical pipeline contains planning, execution, verification, repair, and terminal handoff states. On entry, an in_hook loads durable context, progress records, and phase-specific instructions. The agent performs open-ended tool use within the state, then an out_hook persists progress and receipts. A before_transfer block verifies checklists, predicates, manual approvals, or LLM reviews before a goto operation can commit the next state. The runtime validates the edge, evaluates checks, persists state, evaluates edge guards and hooks, commits the target state, logs the transition, and runs the target in_hook; failures leave the run in the source state and can route it to repair. The system stores run identifiers, current state, transition history, check outcomes, timestamps, and evidence references, allowing restart and context refresh from durable control state. A host stop hook blocks premature termination unless the run is terminal or explicitly externally blocked. The profile-development loop executes the current harness, analyzes failures, abstracts reusable lessons, proposes runbook changes, tests for regressions, and freezes profiles before designated evaluation. Critical design decisions include retaining a single general-purpose agent rather than decomposing it into node-local calls, making the runbook jointly inspectable and editable, and activating controls from visible task semantics rather than benchmark identifiers. These choices are conceptually motivated, but the experiments do not separately quantify their individual effects. The system distinguishes independently executable predicates and commands from manual, checklist, message, or LLM-review attestations; the latter remain fallible and are not treated as correctness proofs. Key Results The main evaluation uses Terminal-Bench 2.1, comprising 89 tasks and five trials per task, for 445 trials. With GPT-5.5 xhigh, StateM achieves 92.1% versus an 83.1% public GPT-5.5 Codex reference, a +9.0-point difference, and solves 88 of 89 tasks at least once across five trials. With GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh, the frozen GPT-5.5-developed profile records 424/445 = 95.28% raw accuracy and at least one success on every task, versus an 84.9% public reference. However, the submission is not merged into the leaderboard, and the authors report that excluding four rewarded trajectories reduces the result to 94.38%, while excluding nine trajectories flagged for possible reward hacking reduces it to 93.26%. GPT-5.6 Luna increases from a 76.7% reference to 85.4% with the frozen profile. Exact frozen transfer fails across providers: DeepSeek-V4-Flash falls from an 82.7% baseline to 82.0% with the unmodified GPT-derived profile. After provider-specific adaptation costing $37.02, DeepSeek reaches 392/445 = 88.09% under standard timeouts and 392/440 = 89.09% on an 88-task common core. Evaluating the remaining latency-sensitive task under an extended timeout produces a descriptive 395/445 = 88.76% aggregate, not a standard-condition score. The final DeepSeek evaluation costs $15.20 in realized API charges, and adaptation plus evaluation costs $52.22, compared with a reported $574.68 model cost for a GPT-5.6 Sol max public submission; these cost comparisons use different providers, harnesses, evaluation artifacts, and in some cases different scoring conditions. On BusinessBench, the first frozen held-out evaluation over six treated families improves equal-family macro accuracy from 84.67% to 85.22% (+0.55) and instance-weighted micro accuracy from 84.44% to 85.78% (+1.34). The mechanism-matched Budget Approval and Machine Operating subgroup improves from 71.91% to 81.94% (+10.04), while RefactorBench declines by 2.78 points and WooCommerce Stock declines by 3.70 points. Later post-evaluation refinements improve selected reruns, but those results are explicitly not untouched held-out evidence. The paper also reports one 22-hour profile-development run that retained durable control state through context refresh and stop-hook continuation, although terminal-output accumulation caused slowdown. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The paper’s genuine contribution is the specific agent-native integration of phase-level context refresh, checked transition contracts, shared human/agent runbook editing, and failure-driven procedural-memory updates; finite-state execution, persistent workflow state, hooks, recovery, harness adaptation, and benchmark-specific prompt engineering are individually established ideas, and the authors explicitly position StateM as a combination rather than a new primitive. The empirical novelty lies in the reported hierarchy of fixed-model improvement, frozen cross-generation transfer, adapted cross-provider transfer, and task-family generalization, although the strength of that finding depends on the evaluation controls and benchmark-adapted profiles. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides explicit evaluation regimes, task counts, trial counts, transfer boundaries, cost accounting, profile-freezing rules, and a useful distinction between raw, adjudicated, standard-timeout, common-core, and extended-timeout results. It states that routing avoids hidden tests, verifier implementations, task hashes, public solutions, answer artifacts, and manually enumerated task identifiers. It reports no component ablations, multiple-seed analysis, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or controlled experiments that compare the full system against matched variants with only state persistence, only checks, only prompts, only stop hooks, or only runbook practices. The GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 reference scores are reproduced public results rather than newly rerun, agent-version-matched A/B controls, and the key 95.28% result is a public pre-adjudication submission whose pull request remains open; the authors themselves disclose possible reward hacking and four or nine questionable trajectories depending on the scoring policy. Terminal-Bench profile development is explicitly benchmark-adapted, so the large gains should not be interpreted as evidence that the generic runtime alone generalizes. BusinessBench uses one stochastic trajectory per arm and excludes the 72-instance Attendance-Payroll family from efficacy aggregates through abstention, while later refinements use evaluation feedback and therefore cannot support the untouched generalization claim. Core code and several runtime cases are reported as open source at GitHub, but the paper does not state an exact repository URL; availability of complete runbooks, all traces, evaluation scripts, model configurations, and model weights is not stated. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper builds and evaluates a runtime/tool, while its conclusions are primarily empirical. Practical: StateM is implemented as a YAML and CLI runtime and was run on a 2025 MacBook Pro with an M4 chip and on an AWS m7i.4xlarge instance, so it can run on commercially available hardware, subject to the host environment, model-provider access, sandbox, and tool requirements. Efficient: The runtime overhead is not quantified, but the reported DeepSeek final evaluation costs $15.20 and the full adaptation-plus-evaluation campaign costs $52.22; these figures include neither a complete accounting of engineering labor nor a matched runtime-overhead comparison against alternative harnesses, and the GPT comparison uses a separately reported submission cost. Effective: Evidence supports substantial gains on the authors’ Terminal-Bench setup and concentrated gains on mechanism-matched BusinessBench families, but it does not establish that the generic runtime solves long-horizon reliability independently of benchmark-specific runbook content, and negative transfer occurs on at least RefactorBench and WooCommerce Stock. Scalable: The system survives one reported 22-hour development run and 445-trial benchmark submissions, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger task suites, longer-lived production workloads, many concurrent runs, larger runbooks, or substantially more complex state graphs; scalability beyond the tested scale remains a claim. The work delivers a software artifact consisting of the StateM runtime and runtime cases, plus YAML runbook examples and benchmark-specific control profiles; it does not deliver a new trained model or a formal proof of correctness. Security and operational concerns remain host responsibilities: hooks execute with surrounding host permissions, YAML editability is not itself an authorization boundary, and arbitrary external side effects are not transactionally rolled back. Strengths - The runtime cleanly separates reusable execution semantics from workflow-specific control profiles, which prevents the headline benchmark gains from being conceptually conflated with the generic state-machine mechanism. - The transfer protocol is more informative than a single in-domain score: it tests fixed-model lift, frozen transfer across GPT generations, failed exact transfer across providers, inexpensive provider adaptation, and held-out task-family generalization. - The paper reports unfavorable evidence rather than only aggregate wins: frozen transfer to DeepSeek drops performance, and initial profiles produce negative transfer on RefactorBench and WooCommerce Stock; the subsequent analysis links these failures to incorrect control boundaries. - The authors disclose important evaluation caveats, including the unmerged leaderboard status, possible reward-hacking trajectories, pre-adjudication scoring, extended-timeout aggregation, and the distinction between standard-timeout and descriptive results. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that StateM provides control points rather than a correctness oracle; semantic checks, receipts, and LLM reviews remain fallible; it cannot recover unpersisted work, hidden context, or arbitrary external side effects; and hook safety, sandboxing, permissions, idempotence, and compensation remain host responsibilities. They acknowledge that static runbooks do not dominate every model, task, provider, or benchmark; exact profiles may fail across providers; concrete controls transfer locally; one universal workflow is inappropriate; BusinessBench aggregate gains are modest; and later refinements are post-evaluation diagnostics rather than untouched evidence. They also explicitly identify evaluator-induced practices, ambiguous benchmark specifications, incorrect abstraction of failure lessons, and the possibility of storing the wrong lesson as procedural memory. The paper limits its scope to single-agent control flows and leaves multi-agent isolation and coordination for future work. These limitations are generally confronted directly, although their implications for the headline benchmark claims remain understated by the surrounding performance framing. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central causal attribution is unresolved: the reported Terminal-Bench gains combine the runtime with a manually guided, agent-generated, benchmark-adapted control profile, so the experiments do not establish how much comes from durable states and transition semantics versus additional prompts, task-specific checks, domain knowledge, stop persistence, or ordinary iterative engineering. - There is no matched ablation or factorial study for the principal mechanisms, nor a baseline using an equally developed conventional checklist, prompt-only harness, LangGraph-style controller, or independently authored state machine. - The reference comparisons are not consistently controlled for agent version, provider, timeout, scoring protocol, evaluation date, or realized cost; the cost frontier is therefore suggestive rather than a clean economic comparison. - The 95.28% result is particularly fragile as evidence of practical reliability: it is raw and pre-adjudication, has nine potentially reward-hacked trajectories under the broadest disclosed concern, and five-trial coverage does not estimate single-run reliability. Per-task confidence intervals or a task-stratified analysis are absent. - BusinessBench generalization is narrow because profiles are developed separately by family, one family is excluded through abstention, each arm receives one stochastic trajectory per instance, and the strongest subgroup result is selected around mechanism-matched families; the aggregate held-out gain is only 0.55 macro points. - The adaptation process and human involvement are not fully costed or operationally specified. The reported $52.22 counts recorded DeepSeek API charges, but not the human design effort, Codex-plan cost, infrastructure, or the opportunity cost of repeated profile engineering. - Security, authorization, multi-user concurrency, runbook poisoning, malicious or incorrect agent edits, hook isolation, and failure recovery under partial external side effects are described as deployment responsibilities but not evaluated. Bottom Line This is a useful systems paper and a credible demonstration that carefully engineered execution controls can outperform model upgrades on selected agent benchmarks, but practitioners should read it for the runtime design and transfer methodology—not accept the 95.3% headline as isolated evidence that StateM itself, rather than benchmark-specific harness optimization, delivers the gain.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses evaluation of LLM agents that must understand a machine-learning problem description, manipulate heterogeneous data, and produce executable training and prediction code. This matters to organizations and researchers deploying ML automation for users who describe tasks in languages other than English. Existing end-to-end ML-code benchmarks such as MLE-Bench, DA-Code, and Weco-Kaggle use English descriptions, while multilingual code benchmarks mostly evaluate snippets or programming exercises. The paper also targets two validity problems: benchmark-task leakage into model training data and implementation leakage caused by allowing preprocessing to access both training and validation data. The stated gap is therefore an evaluation setting that jointly tests multilingual task comprehension, executable full-pipeline generation, leakage resistance, and reproducible isolated execution. Key Idea The central insight is to treat cross-lingual ML-pipeline generation as a benchmark-infrastructure problem rather than merely a prompt-translation problem: preserve the same underlying competition and executable grader across languages, while separating training from prediction through a modular API and reducing memorization through private competitions and runtime access controls. This makes language the principal manipulated factor, although the benchmark still contains substantial task and translation confounds. Methodology ML²B starts from Code4ML 2.0 and selects 22 eligible post-2020 competitions with reproducible metadata, public data, documented metrics, and tabular prediction formats; it adds three public 2025 competitions and ten closed competitions without public solution code or forum discussions, yielding 35 tasks. The benchmark covers tabular, text, and image data across nine domains, but the main experiments use a chosen subset of 15 competitions: five public and ten private. Domain labels, task descriptions, data cards, metrics, and schemas are translated from English into Arabic, Belarusian, Chinese, French, Italian, Japanese, Kazakh, Polish, Romanian, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, and Ukrainian using GPT-4o, followed by single-annotator bilingual validation. Agents generate a Python submission in either a monolithic `train_and_predict` format or a modular `train`, `prepare_val`, and `predict` format. The grader AST-recompiles submissions, loads data through a controlled DataLoader, executes the required functions, and computes the competition metric in a network-isolated container; the generation runtime retains internet access, but the grader blocks Kaggle and GitHub while allowing selected ML infrastructure. Static analysis checks possible preprocessing leakage. The experiments run GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-OSS-120b, and Gemini-2.5-Flash with AIDE, plus GPT-OSS-120b with a modified ReAct agent, three runs per task-language condition and a three-hour limit. Performance is normalized against both a manually developed Gemini-3-Pro-assisted baseline and AutoGluon using an error ratio, where lower than one is better; the paper aggregates ratios with standard and weighted areas under a performance profile. Critical design choices are the private-competition split, modular API, and normalized cross-task metric. The paper gives reasonable motivations for each, but does not fully establish that private competitions are absent from model pretraining, that the random split reflects realistic deployment, or that the custom weighted AUP is preferable to simpler hierarchical statistical analyses. Key Results The main evaluation comprises 2,520 runs across 15 competitions, 14 languages, four model-framework configurations, and three repetitions. Relative to the LLM-assisted baseline, GPT-4.1-mini with AIDE obtains the highest average near-baseline-weighted AUP, 0.768 ± 0.112, but only a 61% pass rate. Gemini-2.5-Flash with AIDE obtains AUP 0.732 ± 0.091 and the highest average pass rate, 76%. GPT-OSS-120b with AIDE obtains AUP 0.630 ± 0.083 and an 81% pass rate, while GPT-OSS-120b with ReAct obtains AUP 0.705 ± 0.081 and a 76% pass rate. Results are similar in ranking under AutoGluon normalization, although Gemini's AUP rises to 0.775 and GPT-4.1-mini's falls to 0.736. Language effects are not monotonic by resource level: GPT-4.1-mini's AUP ranges from 0.622 for Ukrainian to 0.867 for Polish and Kazakh, while GPT-OSS AIDE ranges from 0.533 for Italian to 0.711 for Polish and Ukrainian. The authors report that feature count correlates with cross-lingual variance at ρ=0.50, p=0.055, and domain-specific-term count at ρ=0.44, p=0.100, based on only 15 competitions; description length is essentially uncorrelated, ρ=0.04, p=0.874. The main failure categories are execution errors, data handling and preprocessing inconsistencies, signature violations, global dependencies, and environment/API incompatibilities. Static leakage analysis flags fewer than 10% of modular submissions, with 4% remaining after reported false positives are removed, although the authors acknowledge residual leakage. The structured prompt comparison on ten shared competitions improves performance on five and produces 3/3 pass rates on all tasks, whereas the obfuscated format fails on five; this comparison uses DeepSeek-Reasoner and is not a controlled ablation of only prompt structure. Token usage for ReAct averages 475,158 total tokens per experiment, with 448,755 input and 26,402 output tokens; reported costs range from $6.36 to $38.48 per configuration run. A preliminary Qwen2.5-72B evaluation fails on 5 of 9 task-language pairs and is not comparable because it uses only a one-hour budget and three competitions. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the benchmark's combination of multilingual end-to-end ML tasks, private competitions, modular leakage-resistant grading, and isolated execution is a substantive evaluation artifact, while the empirical finding that task characteristics can dominate language-resource categories is potentially new in this setting; the agent frameworks, LLMs, AutoGluon baseline, AST transformation, Docker isolation, and performance-profile aggregation are largely existing techniques adapted and combined for this benchmark. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports three runs per condition, standard deviations for aggregate AUP values, a reproducible AutoGluon reference, failure-category analysis, translation back-translation scores, and agreement statistics. It reports 95% confidence intervals for BLEU and Gwet's AC1 on a 15-competition subset, with meaning-preservation AC1 above 0.80 for every language, but nativeness agreement is low for Japanese (0.308), Kazakh (0.359), Chinese (0.450), Ukrainian (0.538), and Romanian (0.560). The benchmark, baselines, and evaluation infrastructure are stated to be open-sourced at https://github.com/enaix/ml2b. Important concerns remain: one annotator validates each language's translations; private status is inferred from limited web indexability rather than verified against model pretraining corpora; the primary results use only 15 of 35 competitions; AutoGluon fails on two tasks; the LLM-assisted baseline is not independently reproducible in the same sense as AutoGluon; no per-task confidence intervals, seed-level significance tests, or corrected model/language comparisons are reported; and the custom AUP weighting, particularly its near-τ=1 singular behavior, receives no comparison with standard aggregate metrics or hierarchical alternatives. The prompt-format study changes from MLE-Bench's obfuscated representation to ML²B's structured task representation and therefore does not isolate all possible format and task-construction effects. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS. - Practical: The benchmark runs on commercially available hardware, specifically a workstation with 64 GB RAM and one RTX 2080 Ti GPU with 12 GB VRAM, although several model calls require external API or hosted-model access. - Efficient: Execution is expensive for routine regression testing: each run has a three-hour limit, a full four-configuration evaluation represents 7,560 sequential compute hours, and reported average run costs range from $6.36 to $38.48; AutoGluon exceeds GPU memory on two of 15 chosen competitions. - Effective: The isolated grader measures whether generated code executes and achieves the competition metric relative to baselines, directly testing pipeline-generation reliability, but it uses a local 80/20 random validation split rather than leaderboard generalization or deployment outcomes. - Scalable: The paper demonstrates 2,520 runs but does not test 10×–100× larger task, language, model, or concurrency scales; it claims parallel execution can reduce wall-clock duration, but does not evaluate infrastructure behavior at that scale. The work delivers a reusable benchmark dataset, Docker-based runtime and grader, baselines, prompt templates, and analysis code through the stated GitHub repository; it does not deliver a new LLM or pipeline-generation algorithm. Strengths - The benchmark targets a meaningful intersection—multilingual natural-language understanding, executable ML engineering, and leakage-resistant evaluation—that existing snippet-level and English-only benchmarks do not cover. - The ten competitions without public solution code and the blocked Kaggle/GitHub grader address a concrete source of benchmark contamination, while the paper explicitly acknowledges that private status does not prove absence from pretraining. - The modular `train`/`prepare_val`/`predict` interface gives the grader a concrete mechanism for reducing preprocessing leakage, and the failure analysis distinguishes false-positive static detections from the remaining 4% of potentially actionable cases. - The quality–reliability trade-off is a useful empirical diagnostic: GPT-4.1-mini leads on AUP but has the lowest pass rate, whereas GPT-OSS achieves a higher pass rate with lower normalized quality. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that modular submissions may still permit residual data access if agents perform late-stage training, so the API does not eliminate leakage. They acknowledge that the exploratory task-characteristic correlations have low statistical power because N=15. They also acknowledge that language selection depends on qualified annotator availability, that domain-level translation BLEU intervals are wide, and that the Qwen evaluation is preliminary and uses a shorter one-hour budget; a matched full evaluation is deferred to future work. These limitations are discussed directly, although their implications for benchmark validity and language comparisons remain underdeveloped. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper claims ML²B contains 35 competitions and 490 task-language pairs, but the principal experiments evaluate only 15 competitions, heavily weighting ten private tasks and leaving the public 25-task set largely untested; this limits evidence for the benchmark-wide conclusions. - The language comparison is confounded by translation quality, tokenization, prompt length, cultural/domain terminology, and potentially different task interpretations. Single-annotator validation and low nativeness agreement for several languages weaken the claim that observed differences reflect model multilingual competence. - The use of a fixed random 80/20 validation split can produce optimistic or unstable estimates for grouped, temporal, image, and competition-specific data, and the paper does not establish that this split matches the original competition's test distribution. - The primary baseline is produced through iterative prompting of Gemini 3 Pro and manual implementation, but its prompts, code-development protocol, model snapshot, and effort budget are not specified sufficiently for independent replication; the benchmark therefore mixes a reproducible AutoGluon comparison with a less reproducible human/LLM reference. - The statistical analysis treats 15 competitions as independent observations despite repeated languages, models, and runs, and does not report mixed-effects models, multiple-comparison corrections for the many language-by-task observations, or uncertainty on the headline language rankings. The reported ANOVA section is also internally difficult to interpret: it gives very small F statistics with p<0.001 and then says Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests find no significant differences. - The benchmark permits full internet access during generation, and only the grader blocks Kaggle and GitHub. This is realistic for some agents but leaves open retrieval from mirrors, search snippets, package metadata, or other sources; the private-task contamination claim is therefore probabilistic rather than demonstrated. - The conclusion that instruction-following, rather than language comprehension, is the primary bottleneck is plausible from failure examples but is not isolated by controlled experiments that provide equivalent code constraints in English and translated prompts or independently measure comprehension. Bottom Line ML²B is a useful and reasonably well-engineered benchmark contribution for multilingual ML-agent evaluation, but its empirical conclusions should be treated as exploratory until the authors expand beyond 15 tasks, control translation and validation-split confounds, and apply stronger statistical comparisons.

Bobo Li, Hao Fei, Tianjie Ju, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 20 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OmniScientist, an end-to-end system that uses raw multimodal scientific data to generate hypotheses, execute computational experiments, verify results, and compile evidence-grounded manuscripts. - Why it's important: Existing AI-scientist systems usually operate on text, labels, code, or precomputed features, which can remove spatial, temporal, cross-channel, and procedural evidence needed for discovery. - How it does it: A modality-aware perception layer feeds three ReAct agents for ideation, experimentation, and writeup, while deterministic code checks enforce provenance, leakage controls, multiple-comparison accounting, anti-HARKing constraints, and claim traceability. - The good: Across 36 public-dataset cases, the system produced manuscripts in all cases, and in five paired comparisons the perception-enabled variant won 85% of head-to-head judgments, with a reported mean overall gain of 1.39 points. - The missing: The central perception ablation covers only five paired cases and uses a relatively weak blind interface, while the paper does not establish scientific validity through expert assessment, independent replication, or comparison with strong multimodal AI-scientist baselines. - Read it or not: AI-for-science and agent-systems researchers should read it for its provenance-gated orchestration design, but practitioners should treat the broad discovery and domain-agnosticism claims as preliminary rather than validated deployment evidence.

Problem & Motivation: Scientific AI systems increasingly automate idea generation, coding, experimentation, and manuscript drafting, but commonly expose scientific data through text, scalar features, labels, or summaries selected before the agent begins reasoning. This interface can erase local morphology in images, temporal order in trajectories and signals, cross-channel relations in waveforms, and procedural information in experiments. The resulting problem affects researchers seeking automated discovery across disciplines: an agent may complete the visible research workflow while being unable to notice the observations that should determine the research question. The paper targets the gap between workflow completeness and evidence completeness, while also addressing risks introduced by open-ended autonomous research, including leakage, multiple testing, post-hoc hypothesis formation, unsupported claims, and fabricated or untraceable numbers. Key Idea: The core insight is to make raw-evidence perception a lifecycle-wide input rather than a local visualization step, and to surround open-ended language-model reasoning with deterministic stage gates. The system allows observations to influence ideation, experimental design, result inspection, and manuscript claims; the execution record then becomes the source of truth against which results and prose are checked. The conceptual contribution is therefore less a new perception model than a control architecture that couples modality-native observation with provenance-constrained autonomous research. Methodology: Each task is specified by a dataset, scientific subject, target property, raw-data member list, and modality information. The perception layer classifies inputs into perceptual, symbolic, quantitative-statistical, or procedural evidence and exposes modality-specific tools: visual readers such as `look_at_image`, `look_at_signal`, `look_at_3d`, and `look_at_audio`, plus native analyzers for signals, audio, 3-D data, trajectories, videos, and traces. Numeric/native analysis is preferred for efficiency, with visual inspection invoked under an adaptive budget. The ideation agent uses a ReAct loop to inventory data, inspect representative records, issue at least three focused literature searches through OpenAlex/Crossref, generate at least five candidate projects, estimate novelty and statistical power, and select a computational, falsifiable idea. A code-enforced idea check requires fields including the question, hypothesis, protocol, falsification criterion, minimal claim, novelty evidence, claim scope, effective sample, leakage analysis, and visual audit. The experiment agent iteratively generates code in a controlled `run_python` environment, loads real data, executes a battery containing a primary test, baseline, ablation, mechanism analysis, breakdown, sensitivity analysis, and group/leakage evaluation where applicable, and stores stdout, data, figures, configurations, and attempted tests in an execution record. Its rigour check requires successful execution, real-data access, number provenance, at least 60% output coverage for reported numbers, accounting for all attempted tests, multiple-comparison correction, an independence/circularity assessment, and a supported headline analysis; weak analyses are demoted and null results can trigger re-ideation. The writeup agent drafts field-specific paper structures from slices of the execution record, and a claim check matches reported numbers and claims to recorded outputs and analyses. These design choices are operationally clear, but their scientific justification is mostly procedural: the paper does not compare alternative perception budgets, gate definitions, prompt policies, or execution environments in a controlled way. Key Results: The evaluation uses 36 real, publicly downloadable datasets spanning five discipline families, four evidence families, and modalities including images, signals, audio, video, 3-D structures, trajectories, tables, formulae, sequences, fields, and graphs; dataset sizes range from 12 equations to a knowledge graph with 5,088,434 edges. With Claude Sonnet 5 as the reasoning backbone, all 36 runs produced compiled manuscripts, 35 of 36 exited through the rigour check, and the papers received a reported mean composite score of 6.3/10 from two cross-family judges across novelty, soundness, clarity, significance, reproducibility, multimodal grounding, and factual accuracy. The all-case dimension means were 6.3 novelty, 7.0 soundness, 7.0 clarity, 6.3 significance, 6.1 reproducibility, 5.1 multimodal grounding, and 7.7 factual accuracy. The paper reports 16 supported, 17 mixed, 2 refuted, and 1 incomplete system verdicts. In the five paired perception-versus-blind cases, the full system won 85% of head-to-head comparisons; macro-average gains were +1.14 novelty, +0.75 soundness, +0.72 clarity, +1.31 significance, +1.03 reproducibility, +1.53 multimodal grounding, +0.72 factual accuracy, and +1.39 overall. The largest case-level gains occurred for plant phenotyping multimodal grounding (+4.0) and mechanical CAD clarity (+3.5), while cardiology used a weaker vision-off comparison and showed a multimodal-grounding decrease of −1.7. Component ablations on the seismology case report composite degradation from 6.9 to 5.7 without prior-art search, from 6.9 to 6.3 without anti-fabrication enforcement, and from 6.9 to 6.3 with a single-pass rather than iterative agentic loop; removing the novelty check reduced judged novelty from 6 to 5. Representative findings include detection of coherent transients in 163/750 noise-labelled STEAD traces (21.7%, 95% CI [18.8, 24.9]), a paediatric-radiograph patchiness classifier reaching held-out AUC 0.851 versus 0.634 for raw pixels, and leave-one-family-out materials RMSE reported as 3.1–7.0 times higher than random k-fold estimates. Backbone coverage is uneven: Sonnet completed 36/36 cases with a reported mean of 6.5 in Table 4, whereas GPT-5.6 completed 9/10, GLM-5.2 17/18, Kimi 6/9, Qwen3.5-122B 30/34, Qwen3.5-27B 32/36, Qwen3.5-9B 18/32, Gemma-4-31B 32/36, and Gemma-4-26B 25/34. These results are promising for workflow automation, but the strongest claims concern manuscript quality and process compliance, not independently confirmed scientific discoveries. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW FORMULATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the integration of raw multimodal perception throughout autonomous research with code-enforced provenance and anti-HARKing gates; the underlying ReAct loops, multi-agent role separation, literature retrieval, code execution, visual-language perception, and manuscript templating are established techniques combined in a broader setting. The 36-case suite functions as an evaluation suite rather than a clearly standardized benchmark, and the individual scientific findings are generated demonstrations rather than validated domain contributions. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides unusually explicit operational checks, publishes Algorithms 1–2, lists all gate conditions, reports 115 rejected finalize attempts across 36 runs, records 67 demoted analyses, and exposes stage prompts in the appendix. It reports Krippendorff's alpha of 0.66 for the two judges, self-preference bias of 0, and score-versus-length correlation of 0.16. The software and skill repository is listed at https://github.com/Omni-Scientist/OmniScientist, and a project page is listed at https://omni-scientist.github.io; the paper does not clearly state whether all execution traces, generated manuscripts, model configurations, or exact evaluation data are released. Ablations exist for perception and several control components, but the main causal ablation is limited to five blind pairs, with one additional vision-off pair noted in the supplementary table. The blind baseline receives only precomputed scalar features, so it tests the value of a deliberately information-reducing interface rather than superiority over a strong multimodal agent or a carefully matched feature-processing system. The evaluation relies on two model judges scoring generated manuscripts, with failed backbone runs excluded from per-backbone means; this creates selection effects and leaves scientific correctness only indirectly measured. The paper also contains an internal reporting inconsistency: the abstract and Table 3 give a Sonnet overall score of 6.3, while Table 4 reports 6.5 for Sonnet on the 36-case suite. The deterministic provenance check verifies that numbers appear in stdout, but this does not establish that the analyses are scientifically appropriate, that the source datasets are representative, or that the generated hypotheses are genuinely novel. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — the paper evaluates a built software system through experiments and reports run-level execution statistics. * Practical: The system runs on commercially accessible infrastructure, including API-accessed closed models and locally served open-weight models; reported complete-run costs range from $0.03 to $4.34 per paper, with wall-clock times from 12 to 30 minutes for the listed backbones. * Efficient: The cost is low for offline exploratory analysis but the reference Sonnet configuration uses approximately 98k input and 191k output tokens per paper, averages 31.8 Python executions, and requires 29 minutes; no comparison against a conventional analyst workflow or a strong multimodal baseline establishes relative efficiency. * Effective: The system reliably produces traceable manuscripts and often finds plausible dataset patterns, but the evidence primarily measures judged paper quality, process completion, and proxy findings rather than independent expert-confirmed scientific discoveries or real-world decisions. * Scalable: The suite includes a graph with roughly 5 million edges and datasets up to 21,263 records, but the agent uses bounded budgets, 150-second Python timeouts, and at most two ideation fallbacks; no 10×–100× stress test demonstrates scaling in data volume, modality complexity, number of experiments, or agent workload. The work delivers a software artifact, including a public repository and described JSON records, Markdown summaries, replayable execution traces, and compiled PDF reports. It does not deliver a new foundation model, a validated scientific dataset benchmark with fixed tasks and ground-truth outcomes, or a reusable formal proof technique. Strengths: - The execution-record design provides a concrete source of truth connecting data I/O, stdout, figures, attempted tests, reported numbers, and manuscript claims; this addresses a real failure mode in autonomous research more directly than prompt-only self-critique. - The perception ablation demonstrates a meaningful mechanism-level difference: direct observation changes the research question and analysis trajectory, not merely the prose or final score, across five qualitatively distinct modalities. - The system handles negative and mixed outcomes explicitly: 19 of 36 runs are classified as mixed or refuted, and 67 analyses are demoted rather than automatically promoted into the final paper. - The cross-domain specification mechanism is a useful systems abstraction: the paper reports adding disciplines through task specification files without modifying the core engine, while supporting native readers rather than forcing every modality through images. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Not stated as a dedicated limitations section in the provided paper text. The authors do acknowledge bounded literature search, the inability to establish absolute novelty, the requirement that experiments be computational rather than physical, dependence on the reasoning backbone, and the fact that perception is not equally useful for all evidence families. They also report one incomplete run, mixed and refuted outcomes, weaker performance from smaller backbones, and the limited scope of the 36-case demonstration suite, but they do not substantially discuss external scientific validation, domain-expert review, or the limitations of the blind baseline. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The principal gap is validation of scientific discovery rather than manuscript production. The 36 tasks are selected by the authors, each supplies a broad open request, and the resulting papers are judged by two model-based reviewers; there is no blinded assessment by independent domain scientists, replication by separate researchers, prospective validation on new datasets, or comparison against human-assisted and strong multimodal agent baselines. The five-case blind ablation is small and asymmetric: the blind system is deprived of raw structural information, making the result expected in cases deliberately chosen because raw structure matters. The system's novelty screening depends on three to eight API searches and cannot verify priority, yet novelty scores remain a central outcome. The paper does not provide per-case seeds, stochastic variability, confidence intervals for judge scores, or statistical tests for the perception win rate and score gains. Group-disjoint evaluation is mandated in the prompt, but the paper does not document whether it was correctly performed for every dataset with station, subject, patient, site, recording, or other grouping identifiers. The provenance gate ensures textual traceability but does not prevent an incorrect algorithm, inappropriate statistical model, biased dataset, or common-source artifact from producing a fully traceable claim. The claimed discipline agnosticism is also only partially demonstrated: 28 of 36 cases are perceptual, most tasks are retrospective analyses of established public datasets, and no physical experiments or closed-loop laboratory interventions are evaluated. Finally, the paper is an arXiv preprint dated 13 August 2026, so the reported results should be treated as pre-peer-review and the future-dated model and citation ecosystem warrants independent verification. Bottom Line: This is a useful and technically concrete systems paper for researchers building auditable AI-scientist pipelines, but its evidence supports improved multimodal workflow coverage and claim bookkeeping—not yet broadly capable, independently validated scientific discovery.

MOSS-VL Technical Report (38 ▲ )

Pengyu Wang, Chenkun Tan, Shaojun Zhou, Qirui Zhou, Yanxin Chen, Xingyang He, Huazheng Zeng, Jijun Cheng, Chenghao Wang, Xiaomeng Qian, Pengfei Wang, Zhan Huang, Shanqing Gao, Wei Huang, Longjun Cao, Wu Ran, Jie Liu, Changtai Zhu, Hongkai Wang, Yixian Tian, Chenghao Liu, Zhen Ye, Xinghao Wang, Botian Jiang, Guoguo Feng, Zhaoye Fei, Ruixiao Li, Mingshu Chen, Yang Gao, Qinyuan Cheng, Shimin Li, Xipeng Qiu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an open 11.3B-parameter vision-language model family with gated cross-attention, streaming interaction training, and released real-time inference infrastructure for video assistants. - Why it's important: Live assistants must decide when to speak while video is still arriving, maintain low latency as visual history grows, and potentially revise responses when new evidence appears. - How it does it: It keeps visual patch tokens outside the autoregressive text sequence, appends new frames to a cross-attention cache, and trains explicit silence/response state tokens using synthesized, timestamped interaction streams. - The good: MOSS-VL-Realtime achieves the best average on OVO-Bench (70.2), OmniMMI (32.7), and ProactiveVideoQA (47.2), and leads all three reported proactive-response subsets, including 66.0 versus 37.5 on OmniMMI Proactive Alerting. - The missing: The defining L5 capability—perceiving while generating, revising, or interrupting a reply as evidence changes—is demonstrated only through qualitative demos, with no quantitative benchmark, ablation, or systematic measurement of revision quality. - Read it or not: Researchers and engineers building open streaming video assistants should read it for its end-to-end architecture, training formulation, and released implementation; readers interested only in general offline VLM accuracy can find stronger models on several standard benchmarks.
