Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify the lack of future-covariate conditioning as a limitation on fev-bench, the multivariate and long-horizon probabilistic bottleneck relative to Toto-2.0-2.5B, weaker economic/financial point forecasting, and domain-specific retail weaknesses. They also describe diminishing marginal returns during training. These limitations are confronted with subgroup results, although the paper does not discuss the missing alignment ablation, training cost, uncertainty estimates, or unexplained score discrepancies. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper presents Rank-Guided Cross-Depth Alignment as a contribution but provides no controlled no-alignment baseline, no sweep over alignment weights or layer pairs, and no quantitative evidence that rank transfer improves forecasting. - Domain-aware weights are central to ORBIT but are not disclosed, so the main causal claim about source balancing cannot be independently reproduced or separated from the effects of stochastic window and horizon sampling. - The main baselines appear to rely on heterogeneous leaderboard reports, and the paper does not establish matched preprocessing, compute budgets, checkpoint selection, or repeated-run variance. - The mismatch between Figure 10's final scores and the headline benchmark scores is not explained and could reflect different checkpoints or aggregation pipelines. - The evaluation does not measure calibration coverage, interval sharpness, or quantile crossing despite emphasizing 21-quantile probabilistic forecasting; CRPS and WQL alone do not establish calibrated uncertainty. - The use of uniform record and variable sampling may underweight long, information-rich series and may not be optimal across domains; the paper does not compare alternative exposure objectives or quantify the realized distribution after filtering and feasible-horizon constraints. - The reported corpus includes synthetic KernelSynth data and TSMixup recombinations, but the contribution of these augmentations is not ablated. Bottom Line: ORBIT is a useful and empirically consequential training-pipeline contribution for time-series foundation-model researchers, but the paper's strongest claims should be limited to stochastic example construction and mixed-range training until alignment, weighting, reproducibility, calibration, and compute-cost evidence are resolved.

Tong Zhang, Motasem Alfarra, Carlos Hinojosa, Christos Louizos, Bernard Ghanem · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DiSCO, a strictly black-box prompt-defense module that appends optimized suffixes to text-to-image prompts to reduce unsafe image generation without modifying the target model. - Why it's important: Existing white-box defenses cannot be applied to proprietary generators, while text-only sanitization misses linguistically benign prompts that still induce harmful images. - How it does it: DiSCO uses beam search over suffix tokens generated by LLaMA-3-8B, scoring each candidate image by its CLIP similarity to model-specific safe references minus its similarity to unsafe references. - The good: Across 32 model/defense–attack settings and five seeds, the reported mean ASR falls from 23.6% to 2.4% under NudeNet and from 8.3% to 1.7% under Q16, with held-out ShieldGemma evaluation also showing reductions. - The missing: The method requires approximately 146–273 seconds and up to 256 candidate image generations per prompt under default settings, and the paper does not evaluate adaptive attackers designed specifically to anticipate DiSCO. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners working on black-box safety for text-to-image systems should read it for its output-distribution-guided defense design, but deployment engineers should treat the current latency and untested adaptive-threat robustness as major obstacles.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses unsafe image generation by text-to-image systems, especially the case in which a prompt passes language-level moderation or rewriting but still produces nudity, violence, or other harmful content because of the generator's learned visual distribution. This problem affects deployment of both open and proprietary generators: internal weight editing, gradient-based optimization, and inference-time representation steering require model access, whereas LLM-based prompt rewriting can remove explicit unsafe language without correcting unsafe prompt-to-image associations. The paper formalizes a prompt as benign adversarial when it passes a text-safety check but produces unsafe images with probability at least 0.5. The target gap is therefore not merely unsafe wording, but the lack of a portable mechanism that observes a black-box generator's outputs and steers a safe-looking prompt toward safer regions of that generator's output distribution while retaining semantic intent. Key Idea The central insight is to use the target generator's own safe and unsafe image distributions as a contrastive optimization signal for prompt modification. Rather than judging only whether the prompt text looks safe, DiSCO generates candidate images for candidate prompt suffixes and favors candidates close to safe reference images and far from unsafe reference images in CLIP image-embedding space. The distinctive aspect is the combination of model-specific output-distribution references with autoregressive suffix beam search under a black-box interface; the individual ingredients—CLIP similarity, beam search, language-model prompt extension, and image safety classifiers—are established techniques. Methodology DiSCO first queries the target text-to-image generator with I2P prompts to construct model-specific reference pools. Images enter the safe pool only when both NudeNet and Q16 classify them as safe, and enter the unsafe pool only when both classify them as unsafe; disagreements are discarded. For an input prompt, typically after any existing language-level rewriting, a suffix generator M (LLaMA-3-8B) proposes continuations token by token. At each of T expansion steps, DiSCO retains a beam of K prompts, renders candidate images through the unchanged target generator, samples R safe and R unsafe references, embeds all images with a frozen CLIP image encoder, and scores each candidate using J(p_hat) = (1/R) sum_i cos(phi(x_hat), phi(x_i_safe)) - (1/R) sum_j cos(phi(x_hat), phi(x_j_unsafe)). It returns the surviving prompt with the highest score. Default settings are K=4, T=16, branching factor b=4, and R=8. The main design decisions are: (1) using both positive and negative reference pools, which the ablation supports over either pool alone on average; (2) resampling references at every search step, which the authors argue supplies diverse stochastic guidance, although the explanation is not theoretically established; and (3) appending rather than rewriting the original prompt, which preserves the input text but can still cause semantic drift. The paper describes adaptive feedback in the abstract, but the main algorithm presents a fixed contrastive objective rather than a clearly specified severity-dependent objective; the more general preference-weighted formulation remains unevaluated. Key Results The principal evaluation covers SD v1.4, SD v2.0, SD 3, and Flux as undefended generators, plus SLD-Max, SAFREE, RECE, and ESD applied to SD v1.4. It tests Ring-A-Bell, UnlearnDiffAtk, MMA-Diffusion, and P4D, using NudeNet and Q16 ASR. Across 32 system–attack settings and five seeds, the headline aggregate is a reduction from 23.6% to 2.4% NudeNet ASR and from 8.3% to 1.7% Q16 ASR. For undefended models, mean NudeNet reductions across attacks are 42.6 percentage points for SD v1.4, 33.0 for Flux, 26.5 for SD v2.0, and 11.6 for SD3; Q16 reductions range from 3.3 to 11.1 points. Representative changes include SD v1.4 under Ring-A-Bell falling from 84.2% to 7.8%, Flux from 89.7% to 5.0%, and SD3 from 34.5% to 2.1%. Among defended systems, average NudeNet reductions are 21.1 points for SLD-Max, 20.8 for SAFREE, 5.8 for RECE, and 8.0 for ESD. CLIP alignment to the original prompt increases by 0.036–0.086 across the eight reported systems, while ImageReward also increases in the aggregate tables; these are proxy quality measures rather than human judgments. On 1,000 unseen T2I-RiskyPrompt prompts, relative ASR reductions range from 48.8% to 65.5% for undefended models and 81.7% to 93.8% for defended models, leaving 0.1%–1.1% residual ASR in the latter group. A held-out ShieldGemma2-4B evaluator also reports reductions in all 32 settings, but the evaluation remains based on automated safety classifiers. The strongest counterpoint is that the method's default optimization takes 146–273 seconds per prompt on one A100; reducing candidate denoising to four steps lowers the cost to 33.8 seconds while producing NudeNet ASR of 8.2% versus 7.1% with 50-step scoring in the tested SD v1.4/Ring-A-Bell setting. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily a NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an engineering component: it formulates text-to-image safety failures as black-box distributional alignment and instantiates this with contrastive safe/unsafe image-pool scoring and suffix beam search. The underlying mechanisms are largely standard combinations of language-model generation, beam search, CLIP embeddings, and classifier filtering, so the main novelty lies in their application to benign adversarial prompt defense and in the cross-model empirical demonstration rather than in a new optimization theory or new dataset. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes ablations for reference sampling size R, total reference-pool size, safe-only versus unsafe-only versus contrastive scoring, and beam width/suffix length. The contrastive objective obtains average residual ASR of 15.6% in one SD v1.4 ablation, compared with 21.6% for safe-only and 20.6% for unsafe-only scoring, although the contrastive method loses to single-pool variants on UnlearnDiffAtk. Pool-size experiments find similar results using 25% of the pool, approximately 653 benign and 21 harmful images, but are limited to SD v1.4. Results generally report five seeds and means with standard deviations, while some ablations use fixed generation and search seeds or only a small number of pool-subsampling seeds. The paper directly addresses evaluator circularity: NudeNet and Q16 construct the pools and serve as primary evaluators, but ShieldGemma2-4B is used as an independent held-out classifier and still shows reductions. Important limitations remain: no statistical significance tests are reported; no human safety or quality evaluation is provided; the reference pools and some hyperparameters are derived from I2P-related data; only one independently reimplemented attack, APT, is used in the supplementary stress test; and APT is not adaptive to DiSCO. Code, datasets, model weights, and a repository URL are not stated, although the algorithm and many hyperparameters are specified. The reported safety metric is classifier-defined ASR, so improvements establish reduced classifier-detected unsafe content rather than complete prevention of harmful outputs. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a prompt-level system component but no reported public software artifact. Practical: The method can run on commercially available hardware, and the experiments use a single NVIDIA A100, but its black-box requirement still assumes permission to issue many image-generation queries to the target service. Efficient: It is substantially more expensive than ordinary prompt rewriting or existing inference-time defenses: the default configuration requires T × b × K = 256 candidate image generations and approximately 146–273 seconds per prompt, although four-step candidate renders reduce one tested case to 33.8 seconds and the final generation has no extra cost once the suffix is cached. Effective: The evidence shows large reductions in NudeNet and Q16 classifier ASR across four generators, four attacks, four existing defenses, and an additional dataset, with ShieldGemma confirmation; it does not establish safety against human judgments, all harmful-content classes under adversarial attack, or adaptive attacks optimized against DiSCO. Scalable: The experiments cover standard model and benchmark scales but do not test 10×–100× higher request volume, larger beam/search budgets, high-concurrency service operation, or proprietary API rate limits; the per-prompt query cost is therefore a substantial untested scalability constraint. The work delivers a specified prompt-optimization algorithm and an experimentally evaluated method, but the paper does not state that it releases a library, CLI, dataset, or trained model. Strengths - It identifies and formalizes a practically important failure mode—textually benign prompts that still induce unsafe images—rather than treating text sanitization as equivalent to image safety. - The output-distribution-guided objective is compatible with generators for which gradients, weights, and intermediate representations are unavailable, and the experiments span UNet-based and DiT-based generators as well as multiple existing defense families. - The evaluation includes useful component ablations and directly tests potential detector circularity with ShieldGemma2-4B; the held-out evaluator reduces concern that the method merely exploits NudeNet/Q16 boundaries. - The supplementary analysis quantifies a real deployment trade-off: four-step candidate scoring produces a 6.2× speedup, but the full method remains far slower than conventional safety filters, making the cost claim unusually concrete. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge semantic drift caused by suffixes that inject visually dominant concepts, such as popular characters or common animals, and suggest adding an explicit semantic-preservation constraint. They also identify multi-level safety-pool construction and deployment-specific preference calibration as future work. In the APT stress test, they acknowledge that the attack is not adaptive to DiSCO, that it uses an author reimplementation because no official implementation is available, and that SD v2.0 does not fully recover its unattacked baseline. The paper also reports the substantial per-prompt optimization overhead, though it frames caching and reduced denoising as mitigations. These limitations are confronted in supplementary experiments, but the implications for real-time or high-volume deployment are not fully resolved. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central threat model is not adaptive: an attacker who knows that DiSCO appends a suffix and optimizes against CLIP safe/unsafe separation could search for prompts that survive the defense, but this setting is not evaluated. - The method relies on the same two safety classifiers for reference-pool construction and primary evaluation, and the independent ShieldGemma test is reassuring but still only one automated evaluator with a sexually explicit-content policy; broader human or policy-based assessment is missing. - The paper claims architecture agnosticism and applicability to any text-to-image system, but experiments cover four named generators and do not test proprietary API models, non-diffusion generators, different CLIP/tokenizer interfaces, or systems that reject unusually long suffixes. - The reported quality improvements may reflect CLIP/ImageReward preferences for generic or common safe imagery rather than preservation of detailed user intent; the authors' own semantic-drift examples show that high embedding similarity can coexist with concept injection. - The optimization is evaluated selectively after an initial unsafe generation in the proposed deployment flow, which requires an initial image and a reliable image-safety detector; the latency and false-positive implications of this gate are not fully measured. - Some headline gains aggregate heterogeneous baselines and attack settings with very different starting ASRs, while several ablations evaluate only residual failures or fixed-seed subsets; this complicates direct comparison of absolute ASR and does not establish robustness under repeated stochastic generations per prompt. - No human annotation, confidence intervals over prompts beyond seed variation, significance testing, or analysis of failure cases by harm category under the adversarial attacks is reported. Bottom Line DiSCO is a useful and empirically credible black-box defense concept for researchers studying text-to-image safety, but its 34–273-second optimization cost and lack of adaptive-attacker evaluation make it a research prototype rather than a convincing general-purpose production safeguard.

Problem & Motivation: High-order DG spectral-element discretizations provide accuracy and geometric flexibility, but their element-interior coupling, large polynomial orders, mesh anisotropy, curved elements, irregular topology, and local refinement make iterative elliptic solves difficult. Existing adaptive multigrid approaches commonly use a globally represented finest mesh with hanging nodes or transition elements, complicating conservative DG operators and purely hexahedral mesh management. The paper targets elliptic systems arising in computational fluid dynamics, meteorology, astrophysics, and related PDE applications, with particular relevance to pressure and diffusion solves in incompressible flow. The claimed gap is the absence of an FAS multigrid method demonstrated for high-order adaptive DG-SEM on unstructured curvilinear hexahedral meshes while retaining tensor-product fast diagonalization. Key Idea: Store the full approximate solution on a hierarchy of locally present refinement-zone meshes, rather than representing the entire domain on the finest adaptive mesh. Refinement boundaries are surrounded by frozen child elements whose values are interpolated from parent leaves and are incorporated directly into the DG operator. This avoids hanging nodes while preserving DG coupling. The solver's second key mechanism is an element-centered overlapping Schwarz smoother that retains edge and vertex-neighbor information through node restriction/merging, then approximates each curved subdomain by a volume-preserving Cartesian tensor-product surrogate. Fast diagonalization supplies cheap approximate subdomain inverses, while inexact CG acceleration compensates for the surrogate's geometric and coefficient approximations. Methodology: The paper discretizes the three-dimensional reaction-diffusion problem \(\kappa u-\nabla\cdot(\nu\nabla u)=f\) using nodal tensor-product DG-SEM basis functions at Gauss-Legendre-Lobatto points and an interior-penalty formulation. A hierarchy is formed through successive global or local h- or p-refinements; each level has a uniform polynomial degree, so mixed p-levels are not supported within one level. Regularly refined children become active twigs or leaves, while neighboring irregular children become frozen elements. Prolongation uses embedded interpolation; residual restriction is its transpose; solution projection uses either embedded interpolation or an L2 projection. The FAS equations retain full solutions and construct modified right-hand sides for twig elements from projected child solutions, restricted residuals, and DG couplings to frozen elements. The V-cycle applies pre-smoothing, residual formation, solution projection, coarse FAS correction, frozen-element update, prolongation, and post-smoothing. The weighted additive Schwarz smoother restricts residuals to element-centered overlapping subdomains, merges irregular edge/vertex nodes, approximates geometry by a parallelepiped/cuboid with preserved volume, replaces variable diffusivity by an element average, and solves the resulting tensor-product operator by precomputed generalized eigendecompositions and fast diagonalization. The inexact preconditioned CG variant uses one Schwarz sweep per inner step and serves both as a smoother and root-level solver. Three important design choices are only partly justified: the Cartesian surrogate and averaged coefficient are empirically motivated rather than analytically bounded; the choice between interpolation and L2 projection is tested but not theoretically analyzed; and the fixed per-level polynomial degree and frozen-layer construction simplify implementation but restrict general hp adaptivity. Key Results: The paper reports residual-reduction counts and normalized runtimes for manufactured elliptic problems on Cartesian, anisotropic, curved, irregular, and blade meshes. On uniform Cartesian meshes with p from 4 to 32, the fastest reported p-FAS-FMG-SCG configurations achieve \(\tau_{10}=2.66,1.23,0.60,0.43\) microseconds per DOF/core for p = 4, 8, 16, 32, while h-FAS-FMG-WAS achieves \(\tau_{10}=1.76,0.29,0.34,0.78\), respectively; the corresponding residual-reduction counts range from 1 to 2 in the fastest tuned cases. For aspect ratios up to 48 at p = 16, FAS-FMG-SCG with sufficiently many smoothing steps maintains approximately 3–4 iterations and normalized runtimes below about 5, whereas unaccelerated WAS becomes inefficient or unstable and CS-CG-WAS degrades substantially. On the spherical-shell curved mesh, selected methods require 1–3 iterations for p-FAS-FMG-SCG and 2–7 for h-FAS-FMG-SCG, with normalized runtimes from 1.50 to 18.6 depending on p and aspect ratio. On the highly irregular diamond mesh, WAS-based methods fail to converge, while p-FAS-FMG-SCG requires 1–2 iterations and h-FAS-FMG-SCG 1–3 iterations. The blade case combines curvature, deformation, aspect ratios up to 10, variable diffusivity, and irregular topology: the global configuration has 1.102 billion total DOFs and 963 million leaf DOFs, while the local configuration has 79 million total and 46 million leaf DOFs; both report one iteration to reduce the residual by 10 orders of magnitude, with 32-rank runtimes of 53.14 s and 5.22 s and per-DOF/core times of 1.54 and 2.12 microseconds. The spherical-front adaptation benchmark reports 93–98% DOF savings relative to global refinement, and adaptation plus operator setup each consume about 10% of solver time in the reported runs. The paper compares single-core normalized times to Fehn et al.'s Chebyshev-Jacobi results, claiming a factor-of-20-or-more advantage for p ≥ 8, but this is not a matched implementation comparison. The Navier–Stokes cylinder example uses 6.34 million velocity-and-pressure DOFs and shows a qualitative field at time 5, not a quantitative flow-validation study. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the FAS formulation with active, twig, leaf, and frozen DG elements and direct frozen-element coupling is the central formulation contribution; the Krylov-accelerated tensor-preserving Schwarz method extends existing Schwarz/fast-diagonalization ideas to irregular curvilinear meshes, so it is an integration and generalization of established components rather than an entirely new preconditioning principle; the HiSPEET implementation and its large adaptive demonstrations provide a system contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.14123v1, dated 14 August 2026), not identified as peer-reviewed in the supplied document. It gives algorithmic equations, pseudocode, hardware/compiler/MPI details, parameter sweeps, several robustness studies, and manufactured solutions. It includes useful sensitivity experiments for penalty, overlap, projection, smoothing counts, aspect ratio, curvature, and topology, and explicitly reports failure of WAS on the irregular diamond mesh. However, it does not provide convergence/error bars, multiple random-start seeds, statistical tests, or a formal convergence theory for the adaptive FAS construction. Many headline configurations are selected as the fastest among extensive parameter searches, so the reported numbers reflect tuning and may not transfer without equivalent search effort. Comparisons to contemporary methods are indirect, use different codes and hardware, and do not establish equal accuracy or equal implementation scope; the paper does not present a controlled comparison with the strongest local adaptive DG solvers such as matrix-free block-preconditioned or task-based alternatives. The authors state that source code and examples are available at https://github.com/HiSPEET/hispeet.git, built on FD4 and LIBXSMM; data-generation scripts, exact run configurations, and independent reproduction results are not stated. The adaptation criterion includes a manually selected threshold of 0.7 of the maximum element error and unconditional refinement of elements cut by the front, which makes the benchmark partly hand-engineered. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper delivers and evaluates the HiSPEET library and an MPI-parallel adaptive solver, although most quantitative tests solve manufactured elliptic systems rather than deployed application workloads. Practical: The implementation runs on commercially available Intel Xeon CPUs using MPI, and the authors provide a GitHub repository, but GPU portability and dependencies beyond the stated HPC stack are not evaluated. Efficient: The method uses matrix-free tensor-product operator evaluation and fast diagonalization; reported costs are 0.29–2.12 microseconds per DOF/core in selected standard or application cases, but overlap, ghost, setup, and communication costs are simplified or omitted in the analytical cost model. Effective: It reduces residuals by 10 orders of magnitude in the reported elliptic tests and achieves 93–98% DOF savings in the spherical-front adaptation benchmark, but solution-error accuracy, conservation across levels, and flow quantities of interest are not comprehensively measured; the authors explicitly note that interlevel coupling is generally not conservative. Scalable: It reaches 1024 MPI ranks for the 963-million-DOF blade case and shows near-ideal strong-scaling behavior in the plotted global case, but local refinement loses efficiency at high rank counts, lower levels can contain only 13–14 active elements per partition, frozen-element workload is excluded from balancing, and behavior at 10–100 times larger scale is not tested. The work delivers the HiSPEET software artifact and examples; it does not deliver a validated production flow solver or a formal proof of multigrid optimality. Strengths: - The active/twig/leaf/frozen hierarchy gives a concrete way to combine FAS with locally refined DG meshes while avoiding hanging nodes and preserving the DG discretization on each level. - The Schwarz construction addresses a real tension between geometric robustness and fast diagonalization: it retains edge/vertex information while mapping irregular curved subdomains to cheap tensor-product surrogates. - The evaluation stresses several failure modes that commonly break high-order multigrid—aspect ratios up to 48, curved geometry, irregular neighbor topology, variable coefficients, and a 963-million-DOF blade mesh—instead of reporting only uniform Cartesian results. - The open HiSPEET implementation, explicit pseudocode, and large-scale MPI experiments make the engineering contribution more reusable than a paper-only algorithm description. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that interlevel coupling is generally not conservative and leave its advantages or disadvantages for future work. They restrict every level to one polynomial degree and do not perform simultaneous h- and p-refinement within a level. They acknowledge that parallel efficiency, especially under local refinement, can improve through better partitioning because frozen-element workload is not included in the balance metric and coarse levels become underpopulated at high process counts. They describe the Navier–Stokes results as preliminary, defer thorough flow and turbulent-flow investigations, and identify error-estimation-driven adaptation as future work. They also note that the discrete energy estimator underestimates error at insufficient resolution and compensate with an additional rule refining all elements cut by the wavefront. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central FAS-DG construction lacks a theorem establishing stability, approximation properties, conservation across refinement interfaces, or mesh-independent convergence; the authors' statement that the final formulation is conservative on each level does not establish conservation of the composite multilevel solution. The method is evaluated mainly on manufactured elliptic problems with smooth or prescribed solutions, and the adaptive front test uses a known exact solution and hand-crafted refinement safeguards, leaving general estimator reliability and robustness under singularities or discontinuous coefficients unresolved. The comparison section makes strong speed claims from non-matched hardware and implementations, without reporting equal residual/error tolerances, memory traffic, setup time, communication time, or tuning cost. The reported one-iteration blade results may reflect a favorable full-multigrid startup and selected smoothing parameters rather than a general convergence guarantee. Mixed local hp refinement, highly variable diffusivity, non-affine mappings beyond the tested geometries, nonlinear flow coupling, GPU execution, and weak scaling are not evaluated. Finally, the paper does not quantify solution accuracy or physical quantities for the cylinder flow, so its practical impact for Navier–Stokes applications remains demonstrated only at the infrastructure level. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile systems-and-algorithms paper for high-order DG researchers because it supplies a credible, open implementation of a hanging-node-free adaptive FAS hierarchy and demonstrates strong tuned performance on difficult meshes, but its novelty and practical superiority remain less conclusive than its headline speed claims because theory, matched baselines, general hp adaptivity, and quantitative flow validation are missing.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive coding agents are executed model–runtime systems rather than bare language models. The runtime controls prompt and context construction, tool schemas, session state, provider adaptation, retries, compaction, permissions, verification, and stopping; these choices alter both the trajectories reachable by a fixed model and the data available for later learning. Prior work has explored agent–computer interfaces, workflow evolution, and harness adaptation, but the paper identifies a narrower systems gap: heterogeneous harness modifications often lack persistent intervention identity, source provenance, comparable evidence, and a structured handoff into model updating. The target domain is software-engineering agents, especially repository repair under executable tests. Key Idea: Treat the harness as an explicit, persistent intervention variable and evaluate a matched portfolio rather than only a winning runtime. A harness both determines current execution and acts as a curriculum/data-generation policy: different harnesses produce sibling trajectories on the same model and task, including successes, regressions, near misses, no-action outcomes, and alternative patches. HELIX preserves the identity and evidence of each sibling so those contrasts can later support SFT, critic, filtering, or preference learning. The build–update–rebuild loop is conceptually clear, but only the build and evidence-generation portions are implemented and tested in this paper. Methodology: HELIX represents a harness as eight dimensions—shell, session/hooks, configuration, prompt, tools, turn loop, acceptance, and runtime policy—and decomposes OpenCode, Pi Mono, Nanobot, and Hermes Agent into source-derived atoms connected through typed ports. Recipes bind atoms, strategies, policies, and product shells; a compiler resolves dependencies and bindings and emits a deterministic lockfile. Pre-execution conformance, boundary, and source-purity checks screen compositions, after which an assembled runtime executes a multi-step loop: create or restore the session, normalize the request and context, stream model output, normalize tool calls, run permission and tool preflight, execute tools, apply hooks and retries, test acceptance and stopping conditions, and persist traces and workspace effects. The evidence plane records recipe and model–task–attempt identity, runtime traces, workspace diffs, verifier outcomes, policy evidence, cost/cadence, and artifacts. Formally, the paper defines trajectory sampling under model and harness conditions, verifier labels that may distinguish resolution, target miss, regression, no action, policy violation, patch noise, and evaluator gaps, and a deployment objective combining reward with cost and policy-risk penalties. It also defines fixed-harness coverage and post-hoc portfolio oracle coverage separately. The main live study evaluates Pi Mono plus 64 Pi-centered source-pure recipes that vary session/hooks, configuration, and tools over 100 LiveCodeBench-derived repair fixtures; selected members receive ten-attempt repeated evaluation on the same fixtures and two-attempt evaluation on 55 SWE-bench Verified instances. Critical design decisions—typed bounded composition, persistent lockfile/provenance identity, and sibling grouping by task and model—are well motivated for auditability, but the paper does not establish that these mechanisms improve model learning because no model update is run. Moreover, multiple components change together in most comparisons, preventing component-level causal attribution. Key Results: In the 65-candidate, one-attempt matrix over 100 LiveCodeBench-derived fixtures, Pi solves 50/100 tasks, the best fixed candidate solves 52/100, and the second-best solves 51/100; only two of 64 non-baseline candidates exceed Pi, while 23 candidates solve zero tasks. The full portfolio produces 1,014 trace-strict successful slots out of 6,500 and a post-hoc union of 79/100 tasks, 29 more than Pi and a 58.0% relative coverage increase, but this is not a deployable fixed-harness score because outcomes are observed before selecting a candidate. In ten-attempt repeated evaluation, Pi covers 72/100 tasks with 529/1,000 successful slots, while two selected OpenCode-family variants each cover 75/100 with 549/1,000 and 546/1,000 successful slots. On 55 SWE-bench Verified instances with two attempts per member, Pi resolves 44/55 tasks and 81 slots; the strongest selected OpenCode variant resolves 46/55 and 86 slots, while the selected-member union covers 49/55. The deeper SWE-bench matrix contains 411 resolved slots, 132 gaps, seven empty patches, 486 nonempty production-only patches, 57 patches touching tests, and 248 patches with symlink/path noise; only 205 resolved patches are both production-only and path-clean. A curated 200-slot slice from 20 instances yields 438 derived, non-independent records: 63 clean SFT examples, 56 cleanup-needed SFT examples, 52 critic negatives, 113 filter samples, and 154 preference pairs. Case studies show that target-test success can conceal regressions, as in pytest where a Pi patch passes 2/2 target tests but fails 2/123 regression tests, and that a clean patch can still be semantically wrong, as in xarray where both candidates pass all 247 regression tests but only one passes the target. The results support modest fixed-harness gains and portfolio complementarity, not recursive model improvement or causal explanations for individual component effects. The paper is an arXiv v1 preprint dated 14 August 2026, so the evidence is pre-publication. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the source-traceable representation and evidence-linked sibling export that connects heterogeneous harness recomposition to potential model-update data; the broad claim that runtime interfaces affect agent behavior and the general build–update–rebuild abstraction overlap with prior harness-evolution and recursive-improvement work, while the evaluated recipes are largely combinations of existing harness components. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study reports a complete 65-candidate matrix for the primary one-attempt experiment, clearly separates fixed-candidate coverage from post-hoc oracle coverage, uses repeated runs and the official SWE-bench evaluator for selected members, and includes detailed verifier-grounded traces and patch-quality accounting. It also prevents sibling leakage by keeping each task group within one train/dev split. However, no confidence intervals, standard errors, statistical tests, or multiple independent seeds are reported; rollouts use a nondeterministic MiniMax-M2.7-highspeed model, and selected follow-up candidates are not evaluated under a common budget across the full portfolio. The main LCB fixtures are the first 100 eligible examples rather than a random or held-out sample, use public tests rather than official hidden-test evaluation, and appear to be benchmark-derived in the same environment used for candidate selection. Comparisons vary several harness dimensions jointly, and only Pi is the principal baseline; no strong contemporary coding-agent baselines or compute-normalized alternatives are reported. The authors release code at https://github.com/HKUDS/HELIX; data, model weights, and a trained updated model are not stated as released. The 438 rows are derived records rather than independent examples, and the paper does not validate whether training on them improves any downstream model. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile. Practical: The runtime and compiler appear implementable on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not report hardware requirements, installation burden, or operational deployment beyond controlled experiments. Efficient: Portfolio construction is expensive—6,500 primary rollout slots plus repeated and SWE-bench follow-ups—and the paper reports modest per-slot overheads for selected LCB recompositions, including approximately 5.4–7.8 additional seconds and up to 0.171 additional tool calls per slot, but provides no end-to-end cost comparison against stronger baselines or a router. Effective: Evidence shows small fixed-harness improvements and complementary outcomes under coding benchmarks, while it does not show that the exported records improve a model, that a selector can exploit the 79/100 or 49/55 unions, or that the method solves the broader recursive-self-improvement problem. Scalable: HELIX enumerates up to 1,024 or 4,096 recipes, but live evaluation covers only 65 candidates, 100 LCB-derived tasks, and 55 SWE-bench instances; behavior at 10×–100× the candidate, task, rollout, or co-evolution-round scale is not evaluated. The work delivers a released software substrate and exported training-record format, but not a trained model, deployable router, or completed multi-round RSI system. Strengths: (1) The paper makes an often implicit source of agent variance explicit by representing session behavior, tools, configuration, turn control, acceptance, and policies as inspectable intervention dimensions rather than treating the runtime as an opaque product label. (2) Persistent recipe, lockfile, model, task, attempt, trace, workspace, and verifier identity is a concrete reproducibility and attribution contribution for agent-runtime experiments. (3) The distinction between fixed-harness performance and post-hoc portfolio yield is methodologically important and prevents the 79/100 union from being presented as a single deployable score. (4) The regression-aware examples and the 438-record accounting demonstrate that executable verification can distinguish clean positives, noisy patches, semantic near misses, and target-passing regressions—labels more useful for learning than a binary success bit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the main evaluation uses only 100 non-random AtCoder/LiveCodeBench-derived fixtures and public tests, the SWE-bench follow-up covers only 55 instances, and results concern coding agents. They acknowledge that multiple components change simultaneously, so individual causal effects cannot be identified; that attempt budgets and selected-member follow-ups are not directly comparable; that post-hoc oracle coverage is not deployable without a router; and that automated tests miss some semantic, artifact, evaluator-exploit, timeout, and environment failures. They also state that no updated model is trained, the sibling dataset remains small, recursive updating needs methods beyond simply adding data, larger portfolios are token-expensive, and safety, trace leakage, permissions, and upstream harness maintenance require additional controls. These limitations are confronted directly and materially narrow the paper's claims. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central claimed co-evolution loop is not empirically closed: there is no model update, no rebuilt portfolio conditioned on a changed model, and no measurement of improvement across rounds. The fixed-harness gains are small—2 tasks on the primary 100-task matrix and 2 tasks on the 55-task SWE-bench follow-up—and may be unstable without confidence intervals or repeated evaluation of every candidate. The portfolio union is an oracle upper bound and may substantially overstate practical benefit because the paper evaluates no pre-outcome router, early stopping policy, or compute-normalized selection strategy. Candidate selection and follow-up analysis create potential selection bias, while the first-100-task choice and public-test use limit generalization. The comparison set lacks strong current coding-agent baselines and does not establish whether HELIX's provenance machinery, rather than the particular source implementations or changed prompts/tool behavior, causes the gains. Finally, the training-record taxonomy is plausible but unvalidated: record counts, including overlapping multi-purpose rows, are not evidence of learning value until downstream model training, held-out regression testing, and preservation of general capability are measured. Bottom Line: HELIX is a useful and reproducible infrastructure contribution for auditing and harvesting interaction data from coding-agent harness portfolios, but it does not yet demonstrate recursive self-improvement and should not be ranked as evidence that model–harness co-evolution improves a model across rounds.

Generating High-Diversity Synthetic Tabular Data via Less-Constrained Prior

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SPT, a two-stage VAE–latent-diffusion method for mixed-type tabular synthesis that removes the fixed-prior regularization used by prior two-stage models. - Why it's important: Better coverage of rare and low-density modes can improve synthetic-data usefulness while avoiding the fidelity–diversity trade-off that limits tabular generators. - How it does it: It derives stage-one training from a single KL divergence between the real distribution and the final generative model, replacing KL regularization toward a fixed prior with self-regularization against the aggregated posterior, followed by diffusion modeling of that posterior. - The good: Across 12 datasets and 5 seeds, SPT obtains the best aggregate results on 8 of 10 reported metrics, including β-recall of 0.526, coverage of 0.953, clipped coverage of 0.923, and TOPSIS of 0.969. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish formal privacy guarantees, compute efficiency, or performance at substantially larger datasets, and it appears to use TOPSIS for hyperparameter selection based on the same evaluation metrics. - Read it or not: Researchers working on VAE-based or latent-diffusion tabular synthesis should read it for the latent-support formulation and ablations, but deployment-focused readers should treat the privacy and scalability claims as unverified.

Problem & Motivation: Tabular synthesis must reproduce mixed continuous–categorical joint distributions while preserving fidelity, diversity, and downstream utility. Existing two-stage methods such as TabSyn first train a VAE with a fixed prior, commonly a standard Gaussian, and then fit a trainable generative prior to the aggregated posterior. The paper argues that the fixed prior is used only as a stage-one representation regularizer and is not the prior used for final sampling; consequently, the stage-one KL term imposes an extra constraint on the aggregated posterior. The claimed consequence is reduced effective latent support, especially in low-density or minority regions, which limits coverage and diversity even when conventional fidelity metrics are already strong. Key Idea: The central insight is to optimize the final generative-model objective directly rather than decompose training around a fixed stage-one prior. Algebraically, the fixed-prior VAE regularizer decomposes into self-regularization of each posterior around the aggregated posterior plus an additional KL term between the aggregated posterior and the fixed prior. SPT removes this second term, allowing the learned latent distribution to retain broader, potentially multimodal support before a diffusion model learns that distribution. The paper connects this removal to reachable regions in data space through bounds on the mass of latent likelihood-ratio regions, although the propositions establish concentration bounds rather than a direct theorem that diversity must increase. Methodology: SPT has two sequential stages. In stage one, an encoder with diagonal Gaussian posterior q(z|x) maps each mixed-type row to a d-dimensional latent representation, and a decoder models continuous columns with Gaussian distributions and discrete columns with categorical distributions. The training objective is the reconstruction negative log-likelihood plus E_x[KL(q(z|x)||q(z))], where q(z) is the aggregated posterior, rather than the conventional E_x[KL(q(z|x)||p(z))] for a fixed prior. The paper derives an upper bound for the self-regularization term under a diagonal Gaussian encoder and implements it in closed form; it fixes encoder variance rather than learning it because the objective can otherwise encourage variance inflation. In stage two, a score-based diffusion model is trained on the aggregated posterior q(z), with the encoder and decoder held fixed, and ancestral latent samples are decoded into synthetic rows. A decoder-variance parameter β is annealed during stage-one training to adapt regularization over time. The key design decisions—removing fixed-prior regularization, fixing encoder variance, and β-annealing—are supported by ablations, but their selection remains partly empirical and the exact final objective and training details are deferred to the appendix. Key Results: On 12 real-world Kaggle and UCI datasets, results averaged over 5 random seeds show SPT outperforming six baselines—CTGAN, TVAE, TabMT, STaSy, TabDDPM, and TabSyn—on 8 of 10 aggregate metrics. Relative to the second-best method, SPT reports GoF 0.020 versus 0.025, MMD 0.008 versus 0.010, PCD 0.441 versus 0.469, β-recall 0.526 versus 0.485, coverage 0.953 versus 0.939, clipped coverage 0.923 versus 0.877, classification accuracy 0.741 versus 0.738, and feature-selection consistency 0.830 versus 0.826; it ranks second on α-precision at 0.962 and model-selection consistency at 0.867. Its TOPSIS score is 0.969 versus 0.934 for TabSyn, and it ranks first on 9 of 12 individual datasets and second on the other 3. Against the paper's controlled AutoDiff/TabSyn/SPT comparison, SPT improves TOPSIS from 0.922 for AutoDiff and 0.934 for TabSyn to 0.969. Fixing encoder variance at 0.1 improves MMD by 11.6% and β-recall by 26.4% relative to trainable variance in the reported ablation. β-annealing improves all listed metrics, including MMD from 0.016 to 0.008 and β-recall from 0.343 to 0.528. The privacy experiment varies latent noise scaling c from 1 to 6 and reports a quality–attribute-disclosure trade-off, but the parsed text does not provide complete numerical k-anonymity, AD, or DCR results. The datasets are standard small-to-moderate benchmarks; dataset sizes, model parameter counts, training times, and stress-scale evaluations are not stated in the provided text. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the derivation and implementation of a single-prior two-stage objective that removes the fixed-prior constraint on the aggregated posterior; the encoder-variance choice, β-annealing, and latent diffusion components are largely established techniques adapted and combined for this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study evaluates 12 datasets, six named baselines, ten quality metrics, five random seeds, and reports means with standard errors, while including controlled comparisons and ablations for latent regularization, encoder variance, and β-annealing. Code is stated to be available at https://github.com/Optim-Lab/SPT; no separate dataset release or trained-model release is mentioned. The theoretical analysis is explicit about Gaussian decoder and absolute-continuity assumptions, but its propositions are relatively weak concentration/coverage bounds and do not prove that SPT improves empirical diversity. Statistical significance tests, confidence intervals beyond reported standard errors, and per-dataset variance details are not stated. The use of TOPSIS to identify the best hyperparameter configurations, apparently using the evaluation metrics themselves, creates a possible model-selection/evaluation leakage risk unless a separate validation protocol is used. The baseline set includes strong recent latent-diffusion and tabular-diffusion models, especially TabSyn and TabDDPM, but omits some relevant methods cited in the related-work discussion, such as GReaT, GOGGLE, CoDi, and MaCoDE. The privacy evaluation uses heuristic metrics and latent noise, not differential privacy or a formal disclosure bound. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: The method runs in PyTorch on an NVIDIA RTX A6000, so it is implementable on commercially available GPU hardware, although required memory and inference latency are not quantified. Efficient: The paper provides no training-time, sampling-time, parameter-count, or memory comparison against the baselines, so efficiency relative to latent or data-space diffusion is not evaluated. Effective: On the tested benchmarks, SPT improves statistical diversity while maintaining or slightly improving fidelity and utility, but these metrics remain proxies for domain-specific usefulness and no real deployment task is evaluated. Scalable: The paper tests 12 benchmark datasets but does not report dataset sizes, scaling curves, or experiments at 10×–100× scale; scalability is therefore not demonstrated. The work delivers a reusable software artifact through the stated GitHub implementation, but no standalone library, CLI, dataset, or trained model release is described. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete structural redundancy in two-stage VAE formulations and expresses it through an explicit KL decomposition rather than presenting SPT as an unexplained architectural modification. - The method targets diversity directly and evaluates it with β-recall, coverage, and clipped coverage in addition to standard fidelity and downstream-utility metrics; the reported gains are largest on these diversity measures. - The controlled AutoDiff/TabSyn/SPT comparison and the encoder-variance and β-annealing ablations provide evidence that the gains arise from more than merely replacing the baseline architecture. - The analysis links latent-support restrictions to reachable regions in data space, giving a useful conceptual framework for understanding why a fixed prior may suppress rare modes. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that synthetic-data quality is particularly sensitive to the encoder-variance hyperparameter, and they treat this dependence as a limitation. They also state that it is unknown whether the less-constrained-prior idea transfers to other domains such as images. They do not explicitly acknowledge the absence of formal privacy guarantees, missing efficiency measurements, possible benchmark-selection issues, or the lack of large-scale evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unaddressed concern is evaluation protocol: the paper says TOPSIS is used to identify the best hyperparameter configurations, but does not clarify whether those metrics are computed on held-out validation data or on the reported test data. The study also does not compare training and sampling cost, parameter counts, or memory, despite introducing a two-stage diffusion pipeline. Its privacy section calls latent noise "controllable privacy" without differential privacy guarantees, attack-based auditing, or a clear threat model, and it reports only qualitative trade-off conclusions in the main text. The benchmark evaluation is limited to 12 Kaggle/UCI datasets with no explicit large-scale or highly imbalanced stress tests, and the paper does not establish whether higher coverage corresponds to better domain-specific downstream performance beyond aggregate utility proxies. Finally, the theoretical argument assumes Gaussian decoding and absolute continuity and provides a bound on reachable-region mass, but it does not quantify how the proposed objective changes actual support coverage or rule out increased off-manifold sampling. Bottom Line: This is a useful and empirically well-supported formulation-level improvement for latent-diffusion tabular synthesis, worth reading for researchers studying VAE regularization and diversity, but its practical significance is limited until leakage-controlled evaluation, compute/scaling measurements, and formal privacy analysis are added.

Problem & Motivation: Interactive game video models must preserve geometry, pose, identity, occlusion, metric motion, and action effects while repeatedly conditioning on their own generated outputs. Pixel- or latent-space autoregression leaves these properties implicit, so errors can compound over long rollouts and controls may be ignored, delayed, or applied to the wrong entity. The target users are researchers and developers building playable or interactive game-video simulators, particularly for multi-character articulated scenes. The paper addresses the gap between high visual fidelity and explicit, per-entity, per-frame control by separating exact geometric bookkeeping from learned appearance generation; however, it does not address general game logic, arbitrary objects, persistent inventories, physical interaction beyond simple terrain and separation constraints, or broad multi-agent gameplay. Key Idea: The central insight is to choose an intermediate representation according to what must be exact: make an interpretable, metric articulated world state recur through the autoregressive loop, enforce feasibility on that state, and delegate only appearance to a neural generator. The zero-parameter bridge is the critical mechanism: given root deltas, rotations, relative joints, terrain, and a camera, it reconstructs world-space geometry, depth, identity, and occlusion deterministically. This turns controllability into direct editing of explicit action or root channels and turns selected long-horizon failures into post-hoc state projections rather than learned visual corrections. Methodology: Marionette uses two causal-transformer dynamics stages followed by a deterministic renderer and a video-diffusion observation model. ActionGPT has four layers, width 256, approximately 2.5M parameters, and predicts per-entity discrete action ids plus root displacement and 6D root rotation from recent state summaries, action embeddings, animation progress, weapon state, and optionally terrain features. PoseGPT has eight layers, width 512, approximately 25M parameters, and maps the selected action ids and recent 258-dimensional body state to the next body pose; the resulting pose, root channels, weapon state, and rotations form the 276-dimensional state for two entities. At inference, action tokens or root translation and rotation can be overwritten directly. The bridge converts 6D rotations to matrices using Gram-Schmidt, rotates and cumulatively integrates local root deltas, places relative joints in metric world coordinates, attaches a scanned multi-layer height field, applies a follow or ground-truth camera, and rasterizes height, per-joint identity, and inverse depth into a three-channel control video. Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control then synthesizes RGB from this control video and a first-frame appearance reference using 81-frame chunks relayed autoregressively. Training includes autoregressive state prediction and terrain-related auxiliary terms: a penetration hinge, a contact loss, and a root anti-drift term; the authors report that strong joint-level penalties caused bone stretching, so the shipped configuration uses the terrain patch as input, retains only a small penetration regularizer with weight 0.1, drops the contact loss, and uses inference-time collision projection. The major design decisions—discrete decision versus continuous animation, metric state versus latent recurrence, and deterministic geometry versus learned rendering—are conceptually motivated, but their relative contributions are only partially isolated by the reported experiments. Key Results: The dynamics model is trained on 1,395 state segments totaling approximately 16.4M frames at 20 fps, while the RGB model uses 4,008 clips totaling 673.8 hours at 704 x 1280 resolution. On 48 held-out segments at a 120-frame horizon, deterministic free rollout gives 0.281 +/- 0.141 m root-aligned MPJPE, forcing the recorded action ids gives 0.272 +/- 0.135 m, and forcing temporally shuffled action ids gives 0.357 +/- 0.120 m; Force-GT is better than Force-Shuf on 33/48 segments. Error inflation from correct to wrong tokens is reported as 2.3x for stationary actions, 1.7x for in-place attacks, and 1.3x for locomotion. In 12 held-out 16-second windows, generated state without rules has collision-frame ratio 0.337, mean maximum penetration 0.444 m, foot-skate 1.14 m/s, and final entity separation 21.2 m, versus recorded-state values of 0.082, 0.023 m, 1.13 m/s, and 4.8 m. The terrain collider reduces collision-frame ratio to 0.114 and penetration to 0.157 m without changing separation; adding a 6 m separation cap yields 5.1 m separation, 0.155 m penetration, and increases foot-skate to 1.22 m/s. On the observation layer, Marionette obtains FVD16 of 831 [963, 1209] versus 975 [1101, 1346] for an end-to-end pixel-autoregressive baseline, with overlapping bootstrap intervals; final-chunk FVD is 1,013 versus 1,198. Feeding recorded rather than predicted pose to the same observation model gives FVD 799, compared with 831 for predicted pose. The comparisons are informative for the explicit-state decomposition but narrow: the principal quantitative baseline is a same-data pixel-autoregressive model, and the experiments test a standard-scale, single-game, single-monster, one-on-one setting rather than stress-scale or multi-game generalization. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the operational combination of a predicted metric articulated state, a zero-parameter state-to-geometry bridge, and a video-diffusion appearance model with direct action-token injection and state-level repair; the individual ingredients—autoregressive transformers, pose-conditioned video generation, terrain-aware character animation, and deterministic rendering—are established techniques, and the paper does not introduce a new learning objective or general-purpose simulator architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a useful decomposition ablation by holding the observation model fixed while replacing predicted state with recorded state, and it evaluates state-layer properties that FVD cannot measure. The forced-action protocol fixes seeds, contexts, horizons, and decoding so that the injected token is the principal experimental difference; the rule ablation likewise fixes checkpoints, windows, bridge code, and seeds. Bootstrap intervals are reported for FVD, and the controllability table reports mean and standard deviation, but no confidence intervals or significance tests are given for the state metrics, and the small number of rollout windows limits statistical strength. The paper includes a negative result showing that strong differentiable terrain penalties caused bone-length distortion, which improves methodological transparency. The authors state that they will release dynamics, bridge, terrain, observation-model, evaluation, preprocessing, and configuration code, and provide the project page https://alayalab.github.io/Marionette/; the paper does not establish that all promised releases are already available. The evaluation lacks comparisons with structured motion predictors, physics-based character controllers, action-conditioned diffusion or world models, and recent explicit-state alternatives under a common protocol. The observation model is trained only on ground-truth pose-control inputs but evaluated on generated states, creating a distribution shift that is acknowledged but not comprehensively quantified. The RGB corpus includes entities without recorded state, allowing the observation model to hallucinate content outside the explicit state, which weakens the claim that the complete rendered scene is state-governed. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS, because the paper trains and evaluates a composed generation system and describes a released software pipeline. Practical: The dynamics components are modest at approximately 27.5M parameters combined, but the Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control video-diffusion backbone and 704 x 1280 generation pipeline require substantial GPU memory and the paper does not report runtime, throughput, latency, or hardware, so commercial-hardware feasibility is not demonstrated. Efficient: The deterministic bridge is computationally inexpensive relative to diffusion, but no end-to-end compute, memory, frames-per-second, or comparison against the pixel-autoregressive baseline is reported. Effective: Evidence supports explicit token-level pose influence and targeted reduction of terrain penetration and inter-entity drift, while RGB FVD remains comparable to the baseline; it does not establish reliable gameplay semantics, physical correctness, or user-level interactivity. Scalable: The tested dynamics scope is two entities, one monster type, one fixed weapon and combat configuration, with 12 rendered windows and 20 free state rollouts at 1,000 frames; behavior at 10x–100x scale, additional entity types, multiple monsters, cooperative parties, unseen maps, or broader game logic is not evaluated. The work delivers a planned open-source bridge, terrain pipeline, evaluation code, dynamics models, and observation-model training/inference code, plus terrain assets; the dataset is based on the previously released WildWorld corpus, while the underlying commercial-game footage is restricted to non-commercial academic research. Strengths: - The state/observation factorization creates a meaningful causal and diagnostic interface: action compliance, root drift, penetration, separation, and foot-skate can be measured before RGB synthesis rather than inferred from perceptual scores. - The deterministic bridge makes metric geometry, skeleton topology, identity labels, depth ordering, and camera projection explicit and reproducible, while avoiding additional learned parameters in the geometry path. - The state-level intervention experiments are stronger than qualitative claims of controllability: temporally shuffled actions produce a measured 31% increase in root-aligned pose error, and token switching changes pose within a few frames under shared prefixes and seeds. - The terrain-penalty failure is a valuable empirical observation: joint-level differentiable constraints reduced penetration by deforming the skeleton, whereas post-hoc rigid projection avoided that tradeoff; the resulting design lesson is specific and technically useful. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify appearance drift across chunks because appearance has no deterministic state, incomplete state coverage for visible AI companions and small monsters, and a train-test distribution shift between ground-truth pose-control videos and generated pose-control videos. They also state that dynamics currently cover only a single monster type and that the experimental slice fixes one weapon, one-on-one combat, and a restricted subset of the broader WildWorld corpus. They propose persistent per-entity reference images, recording state for all visible entities, state perturbation during observation-model training, and broader feasibility projections as remedies. The authors directly discuss the negative result from differentiable terrain penalties rather than presenting it as a success. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central comparison does not isolate the cost and benefit of explicit state against strong contemporary structured or physics-based baselines; the only quantitative head-to-head is against one same-data pixel-autoregressive model, while commercial systems are compared qualitatively under mismatched text controls. The claimed preservation of visual fidelity rests on FVD, whose intervals overlap and whose sensitivity to identity, entity-level action compliance, geometry, and appearance persistence is limited; no human study or task-specific visual metric tests these properties. The reported rule improvements use hand-selected thresholds, especially the 6 m separation cap, and the paper does not evaluate robustness to threshold changes, alternative constraint sets, or adversarial states. The observation model receives first-frame appearance conditioning and training pairs containing visible entities with no state, so unchanged aggregate FVD does not prove that all visible content remains consistent with the explicit state. The experiments do not report action vocabulary coverage, per-action success rates, unseen-action generalization, multiple random seeds for model training, runtime, or real-time performance. Finally, claims that the approach scales mechanically to additional monsters and hunters are architectural assertions, not demonstrated results; added entities change state dimensionality, action vocabularies, data requirements, and potentially interaction complexity. Bottom Line: This is a useful and technically credible preprint for the structured-world-model and controllable-game-video communities because it turns an abstract state/appearance factorization into an inspectable system with concrete intervention tests, but its narrow single-game evaluation and weak baseline coverage do not yet justify claims of a scalable general interactive world model.

HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds (110 ▲ )

Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, Jun Gao, Jiawei Chi, Hanyang Wang, Qiyu Dai, Yihao Li, Hao Li, Jingnan Gao, Yi-Hsin Hung, Xingzhuo Guo, Shangchen Miao, Zhiyuan Shi, Xiang Li, Fengrui Tian, Weihua Du, Ziqi Huang, Shenyuan Gao, Siqiao Huang, Mingyu Liu, Yifei Li, Shizun Wang, Xi Wang, Tianqi Zhang, Xue Luo, Xiyin Ren, Jinshan Ren, Xiaoyang Shen, Xiaobo Hu, Zhiyang Dou, Mingyu Ding, Yichao Yan, Xinchao Wang, Yizhou Wang, Shilong Liu, Wenzhao Zheng, Yueqi Duan, Yuan Gong, Ziwei Liu, Ming-Yu Liu, Jialong Wu, Jiangran Lyu, Fangfu Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 18 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HarnessEval-W, an agentic benchmark and evaluation pipeline that scores interactive world-model rollouts across eight world-state metrics while producing an auditable evidence tree for every judgment. - Why it's important: Reliable evaluation of physical causality, action compliance, and long-horizon state consistency is a bottleneck for comparing world models, yet scalar benchmark scores provide little indication of why a model succeeds or fails. - How it does it: A case-specific planner routes each evaluation case to reusable skills, decomposes each skill into specialized visual sub-questions, validates the gathered evidence, and aggregates the results into per-axis and overall scores. - The good: On 5,000 human A/B judgments, the evaluator's model rankings correlate with human preferences at Spearman ρ = 0.93 for intentional transitions and ρ = 0.87 for physical transitions; against WBench, physical-transition pairwise accuracy improves from 31.9% to 71.7%. - The missing: The paper does not establish that its LLM/VLM-based judgments remain valid outside its 330 synthetic, agent-authored cases, and it lacks component ablations, detailed human-annotation methodology, evaluator-cost measurements, and independent validation of the generated cases. - Read it or not: Researchers building or evaluating interactive video/world models should read it for the benchmark design and diagnostic-evaluation perspective, but should treat the leaderboard and claims of general evaluation reliability as preliminary because the evaluator and benchmark are both largely model-generated.
Why this rank

Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) reflect a useful evidence-tree formulation for interactive world-model evaluation, though its routing, decomposition, and aggregation largely combine established agentic judging techniques. Rigor (72), Completeness (65), and Resilience (60) are pulled down by synthetic model-generated cases, missing ablations, limited human validation, unclear annotation methodology, absent cost analysis, and lack of cross-evaluator replication.
