Problem & Motivation: Interactive world models must render coherent observations, execute requested interventions, and preserve or evolve latent world state over time. Existing video and world-model benchmarks measure visual quality, prompt adherence, physics, action following, memory, or consistency using largely fixed rubrics and often compress a rollout into a scalar score. This makes failures in target selection, final-state correctness, unintended events, causal response, object persistence, and offscreen evolution difficult to diagnose or verify. The target users are world-model researchers and benchmark developers working with text-conditioned video generators, camera-controlled models, and native action-conditioned interactive simulators. The claimed gap is an evaluation procedure that adapts the tested questions and evidence-gathering process to each case rather than applying every metric uniformly. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat evaluation as a hierarchical, evidence-acquisition workflow rather than as a single judgment or fixed metric. A parent evaluator interprets the case and activates only applicable skills; each skill delegates narrowly defined questions such as target visibility, target specificity, final-state validity, anchor preservation, or absence of extra events to specialized sub-agents; the parent then validates and aggregates their evidence. This is a meaningful procedural extension of agent-as-a-judge and tool-grounded visual evaluation, although the underlying components—LLM/VLM judging, task decomposition, routing, and aggregation—are established techniques. Methodology: The paper first models an interactive world model as a latent-state transition process, with future observations generated by an observation model S(o_i|s_i), a transition model T(s_i|s_{i-1},a_{i-1}), and an initial-state inference term conditioned on history. It maps this formulation to three axes and eight metrics: Render Quality and Physical Observation under Observation Quality; Exploratory, Intentional, and Physical Transition Correctness under Transition Correctness; and Drift Resistance, Revisit Consistency, and Offscreen Evolution under World Persistence. For each case, a planner consumes the initial image, prompt, and evaluation setting and selects applicable skills from a library, recording reasons for both activated and skipped skills. Activated skills generate expected outcomes and invoke specialized sub-agents or visual tools over sampled rollout frames; a parent skill agent scores the sub-questions, validates evidence, and produces a case-level score. Scores initially lie in [0,1], are reported on a 1–100 scale, and are averaged across cases, with observation metrics evaluated on all 330 cases and other metrics evaluated on their corresponding probe subsets. The benchmark itself is built by sampling a six-axis scene taxonomy, assigning one of six probe families, generating an initial image with text-to-image generation, planning an image-grounded action or trajectory, and filtering candidates with a separate LLM validator. The critical design decisions are adaptive skill routing, decomposition into fine-grained evidence questions, and agent-generated case construction; the paper motivates each conceptually but provides limited formal or empirical justification for the routing policy, aggregation rule, or validator thresholds. Key Results: HarnessEval-W evaluates 18 models on 330 frozen cases. Seedance 2.0 ranks first overall at 75.5, followed by Wan 2.7 at 75.0, Kling 3.0 at 74.4, and MiniMax H3 at 74.3. Wan 2.7 leads Intentional Transition at 83.6 and Physical Transition at 71.1; Seedance 2.0 leads Drift Resistance at 79.8; HY-WorldPlay 1.5 leads Revisit Consistency at 81.9; and SANA-WM leads Offscreen Evolution at 72.3. The evaluated models include 10 prompt-based image-to-video systems, two native-action systems, and six camera-pose systems, with several closed-source models accessed through official APIs. In the human-alignment study, 5,000 pairwise judgments over nine models yield ρ = 0.93 and Kendall τ = 0.82 for Intentional Transition, and ρ = 0.87 and τ = 0.74 for Physical Transition. Against WBench on the same videos and GPT-5.5 backend, HarnessEval-W increases pairwise accuracy from 60.2% to 77.8% for intentional evaluation and from 31.9% to 71.7% for physical evaluation; draw rates fall from 36.1% to 11.1% and from 52.2% to 1.8%, respectively, and Brier scores are lower in both settings. Repeated temperature-zero runs produce evaluator-to-human correlations between 0.928 and 0.964, with a fitted-curve envelope of 0.33 Bradley–Terry units versus 1.61 for WBench. Across the 18 models, Intentional and Physical Transition correlate at r = 0.98, while Exploratory Transition correlates weakly with them at r = −0.15 and −0.18. Descriptive comparisons between base and action-conditioned models suggest capability tradeoffs: the paper reports that DreamX-World loses roughly 12 points on Intentional and 8 points on Physical while gaining on exploration and revisit, and HY-WorldPlay loses roughly 23 points on Intentional and 12 points on Physical while gaining roughly 13 points on Revisit. The text and figure report slightly different numerical deltas, which should be reconciled. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuine contribution is an open, agentified evaluation harness that makes case-specific routing and decomposed evidence traces first-class benchmark outputs, while its individual mechanisms are mostly standard agentic judging and visual-analysis techniques applied to interactive world-model evaluation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper uses a common evaluator backend, temperature, and frame-sampling configuration across models and controls the WBench comparison by reusing the same videos and GPT-5.5 backend, which strengthens the protocol comparison. It reports a human A/B study, Bradley–Terry aggregation, rank correlations, pairwise accuracy, draw rate, Brier score, repeated-run stability, and 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples for the fine-tuning comparisons. However, no ablation isolates the value of routing, sub-agent decomposition, tool use, parent validation, or the case validator; no inter-annotator agreement, annotator demographics, sampling procedure, confidence intervals for the main human-alignment statistics, or per-case human labels are stated; and robustness is tested across repeated runs of the same GPT-5.5 backend rather than across independent evaluator families. The benchmark cases are generated from a synthetic taxonomy using image-generation and LLM planning/validation, so the evaluator and data construction process may share model biases. The paper does not report evaluator latency, token usage, API cost, failure rates, or calibration against independently authored expert cases. Code, a project page, and the full pipeline are stated to be available at https://github.com/mirros-lab/harnesseval-w and https://mirros-lab.github.io/HarnessEval-W, but the parsed paper does not specify the release contents, license, exact checkpoints, or whether all generated cases, rollout inputs, traces, and evaluation prompts are included. The work is an arXiv preprint dated August 2026, not a reported peer-reviewed publication. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper delivers and runs an executable benchmark system and evaluates it experimentally. Practical: The pipeline can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but its dependence on proprietary GPT-5.5/VLM APIs, image/video models, and unspecified visual tools makes local deployment requirements and operational constraints Not stated. Efficient: The method invokes multiple sub-agents and validation stages per rollout, so it is likely more expensive than a single rubric-based judge, but the paper reports no latency, memory, throughput, token, or monetary cost comparison. Effective: Evidence supports improved agreement with human preferences and discrimination relative to WBench for intentional and physical transitions, but it evaluates only two of the eight skills against humans and therefore does not establish effectiveness for persistence, observation quality, or broad physical reasoning. Scalable: The released benchmark contains 330 cases and 18 evaluated models, but 10×–100× scaling in cases, rollout length, skill-library size, evaluator compute, or model diversity is not tested; the proposed self-evolving and test-time-scaling behavior remains future work. The work delivers a software benchmark/tool and dataset of evaluation cases, rather than only a paper-form proposal. Strengths: - It reframes benchmark output from a scalar leaderboard number to a structured evidence tree, enabling diagnoses such as wrong-target edits, missing final states, protected-anchor violations, and extra events. - The three-axis/eight-metric decomposition covers complementary capabilities that are often conflated: rendering, action-conditioned transition, and long-horizon persistence, including offscreen evolution. - The controlled WBench comparison is informative: using the same videos and judging backend isolates protocol design and shows large gains in physical-transition discrimination and human agreement. - The benchmark exposes a potentially useful empirical pattern: converting text-to-video models into action-conditioned world models may trade commanded-interaction fidelity for exploration and revisit consistency, although the comparison is descriptive rather than causal. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper does not present a dedicated limitations section. It explicitly frames HarnessEval-W as an initial system and identifies future needs for test-time compute scaling, expansion of the skill library, and recursive self-improvement when the evaluator encounters unsupported scenarios. It also states that capability-shift comparisons between released base and derived models are descriptive rather than controlled ablations. Specific limitations involving synthetic case provenance, evaluator bias, cost, cross-backend robustness, or human-study design are Not stated. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest concern is circularity: LLMs generate initial scenes, plan actions, validate cases, route skills, and judge rollouts, while the human study covers only selected transition settings. The paper does not show that agent-generated cases faithfully represent real interactive-world use or that their expected outcomes are independently correct. The fixed 330-case set is relatively small for eight metrics and has uneven probe-family sizes—108 exploratory, 51 intentional, 66 physical, 34 drift, 34 revisit, and 37 offscreen cases—so leaderboard differences may be sensitive to case composition. Cross-interface comparisons are also difficult because text-to-video, camera-pose, and native-action models receive translated inputs that may not be equally natural or equally expressive. The overall score averages heterogeneous metrics and case subsets without a sensitivity analysis over metric weighting or probe-family balance. No evaluator-human agreement is reported for observation and persistence metrics, no adversarial cases test systematic judge failures, and no independent expert audit checks whether evidence traces are factually grounded rather than merely plausible textual explanations. The fine-tuning analysis compares released systems with potentially different training, inference, duration, and interface details; despite bootstrap intervals, it cannot support the proposed causal explanation about training-data emphasis. Finally, the paper does not quantify computational cost, API dependence, reproducibility across VLMs, or degradation when models produce long, low-quality, or unusual rollouts. Bottom Line: HarnessEval-W offers a useful and potentially reusable benchmark-engineering pattern—decomposed, evidence-traceable evaluation for interactive world models—and is worth reading for benchmark researchers, but its strongest claims should remain provisional until independent case authoring, broader evaluator validation, ablations, cost analysis, and cross-backend replication are provided.

SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science? (56 ▲ )

Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, Yining Zheng, Yuxin Wang, Xipeng Qiu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SWE-bench Science, a repository-level benchmark of 119 scientific software engineering tasks drawn from 98 GitHub repositories across 20 scientific domains, together with a failure taxonomy and a paired scientific-information ablation. - Why it's important: Incorrect scientific software can invalidate experimental, simulation, or analytical conclusions, so passing ordinary software tests is insufficient evidence that an agent preserved scientific meaning. - How it does it: The benchmark freezes reproducible repository snapshots, supplies agents with public tasks and tests, evaluates patches against hidden scientific validators, and separates tasks into Issue-driven, Expert-exploratory, and Engineering-integration paradigms. - The good: The benchmark exposes a large gap between public-test performance and complete scientific correctness: the best overall Pass@1 is 47.90% despite a 96.64% mean public score for the same agent. - The missing: The paper does not report repeated runs, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or inter-rater reliability for its manually assigned failure categories, limiting confidence in comparative and causal conclusions. - Read it or not: Researchers building coding agents or evaluating scientific software should read it for the benchmark and failure taxonomy; readers seeking a new repair algorithm or a validated intervention can largely skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Scientific software increasingly mediates simulations, instrument processing, numerical analysis, machine-learning workflows, and high-throughput experiments. Researchers therefore need repository-level maintenance that preserves scientific contracts such as unit consistency, coordinate invariance, physical conservation, statistical semantics, and end-to-end data-flow behavior. Existing code benchmarks emphasize standalone function synthesis or generic issue resolution, while scientific benchmarks often test self-contained implementations, paper reproduction, or broader research workflows rather than maintenance of interacting production repositories. The gap is an evaluation setting that tests whether an agent can infer and preserve domain-specific semantics under hidden cases, boundary conditions, alternate representations, and cross-module integration. Key Idea: The central insight is to evaluate scientific software repair as preservation of hidden scientific contracts rather than as public-test passing. The benchmark operationalizes this through a Chain-of-Evidence Protocol: public materials expose a reproducible symptom and executable context, while private validators vary scientific cases and test semantic equivalence, boundary behavior, regression preservation, and system integration. The paper also treats explicit scientific guidance as a separable information factor, enabling paired comparison without removing repository-intrinsic engineering evidence. Methodology: The authors construct 119 tasks from 98 repositories by sampling issues, pull requests, commits, literature, and scientific scenarios; freezing pre-fix snapshots; reproducing the defect or capability gap in containers; abstracting public descriptions and domain context; and creating hidden validators with alternative cases and anti-overfitting checks. Tasks are assigned to three paradigms: 52 Issue-driven tasks test repair of known defects, 49 Expert-exploratory tasks require root-cause discovery from a scientific discrepancy, and 18 Engineering-integration tasks require completion of multi-module capability chains. Agents receive a repository snapshot, problem statement, required scientific context, and public tests, then inspect, edit, execute, and revise code; submitted patches are evaluated in a clean environment with public and private tests. Metrics include mean PublicScore, mean PrivateScore, Fail2Pass, Pass2Pass, and binary Pass@1, where Pass@1 requires every applicable private test to pass. The main design decisions are hidden semantic validation, preservation of executable repository context when removing auxiliary science information, and classification by task paradigm; the paper motivates these choices, but does not quantify validator coverage, establish independent annotation reliability, or show that the paradigms are statistically separable. Key Results: Across eight model–harness configurations on the common 119 tasks, Claude-Opus-5 with Claude Code achieves the highest overall Pass@1 at 47.90%, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with Codex at 46.22% and DeepSeek-V4-Pro with Claude Code at 42.02%. Claude-Opus-5 leads Issue-driven tasks at 38.46% and Expert-exploratory tasks at 65.31%, while DeepSeek-V4-Pro leads Engineering-integration at 44.44%. GPT-5.6-sol has the highest mean PrivateScore at 78.82%, Fail2Pass at 72.30%, and Pass2Pass at 97.66%; DeepSeek-V4-Pro has the highest PublicScore at 100.00%. Public scores range from 93.28% to 100.00%, whereas Pass@1 ranges from 14.29% for Qwen3.5-397B to 47.90%, demonstrating that visible tests substantially overestimate complete repair. On the 91-task paired subset, adding scientific information raises DeepSeek-V4-flash Pass@1 from 16.48% to 23.08%, but lowers GPT-5.6-sol from 36.26% to 31.87%; the intervention raises DeepSeek-V4-flash input/output consumption from 4.84 million/128.43 thousand tokens to 7.40 million/159.26 thousand, while reducing GPT-5.6-sol consumption from 3.86 million/43.75 thousand to 3.70 million/40.25 thousand. These are descriptive paired differences, not statistically established causal effects. The benchmark spans repository contexts from 174 to 2,029,051 non-empty lines and reference patches averaging 117.81 additions and 44.53 deletions, but the paper does not report performance by scientific domain or stress results at larger task counts. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION. The substantive contribution is a cross-domain repository-level benchmark with hidden scientific-contract validation, three task paradigms, and a scientific-information ablation; the agent execution loop, patch-based evaluation, public/private tests, and most coding-agent comparisons are standard components applied to scientific software. Rigor & Reproducibility: The benchmark code, dataset, and leaderboard are publicly linked at https://github.com/OpenMOSS/SWE-bench-Science, https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science, and https://swescience.github.io, respectively; the paper does not mention released model weights because it evaluates external agents. The task schema, repository snapshots, public/private separation, task provenance inventory, and exact aggregate metrics are described in detail. However, the experiments appear to use one attempt per task/configuration, with no seeds, repeated stochastic trials, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Failure mechanisms are manually audited, but annotation procedures, annotator counts, adjudication, and inter-rater agreement are not reported. The comparison confounds model identity with harness, reasoning mode, and likely proprietary implementation details, and the scientific-information ablation compares only GPT-5.6-sol and DeepSeek-V4-flash on 91 tasks. The authors claim leakage controls and contamination metadata, but provide no quantitative contamination audit in the paper. Domain imbalance is substantial: Chemistry contributes 24 tasks, while six domains contribute one task each, and the five largest domains account for 76 of 119 tasks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The benchmark can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not report hardware requirements, wall-clock time, external API cost, or the resources needed to execute the largest repositories. Efficient: Token use varies widely—mean input consumption is plotted for the agents and the ablation reports 3.70–7.40 million input tokens per task—but runtime, memory, dollar cost, and comparison with non-agent repair tools are not evaluated. Effective: Hidden scientific validators provide stronger evidence than public tests, and the best agent solves 47.90% of tasks exactly, but this remains a proxy for real scientific reliability because no downstream scientific workflows, human expert judgments, or consequential deployments are measured. Scalable: The dataset includes repositories up to 2,029,051 non-empty lines, yet only 119 tasks are evaluated; the paper does not test performance at 10×–100× task volume, larger private suites, longer interaction horizons, or substantially larger repositories. The work delivers a reusable benchmark dataset, evaluator, code repository, and leaderboard, but not a new coding agent or repair algorithm. Strengths: - The benchmark targets a meaningful failure mode that generic repository repair scores miss: patches can pass visible tests while violating scientific invariants, boundary semantics, alternate representations, or system-wide contracts. - Its 119 tasks cover 20 scientific domains and three explicitly differentiated task paradigms, providing broader scientific repository coverage than the comparison benchmarks summarized in the paper, although coverage remains uneven. - The public/private evaluation design and example of a patch passing a public diagnostic while failing 3 of 10 private scientific cases directly demonstrate why exact hidden validation matters. - The paired ablation isolates the marginal role of explicit scientific information while retaining code structure and executable context; the opposite effects for GPT-5.6-sol and DeepSeek-V4-flash are a useful empirical warning against assuming that more domain guidance uniformly helps. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the number of tasks per scientific domain is limited, reducing the reliability of domain-level comparisons. They also acknowledge that their analysis of how agents use scientific knowledge remains preliminary and does not sufficiently explain how domain knowledge should be supplied to improve task completion. The conclusion calls for broader model coverage. These limitations are stated directly, but the paper does not discuss the absence of repeated trials, statistical testing, annotation reliability, cost measurement, or possible benchmark-selection bias. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The benchmark construction depends heavily on author-defined scientific contracts and hidden validators, but the paper does not establish that these validators are complete, unbiased, or independently reviewed by domain experts; a hidden test can itself encode the reference implementation’s assumptions. The dataset is partly derived from historical issues and pull requests, and the paper does not provide a quantitative contamination analysis despite evaluating models that may have seen public repositories or fixes during training. Model comparisons are not controlled for harness, maximum reasoning settings, context policies, or API versions, so leaderboard differences cannot be attributed cleanly to model capability. The failure taxonomy is useful but may be subjective and mutually exclusive categories can oversimplify multi-cause failures; no inter-rater agreement is reported. The study lacks strong non-LLM baselines, human developer performance, conventional program-repair systems, multi-sample success rates, and domain-stratified confidence estimates. Finally, exact Pass@1 treats all tasks as equally weighted despite large differences in repository size, scientific complexity, and number of private tests, and the paper does not evaluate whether benchmark success transfers to real scientific users or downstream scientific conclusions. Bottom Line: Read this preprint if you work on coding-agent evaluation or scientific software reliability—the benchmark and public/private scientific-contract framing are useful—but treat its model rankings and scientific-information conclusions as preliminary until repeated controlled experiments, independent validator audits, and stronger baselines are provided.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Harness-IF, a rule-level benchmark and Against-Prior Accuracy (AP-Acc) metric for evaluating instruction following by coding agents across system prompts, tool descriptions, skill descriptions, project files, and user instructions. - Why it's important: Aggregate task-success or instruction-following scores can count behavior as compliant even when the agent would have produced the same behavior without the instruction, obscuring failures that matter in deployed multi-surface agent workflows. - How it does it: It executes 60 multi-turn coding tasks containing 25–35 atomic rules each, extracts pass/fail verdicts from traces and artifacts, and compares ordinary accuracy with accuracy on rules labeled as opposing the agent's unprompted default behavior. - The good: Across 12 model builds and 37,616 eligible verdicts, every model performs worse on against-prior rules, with an Acc–AP-Acc gap of 3.6–7.4 percentage points that remains positive under common-support, item-clustered analysis. - The missing: The main evaluation is heavily dependent on an LLM judge—86.8% of verdict rows involve GPT-5.2—and a judge swap yields only 62.1% agreement and κ = 0.163 on 116 paired clean verdicts, limiting confidence in absolute scores and fine-grained rankings. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners building coding-agent evaluations should read it for its prior-controlled measurement design, but should not use its leaderboard or surface accuracies as definitive without independently validating the released scoring judgments.

Problem & Motivation: Coding agents receive instructions through a distributed operational stack rather than a single user prompt: platform defaults, system prompts, tool and skill descriptions, project files, and current user requests. Existing instruction-following benchmarks largely place constraints in user messages, while coding-agent benchmarks usually collapse long trajectories into final task success. This leaves two gaps: evaluators cannot reliably determine whether an observed behavior resulted from following a particular operational rule or from an unprompted default, and they cannot cleanly study how delivery surface affects compliance or precedence. The target users are researchers evaluating agent behavior and developers deploying coding agents whose intermediate actions, edits, tool use, and final reports must satisfy project- and platform-level policies. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat instruction following as an execution-level, rule-by-rule attribution problem and to control for coincidental compliance by evaluating rules that oppose observed unprompted defaults. Harness-IF separates the delivery surface of a rule from its semantic content, while AP-Acc restricts measurement to against-prior rules. This is more than ordinary constraint checking, but the prior-control idea depends on behavioral labels that are partly generated from zero-injection probes and partly curated rather than established through an independent causal intervention for every rule. Methodology: The benchmark begins with a 642-rule library covering seven families—professional writing, output control, code style, workflow, quantitative limits, conditional logic, and tool use—and seven logical modalities, including require, forbid, conditional-require, maximum/minimum limits, prefer, and allow. Rules are tagged for behavioral prior, observability, verifiability, universality, and surface fit. Authors assemble 80 candidate coding items and retain 60 after human quality and discriminativeness review; each retained item combines a realistic code fixture, tests, a multi-turn task, 25–35 injected rules, surface-specific renderings, and scoring scripts. The main panel assigns admissible rules to one of five configurable surfaces—system prompt, tool description, skill description, project file, or user instruction—while keeping a harness default fixed. Twelve model builds run each of the 60 items for three rounds, producing 2,160 agent-item-round runs and 40,104 method-level verdict rows. Evidence includes traces, file differences, tests, artifacts, logs, and final outputs. Rules receive pass, fail, or not-applicable labels through deterministic checks, AST and cross-file checks, command-output checks, hybrid checks, or an LLM judge; rubric and hybrid judgments use three GPT-5.2 votes at temperature 0.3. The primary accuracy metric averages eligible binary pass/fail rule instances, while F-Acc removes nondiscriminative rules and DW-Acc weights rules by correlation with overall agent accuracy. AP-Acc averages only eligible rules labeled against-prior. Prior labels come from a nine-build zero-injection probe when a 5-of-9 consensus is available, and from curation or prior records otherwise. A separate E0 pilot uses 916 runs from nine older builds, four synthetic conflict pairs, counterbalanced surface assignments, deterministic scoring, and Bradley–Terry analysis to study precedence rather than isolated compliance. The key design decisions are rule-level scoring, exclusion of no-opportunity cases, and prior stratification; the first two are appropriate for the stated measurement goal, while the justification for mixed empirical and curated prior labels and for selecting items partly by discriminativeness is weaker because both can affect validity and generalization. Key Results: On the main coding panel, ordinary accuracy ranges from 72.1% to 85.9%, while AP-Acc ranges from 66.1% to 78.6%. Claude-Opus-4.7 scores highest on both metrics at 85.9% Acc and 78.6% AP-Acc; StepFun-3.5 is lowest at 72.1% and 66.2%, respectively. Every model has a positive Acc–AP-Acc gap, ranging from 3.6 points for GLM-5.1 to 7.4 points for Seed-2.0-Pro, with a mean gap of 5.81 points over 37,616 eligible verdicts and 19,449 against-prior verdicts. A common-support analysis retains 2,430 of 3,342 observation keys, or 72.7%, and item-clustered intervals remain positive for all 12 models; however, all adjacent model comparisons include zero, so the leaderboard is not statistically resolved at neighboring ranks. Prior control leaves the top model unchanged but swaps three adjacent rank pairs. Failures total 8,440: 77.1% concern shortfall rules, 20.8% overstep rules, and 2.1% preferences, although shortfall and overstep fail rates are similar at 23.8% and 20.8%, indicating that failure mass mainly reflects rule exposure. Output control has the lowest family accuracy at 70.9%, versus 82.6% for quantitative limits, and is the lowest family for 11 of 12 models. Commanding rules are the hardest modality at 76.0%, while preferences reach 90.6%. In E0, pooled mean precedence ranks are system prompt, project file, and user instruction tied at 2.22, followed by tool description at 3.78 and skill description at 4.56; the complete ordering appears in 9,652 of 10,000 crossed model-and-pair bootstrap samples. Only six of nine individual model fits reproduce the exact ordering, so this supports a pooled tendency over four synthetic conflicts rather than a universal hierarchy. The exploratory non-coding panel reports case-macro pass rates from 65.8% to 84.8%, led by GPT-5.5 rather than Claude-Opus-4.7, but uses a different population, metric, and model snapshot and is not directly comparable. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely new elements are the surface-aware rule-level benchmark construction and AP-Acc's explicit stratification of compliance by opposition to observed defaults; the execution stack, deterministic/rubric checking, multi-turn coding tasks, and conflict-precedence analysis combine established evaluation practices rather than introducing a new learning algorithm or theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides multiple rounds, common-support restrictions, item-clustered bootstrap intervals, test–retest statistics, deterministic-only sensitivity analysis, prior-label threshold sweeps, and extensive E0 leave-one-model/pair-out and error-assignment checks. The main panel contains 37,616 eligible binary verdicts, but the effective independent sample is much smaller because observations share 60 items, 12 models, and repeated rounds. Test–retest ICC is 0.725 at the agent level and 0.599 at the agent-item level, with a mean per-cell accuracy range of 15.6 percentage points across rounds. The dominant scoring mechanism is an LLM judge or hybrid method covering 86.7% of eligible verdicts. The judge-swap analysis is concerning: GPT-5.2 versus Claude Opus yields 62.1% agreement and κ = 0.163 on 116 paired clean verdicts, with per-agent pass-rate changes from −40 to +33 points. A related, historical five-vote human-reference audit reports 69.0% agreement and κ = 0.515 over 919 rows, but its sampling frame, raw labels, rater assignments, and exact protocol are not fully retained, and it does not directly validate the frozen three-vote panel. Prior labels are independent of the evaluated cohort for only part of the data: 44.1% of against-prior verdicts derive from zero-injection consensus, and those probes overlap five evaluated model identifiers, although seven evaluated models are absent from the probe cohort. Item selection used observed difficulty and discriminativeness, creating explicit selection optimism. The authors state that code, the rule library, 60 items, scoring scripts, sanitized verdict records, and analysis scripts are intended for public release; no URL is given, and raw provider outputs and workspaces are not redistributed, preventing full end-to-end trajectory replay. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper evaluates a benchmark and scoring pipeline on executed coding-agent runs rather than proving a theorem or reporting a deployed service. Practical: The benchmark can run on commercially available API-accessible models and a coding-agent harness, but it requires access to a separate judge model and realistic execution environments. Efficient: The reported evaluation costs 2,160 agent runs plus judge inference for approximately 40,104 method rows; no token, latency, monetary, or hardware cost comparison is provided. Effective: The evidence supports detection of systematic differences between aggregate and against-prior rule compliance, but judge instability and the lack of direct causal isolation for every prior label limit claims about true instruction-following ability. Scalable: The study tests 60 items, 12 models, and three rounds, not 10×–100× larger panels; scalability is plausible for offline verdict regeneration, but construction, judging, and execution costs at larger rule libraries are not evaluated. The work delivers a benchmark/data package, scoring scripts, analysis code, and sanitized result records in planned form; it does not yet provide a stated public repository URL or a trained model. Strengths: - It identifies a real measurement failure in conventional instruction-following scores: compliance can be indistinguishable from default behavior, and the paper quantifies this inflation for every evaluated model rather than merely asserting it. - The rule-level representation preserves execution evidence and supports decomposition by family, modality, observability, and surface, giving the benchmark diagnostic value beyond a single task-success number. - The prior-alignment finding is unusually resilient across like-for-like scoring, common support, deterministic-only checks, prior-label threshold sweeps, and all 12 model builds. - The E0 pilot uses counterbalancing, crossed model/pair resampling, leave-one-out analyses, and conservative treatment of errors; importantly, the authors avoid presenting its pooled surface order as a universal instruction hierarchy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the main claims to 60 selected coding items, 302 instantiated rules, and 256 rules receiving verdicts, with professional-writing rules evaluated only in a separate non-coding extension. They acknowledge that item selection based on difficulty and discriminativeness may cause selection optimism; AP-Acc is a behavioral stratification rather than a training-provenance claim; almost 87% of verdicts involve an LLM judge whose labels change under judge substitution; F-Acc and DW-Acc are cohort-adaptive; fine-grained neighboring rankings are not reliable; the main panel does not identify causal surface effects because admissible placement, wording, family, and surface co-vary; and E0's result is a pooled tendency from four synthetic conflicts and nine older builds. They also document incomplete provenance and release boundaries, including unavailable raw provider traces and qualified human calibration evidence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most consequential unacknowledged—or insufficiently resolved—issue is construct validity of AP-Acc: a rule can be labeled against-prior because of a broad default tendency or curator judgment, but the paper does not run a paired with-rule/without-rule intervention for every scored rule and model, so lower AP-Acc cannot by itself establish that the instruction caused a behavioral departure. The judge-swap result is strong evidence that absolute pass rates and possibly family/prior effects are judge-dependent, yet the paper does not report an alternate-judge AP-Acc gap or row-level adjudication sufficient to test whether the headline effect survives judge substitution. The 60-item panel is selected after observing pilot difficulty and discriminativeness, and the paper does not provide a held-out confirmatory set showing that the 5.81-point gap generalizes beyond optimized items. The E0 conflicts are synthetic and few, and the fixed AB-before-BA collection order leaves a residual temporal or session-order confound. The main surface-level accuracy table is especially easy to misread: user-instruction placements are exclusively against-prior, and other surfaces have different rule-family compositions, so it cannot estimate surface difficulty. Finally, the benchmark omits specialized coding-only and fine-tuned models and lacks human-authored scoring validation for the exact frozen protocol. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile benchmark-design paper with a credible and repeatedly supported warning that aggregate instruction-following scores overstate compliance, but its AP-Acc construct and LLM-judged measurements require independent validation before the benchmark should serve as a definitive model ranking or deployment certification.

XBridge: Entity-Grounded Latent Bridge for Heterogeneous LLM Communication

W Yang, WC Huang, W Zhang, Y Wang, PS Yu, J Lee · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces XBRIDGE, a decode-free communication protocol that combines receiver-vocabulary token mapping with a learned cross-attention bridge for transferring context and hidden states between heterogeneous LLMs. - Why it's important: Heterogeneous multi-agent systems can avoid redundant reasoning, but existing text communication is slow and lossy while latent communication often loses exact entity identity or assumes architectural compatibility. - How it does it: Lexical Anchor Mapping (LAM) prepends receiver-native embeddings of the sender’s context, while a 264M-parameter Latent Enrichment Bridge (LEB) lets the receiver query the sender’s hidden states through gated cross-attention at four receiver layers. - The good: Across three model families and seven benchmarks, XBRIDGE beats heterogeneous natural-language communication on every task and direction tested, with 11× lower reported latency; on Llama→Qwen it raises average F1 from 41.8% to 63.2%. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish whether XBRIDGE is competitive under realistic communication-bandwidth and memory constraints, because it transmits the full mapped context in addition to sender hidden states and omits a strong cross-architecture latent baseline such as C2C from the main comparisons. - Read it or not: Researchers working on latent LLM communication or multi-agent inference should read it for the discrete-anchor/continuous-enrichment decomposition, but practitioners should wait for evaluations that measure end-to-end cost, context-length scaling, and stronger cross-architecture baselines.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses asymmetric multi-agent question answering in which a sender sees a context document and a receiver sees only the question, with the two agents drawn from different LLM families, tokenizers, hidden dimensions, and architectures. Existing natural-language communication is architecture-agnostic but requires autoregressive summary generation and can discard internal contextual structure; latent transfer avoids decoding but commonly assumes shared architecture or directly projects continuous states without reliably preserving rare names, numbers, dates, and other exact entities. The paper calls this failure the entity grounding problem: contextual information may cross the bridge while the receiver loses the discrete lexical identity to which that information refers. The motivation is therefore strongest for heterogeneous, asymmetric communication rather than general multi-agent dialogue. Key Idea: The central insight is to separate discrete entity identity from continuous contextual reasoning. LAM copies the sender’s entire tokenized context into the receiver’s vocabulary through deterministic token mapping, ensuring that entity anchors exist in the receiver’s native embedding space; LEB then uses receiver-conditioned cross-attention to retrieve contextual information from sender hidden states. The receiver’s self-attention propagates the LAM anchors into its intermediate states, which become queries that bind LEB’s contextual signal to particular entities. This is a clear decomposition, although LAM is more than an entity-only channel because it transmits the full context rather than a compressed set of entity mentions. Methodology: The sender performs one frozen forward pass over context C and emits sender tokens and last-layer hidden states H_S. LAM maps each sender token to one or more receiver tokens using direct surface-string/ID lookup when possible and string decoding plus receiver retokenization otherwise; the resulting receiver embeddings are prepended to the receiver’s question embeddings. LEB inserts four independently parameterized gated cross-attention modules into receiver layers 6, 13, 20, and 27 of a 28-layer Qwen receiver. At each module, receiver states are layer-normalized and projected to queries, while sender last-layer states are separately normalized and projected to keys and values; scaled dot-product attention produces a retrieved signal that is added through h'_R = h_R + tanh(alpha) A. Only the bridge parameters are trained; sender and receiver remain frozen. Training uses answer-token next-token prediction, with 264M trainable bridge parameters and a balanced 587-example set spanning seven domains. Important design choices—four modules, last-layer sender states, and gate initialization alpha=1.0—receive ablations: four modules outperform one, two, and seven; the last sender layer reaches 78.8% F1 versus 64.6–70.2% for earlier layers; and warm gating reaches 78.8% versus 72.7% for zero initialization. The justification is empirical, but the experiments do not fully separate bridge capacity from parameter count or training dynamics. Key Results: On Llama-3.1-8B→Qwen2.5-7B, XBRIDGE obtains 63.2% average F1 across Countries, Tipsheets, HotpotQA, QASPER, MuSiQue, MultiFieldQA, and 2WikiMQA, versus 41.8% for heterogeneous NLComm, 20.8% for NoComm, and 55.2% for FullComm. On Qwen→Llama it obtains 61.9% versus 47.6% for NLComm and 61.2% for FullComm; on Mistral→Qwen it obtains 65.0% versus 44.1% for NLComm and 55.2% for FullComm. It beats NLComm on all seven tasks for all three heterogeneous pairs, with average gains of 21.4, 14.3, and 20.9 percentage points. The strongest gains occur on Countries, where Llama→Qwen improves from 22.6% to 72.5%, and on MuSiQue and 2WikiMQA; the smallest gain is on structured Tipsheets. On HotpotQA, the grounding ablation gives 24.6% NoComm, 30.3% LEB without LAM, 56.5% LAM without LEB, and 78.8% full XBRIDGE, supporting complementarity. Reported HotpotQA latency is 0.15 seconds per sample for XBRIDGE versus 1.70 seconds for NLComm, a nominal 11× reduction, but 0.13 seconds for FullComm and KVComm, so XBRIDGE is not the fastest latent or full-context alternative. In the same-architecture Qwen→Qwen setting, XBRIDGE averages 63.1% versus 51.1% for KVComm and 42.9% for homogeneous NLComm, beating KVComm on six of seven tasks but losing on MultiFieldQA. Dual independently trained bridges reach 70.4% on HotpotQA versus 56.8% for dual NLComm and 67.0% for a single Llama sender with both documents. Sender scaling is weak under the fixed training budget: Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 14B senders yield 59.5%, 61.9%, and 62.1% seven-task averages. The entity perturbation study reports that swapping LAM shifts target outputs toward the substituted entity, whereas swapping LEB alone does not; however, 55–59% of outputs mention neither target entity, limiting the strength of the role-separation conclusion. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the explicit formulation of rare-token/entity grounding as a failure mode of continuous cross-architecture communication and the paired use of receiver-native lexical anchors with receiver-queried latent enrichment; cross-attention, token remapping, gated residuals, and frozen-backbone training are individually standard components, and the work does not introduce a new dataset or benchmark. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports component ablations, module-count and sender-layer sweeps, gate initialization, auxiliary-loss, training-data-composition, sender-size, same-architecture, entity-perturbation, latency, and composability analyses. The balanced 587-example bridge training set outperforms 20K HotpotQA-only and 42K skewed training sets, which usefully exposes task-distribution sensitivity. Evaluation covers three model families, three heterogeneous directions, seven datasets, and disjoint training/evaluation splits. However, most accuracy tables provide single F1 values without multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the only reported statistical test concerns a 196-sample cosine-alignment diagnostic. The main heterogeneous comparison omits a direct C2C or other strong cross-architecture continuous-transfer baseline, despite discussing such methods. The public implementation is stated at https://github.com/WooseongYang/XBridge, but the paper does not state whether training data, preprocessing scripts, cached hidden states, exact evaluation code, or trained bridge weights are released. A major methodological issue is that XBRIDGE transmits the full context as receiver-native embeddings plus hidden states, while NLComm transmits a 128-token decoded summary; therefore the latency comparison is favorable but does not compare equal communication bandwidth, sequence length, or memory footprint. The FullComm comparison is also not an independent communication baseline because LAM gives the receiver the full context, and the reported improvements over FullComm may reflect the added sender representation rather than better context delivery. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a substantial SYSTEMS artifact component. Practical: The evaluated 7B–8B models and H200 measurements indicate that the method can run on commercially available accelerator hardware, but the paper does not report consumer-GPU, CPU, batching, or multi-request behavior. Efficient: XBRIDGE avoids autoregressive sender decoding and reports 0.15 seconds per HotpotQA sample versus 1.70 seconds for NLComm, but it adds 264M trainable bridge parameters, cross-attention over all sender positions at four layers, and full-context receiver processing; end-to-end memory, communication bytes, and throughput are not measured. Effective: The experiments show large F1 gains over the selected NLComm baseline and strong entity-rank and perturbation diagnostics, especially for reasoning tasks, but effectiveness is demonstrated primarily on seven QA benchmarks and does not establish robustness to noisy, adversarial, multilingual, conversational, or open-ended agent interactions. Scalable: The paper tests context lengths from approximately 11 to 6,979 tokens and combines two senders, but it does not evaluate 10×–100× context length, many-agent composition, multi-turn exchange, or bandwidth-constrained deployment; larger-sender scaling is nearly flat from 7B to 14B under the fixed 587-example training budget. The work delivers a public software implementation and trained bridge methodology, but the paper does not clearly state that model weights or all reproduction assets are released. It stops short of a deployed multi-agent infrastructure system: communication is one-way, single-exchange by default, and only a two-sender composition experiment is reported. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete failure mode—loss of discrete entity identity during continuous cross-architecture transfer—and gives it operational diagnostics through answer-token rank, entity representation alignment, and controlled entity substitution. - The LAM/LEB factorization is technically simple and conceptually useful: the ablation changes HotpotQA from 30.3% with LEB alone and 56.5% with LAM alone to 78.8% with both, directly supporting the claimed complementarity. - The evaluation spans three model families, both communication directions represented among heterogeneous pairs, seven task types, same-architecture transfer, sender-size variation, latency, and two-bridge composition rather than relying on one model pair. - The method achieves a meaningful practical latency advantage over autoregressive communication and requires training only a small fraction of the receiver, while the balanced-data experiment exposes that generalization depends more on task coverage than raw bridge-training volume. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that XBRIDGE currently supports one sender-to-receiver direction and one exchange, and that bidirectional multi-turn dialogue is not evaluated. They also acknowledge that many-agent composition remains open, despite demonstrating composition of two independently trained bridges. They note that the 587-example training budget becomes a bottleneck for the 14B sender, whose 62.1% average only matches the 7B sender’s 61.9%, and leave larger training sets for future work. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, but the discussion does not address bandwidth, memory, privacy, sequence-length, or fairness implications of transmitting the full context. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central unaddressed issue is cost accounting: because LAM sends the entire context, the method may shift work from autoregressive decoding to long-context embedding, receiver attention, and transmission, and the paper does not report bytes transferred, peak memory, token expansion, or throughput at long contexts. The comparison set is incomplete for the stated cross-architecture problem; C2C and other learned projection methods are discussed but not directly evaluated in the main heterogeneous experiments. FullComm is treated as an upper reference even though XBRIDGE receives the same full context through LAM and an additional sender-state signal, making claims that it exceeds FullComm difficult to interpret as communication efficiency or information preservation. The evaluation uses small fixed subsets—often 75–200 examples per task—and lacks seed variability and uncertainty estimates for the headline F1 results. The entity-fidelity diagnostic focuses on the first answer token for multi-token entities, while the perturbation experiment has a majority of outputs in the “neither” category, so the evidence for exact entity grounding is weaker than the aggregate claims suggest. Finally, the method’s apparent task generalization may depend on training on approximately 100 examples from every evaluation domain; this is a useful protocol for transfer, but it should be tested against broader unseen domains and distribution shifts before claiming general cross-task communication. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers studying latent LLM communication because it offers a clear discrete-plus-continuous design and strong controlled evidence, but its practical advantage is overstated until full-context bandwidth costs and competitive cross-architecture baselines are evaluated.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation The paper addresses zero-to-all repository generation: constructing an entire software project from high-level natural-language requirements without a predefined file layout, component decomposition, or dependency graph. The affected domain is long-horizon software engineering, where an agent must coordinate requirements, architecture, interfaces, implementation, and testing across many files. Existing repository-generation systems such as RPG generally create a static planning graph and then execute it, while other benchmarks provide architectural or interface priors. The claimed gap is that repository modularity is only partially observable from requirements and becomes clearer during decomposition and implementation; a one-shot plan may therefore create diffuse components, redundant responsibilities, excessive coupling, and inconsistent cross-file interfaces. Key Idea The central insight is to treat repository architecture as a persistent state that should be optimized incrementally rather than as a one-shot plan. Repo0 separates functional coordination among requirements from implementation dependencies among components using two linked DAGs, then uses cohesion and responsibility metrics to identify components that should be split and coupling/connectivity metrics to identify components that should be merged. This makes architectural refinement an explicit convergence process and preserves requirement-to-component traceability during restructuring. Methodology Repo0 has three main phases. First, an LLM extracts capability-level candidate requirements from the input document, merges redundant or subsumed items into high-level requirements, expands each high-level requirement into sub-requirements, and labels functional coordination edges to form the requirement DAG. It then maps sub-requirements to bounded implementation components, creates the many-to-many alignment relation, and infers a separate component-dependency DAG. Second, the system repeatedly evaluates the architecture. For component c, responsibility is the set of aligned sub-requirements, while cohesion is the density of requirement-DAG edges internal to that set; components below cohesion threshold gamma_split and above a size threshold become split candidates. Pairwise coupling is Jaccard similarity between responsibility sets, and pairs with coupling above theta_merge and connectivity greater than one become merge candidates. An LLM validates candidate actions and performs split, merge, revise, or save operations; the loop stops when a full round has no eligible split or merge, followed by a semantic alignment/revision pass. Third, the converged component DAG is converted into package assignments, file paths, symbols, and dependency-aware generation order. Each component receives context from its responsibility, aligned requirements, and upstream components; Repo0 generates an importable skeleton, synthesizes tests, fills in implementation, runs import/interface/pytest checks, and applies localized repairs. The paper does not define a single learned or globally optimized objective; the main control mechanism is thresholded modularity heuristics plus LLM judgment. The Dual-DAG separation is conceptually motivated and supported by ablations, but the choice of cohesion/coupling thresholds is empirically tuned through manual comparison with held-out golden architectures rather than justified analytically. Key Results The evaluation uses six paraphrased real-world Python repositories from RepoCraft: requests, statsmodels, django, scikit-learn, pandas, and sympy, ranging from 17 to 699 files and 2,793 to 218,924 effective lines of code. The main table reports requests, statsmodels, and django, using GPT-5 mini and DeepSeek V3.2, with mini-SWE-agent, Paper2Code, and RPG as baselines; the remaining repositories are stated to appear in the supplement. Repo0 achieves 100.00%, 80.68%, and 80.50% Functionality Coverage on requests, statsmodels, and django with GPT-5 mini, and 100.00%, 78.41%, and 79.17% with DeepSeek V3.2. Its corresponding Pass Rates are 50.98%, 85.51%, and 74.36% for GPT-5 mini, and 78.08%, 69.03%, and 74.07% for DeepSeek V3.2. Relative to RPG, the reported Pass Rate gains are 19.47, 7.61, and 27.03 points under GPT-5 mini; across the six-repository evaluation, the abstract reports maximum gains of 29.74 points for Pass Rate and 20.08 points for Coverage. Repo0 also has the highest Voting Rate in all six main settings. In the ablation study, removing structural evolution reduces Coverage by 5.68 points and Pass Rate by 8.47 points on requests, and reduces Coverage by 5.92 points and Pass Rate by 13.33 points on django. Removing component-graph ordering reduces statsmodels Pass Rate by 30 points while leaving Coverage unchanged. On statsmodels with GPT-5 mini, metrics-guided evolution improves Coverage from 75.90% without evolution to 80.68%, Pass Rate from 81.90% to 85.51%, and Voting Rate from 93.00% to 98.65%; fixed one-, three-, and five-round LLM-only evolution performs worse, although the five-round variant increases Functionality Novelty to 13.37% versus Repo0's 11.48%. These results support the claim that controlled refinement is more useful than simply allowing more structural actions, but the evaluation metrics include semantic matching and adapted tests, so they measure functional coverage and proxy correctness rather than complete software quality, maintainability, security, or architectural quality. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the substantive contribution is the formulation of zero-to-all repository generation as modularity-guided structural evolution with a linked requirement/component Dual-DAG and explicit convergence, while the underlying LLM prompting, graph representation, cohesion/coupling heuristics, dependency ordering, and TDD repair are largely standard techniques combined in this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility The study reports three independent runs per experimental setting and averages results, but it does not report standard deviations, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or per-run variance. It includes component ablations for requirement context, component-graph ordering, Dual-DAG representation, and structural evolution, plus a comparison against fixed-budget LLM-directed evolution. The ablations are useful, although several effects are measured on only three prominently reported repositories and some ablated variants improve Functionality Novelty while reducing required-functionality coverage, indicating metric tradeoffs. The authors state that code and data are available at https://github.com/cslsolow/Repo0 and provide a supplementary document with prompts and results for the remaining repositories. Generation uses deterministic decoding at temperature zero, which reduces sampling variance but does not establish robustness to stochastic generations. Thresholds gamma_split = 2/3 and theta_merge = 0.7 were selected on two held-out repositories by manually comparing evolved structures with golden repository architectures; although the repositories were held out from the final benchmark, this procedure introduces architectural-target tuning and relies on human judgment. All methods share the same downstream TDD, validation, and repair scaffold, which helps isolate architecture planning, but the evaluation pipeline itself follows RPG and uses LLM-based semantic voting and test rewriting. The principal concerns are the small, single-language benchmark, incomplete reporting of variability, dependence on potentially benchmark-specific evaluation procedures, and lack of direct measurements of modularity, maintainability, interface quality, or generated-code security. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a system artifact. Practical: Repo0 is implemented as an LLM-agent pipeline and can run on commercially available hardware, although it depends on access to GPT-5 mini or DeepSeek V3.2 and an execution environment for generated repositories. Efficient: The paper reports DeepSeek V3.2 total costs of $21.28 for requests, $41.12 for statsmodels, and $100.06 for django; generation costs are $11.95, $28.19, and $27.24 respectively, but evaluation dominates for django, and full cost comparisons across all methods and repositories are deferred to the supplement. Effective: The evidence shows improved benchmark Functionality Coverage, Pass Rate, and Voting Rate over the tested baselines, but these metrics rely on adapted tests and LLM semantic evaluation and do not establish production reliability or architectural maintainability. Scalable: The system is tested on repositories up to 699 files and 218,924 lines, but the paper does not test 10x–100x larger projects, multilingual repositories, repeated architectural evolution over extended development, or the cost and context behavior of such scaling. The work delivers a reusable software artifact and accompanying data through the stated GitHub repository, rather than stopping at a paper-only design. Strengths - The paper identifies a meaningful limitation in current repository-generation systems: architecture is treated as a fixed planning artifact even though implementation exposes architectural errors. - The Dual-DAG representation gives a concrete separation between requirement-level coordination and implementation-level dependency, with an explicit many-to-many alignment relation that supports traceability during restructuring. - The convergence analysis is stronger than a simple before/after comparison: fixed-budget LLM evolution performs worse than metric-guided stopping, supporting the specific claim that action selection and termination criteria matter rather than refinement count alone. - The controlled shared downstream scaffold and component ablations provide evidence that architectural planning, rather than only a different code-generation or repair policy, accounts for much of the reported improvement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that structural-update quality depends on the backbone LLM's architectural reasoning ability, because the LLM still instantiates split, merge, revise, and alignment changes even when metrics select candidates. They also acknowledge that the evaluation covers only six Python repositories from one benchmark and that effectiveness in other programming-language ecosystems remains untested. They argue that the representation and metrics are not inherently Python-specific but leave multilingual and additional-benchmark evaluation to future work. These limitations are stated directly, although the paper does not discuss several other concerns such as evaluation cost, metric validity, architectural quality independent of golden structures, or statistical uncertainty. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The main evidence does not establish that higher cohesion and lower coupling measured on the requirement graph correspond to better maintainability or architecture in the generated source code; direct code-level modularity, dependency-cycle, API-stability, defect, security, and human-review measures are absent. - Threshold selection uses manual similarity to golden repository architectures, which may favor reproducing benchmark structures and undermines the claim that the method can discover appropriate architectures without structural priors. - The benchmark contains only six repositories, all in Python, and the prominent results cover only three; there is no evaluation on independently collected requirements, unseen domains, other languages, larger project scales, or requirements whose best architecture differs substantially from the reference repository. - The paper reports averages over three deterministic runs but omits variance and significance testing, making it difficult to determine whether some smaller gains are robust. - The shared downstream scaffold helps isolate planning but may conceal interactions between architecture quality and alternative code-generation strategies; comparisons against stronger current agentic baselines or multiple independent implementation backends are limited. - The evaluation uses adapted ground-truth tests, semantic voting, and functionality matching, but does not quantify false positives, test adequacy, hidden-test performance, or whether generated extra functionality is correct; the paper itself observes that increased Functionality Novelty can accompany lower required-functionality coverage. - The structural loop is described as continuous, but architecture is fixed before the principal code-generation phase except for localized revision, so the evidence does not fully test architecture changes driven by substantial implementation discoveries or cross-component failures. Bottom Line Repo0 is a worthwhile paper for researchers studying repository-generation agents because it offers a clear evolving-architecture formulation backed by useful ablations and sizeable benchmark gains, but its claims should be treated as preliminary until independent evaluations remove golden-architecture tuning and test multilingual, larger-scale, code-quality, and statistically robust outcomes.

FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis (105 ▲ )

Kou Shi, Zun Wang, Qisheng Su, Shiting Huang, Ziao Zhang, Zhen Fang, Qingnan Ren, Jin Liu, Yu Zeng, Yiming Zhao, Lin Chen, Zehui Chen, Feng Zhao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 21 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FACET, a pipeline that synthesizes Harbor-format terminal tasks by reconstructing multi-skill scenarios, grounding instruction/solution/verifier generation in a realized container state, and validating and repairing the resulting executable bundle. - Why it's important: Invalid or internally inconsistent synthetic tasks waste generation and training compute, while dense, reliable terminal supervision is needed to improve agents on long-horizon command-line workflows. - How it does it: FACET generates the environment before the task artifacts, exposes the observed initial state to downstream generators, creates the solution before the verifier, and uses execution traces for targeted repair. - The good: On 500 common skill-pair inputs, FACET produces 350 validated tasks—a 70.0% yield versus 27.8% for a TerminalWorld-style reproduction and 15.6% for a simplified baseline—and its 1,200 successful trajectories improve Qwen3.5 scores on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 6.75–8.24 points. - The missing: The paper does not isolate the contributions of scenario reconstruction, shared-state grounding, artifact ordering, and targeted repair through controlled component ablations, so the source of the end-to-end gain remains uncertain. - Read it or not: Researchers building synthetic interactive-agent data should read it for its executable-task construction and validation design; readers seeking evidence of broad agent capability gains should treat the single-benchmark SFT results as preliminary.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (76) are meaningful because FACET makes realized executable state the shared grounding interface for task synthesis and uses targeted repair rather than merely generating text artifacts. Rigor (70) is supported by explicit acceptance criteria, clean-container validation, generation-order testing, and cross-scale SFT gains, but no component ablations, matched SFT controls, multiple seeds, or human realism and verifier-quality assessments limit confidence. Completeness (74) and Resilience (69) are reduced by end-to-end confounding, unequal repair budgets, benchmark dependence, and possible verifier shortcuts; Impact (68) reflects a useful synthesis pipeline and dataset but no confirmed public artifact.
