Problem & Motivation The work addresses short-horizon demand forecasting for commerce categories and retail items whose future demand depends both on recurring numerical patterns and on future events such as holidays, promotions, mega-sales, price changes, and platform interventions. Numerical time-series foundation models capture historical dynamics but cannot infer events absent from their inputs; text-enhanced models can supply this information but often fuse it uniformly, duplicating temporal evidence or introducing noise. The specific gap is instance-level control over whether semantic information should be used, where it should interact with temporal representations, and how it should alter local trajectory shape versus overall demand level. Key Idea The central insight is to treat event semantics as a conditional intervention with marginal utility rather than as an always-on forecasting modality. ReasonCast first decides whether intervention is warranted, then expresses the event effect in structured forecast-specific fields and applies it only to an event-related temporal subspace, with separate additive and multiplicative paths for local shape changes and level shifts. The exact Skip path makes this idea operationally robust by preserving the numerical forecast unchanged when semantics are not selected. Methodology For each item or leaf category, the system receives a history of length L and predicts the next H=7 observations. A pretrained Chronos-2 model produces a no-text forecast and entropy estimate. A Qwen3-32B-based agent chooses Skip, Basic, or Tool; holidays and mega-sales forcibly disallow Skip. Basic uses available context, while Tool additionally retrieves event evidence or temporal statistics, although the paper does not quantify actual tool usage. For non-Skip cases, the reasoner produces structured fields for relevance, dominant event, demand direction, temporal shape, amplitude, peak, and a short trend narrative. A text encoder and MLP align these semantics into tokens. At the Chronos-2 future-token interface, a learned basis is QR-orthogonalized into an event projector P_E, decomposing temporal tokens into event and complementary components. Only the event component queries semantic tokens through cross-attention, yielding Delta H. The fused representation adds alpha times an instance gate g_i times Delta H to the temporal representation, while a separate multiplicative correction predicts y_hat_i = y_hat_i^lat elementwise multiplied by exp(m_i beta g_i rho_i) to model level shifts. The gate uses semantic features, recent-demand volatility, no-text entropy, and event descriptors. Training proceeds through schema SFT on 4,590 filtered teacher examples, semantic-field GRPO using forecast-derived direction/shape/amplitude/peak rewards, contrastive event-subspace grounding and text-event alignment, selective fusion training, and forecast-utility GRPO against a frozen forecaster. The key design choices—mandatory event routing, orthogonal event-selective interaction, and dual-path correction—are motivated by the authors' decomposition of event effects, but the causal or global identifiability of the learned event subspace is explicitly not established. Key Results On 15 proprietary seven-day windows from 15,696 daily leaf-category series, ReasonCast obtains WMAPE/MAE of 39.10%/1080.71 on holiday-sensitive categories, 25.08%/331.09 on holiday-insensitive categories, and 21.06%/322.24 overall; the strongest listed non-ReasonCast values are 42.39%/1185.03, 31.64%/390.67, and 25.59%/370.86 from Chronos-2-small fine-tuned variants. On mega-sale windows, it obtains 20.89%/589.94 on sensitive categories, 9.71%/215.61 on insensitive categories, and 12.87%/339.68 overall, compared with best non-ReasonCast WMAPEs of 22.14%, 10.02%, and 13.35%. On 3,049 M5 item series aggregated across ten stores and 14 event-centered windows, it reaches 32.63% WMAPE and 4.00 MAE, versus 33.10% and 4.06 for Chronos-2-small Multi-FT and 33.21% and 4.08 for Uni-FT. Relative to the strongest non-ReasonCast comparators, the authors report WMAPE reductions of 7.8% on holiday-sensitive categories, 5.6% on mega-sale-sensitive categories, and 1.4% on M5 event windows. On stable-sales periods, Chronos-2-small scores 7.91%/185.15; forced always-on ReasonCast semantics degrade this to 9.59%/224.43, whereas agent-routed ReasonCast exactly matches the backbone. Removing multiplicative correction worsens holiday-sensitive WMAPE by 5.19 percentage points, removing additive correction worsens it by 1.02 points, and removing orthogonal decomposition/alignment worsens stable forced-Basic WMAPE by 1.72 points. Forecast-utility RL reduces event WMAPE from 20.52% for the original LLM to 18.96% and negative-transfer rate from 23.59% to 15.08%. In semantic inversion tests, incorrect fields increase WMAPE in 13 of 15 windows, by 2.67 points on average, with a 25.33-point worst-case increase. These results support content-sensitive intervention, but only across a small number of evaluation windows and without statistical variability estimates. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily a NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an engineering-system component: the paper reframes multimodal forecasting as selective semantic intervention and combines routing, structured semantic fields, event-subspace interaction, entropy-conditioned gating, dual-path corrections, and forecast-utility RL. Individual ingredients such as LLM reasoning, cross-modal alignment, adaptive fusion, RL post-training, and tool routing are established, so the main novelty lies in their forecast-specific integration and the explicit exact-preservation abstention path rather than in a wholly new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility The study includes useful component ablations, cumulative post-training comparisons, entropy-tier analysis, a semantic inversion stress test, window-level results, chronological splits, and leakage controls that restrict event information to records available before each forecast origin. However, it reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, significance tests, confidence intervals, or sample-level negative-transfer distribution beyond the aggregate rate. The proprietary commerce dataset, teacher-generated corpus, trained ReasonCast models, and implementation are not stated to be released; no code or repository URL is mentioned. The evaluation relies heavily on the authors' 15-window proprietary test set, and the M5 evaluation uses only 14 event-centered windows rather than the full benchmark protocol. The teacher corpus is filtered using future-grounded trajectory information, which may be legitimate training supervision but requires clearer separation from evaluation windows and more detail about overlap. Baselines include relevant numerical and text-enhanced models, but the comparison does not establish robustness against every recent event-aware multimodal forecasting method, and the paper does not report route frequencies or verify that Tool materially improves results over Basic. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The components can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but Qwen3-32B inference combined with Chronos-2 and possible retrieval/statistics tools may be expensive; hardware requirements are not reported. Efficient: The method adds LLM reasoning, semantic encoding, routing, and possibly tool calls relative to Chronos-2, but the paper provides no latency, memory, throughput, token, tool-call, or monetary-cost measurements. Effective: The evidence directly measures point-forecast accuracy and shows improvements on event-centered WMAPE/MAE while preserving the backbone under Skip, although the strongest gains concentrate in a small set of event windows and do not establish causal event understanding. Scalable: The method is tested on 15,696 proprietary series and 3,049 M5 series but not at 10x–100x scale; the paper explicitly leaves route frequency, tool cost, latency, and production-scale resource trade-offs unevaluated. The work describes a forecasting system and trained-model pipeline, but it does not state that a library, CLI, dataset, model weights, or other reusable software artifact is released. Strengths - The selective-intervention formulation addresses a real failure mode of multimodal forecasting: useful event context is conditional, and always-on text can degrade stable-period accuracy. - The exact no-text identity is stronger than a learned soft gate: when Skip is selected or context is unavailable, the fusion interface mathematically returns the Chronos-2 forecast rather than merely attempting to approximate it. - The dual-path correction has interpretable functional roles, with ablations showing that multiplicative correction matters particularly for holiday-driven level shifts while additive correction helps local event trajectories. - The paper tests semantic dependence rather than only text presence: inverting the structured fields harms 13 of 15 windows, including a 25.33-point WMAPE failure on a difficult overlapping-event window. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors acknowledge non-stationary event effects across products, regions, and seasons; variable timeliness, completeness, and reliability of external signals; the accuracy-latency-cost trade-off introduced by tool reasoning; limited ability to distinguish causal event effects from associations; and the absence of a complete accounting of tool-call frequency, end-to-end latency, and realized inference cost. They also state that orthogonal decomposition does not make the event subspace causally or globally identifiable and that adaptive gating does not guarantee immunity from sample-level negative transfer. These limitations are confronted directly in the discussion rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The evaluation aggregates only 15 proprietary commerce windows and 14 M5 windows, so the reported improvements may be sensitive to a small number of event alignments; broader rolling-origin and cross-domain tests are needed. - No variance estimates or repeated runs support the significance of differences that are sometimes below one WMAPE percentage point, especially on M5. - The mandatory Basic-or-Tool rule for holidays and mega-sales limits the claimed abstention behavior precisely on the event regimes where the method is most heavily evaluated; the paper does not test whether Skip would sometimes be preferable there. - The Tool route is conceptually central but operationally under-evaluated: route proportions, retrieval quality, tool accuracy, latency, and incremental benefit over Basic are missing. - The learned event subspace is treated as semantically meaningful despite lacking identifiability tests, probing against independently labeled event factors, or comparisons with simpler covariate injection mechanisms. - The forecast-utility RL reward uses realized future errors and a frozen forecaster; the paper does not fully establish that this optimization transfers to unseen event types, changing policies, or a different backbone. - The main proprietary dataset may contain platform-specific event semantics and signals, limiting conclusions about settings where event descriptions are noisier, less complete, or available in other languages. Bottom Line This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers studying event-aware multimodal forecasting because it turns text fusion into a measurable intervention-and-abstention problem and provides credible ablations, but its practical claims remain premature until the authors report route costs, statistical variability, broader event diversity, and independent large-scale deployment results.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the engineering-to-manufacturing information gap in complex railway production, including locomotives, maintenance-of-way equipment, and railcars. Engineering BOMs encode design intent and engineering decomposition, whereas manufacturing BOMs must represent assembly sequence, plant-specific structures, production-only materials, tooling, workstations, and executable operations. Premature ERP synchronization, manual MBOM restructuring, inconsistent release states, disconnected raw-material spreadsheets, and lightweight visualization data can break traceability and prevent reliable process simulation. The paper argues that prior work treats digital twins, digital threads, and EBOM-to-MBOM transformation largely as separate topics, with limited empirical evidence from integrated railway deployments or comparisons across railway manufacturing contexts. Key Idea: The central insight is that a digital manufacturing program must treat manufacturing data governance as a prerequisite architecture layer rather than as an implementation detail after simulation or execution systems are deployed. A dedicated manufacturing boundary object—exemplified by Case C's MFGPART and Case B's manufacturing assembly revision—preserves identity linkage to engineering parts while allowing independent BOM structures, revisions, lifecycle states, plant variants, and manufacturing attributes. The paper couples this boundary-object pattern with separately governed BREP-enabled JT data, arguing that ordinary lightweight PLM visualization cannot support collision detection, ergonomic analysis, robot-path planning, or high-fidelity process simulation. Methodology: The study uses a qualitative multiple-case design with purposive theoretical sampling across three anonymized organizations sharing a common PLM-platform foundation: a European locomotive OEM, a North American maintenance-of-way manufacturer, and a multinational railcar manufacturer. Evidence includes published case documentation, internal system specifications, PLM configuration records, workflow definitions, deployment summaries, program reviews, and practitioner knowledge from implementation roles; no formal structured interviews were conducted. Analysis proceeds through independent within-case mapping against five constructs—digital-thread integrity, BOM-transformation governance, visualization-pipeline capability, process-simulation readiness, and change-management maturity—followed by cross-case classification into convergent, partial, and single-case patterns. Architecture elements are elevated to transferable patterns only when supported by at least two cases and consistent with prior literature. The operational pipeline begins with DBOM/EBOM establishment, applies closure and revision rules, creates or derives manufacturing-specific objects and MBOM structures, performs accountability and traceability checks, generates and associates BREP-enabled JT data at MBOM BOM-line positions, builds a Plant BOP hierarchy from plant to operation, assigns components and resources, and exports execution structures to ERP/MOM systems. Case A additionally integrates parameterized operation-time estimation and process simulation; Case B redesigns engineering-release and ERP-synchronization workflows; Case C specifies conditional MFGPART instantiation and multi-site MBOM variants. The major design decisions are plausible and practically motivated, but their comparative superiority over alternative PLM data models, integration patterns, or visualization formats is not experimentally established. Key Results: The principal result is a five-layer architecture: (1) PLM collaboration and governance; (2) BOM transformation using manufacturing-specific items, closure and revision rules, constraints, and accountability checks; (3) a separately governed BREP-enabled JT visualization and simulation pipeline; (4) Plant BOP and process planning linking product structures to operations, resources, tooling, and time analysis; and (5) execution and feedback through ERP/MES/MOM, quality data, and as-built records. Layers 1 and 2 are supported by mechanisms observed across all three cases. Layers 3 and 4 are supported by Case C specifications plus Case A deployment evidence and, for Layer 4, Case B target-state design intent. Layer 5 is explicitly the least validated: Case A demonstrates MBOM export, work-instruction updates, and shop-floor actuals used by a duration-calculation engine, while Case B and Case C mainly provide planned or specified integrations. In Case A, a 54-locomotive project used process simulation to evaluate assembly and welding sequences; a coupling/crash-box example reportedly found that installing the crash box before the coupling reduced interference and eliminated additional rework steps. The paper reports an estimated 15–25% reduction in manufacturing-planning time, improved pre-production error detection, reduced reliance on paper instructions, and better change propagation, but supplies no sample sizes, baselines, variance, cost data, defect counts, throughput figures, or statistical tests. Cases B and C report governance mechanisms and expected benefits rather than post-deployment performance measurements. No strong quantitative or external benchmark baselines are used. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION; NEW SYSTEM/TOOL; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The paper's genuinely distinctive contribution is a cross-case, railway-focused formulation that makes the manufacturing boundary object, separately governed BREP-JT pipeline, and governance-first deployment sequence explicit within a five-layer architecture; the underlying PLM, BOM, ERP, BOP, and process-simulation technologies are commercial and established rather than newly invented. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper improves qualitative validity by using three contrasting cases, within-case analysis before comparison, explicit evidence mapping, and a stated two-case threshold for elevating patterns into the architecture. It also openly separates post-deployment evidence in Case A from specification-stage intent in Cases B and C and acknowledges insider positionality. However, the evidence is asymmetric: Case C is the principal source for the architectural detail in Layers 2–4, Case A supplies most deployment outcomes, and Cases B and C lack post-deployment measurement. There are no quantitative ablations, multiple seeds, error bars, significance tests, formal interview protocol, independent coding reliability, or alternative-architecture comparisons. The organizations are anonymized, and the underlying internal documents are not publicly available; data are stated to be available from the corresponding author upon request. No code, dataset, reusable software implementation, or model weights are released. The common PLM-platform foundation improves comparability but also narrows external validity and may make the architecture partly specific to one vendor ecosystem. The 15–25% planning-time estimate is based on post-mortem documentation and practitioner assessment, creating substantial risk of attribution and confirmation bias. Deployability (4-property check): Profile used: EMPIRICAL, because the paper reports qualitative evidence from implemented and planned manufacturing systems rather than presenting a purely theoretical architecture or evaluating a newly built infrastructure artifact. Practical: The architecture uses commercially available PLM, ERP, CAD-to-JT translation, process-planning, simulation, EWI, and MES components and can therefore run on industrial computing infrastructure, although licensing, integration, data migration, and governance costs are not quantified. Efficient: The paper gives no compute, storage, translation-time, BOM-processing, licensing, or memory measurements, so efficiency relative to manual workflows or alternative PLM architectures is not established. Effective: Case A provides reported evidence of virtual sequence validation, work-instruction change propagation, and an estimated 15–25% planning-time reduction, but the broader claim that the architecture improves delivery, quality, and assembly performance rests mainly on organizational assessments rather than controlled causal evaluation. Scalable: The design targets products of approximately 400,000 parts and high customization and includes multi-site variants, but the paper does not report stress tests, throughput at 10×–100× scale, or evidence that the five-layer architecture remains operational under substantially larger product, plant, or feedback-data loads. The work delivers a reference architecture and implementation patterns, not a released software artifact, library, CLI, dataset, or trained model. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete and operationally important distinction between lightweight JT visualization and BREP-enabled JT required for simulation, then places the latter in a separately governed pipeline rather than treating it as an automatic PLM output. - The manufacturing boundary-object pattern provides a clear way to preserve engineering identity while permitting independent manufacturing structure, lifecycle control, plant variants, and production-only content. - The three cases cover distinct product types and maturity stages, allowing the study to connect mature deployment evidence from the locomotive case with governance failures and remediation in the maintenance-of-way case. - The authors explicitly label design intent, single-case observations, partial replication, and post-deployment evidence instead of presenting all architecture layers as equally validated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge insider positionality in two cases, possible confirmation bias, reliance on specification-stage documentation for Cases B and C, absence of structured interviews, the lack of empirical validation for the as-built/as-operated Layer 5 feedback loop, and the use of practitioner assessments rather than controlled pre/post KPI measurement. They also state that no formal ROI study was conducted, that all cases involve medium-to-large organizations with existing PLM infrastructure, that SME applicability is unexamined, and that confidentiality restricted the available evidence. These limitations are confronted directly and materially weaken claims about quantified benefit, full digital-twin realization, and generalization. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not provide enough raw evidence to independently audit the case findings: organizations, implementation timelines, document counts, coding procedures, stakeholder perspectives, and detailed before/after process measures are absent. The common PLM-platform sampling frame limits the ability to distinguish domain requirements from vendor-specific configuration choices, while the claimed transferability to aerospace, defense, and other industries is not tested outside rail. The architecture's layer ordering is inferred from dependencies and one case's failures, but competing deployment sequences are not compared and necessity is not experimentally demonstrated. The paper also treats ERP/MOM feedback and digital-twin behavior broadly without specifying data schemas, latency, synchronization semantics, quality-data models, conflict resolution, cybersecurity, or governance of as-built/as-operated updates. Case A's reported 15–25% planning-time improvement and qualitative quality benefits lack denominators, measurement windows, counterfactuals, uncertainty, and independent verification. Finally, the paper is an unedited Article in Press manuscript, and the first page warns that further editing may reveal errors; confidence should therefore be lower than for a finalized peer-reviewed version. Bottom Line: This is a useful practitioner-oriented qualitative architecture paper for teams planning PLM-based EBOM-to-MBOM transformation, especially its governance-first and BREP-JT pipeline guidance, but it should not be treated as strong evidence that the proposed architecture delivers measured digital-twin, productivity, or closed-loop manufacturing gains.

Problem & Motivation: Knowledge-tracing systems estimate student mastery and predict future responses, but their predictions generally do not identify which earlier concepts a teacher should remediate. Neuro-symbolic approaches often attach prerequisite graphs to these models and implicitly assume that the graph can be learned from interaction logs, avoiding costly expert annotation. The paper addresses whether log-only temporal association contains a usable prerequisite signal and, if not, how expert curricular knowledge can be exploited transparently. The application domain is teacher-facing analytics for middle-school mathematics and adaptive learning. The paper distinguishes this log-only problem from content-based prerequisite discovery using item text or NLP/LLM methods. Key Idea: The core insight is that prerequisite structure should be treated as expert-supplied symbolic knowledge rather than inferred from learner-response co-occurrence, because learner ability and item difficulty induce positive associations between nearly all skills. Given a trusted graph, a fixed fuzzy rule layer can expose graph-grounded explanations without training additional parameters; its claims are then separated from the neural model's behaviour through a controlled audit that measures whether each model actually encodes a prerequisite and whether post-hoc attribution can find it. Methodology: The study has two main components. First, it ranks candidate directed skill pairs using three log-only induction families: transfer entropy; a confound-controlled mastery-lift score based on residualising correctness using learner mean performance and skill difficulty; and a semi-supervised logistic classifier trained from four expert edges using mastery-lift, temporal precedence, difficulty gap, and co-count features. It evaluates rankings against 16 expert edges on ASSISTments 2009 and checks the association confound on ASSISTments 2012 and Junyi. Second, D-FIS consumes per-skill mastery estimates from a DKT or SAKT model and an expert graph, maps mastery to fixed weak/moderate/strong fuzzy memberships, and emits one rule-based explanation per weak prerequisite of an at-risk target. The default confidence is the conjunction of prerequisite weakness and target weakness, compared under product, minimum/Gödel, Łukasiewicz, and drastic t-norms. The localisation audit constructs matched learner histories differing only in whether prerequisite A is answered correctly, measures the change in predicted mastery for target B, and labels an edge model-respected when the lower 95% confidence bound exceeds a threshold. For model-respected edges, it tests whether Integrated Gradients or occlusion-based SHAP places an interaction with A in the top three attributed interactions. The use of a fixed linear membership mapping and a parameter-free rule base is clearly motivated by auditability, but the 0.5 membership breakpoint, linguistic thresholds of 0.4 and 0.7, effect threshold, background-history generation, and choice of 50 or 30 samples per edge receive limited justification. Key Results: On ASSISTments 2009, the LSTM-DKT reaches test AUC 0.848 on 446,000 interactions from 3,862 learners and 110 skills. Transfer entropy performs approximately at chance. Confound-controlled mastery-lift gives a median expert-edge rank of 3,622 among 7,144 candidate pairs, versus a chance rank of approximately 3,572, with 0 of 16 expert edges in the top 100. The semi-supervised method reaches a median relative rank of 0.36 for held-out expert edges, with 22% in the top 10% and 41% in the top 25%, compared with 10% and 25% chance expectations respectively. The reported association confound appears in ASSISTments 2012, where 98% of sampled skill pairs have positive correlation with mean r = +0.23, and Junyi, where 100% of sampled exercise pairs are positive with mean r = +0.19 across 25.9 million interactions and 247,606 students. In the localisation audit, DKT respects 12 of 16 expert edges, with measured effects from +0.07 to +0.50; four edges are null or reversed. SAKT, with test AUC 0.799, respects 11 of 16. On model-respected edges, top-3 localisation averages 66% for Integrated Gradients and 61% for occlusion-SHAP on DKT, while SAKT gives 69% and 27%, respectively. D-FIS achieves 100% localisation by construction when the graph is correct and the model-respected edge is supplied, so this is not an independent empirical comparison. For t-norm selection, product, minimum, and Łukasiewicz achieve Spearman correlations of 0.495, 0.445, and 0.290 with measured prerequisite effects, firing 4, 7, and 1 of 16 rules at confidence above 0.1; the product result has parametric p = 0.051, bootstrap positive-correlation frequency 97.6%, and one-sided permutation p = 0.026. The findings support a log-signal limitation and conditional graph-grounded localisation, but do not establish improved prediction, teacher utility, remediation quality, or student learning. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW METHOD, and NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION, with a secondary NEW SYSTEM/TOOL classification: the log-only prerequisite-induction failure and its ability/difficulty explanation are the main empirical contribution, while D-FIS combines standard fuzzy membership and t-norm operations with an architecture-independent matched-counterfactual audit in a teacher-facing knowledge-tracing setting; the fuzzy layer itself is technically simple and not a fundamentally new fuzzy-inference mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper evaluates three induction families, two KT architectures, three public datasets for the confound analysis, four t-norms, and two attribution methods. It reports confidence intervals for audit effects, a 5,000-resample bootstrap, a 10,000-permutation test, and a Wilcoxon comparison for attribution methods. However, the induction comparison does not include several potentially stronger modern baselines, such as causal or longitudinal latent-variable models, content-based methods, graph-learning KT systems, or carefully calibrated negative-control analyses; consequently, the conclusion concerns the tested log-only estimators rather than all feasible log-only induction. The audit's ground truth is defined by the model's response to synthetic matched histories, making D-FIS's 100% localisation guarantee tautological and validating model-consistent localisation rather than causal correctness in students. The paper states that code, trained models, expert graph, anonymised data, and scripts are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request, but it does not provide a public repository URL in the manuscript, so public reproducibility is not yet demonstrated. Multiple seeds and full training variability are not clearly reported, and the small n = 16 edge-level t-norm comparison makes the effect-size ranking fragile despite resampling. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL): Practical: D-FIS requires only commercially available hardware and adds a linear-time rule evaluation over an existing KT model, although deployment depends on obtaining a correct expert graph and reliable mastery estimates. Efficient: The rule base contains one independent rule per prerequisite edge and costs O(|E|) per explanation, with no trainable parameters or additional inference model; the paper does not quantify wall-clock latency or memory relative to attribution methods. Effective: The evidence shows that D-FIS produces graph-localised, readable explanations when the graph is correct and the model encodes the edge, but it does not show that teachers find the explanations useful or that they improve instructional decisions or student outcomes. Scalable: The algorithmic cost scales linearly with graph edges and is independent of the number of skills for each target explanation, but experiments cover only a 16-edge graph, so behaviour at 10×–100× graph scale and under dense or cyclic prerequisite structures remains untested. The work delivers a D-FIS implementation, trained KT models, an expert graph, induction and audit scripts, and anonymised data, but the stated release is by reasonable request rather than a clearly public software repository. Strengths: - The paper isolates a frequently implicit assumption—recoverability of prerequisite relations from response logs—and tests it with three methodologically different induction families rather than relying on one failed estimator. - The ability/difficulty confound is supported across ASSISTments 2009, ASSISTments 2012, and the much larger Junyi dataset, making the negative result more informative than a single-dataset ranking failure. - The localisation audit cleanly separates whether a KT model encodes a prerequisite from whether an explanation method identifies it, and it exposes architecture-dependent degradation of occlusion-based SHAP on SAKT. - The paper is appropriately candid that D-FIS's 100% localisation is a design guarantee, not evidence that the layer recovers causal model use, and it reports four expert relations that the DKT does not respect. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the study to log-only induction, a single compact 16-edge middle-school mathematics graph, and a proof-of-concept involving DKT and SAKT. They state that content-based prerequisite methods are not evaluated, that the audit measures model behaviour rather than classroom learning, and that no teacher user study, classroom field study, instructional-decision evaluation, or student-outcome evaluation is provided. They also acknowledge that ordinary fuzzy memberships do not represent epistemic uncertainty, that the intuitionistic fuzzy extension is unevaluated, and that larger or more networked prerequisite graphs require new validation. These limitations are confronted directly and framed as future work rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unacknowledged concern is that the paper's central localisation ground truth is model-defined: a matched perturbation demonstrates sensitivity of the model to A, but not that A is the true educational cause or that the expert edge is valid for the learner. The expert graph is treated as ground truth despite containing only 16 edges and no inter-rater agreement, alternative curricular graphs, or graph-noise robustness analysis. The induction evidence is persuasive against the three selected families but does not establish an information-theoretic impossibility for log-only discovery; the confound replication reports sampled-pair percentages without enough detail on sampling procedure, uncertainty, conditioning, or controls for shared item exposure. The study also lacks comparisons with stronger causal sequence models and graph-based KT explainers, does not quantify D-FIS runtime or explanation coverage in realistic deployment, and does not test sensitivity to membership breakpoints, confidence thresholds, graph errors, sparse histories, or prerequisite chains with multiple parents. Because DKT and SAKT are trained and evaluated on the same benchmark split and the audit is applied to their own predictions, the results say little about transfer to other datasets or modern KT architectures. Bottom Line: This preprint is worth reading for its well-motivated negative result about log-only prerequisite induction and its reusable audit protocol, but its simple fuzzy layer and model-defined evaluation do not yet provide evidence of educational impact or broad superiority over existing explainability systems.

GLaQ: Grounding Latent Queries in Visual Evidence for Multimodal Reasoning

Z Yang, L Zhang, X Zhang, C Zhang, P Li, H Wang… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GLaQ, a fixed-block grounded latent-query interface that retrieves visual evidence from source image tokens and reinjects it into a multimodal language model during reasoning. - Why it's important: Fine-grained visual details can be lost in textual chain-of-thought or redundant autoregressive latent states, while external crop/zoom tools add inference-time complexity and operational constraints. - How it does it: GLaQ first contextualizes jointly inserted query slots, grounds them through a lightweight cross-attention/self-attention LQFormer over the original visual tokens, and then uses the grounded queries as soft prompts for answer generation. - The good: On five benchmarks, GLaQ-7B improves over its Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone by 5.99–9.66 percentage points and beats all compared visual-latent methods in the reported table; controlled ablations show that both LQFormer grounding and ROI-teacher alignment contribute materially. - The missing: The evaluation uses only one 7B backbone, lacks reported variance or statistical testing, and does not establish whether the gains persist without training examples selected specifically from cases where the base model fails on the full image but succeeds with an auxiliary view. - Read it or not: Researchers working on multimodal latent reasoning should read it for the fixed-query grounding and teacher-alignment design, whereas practitioners seeking deployment evidence should treat the results as preliminary because scale, hardware, and broader workload tests are absent.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) are strong for replacing autoregressive visual-latent trajectories with fixed, jointly contextualized queries grounded in source visual tokens and ROI-teacher alignment. Rigor (55) is substantially reduced by the preprint status, single-backbone evaluation, curated failure-selected training data, absent variance and statistical tests, and unclear compute-matched baselines; Completeness (70) and Resilience (62) are also limited by unverified grounding claims and missing robustness analysis. Problem & Motivation: Multimodal reasoning systems need to preserve and reuse localized visual evidence across multiple reasoning steps. Textual rationales compress visual attributes and spatial relations, while existing thinking-with-images systems recover evidence by cropping, zooming, annotating, or otherwise manipulating images at inference time. Continuous visual-latent methods avoid external tools but commonly generate latent states autoregressively; the paper argues, based partly on pairwise cosine-similarity visualizations, that later states can become increasingly similar and therefore fail to add complementary evidence. The target domain is fine-grained visual perception and multimodal reasoning, especially high-resolution, localized, and subtle visual-recognition tasks. Key Idea: Replace an autoregressive latent trajectory with a fixed set of jointly contextualized query slots that independently access the original visual-token pool, followed by self-attention to coordinate the slots. The queries act as learned, context-dependent requests for visual evidence rather than as successive latent states whose content is generated from preceding latent states. This is the paper's central conceptual contribution; the surrounding Q-Former-style attention, EMA teacher, self-distillation, and DePO components are adaptations or combinations of existing mechanisms. Methodology: A frozen visual encoder maps image I to visual tokens V. The MLLM processes the image and text prefix until a latent-start marker, then inserts K=16 learnable continuous query slots jointly. In the first pass, the MLLM contextualizes these slots into UQ. A two-layer LQFormer then applies, at each layer, cross-attention from UQ to V, slot self-attention, and an FFN with residual connections and RMS normalization, producing grounded queries ZQ. The model replaces the original slots with ZQ and performs a second forward pass for ordinary autoregressive text generation. During SFT, a full-image student and an EMA-updated teacher process the same contextualized queries, but the teacher receives a paired ROI image. A projector aligns slot-wise normalized student and teacher representations with a cosine-distance loss, combined with next-token prediction as L = 0.3 Llatent + Lntp. Stage 1 uses 80K Visual-CoT examples selected where Qwen2.5-VL-7B fails on the original image but succeeds with an auxiliary view; Stage 2 uses 30K Zebra-CoT interleaved visual-search trajectories. The model is then trained with DePO on 10K filtered samples, optimizing both categorical text actions and continuous grounded-query actions using task-level accuracy and formatting rewards, with reward R=(1-0.1)Racc+0.1Rfmt. The key design decisions—joint rather than autoregressive slots, ROI-view EMA supervision, and DePO's optimization of continuous queries—are supported by ablations, although the paper does not fully disentangle the effects of additional compute, training-data curation, or architecture-specific tuning. Key Results: On V, HRBench-4K, HRBench-8K, MME-RealWorld-Lite, and MMVP, GLaQ-7B scores 85.34, 73.37, 70.37, 53.31, and 75.33, respectively. Relative to Qwen2.5-VL-7B scores of 76.44, 67.38, 63.75, 43.82, and 65.67, the reported absolute gains are +8.90, +5.99, +6.62, +9.49, and +9.66 points. GLaQ-7B also exceeds the strongest listed visual-latent baseline on each benchmark: for example, it exceeds HyLaR by 4.19 points on V and 3.12 points on MMVP, while the exact per-benchmark margins against every strongest baseline are not summarized in the text. The largest resolution-related gain is on HRBench-8K single-instance questions (+10.00 points over the base), while the cross-instance gain is only +3.25 points, indicating weaker evidence integration across multiple instances. GLaQ-SFT without RL scores 82.72, 71.13, 65.63, 51.80, and 70.00; text-only GRPO reaches 84.82, 72.00, 69.38, 52.42, and 74.00; full DePO adds 0.52–1.37 points over text-only GRPO on every benchmark. In Stage 1 ablations, removing the EMA teacher reduces scores to 80.15, 69.38, 62.75, 47.99, and 67.67, while removing LQFormer reduces them to 78.54, 67.13, 62.38, 46.87, and 66.67. The efficiency plot reports V* accuracy improvements of 8.90, 2.09, and 4.19 points and throughput improvements of 7.62%, 20.11%, and 5.70% relative to Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DeepEyes, and HyLaR, respectively, but the parsed paper does not provide the underlying hardware, absolute throughput values for all systems, or confidence intervals. The work is an arXiv preprint (v2, dated 18 August 2026 in the document), not a peer-reviewed publication according to the supplied text. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the fixed context-conditioned query block with source-token grounding is a distinct formulation of visual latent reasoning, while the LQFormer, ROI self-distillation, and DePO training pipeline largely combine Q-Former-style attention, EMA/BYOL-style targets, supervised fine-tuning, and an existing continuous-action policy-optimization method in a new multimodal setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for the EMA teacher, LQFormer, text-only SFT, text-only GRPO, and DePO; sensitivity studies for latent-alignment weight and query count; and comparisons with open-source, proprietary, thinking-with-images, and visual-latent systems. These experiments support the claim that grounding and teacher alignment matter: with Stage 1 SFT, λlatent=0.3 outperforms λlatent=0 on all five benchmarks, and K=16 beats K=8 and K=32 under the reported setting. However, no error bars, multiple random seeds, significance tests, or per-example error analyses are reported. The results are described as reproductions evaluated with VLMEvalKit, but no code, dataset release, model weights, or repository URL is mentioned. The training data are heavily curated: Stage 1 retains examples on which the base model fails with the original image but succeeds with an auxiliary view, creating a selection mechanism closely tied to the proposed method's intended strength. Baselines may also differ in training data, inference procedures, and implementation provenance, and the paper does not report matched compute, token counts, image-resolution preprocessing, or hardware for the throughput comparison. The similarity heatmaps are qualitative and do not establish that reduced pairwise similarity corresponds to more useful or complementary evidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a model architecture and training procedure rather than a released software system. - Practical: The method runs on a commercially available 7B MLLM backbone in principle, but the paper does not state hardware requirements, memory use, latency, or serving details. - Efficient: Fixed K=16 grounding avoids variable-length autoregressive latent rollouts; the paper reports throughput gains of 7.62% over Qwen2.5-VL-7B, 20.11% over DeepEyes, and 5.70% over HyLaR on the plotted V* setup, but does not provide enough hardware and absolute-cost detail to verify general efficiency. - Effective: The method improves five benchmark scores and ablations attribute gains to source-token grounding and ROI-teacher alignment, but the evidence measures benchmark accuracy rather than reliability in deployed visual decision-making. - Scalable: Not evaluated beyond one Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, K values of 8/16/32, and the reported benchmark sizes; behavior at 10×–100× model, image, query-block, or workload scale is unknown. The paper delivers a trainable multimodal model interface and associated training recipe, but no software artifact, dataset, or trained weights are identified in the supplied text. Strengths: - The fixed-query formulation directly addresses a specific weakness of autoregressive visual-latent rollouts while preserving access to the original visual representation. - The ROI-teacher/full-image-student setup converts localized-view supervision into an inference-compatible full-image pathway, and the slot-wise alignment objective matches the fixed query layout rather than relying on dense feature reconstruction. - The ablation structure is informative: removing LQFormer makes performance worse than text-only SFT on all five benchmarks, and DePO improves over matched text-only GRPO on every benchmark, supporting the claimed roles of grounding and latent-action optimization. - The method improves both accuracy and the reported V* throughput relative to several relevant baselines, rather than trading accuracy for additional inference computation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the evaluation to one 7B backbone, fixed query capacity, and auxiliary localized-view supervision. They identify model scaling, adaptive query allocation, and reducing reliance on localized views as future work. They also acknowledge through the discussion of HRBench cross-instance results that integrating evidence across multiple instances remains more difficult, and they caution that varying K is not a test-time scaling experiment. These limitations are stated directly in the conclusion, although their impact is not experimentally quantified. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The principal unacknowledged concern is data-selection and supervision bias: 80K Stage 1 examples are selected precisely when the base model benefits from an auxiliary reasoning view, so the evaluation may overrepresent cases favorable to localized-evidence transfer. The paper does not compare against equally trained baselines using the same 80K/30K data, matched extra forward passes, or alternative ROI distillation objectives, leaving the contribution of data adaptation versus architecture unclear. It also does not report random-seed variance, statistical significance, failure cases, calibration, hallucination rates, or whether latent queries actually attend to semantically correct regions; cosine diversity is used as suggestive evidence rather than a grounding measurement. The efficiency claim lacks hardware, batch size, sequence length, image preprocessing, and training-cost accounting, and the use of deterministic decoding may not reflect deployment workloads. Finally, comparisons with proprietary models and recently published methods may not be fully time- or protocol-matched, and the paper provides no evidence that DePO remains stable or beneficial at larger models, longer reasoning trajectories, more query blocks, or distribution-shifted images. Bottom Line: GLaQ is a credible and technically focused contribution for visual-latent-reasoning researchers, with strong within-setting ablations and benchmark gains, but its practical and scientific significance remains bounded until the authors demonstrate robustness across backbones and data regimes and release reproducible implementation and variance measurements.

KV-Pipe: On the Relation Between KV Sharing and Pipeline Parallel Efficiency in LLMs

M Dialameh, H Rajabzadeh, HK Murali, W Ahmed… · arxiv.org · inference optimize llm faster inference throughput - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces KV-Pipe, an offline stage-aware policy that converts selected Transformer attention layers to cross-layer KV sharing to rebalance pipeline-parallel LLM training workloads while also reducing inference KV-cache cost. - Why it's important: Pipeline stage imbalance and bubbles waste accelerator capacity, particularly at high pipeline degrees and long sequence lengths, while KV-cache growth limits long-context serving throughput. - How it does it: It computes a FLOPs Imbalance Ratio (FIR), starts by sharing KV in the tail stage, then greedily retargets whichever stage becomes the bottleneck until the stage-FLOP profile is approximately balanced. - The good: On LLaMA2-7B with 8 Ascend 910B devices, it improves MFU by 3.10%, 4.32%, and 9.17% at PP=2, 4, and 8, respectively, while reducing iteration time by 4.90%–9.80%; it also remains beneficial when combined with Seq1F1B. - The missing: The strongest claims are supported mainly by dense LLaMA-family models and PP degrees no higher than 8; quality preservation is directly evaluated only for LLaMA2-7B, and the method is not tested at PP=16/32, on MoE or hybrid architectures, or with a joint placement-and-quality optimizer. - Read it or not: Systems researchers working on pipeline-parallel LLM training or long-context serving should read it for the workload-reshaping perspective and empirical results, while readers seeking a generally validated KV-sharing method or principled global optimizer can wait for broader evidence.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (70) and Non-Obviousness (72) come from treating cross-layer KV sharing as a pipeline-balancing control variable rather than solely an inference-memory technique. Rigor (65) and Resilience (62) are pulled down by narrow quality validation, no statistical variation, limited PP scale, insufficient training-semantics detail, and weak equal-quality comparisons. Completeness (68) benefits from candid discussion of heuristic limitations, while Impact (65) is constrained by the lack of released software and limited evidence beyond dense LLaMA-family settings.
systems Novelty 70 Rigor 65 Non-Obv 72 Completeness 68 Resilience 62 Impact 65
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM pipeline parallelism partitions layers across accelerator stages, but heterogeneous components such as embeddings, LM heads, attention variants, MoE blocks, and long-context attention create unequal stage costs and pipeline bubbles. Existing scheduling, partitioning, and bubble-mitigation methods generally treat the model's layer-cost profile as fixed, while cross-layer KV sharing has primarily been studied for inference memory and decoding efficiency. The specific gap is whether KV layout itself can be used to alter per-stage computation and cache growth so that a fixed pipeline partition becomes better balanced without changing the scheduler or micro-batching policy. Key Idea: The central insight is to use cross-layer KV sharing as a controllable reduction in the cost of selected attention layers, placing that reduction on the current critical pipeline stage rather than distributing it uniformly. In the evaluated LLaMA2 configurations, the tail stage is initially expensive because it includes the LM head, so tail-first sharing reduces its cost; as the bottleneck moves, the algorithm retargets the new maximum-cost stage. The paper's more general contribution is the system-level coupling of architectural KV reuse with pipeline balancing, although the tested LLaMA2 cases mostly reduce to selecting an appropriate number of late shared-KV layers rather than demonstrating frequent non-tail retargeting. Methodology: The method assumes a decoder-only Transformer with layers partitioned into fixed pipeline stages. A full-attention layer computes separate Q, K, and V projections and stores its own K/V cache; a shared-KV layer retains its query projection and attention computation but reuses K and V from an earlier layer, reducing K/V projection FLOPs and one layer's cache growth. For each layer, the method estimates full-attention and shared-KV FLOPs, computes stage totals including embedding and LM-head costs, and defines FIR as the maximum stage FLOPs divided by average stage FLOPs. Algorithm 1 initializes all layers as full attention, starts at the final stage, converts the deepest remaining full-attention layer, updates that stage's cost and FIR, and switches to the current maximum-cost stage once the tail is within a tolerance of the average. It stops when FIR is at most 1 plus epsilon, a conversion budget is exhausted, or no convertible layer remains. The paper compares uniform, symmetric-bipolar, and architecture-balanced placement policies. The critical decisions are tail-first ordering, greedy bottleneck retargeting, and FIR-based offline stopping. These choices are intuitive and cheap, but the paper does not establish that FLOPs predict actual forward/backward stage time in general; an ablation shows measured max-stage-time guidance is slightly worse in one setting, not that FIR is universally preferable. The treatment of training semantics and gradients for cross-layer K/V reuse is also not described at sufficient algorithmic depth to independently verify that the modified architecture preserves the intended training dynamics. Key Results: On 8 Ascend 910B NPUs using LLaMA2-7B and 1F1B, the best architecture-balanced configurations improve MFU from 62.45% to 64.39% at 4K/PP=2 with 8 shared layers, from 61.28% to 63.93% at 8K/PP=4 with 6 shared layers, and from 56.32% to 61.49% at 8K/PP=8 with 4 shared layers. Corresponding iteration times fall from 104.14 to 99.27 seconds, 241.96 to 224.95 seconds, and 263.3 to 237.5 seconds. At 8K/PP=8, FIR changes from 1.1194 to 1.0004, supporting the claimed relationship between stage balance and utilization. The MFU-versus-sharing curves are non-monotonic: increasing sharing lowers total FLOPs but eventually over-corrects the original bottleneck and shifts the critical stage. On 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, experiments cover LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA2-13B, LLaMA3-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B at 4K, 8K, and 16K with PP=2, 4, and 8; the reported compact table shows KV-Pipe consistently above 1F1B and Seq1F1B in MFU and below them in iteration time. For example, LLaMA2-13B at 16K/PP=8 improves from 39.5% MFU and 960 seconds with 1F1B to 52.0% and 750 seconds with KV-Pipe, although the table's presentation does not expose all implementation and statistical details. Combining KV-Pipe with Seq1F1B yields 50.0% MFU and 248 seconds for LLaMA2-7B at 8K/PP=8, versus 47.0% and 265 seconds for Seq1F1B alone; for LLaMA2-13B at 16K/PP=8, it yields 52.0% and 750 seconds versus 48.5% and 820 seconds. A separate MHA inference case study reports throughput ratios of 1.22x, 1.35x, 2.72x, 2.57x, and 2.77x at 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, and 128K, respectively. GQA validation reports 620 to 665 tokens/s for LLaMA3-8B at 32K and 170 to 184 tokens/s for Qwen2.5-14B at 128K. Against DawnPiper in an A100 evaluation setting, the paper reports approximately 4.5% and 5.2% throughput gains on GPT-2 770M and T5 780M, respectively, but these comparisons also change pipeline mode and rely on the paper's modified KV-sharing architecture, so they are not direct comparisons of an unchanged model under equal quality constraints. Baseline coverage includes 1F1B, Seq1F1B, vPipe, DawnPiper, and GPipe, but not all current partitioning, scheduling, or production serving systems are measured head-to-head. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and arguably NEW FORMULATION; the genuinely new element is treating cross-layer KV sharing as a stage-cost and pipeline-balance control variable with an explicit FIR-guided allocation policy, while the underlying KV sharing, pipeline parallelism, greedy allocation, and cache-reduction mechanisms are established ideas combined in a new systems setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes placement comparisons, sharing-budget sweeps, tolerance sensitivity, FIR-versus-measured-time guidance, quality checks, composability with Seq1F1B, GQA inference validation, and a comparison with DawnPiper and vPipe. At PP=8/8K on LLaMA2-7B, uniform, symmetric-bipolar, and architecture-balanced placement with four shared layers produce MFU improvements of 6.40%, 7.10%, and 9.17%, respectively; changing epsilon from 0.02 to 0.10 selects 5, 4, and 3 layers while MFU improvements remain between 8.60% and 9.17%. Quality evaluation reports validation perplexity and an average over MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, and TruthfulQA for LLaMA2-7B; the best PP=8 configuration changes PPL from 5.47 to 5.49 and leaves the downstream average at 52.2 versus 52.2. However, the paper reports no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and it does not state whether the timing results are averaged over repeated runs or how warm-up, communication, and compiler effects are handled. No code, data, model weights, or repository URL is mentioned. The quality study is narrow, the main Ascend experiments use a single model and a fixed workload, and the method changes the model architecture while the paper provides limited detail on training convergence, final task quality beyond one model, or the exact implementation of cross-layer reuse in forward and backward passes. The inference comparison is presented as a case study rather than a broad comparison against modern KV-compression and serving baselines. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile. Practical: The algorithm itself runs offline using a pipeline partition and per-layer FLOPs estimates, and the measured experiments use commercially available Ascend 910B and NVIDIA V100 hardware, but deployment requires framework support for cross-layer KV reuse and retraining or evaluating the modified architecture. Efficient: The allocation procedure has negligible cost relative to training, and the reported end-to-end gains reach 9.17% MFU and 9.80% lower iteration time at PP=8; the paper does not provide a full memory, communication, or energy accounting relative to competing systems. Effective: The measured training results show lower iteration time and higher MFU, while the LLaMA2-7B quality table shows nearly unchanged PPL and downstream average for tested configurations; evidence does not establish preservation of quality for other model families, training regimes, or early-layer sharing. Scalable: Results cover PP up to 8, sequence lengths up to 16K for training and 128K for selected inference cases, but PP=16/32, frontier-scale models, MoE, hybrid Transformer-SSM models, and multi-node scaling are not evaluated, so 10x–100x scalability remains a claim rather than a measurement. The work delivers an algorithmic layer-assignment procedure and a modified-model configuration, but no publicly identified software artifact or reusable package is provided. Strengths: - It identifies a non-obvious systems degree of freedom: changing the model's effective layer-cost profile can complement, rather than replace, scheduling and partition-search methods. - The bottleneck-targeted policy explains the observed non-monotonic sharing curves and gives a concrete operational rule for choosing an intermediate sharing budget instead of maximizing cache compression blindly. - The evaluation includes both hardware backends, multiple model families, multiple pipeline degrees, long-context inference, quality measurements, stronger-schedule composition, and a prior-partitioning comparison. - The quality–efficiency analysis makes the practical claim more precise: in the tested LLaMA2 cases, the principal advantage over a fixed 25% tail-sharing rule is adaptive budget selection, with four shared layers at PP=8 outperforming eight shared layers on both iteration time and reported quality metrics. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit quality-preservation evidence to LLaMA2-7B and state that system-only results on LLaMA2-13B, LLaMA3-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B do not establish architecture-independent quality preservation. They do not claim transfer to MoE, hybrid Transformer–SSM architectures, arbitrary training regimes, or PP degrees above 8. They also acknowledge that the greedy procedure is a lightweight heuristic without global optimality guarantees and propose joint optimization of pipeline placement, KV-sharing placement, and explicit quality constraints as future work. The paper additionally notes that direct timing may be preferable when accurate stage profiles are available and that Seq1F1B was unavailable in the Ascend implementation used for the main experiments. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not adequately establish that FLOPs imbalance is the right objective when communication, memory bandwidth, kernel fusion, recomputation, backward execution, and hardware-specific utilization determine actual stage time. The FIR definition appears to be based on forward-style layer FLOPs, but the primary metric is end-to-end training MFU and iteration time; the relationship between FIR and full forward/backward stage time is therefore only partially validated. The central method changes attention behavior and potentially model quality, yet training-loss dynamics, convergence speed, gradient semantics, and comparisons at equal final quality or equal training compute are not reported. The strongest LLM results use LLaMA-family dense models, with only a small number of quality-tested configurations, so the claimed generality to heterogeneous architectures is unsubstantiated. The GPU table reports improvements over scheduling baselines but does not clearly state the selected KV budgets, layer assignments, repeated-run variance, or whether all methods use exactly matched batch sizes and implementation maturity. The inference section lacks comparisons against contemporary cross-layer KV-sharing, quantization, paging, and serving systems, and the MHA case uses an attention configuration less representative than GQA; the later GQA check contains only two model points. Finally, the comparison to DawnPiper and vPipe does not isolate the cost of quality-changing KV sharing from the benefit of partitioning or asynchronous execution, limiting the strength of the claimed advantage over those systems. Bottom Line: This is a useful systems paper with a credible and practically relevant observation—stage-aware KV sharing can improve pipeline efficiency beyond scheduler-only changes—but its novelty is primarily a well-executed coupling of known mechanisms, and broader model-quality, scale, implementation, and equal-quality comparisons are needed before treating KV-Pipe as a generally deployable solution.

HiFloat4 Format for End-To-End Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Large Language Models

HY Mak, S Golestan, H Le, MT Jazi, Y Peng, Y Wang… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces end-to-end FP4 reinforcement-learning post-training with Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ), a sparse residual correction for activation quantization in the rollout path. - Why it's important: Fully quantizing rollout and training could reduce the memory and compute cost of long-horizon LLM reasoning RL, but activation quantization currently causes large accuracy losses and unstable optimization. - How it does it: It decomposes the activation as the FP4-quantized activation plus a quantized residual, then computes the residual correction with a 50%-sparse FP4 GEMM, primarily using hardware-supported 2:4 sparsity. - The good: On Qwen2.5-3B trained on GSM8K, HiF4 with Rollout-ResQ-S2:4 improves Mean@1 from 82.03% to 85.90%, reducing the BF16 gap from 4.93 to 1.06 percentage points, while also outperforming SmoothQuant, RHT, and OCC. - The missing: The paper does not measure execution speed or energy on native FP4 and sparse hardware, so its central efficiency claim remains a theoretical estimate rather than an end-to-end systems result. - Read it or not: Researchers working on quantized LLM training, RL post-training, or accelerator-aware inference should read it for the rollout-side failure diagnosis; readers seeking validated deployment speedups or broad task coverage can defer it.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (76) and Non-Obviousness (75) are driven by isolating rollout activation quantization as the main FP4 failure mode and introducing sparse residual correction specifically in the RL rollout path. Rigor (62) is limited by simulated rather than native FP4 execution, no seeds or uncertainty estimates, sparse ablations, and missing comparisons with several relevant low-precision RL methods. Problem & Motivation: LLM reinforcement-learning post-training requires repeated autoregressive rollouts and training passes, making memory bandwidth, matrix multiplication throughput, and numerical stability important cost constraints. Existing low-precision RL methods generally retain higher precision in gradients or use 8-bit computation, while naïvely applying FP4 to both rollout and training causes substantial degradation. The paper focuses on mathematical reasoning tasks, where long generated trajectories magnify rollout cost and where errors in sampled trajectories can alter the RL learning signal. The specific gap is the lack of a fully 4-bit rollout-and-training recipe that maintains accuracy despite nonstationary activation distributions and activation outliers; static post-training quantization methods such as offline smoothing or calibration are poorly matched to an evolving RL policy. Key Idea: The central insight is that FP4 RL degradation is dominated by activation quantization in the rollout policy, not by quantization in the training pass, and that the lost activation information can be represented as a sparse residual. Instead of relying on a higher-precision rollout or doubling the number of dense FP4 GEMMs, Rollout-ResQ adds a second FP4 matrix product using a 50%-sparse quantized residual. This is a meaningful diagnosis-plus-remedy contribution, although the residual decomposition itself follows a standard quantization-error compensation pattern and the main differentiator is its placement in the RL rollout path and its chosen sparsity structure. Methodology: The system uses GRPO in VeRL, with vLLM for rollouts and FSDP for training. It quantizes linear-layer weights and activations throughout transformer blocks using either HiFloat4 (HiF4), which uses three-level hierarchical scaling over blocks of 64, or MXFP4, which uses block microscaling over blocks of 32. In the training phase, the forward pass computes quantized activation-weight products, while the activation and weight gradient paths are also quantized according to the paper's FP4 recipe. In the rollout phase, for each linear layer it computes the activation residual \(\Delta X=X-Q(X)\), quantizes that residual, applies a sparsity operator, and computes \(Q(X)Q(W)^T + S(Q(\Delta X))Q(W)^T\). It evaluates channel-wise top-50% sparsity, 2:4 semi-structured sparsity, and 50% block sparsity over 32-by-64 blocks; the main reported method is Rollout-ResQ-S2:4. Critical design decisions are: applying correction only during rollout, motivated by the precision-localization experiments; sparsifying the residual rather than the primary activation, supported by one MSE/RMSE analysis; and fixing sparsity at 50%, chosen for hardware compatibility rather than selected through a reported accuracy-efficiency sweep. The GRPO objective uses clipped importance ratios, group-relative token advantages, a KL penalty, and a truncated importance-sampling threshold of 5.0. A potential conceptual concern is that computing \(X-Q(X)\), selecting residual elements, and forming the correction may require higher-precision activation handling and metadata; the paper does not fully specify whether these operations are implemented in FP4 hardware or simulated outside the GEMM path. Key Results: On Qwen2.5-3B trained with GRPO on GSM8K, BF16 reaches 86.96% GSM8K-test and 61.2% Math-500 Mean@1. Naïve HiF4 reaches 82.03% and 44.6%, while MXFP4 reaches 73.31% and 27.8%. HiF4 Rollout-ResQ-S2:4 reaches 85.90% on GSM8K-test and 52.6% on Math-500; HiF4 block-sparse Rollout-ResQ reaches the best Math-500 result, 55.8%. For MXFP4, dense Rollout-ResQ reaches 81.65% GSM8K-test and 48.2% Math-500, while S2:4 reaches 81.65% and 46.4%. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B trained on DAPO-Math-17K, only HiF4 is evaluated: BF16 scores 27.29%, 12.08%, 64.53%, and 74.59% Mean@32 on AIME-2024, AIME-2025, AMC-2023, and Math-500, respectively; naïve HiF4 scores 16.15%, 7.29%, 55.16%, and 59.40%; Rollout-ResQ-S2:4 improves these to 20.73%, 8.54%, 55.78%, and 68.95%. Rollout-ResQ-Dense is slightly better on AIME-2025 and Math-500, reaching 8.96% and 69.02%. SmoothQuant, RHT, and OCC are generally weaker or less stable than Rollout-ResQ, with SmoothQuant especially poor in several settings. The paper claims theoretical effective speedups of 2.0x for dense residual correction and approximately 2.67x for S2:4 relative to FP16, assuming 4x FP4 throughput and ideal sparse execution; these are not measured speedups. The evaluation is standard-scale rather than stress-scale: two model sizes, two training datasets, and primarily mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper contributes a rollout-specific sparse residual correction and the empirical finding that rollout activation quantization, particularly outlier-induced zero collapse, is more damaging than training-side FP4 quantization; the underlying residual decomposition, block-scaled FP4 formats, GRPO, and 2:4 sparsity are existing techniques combined for a new fully quantized RL setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The component localization in Table 1 is useful: with Qwen2.5-3B on GSM8K, FP4 training with BF16 rollout nearly matches BF16, whereas BF16 training with FP4 rollout falls to 78.01% for HiF4 and 50.57% for MXFP4, and activation-only rollout quantization is worse than weight-only quantization. The paper also compares three Rollout-ResQ sparsity patterns and three activation outlier baselines, providing some ablation of the correction placement and sparsity structure. However, it reports no multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the apparent differences may therefore be sensitive to RL stochasticity. It does not report an ablation over sparsity levels, residual selection criteria, quantization block sizes, calibration/update frequency, or which transformer layers require correction. It compares against SmoothQuant, RHT, and OCC but does not provide direct experiments against closely related low-precision RL systems such as QeRL, QuRL, JetRL, or importance-sampling-based rollout correction. The simulated quantization code is publicly available at https://github.com/global-computing-consortium/HiFloat4, but the paper does not state that full training scripts, exact data preprocessing, model checkpoints, native kernels, or trained weights are released. All experiments use simulated FP4 because native FP4 hardware was unavailable, so the claimed throughput and memory benefits are not empirically established. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems-oriented efficiency motivation but no native deployment evaluation. Practical: The workloads can run on commercially available hardware through simulation, but the reported runs require approximately 100 GB peak memory for the 3B experiments and 370 GB for the 7B experiments, and native FP4/sparse-kernel compatibility is not demonstrated. Efficient: The method has a theoretical effective cost of 0.75 times an FP16 GEMM for S2:4 under the paper's idealized 4x FP4 throughput assumption, but actual runtime, memory traffic, residual-selection overhead, and kernel utilization are not measured. Effective: It substantially improves mathematical-reasoning accuracy over naïve FP4 and the tested outlier-mitigation baselines, reducing the HiF4 GSM8K-test gap to 1.06 points, but it does not recover BF16 performance on most out-of-distribution benchmarks and does not establish gains on non-mathematical RL tasks. Scalable: The largest evaluated model is 7B with a 17K-example training set; the authors explicitly did not test very large models or datasets, and no evidence supports extrapolation to 10x–100x scale. The work delivers publicly available simulated quantization code and a method specification, but not a validated native FP4 rollout system or reported hardware kernel implementation. Strengths: - The train-versus-rollout precision matrix isolates the failure source more convincingly than a single aggregate FP4 result: training-side FP4 with BF16 rollout preserves 86.88%/86.20% accuracy for HiF4/MXFP4, while FP4 rollout with BF16 training causes much larger losses. - The activation analysis links outliers, block scaling, and zero collapse, including layers with more than 80% post-quantization zeros, giving a plausible mechanism for why rollout errors damage RL more than ordinary supervised training. - Rollout-ResQ improves both HiF4 and MXFP4 and remains useful across two model sizes and multiple held-out math benchmarks; the S2:4 variant provides a hardware-relevant accuracy/overhead trade-off rather than relying only on a dense correction. - The paper tests several established outlier-mitigation baselines and reports both final accuracy and training-reward curves, exposing cases where faster or smoother reward convergence does not necessarily predict downstream benchmark accuracy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that all experiments use FP4 simulation because native FP4 hardware is unavailable, preventing direct speed and efficiency measurements. They also state that simulation runtime prevented experiments on extremely large models or datasets. The study fixes all sparsity patterns at 50% and leaves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off across sparsity levels for future work. These limitations are directly acknowledged, but they materially restrict the paper's practical systems conclusions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not establish that Rollout-ResQ is genuinely end-to-end FP4 in the full computational sense: residual formation, subtraction, norm or magnitude ranking, sparsity-mask construction, scale handling, and accumulation may use higher precision, but their precision and cost are not specified. Its efficiency argument assumes ideal 4x FP4 throughput and ideal sparse GEMM scaling, omitting quantization overhead, sparse-index storage, kernel launch costs, memory traffic, and residual-selection latency. The evaluation lacks native hardware, wall-clock baselines, energy measurements, seed variation, and direct comparisons with the most relevant 4-bit RL methods. The 7B study omits MXFP4 after the 3B comparison, making the format conclusion less general than the paper's framing suggests. The evaluation focuses entirely on mathematical reasoning and uses the same broad domain for training and testing, leaving robustness to other RL rewards, conversational alignment, coding, agentic tasks, and distribution shifts untested. The reported residual robustness evidence is based on a narrow activation example and MSE/RMSE, not a layerwise or training-level ablation demonstrating that the selected mask criterion is consistently optimal. Bottom Line: This is a useful preprint for quantization and LLM-RL researchers because it identifies rollout activation zero collapse as a concrete FP4 failure mode and offers a promising sparse correction, but its central deployment claim remains unverified and the empirical scope is too narrow for production conclusions.

Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, Ning Ding, Jiaye Ge, Lixin Gu, Yicheng Gu, Qipeng Guo, Ermo Hua, Haian Huang, Haozheng Hou, Jie Hou, Xiangyu Hong, Che Jiang, Minxi Jin, Cheng Liang, Dahua Lin, Dawei Liu, Kuikun Liu, Chengqi Lv, Haijun Lv, Han Lv, Ningsheng Ma, Biqing Qi, Jianmin Qian, Shiya Su, Youbang Sun, Huanze Tang, Zhongbo Tian, Hanjing Wang, Rui Wang, Ting Wang, Yi Wang, Baiting Wu, Jun Xu, Bowen Yang, Hui Wang, Weida Wang, Haochen Ye, Jiashuo Yu, Shan Yu, Xiaoyi Yu, Qirui Zeng, Qi Zhang, Ming Zhang, Wenwei Zhang, Bowen Zhou, Xinyu Zhou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 17 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Mobius-v0, a language-model architecture that separates globally shared FFN-based knowledge memory from Self-Attention-based reasoning modules and uses recurrent latent computation to produce shorter outputs. - Why it's important: If validated, the design could reduce training-data requirements and end-to-end serving cost while preserving the capabilities of similarly sized Transformer models. - How it does it: It replaces layer-local FFNs with a shared, sparsely accessed knowledge-vector repository, allowing every Reasoner to retrieve knowledge across depths and iteratively refine hidden-state latents before parallel multi-token decoding. - The good: A 35B continual-pretraining model reports roughly 4x higher request throughput than Qwen3.5-35B with higher average benchmark scores, while the 7B-from-scratch experiment reaches the Transformer baseline's MMLU score using 62.6% as many training tokens. - The missing: The paper does not provide sufficient controlled ablations, hardware/configuration details, uncertainty estimates, or comparisons against strong inference-acceleration and concise-CoT baselines to establish that the architectural change—not training, conversion, routing, or decoding differences—causes the reported gains. - Read it or not: Researchers working on latent reasoning, language-model architecture, or efficient inference should read it as an ambitious systems hypothesis, but practitioners should not treat the headline speedups as deployment evidence until the evaluation is independently reproducible.
