CoinVE-200K: A Large-Scale High-Quality Dataset for Compositional Instruction-Guided Video Editing (13 ▲ )

Fuchen Long, Cong Wang, Zitao Gao, Wenhao Zhong, Yu Cheng, Xiaolu Hou, Yan Li, Xiao Cao, Xinlong Sun, Xi Chen, Yu Liu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CoinVE-200K, CoinVE-Bench, and CoinVE-Edit: a 200K-pair compositional video-editing dataset, a 361-video benchmark, and a 22B region-aware editing model for executing 2–5 editing operations in one video. - Why it's important: Existing instruction-guided video-editing data and models mainly support isolated edits, limiting reliable use in content creation scenarios requiring simultaneous changes to subjects, objects, and backgrounds. - How it does it: It generates synthetic multi-edit pairs with keyword-grounded SAM3/SAM2 masks and uses instruction-specific mask prediction, local/global gating, and soft Q-Blending cross-attention to route each edit to the appropriate spatiotemporal region. - The good: On CoinVE-Bench, CoinVE-Edit reaches 87.97 semantic accuracy, 89.45 scope accuracy, 89.60 editing persistence, 95.30 motion naturalness, and 90.83 content preservation, exceeding the reported open-source baselines on the main correctness metrics. - The missing: The dataset and benchmark rely heavily on synthetic generation and automated MLLM evaluation, with no reported human-study validation, detailed inter-rater reliability, inference-cost analysis, or evaluation beyond the authors’ benchmark. - Read it or not: Researchers working on controllable video generation, video-editing datasets, or multimodal grounding should read it for the dataset construction and routing design, while practitioners seeking a deployable editor should wait for evidence on inference cost, robustness, and real-user edits.
Why this rank
Systems profile. The compositional video-editing dataset, benchmark, and instruction-specific soft routing provide a meaningful contribution (novelty 74; non-obviousness 70), with useful routing ablations and a public dataset link, but synthetic-data and evaluator coupling, no human validation or uncertainty, unfairly weak composition baselines, and missing inference-cost analysis reduce rigor (50), completeness (52), and resilience (47). The released dataset and model-oriented artifact support impact (78), but deployment claims remain unsubstantiated; weighted score = 0.15*74 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*52 + 0.15*47 + 0.30*78 = 63.85, rounded to 64.
systems Novelty 74 Rigor 50 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 52 Resilience 47 Impact 78
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Instruction-guided video editing must modify specified content while preserving identity, motion, scene structure, and all irrelevant regions across time. The practical gap is compositional editing: a single request may combine additions, removals, replacements, and stylization across humans, objects, and backgrounds. Prior datasets cited by the paper—including OpenVE, Ditto, ReCo, InsViE, and Señorita—are characterized as focusing primarily on one dominant operation or one target region, providing limited supervision for decomposing multiple intents, grounding them to separate spatial-temporal regions, and preventing interference between edits. The target users and domains include content creators, film and advertising workflows, and interactive visual storytelling systems. Key Idea: The central insight is to represent each atomic instruction as a separate semantic condition with its own predicted spatiotemporal mask and local/global gate, then combine the resulting instruction-specific cross-attention outputs through soft query-wise blending rather than hard attention masking. This makes the model’s edit routing region-aware while retaining the pretrained video generator’s attention distribution and generative prior. Methodology: CoinVE-200K is built from OpenVid-HD videos filtered to at least 81 frames, a short-side resolution of at least 1080 pixels, suitable aesthetic scores, and appropriate optical-flow magnitude; 420K videos enter subsequent synthesis. Qwen3.6-27B parses each source into subjects, objects, and background regions. Operation templates for addition, removal, replacement, and stylization are instantiated with source-grounded concepts, combined into requests containing 2–5 atomic edits, and checked for compatibility. For synthesis, Qwen3.6-27B extracts edited keywords, SAM3 segments corresponding regions on a representative key frame, and SAM2 propagates masks through the video. HunyuanImage-3.0 or Nano Banana edits the key frame, after which a fine-tuned Wan2.2-Animate-14B or VACE synthesizes the full edited video using the edited key frame, source video, and combined masks. Gemini 2.5 Pro filters samples for per-instruction execution, semantic consistency, temporal consistency, and physical plausibility; a sample is retained only if all checks pass. The resulting dataset contains 200K 1080p pairs with 81–201 frames, six reported atomic edit categories, and an average of 2.55 instructions per video. CoinVE-Edit uses Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, a connector, a mask predictor, GateNet, and a Wan2.1-T2V-14B DiT. For instruction i, the mask predictor produces a probability mask M_i and GateNet produces g_i in [0,1], where local edits use the mask and global edits bypass it. The Q-Blending weight is w_q^i = 1 - beta g_i(1 - M_i), and instruction-specific attention outputs are combined as a normalized weighted sum. Training uses flow matching, binary-cross-entropy plus Dice segmentation loss, and a gate classification loss: L_total = lambda_dit L_dit + lambda_seg L_seg + lambda_gate L_gate, with default weights of 1. The three training phases are image feature alignment, mixed image/video single-instruction editing, and compositional fine-tuning on CoinVE-200K. The separation between instruction-specific conditions, the soft rather than hard routing, and the progressive training schedule are the key design decisions; the paper provides empirical ablations for routing but limited independent justification for the extensive synthetic-data pipeline or the choice of automated evaluators. Key Results: CoinVE-200K contains 200K pairs at 1080p and 81–201 frames. Its reported atomic-operation distribution is local addition 24.1%, background replacement 23.8%, object replacement 22.8%, local removal 18.5%, background stylization 6.4%, and object stylization 4.5%. Videos contain two, three, four, or five instructions in 57.7%, 31.7%, 8.5%, and 2.1% of cases, respectively. The dataset’s reported average editing-quality score is 4.85, compared with 2.66 for InsViE-1M, 2.95 for Señorita-2M, 4.01 for ReCo, 3.52 for Ditto-1M, and 3.82 for OpenVE-3M; the evaluator and scoring procedure for these cross-dataset comparisons are not fully detailed in the parsed text. CoinVE-Bench contains 361 held-out source videos and evaluates 11 metrics across instruction accuracy, physical naturalness, semantic preservation, and video quality. On the compositional benchmark, CoinVE-Edit records SA 87.97, SPA 89.45, EP 89.60, AN 91.85, SC 91.17, MN 95.30, CP 90.83, AQ 4.13, TQ 19.57, CQ 4.31, and TS 0.72. It exceeds Seedance 2.0 on SA, SPA, EP, MN, and TS ties SAMA on TS, but trails Seedance 2.0 on AN 93.19, SC 95.84, CP 93.91, AQ 4.47, and CQ 4.41; it also trails Kling O3 on AQ 4.49. On OpenVE-Bench single-instruction editing, CoinVE-Edit obtains an overall Gemini score of 3.41, below Runway’s 3.51 but above the listed open-source systems; its strongest reported categories are background change 3.11 and local removal 3.81. In ablations, removing both masks and Q-Blending lowers SA from 87.97 to 82.61 and SPA from 89.45 to 84.43; replacing Q-Blending with Q-Bias yields SA 83.35 and SPA 85.49, while physical metrics also decline. Mask Predictor reaches IoU 0.71 and GateNet reaches 0.95 binary accuracy during training. These results support the value of explicit routing, although the largest comparison is against baselines that receive concatenated comma-separated instructions rather than architectures designed specifically for composition. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the dataset’s explicit 2–5-operation composition and benchmark are the clearest contributions, while Q-Blending is a targeted architectural adaptation that combines standard MLLM conditioning, segmentation, gating, diffusion-transformer editing, and synthetic data generation rather than introducing a fundamentally new generative-learning paradigm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations, mask visualizations, comparisons with seven open-source methods and two proprietary systems, and a held-out benchmark described as disjoint from training data. It reports mask IoU, GateNet accuracy, dataset composition, training stages, batch sizes, learning rates, training steps, LoRA ranks, and hardware: all training uses 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The dataset is linked at https://huggingface.co/datasets/FireCRT/CoinVE-200K and the project page is https://coinve200k.github.io; code, model weights, and evaluation scripts are not stated as released. No error bars, multiple random seeds, statistical significance tests, human evaluation, evaluator agreement, or confidence intervals are reported. Dataset filtering and benchmark scoring rely substantially on Gemini-based judgments, while the benchmark comparisons use different model types and concatenate multiple instructions for most baselines. The synthetic pairs are generated with powerful image/video editing systems and then filtered by related automated models, creating possible evaluator-generator coupling and distribution bias. The paper does not provide detailed train/validation/test statistics, source-video licensing analysis, rejection rates from the 420K candidates to the final 200K, per-operation and per-composition performance, or leakage checks against the pretrained models’ data. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile, because the paper trains and evaluates a 22B editing system and releases a dataset, although it does not report deployment measurements. Practical: The model can in principle run on commercially available GPUs, but a 22B model with Qwen3-VL, Wan2.1, video VAE processing, and multi-frame diffusion has no reported inference hardware or latency profile. Efficient: The paper reports 32 H200 GPUs for training but gives no inference memory, runtime, throughput, number of denoising steps, or comparison with alternative editors. Effective: The benchmark shows strong instruction-following, localization, motion-naturalness, and preservation scores, but evidence is mainly synthetic-data evaluation with MLLM and specialized automatic metrics rather than real-user or human-verified editing quality. Scalable: The system is tested on clips up to 201 frames and trained with at most 49 frames and 600x600 pixels in the single-instruction stage; behavior at 10x–100x longer videos, higher concurrency, or substantially more than five edits is not evaluated. The work delivers a public dataset and benchmark links and a described 22B model artifact, but public code and weights are not stated. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete and underrepresented capability gap—joint execution of multiple spatially and semantically distinct video edits—and operationalizes it through a dataset with explicit composition counts, edit taxonomies, and region-aware examples. - The Q-Blending mechanism is technically coherent: it applies instruction-specific spatial routing to attention outputs without modifying attention logits or adding parameters to the DiT backbone, and the ablation shows gains over both instruction concatenation and hard/bias-based routing. - The benchmark separates semantic execution, edit scope, temporal persistence, physical naturalness, non-target preservation, and technical/video quality instead of collapsing evaluation into one score. - The release of 200K high-resolution pairs, a benchmark, and dataset statistics could lower the entry cost for research on compositional video editing, provided the synthetic-data and evaluation biases are characterized. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that CoinVE-200K does not cover reference-based editing, fine-grained motion editing, or complex camera control. They also acknowledge challenges in efficient editing of long videos and highly interactive scenes. Future work is said to target broader editing taxonomies, improved long-range temporal consistency, lower model cost, and unified video-editing agents. These limitations are stated directly, but the paper does not discuss synthetic-data bias, automated-evaluator reliability, licensing, or the absence of inference-cost measurements. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The principal concern is that both the training labels and the quality claims are generated or filtered by automated foundation models, so the dataset may encode the capabilities, stylistic preferences, and failure modes of HunyuanImage, Nano Banana, Wan/VACE, SAM, and Gemini rather than independent ground truth. The strict all-subedits-must-pass filter may improve apparent quality while removing difficult compositions and inducing survivorship bias; the paper does not report candidate rejection rates or human validation. CoinVE-Bench is authored by the same project and evaluated largely with an MLLM checklist, with no human agreement study, evaluator calibration, or independent benchmark. Baseline fairness is uncertain because most competing models receive comma-concatenated multi-instruction prompts and are not adapted or fine-tuned for composition, whereas CoinVE-Edit is trained directly on CoinVE-200K. The paper does not report per-operation results, scaling with the number of edits, performance on motion-heavy or occluded cases, robustness to paraphrases and unseen combinations, or performance on real user-provided edits. It also omits inference latency, VRAM, energy, sampling cost, model-weight/code release status, detailed source-data provenance, and a comparison against a stronger oracle or sequential-editing pipeline. Finally, the claimed 1080p dataset resolution contrasts with the 600x600 and 49-frame training limits reported for an earlier stage, leaving the effective training and inference resolution unclear. Bottom Line: This is a useful dataset-and-system paper with a credible region-routing ablation and strong reported benchmark numbers, but its practical and scientific significance depends on independent human evaluation, fairer composition-aware baselines, and reproducible evidence that the gains transfer beyond a synthetic, author-constructed benchmark.

Overcoming Shortcut Learning in Graph Neural Networks through Active Explanation Guidance

T Younesian, S Azzolin, A Longa, F Ferrini… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces XIGL, an architecture-agnostic human-in-the-loop pipeline that uses actively selected, expert-corrected GNN explanations to reduce shortcut dependence. - Why it's important: Shortcut reliance can produce high in-distribution accuracy but fail under distribution shift, while labeling causal explanations for every graph is expensive. - How it does it: XIGL selects graphs using prediction or explanation uncertainty, obtains node-level relevance corrections, and fine-tunes the GNN with a normalized input-gradient penalty on irrelevant nodes. - The good: On the synthetic ER-color task, passive explanation supervision raises unconfounded-test accuracy from 50.93–60.40% without supervision to 70.53–74.27% across the four tested GNNs, and active selection often beats random sampling. - The missing: The paper does not evaluate real human annotation, explanation faithfulness, modern shortcut-removal baselines, or substantially larger and more realistic graphs, so its annotation-cost and deployment claims remain largely unvalidated. - Read it or not: Read it for work on explanation-guided debiasing and graph active learning; practitioners seeking evidence for real-world deployment should wait for broader datasets, stronger baselines, and human-in-the-loop studies.

Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (78) reflect the useful idea of actively querying explanation corrections, especially the counterintuitive focus on confident concentrated explanations. Rigor (58), Completeness (65), and Resilience (57) are reduced by reliance on small engineered benchmarks, missing human annotation and faithfulness studies, weak modern baselines, large variance, and extensive condition-specific tuning; Impact (52) is only moderate because annotation savings and deployment costs are not measured. Problem & Motivation: GNN classifiers can exploit nodes, edges, or features that correlate with labels in the training distribution but are not causally relevant, causing severe degradation when those correlations change. The problem concerns graph classification applications in which models must remain reliable under distribution shift, including settings with metadata, watermarks, or other spurious graph structure. Existing approaches may require multiple domains or explanation supervision for the entire training set, creating data and annotation requirements that are often unavailable. The paper targets the gap between full explanation supervision and no supervision by asking whether expert corrections can be concentrated on examples whose model explanations are most likely to reveal shortcut behavior. Key Idea: Use the model’s own explanation uncertainty—not only predictive uncertainty—to decide which examples deserve expert annotation. XIGL assumes that input-gradient explanations expose shortcut reliance and argues that both highly diffuse explanations and highly concentrated explanations can be informative: diffuse explanations may indicate uncertainty, whereas concentrated explanations may reflect confident reliance on a simple but spurious feature. Correcting the selected explanations then directly penalizes the model’s sensitivity to marked irrelevant nodes. Methodology: For a graph G with node features and a class prediction, XIGL computes node-wise input gradients, with the paper defining a node score as the sum across class-log-probability gradients. It trains the GNN using cross-entropy plus an explanation loss, L = L_ce + λL_e, where L_e is the ratio of squared gradient mass assigned to irrelevant nodes to total squared gradient mass; the ground-truth explanation marks relevant nodes with 1 and irrelevant nodes with 0. The denominator is intended to prevent the trivial solution in which all input gradients vanish, although the paper does not fully analyze the resulting optimization behavior. In the active-learning loop, the method begins with q explained graphs, trains the model, generates predictions and explanations for unexplained graphs, selects a batch, obtains explanation corrections, adds them to the supervised set, and fine-tunes the model. It evaluates Random and maximum classification entropy (MaCE) as prediction-based strategies, and introduces maximum explanation entropy (MaEE) and minimum explanation entropy (MiEE), computed from softmax-normalized node-gradient scores and normalized by log graph size. Three important design choices are the use of input gradients rather than a learned explainer, the normalized gradient-ratio loss, and MiEE’s deliberate targeting of confident explanations; the first is motivated by simplicity, the second by avoiding gradient collapse, and the third primarily by a simplicity-bias argument rather than a formal analysis. Second-order derivatives arise during optimization, and the paper claims their computational overhead was small but provides no measured overhead. Key Results: The experiments use four GNNs—GCN, GIN, GraphSAGE, and GAT—on two datasets: a synthetic ER-color dataset of 1,000 50-node Erdős–Rényi graphs and CPatchMNIST, an MNIST-derived superpixel graph dataset with label-correlated patch colors in training but randomized colors in validation and test. On unconfounded ER-color test data, passive supervision improves GCN from 60.40±11.36% to 71.20±20.73%, GIN from 52.93±4.23% to 74.20±21.18%, GraphSAGE from 56.80±14.24% to 70.53±17.76%, and GAT from 50.93±4.21% to 74.27±18.74%, with five-seed means and standard deviations. On CPatchMNIST, passive supervision improves GCN from 26.28±12.58% to 30.57±2.90%, GIN from 0.20±0.12% to 33.38±1.13%, and GAT from 22.61±3.93% to 25.25±9.38%, while GraphSAGE slightly decreases from 31.50±6.85% to 30.68±1.88%. In active learning, ER-color accuracy ranges from 50.13% to 73.20% across strategies and architectures; CPatchMNIST ranges from 22.56% to 32.74%. Explanation-based strategies generally outperform prediction-based strategies on CPatchMNIST, MiEE is the most consistently strong strategy overall, and Random is best for GIN on both datasets. Active experiments use an initial 10 explained instances, then 5 instances per round for 20 rounds on ER-color and 50 per round for 10 rounds on CPatchMNIST; the paper claims these budgets use less than 20% of the training data and approach passive performance, but it does not provide a direct annotation-cost measurement. The evaluation is standard-scale and highly controlled rather than stress-scale, and no comparison is reported against a strong existing explanation-guided deconfounding method beyond the no-supervision and active-learning baselines. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the active selection of graph instances for explanation correction, particularly the maximum- and minimum-explanation-entropy queries, while the explanation-guided gradient penalty builds on prior “right for the right reasons” training and existing explanation-based GNN deconfounding; the work is therefore a new integration and active-learning formulation rather than a wholly new explanation or causal-learning principle. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports means and standard deviations over five seeds and evaluates four GNN architectures on two distribution-shifted datasets. It includes passive-versus-no-supervision comparisons and four active query strategies, but it does not provide component ablations isolating the normalized denominator, the gradient explainer, the loss terms, the warm-up schedule, or the choice of minimum versus maximum explanation entropy. No confidence intervals, statistical tests, annotation-time measurements, human annotator agreement, explanation-faithfulness measurements, or computational-overhead measurements are reported. Hyperparameters, training epochs, learning-rate ranges, and λ values are listed in the appendix; the paper states that the implementation is available at https://github.com/TYounesian/xilgraph.git in the abstract, but the appendix also says the full codebase will be released upon acceptance, so the exact reproducibility status is unclear. The synthetic confounders are intentionally constructed and the CPatchMNIST benchmark is closely aligned with the proposed mechanism, limiting evidence against benchmark-specific tuning. The active strategies use different tuned learning rates and λ values for each model/dataset/strategy combination, which may complicate fair comparison. The paper omits comparisons to several plausible debiasing, invariant-learning, explanation-regularization, and active-learning baselines, including a direct experimental comparison with the cited prior explanation-supervision approach. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a proposed software pipeline rather than a demonstrated deployed system. * Practical: The models and datasets are small enough to run on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not report hardware requirements or the cost of computing second-order gradients. * Efficient: XIGL reduces the number of graphs receiving explanation labels, but its relative training and explanation-computation cost versus ordinary active learning or full explanation supervision is not measured. * Effective: The controlled ER-color and CPatchMNIST shifts show improved accuracy in some settings, especially for GIN and ER-color, but the method does not consistently improve every architecture and the evidence uses accuracy as a proxy rather than testing real operational reliability. * Scalable: No experiment tests graphs, datasets, models, or annotation pools at 10×–100× scale; scalability is claimed through architecture agnosticism but not demonstrated. The work delivers a proposed implementation, reportedly hosted at https://github.com/TYounesian/xilgraph.git, but no independently validated dataset, trained model, annotation interface, or production system is described. Strengths: - It identifies a useful interaction between explanation supervision and active learning: the annotation target is not merely an uncertain label but a potentially misleading model rationale. - The normalized explanation loss addresses a concrete degeneracy in gradient-based explanation regularization by discouraging simultaneous collapse of relevant and irrelevant gradients. - The study tests the approach across GCN, GIN, GraphSAGE, and GAT and reports five-seed variability rather than a single run, revealing architecture-dependent behavior such as GraphSAGE’s lack of passive benefit on CPatchMNIST and Random’s advantage for GIN. - The minimum-explanation-entropy strategy encodes a non-obvious hypothesis—that confident, concentrated explanations may be more likely to represent shortcut learning—and obtains comparatively consistent results across the reported settings. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the current study to graph classification, two datasets, four GNN architectures, and synthetic or specially constructed shortcut shifts. They state that they have not evaluated more datasets, more shortcut types, real-world data, self-explainable GNNs, or the role of explanation faithfulness. They also acknowledge that the gap between active strategies narrows as the annotation budget grows and leave the unexplained behavior of Random sampling for GIN to future work. These limitations are directly acknowledged, although the paper still presents annotation-cost reduction without measuring human annotation or cognitive effort. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central causal interpretation is not established: expert corrections are treated as ground-truth relevant-node masks in the experiments, while the practical setting allows users to provide subjective corrections that may not match the true mechanism. The paper does not test whether gradient explanations are faithful to the GNN’s actual decision process, despite citing faithfulness as a known concern. It lacks direct baselines for explanation-guided deconfounding, invariant-risk or domain-generalization methods, graph-specific shortcut-removal methods, and active-learning methods beyond entropy and random selection. The datasets contain only one principal synthetic confounder pattern and one patch-color construction, so gains may reflect matching the supervision and evaluation mechanism rather than robust shortcut removal. The reported standard deviations are large in several ER-color conditions—for example, 21.18 percentage points for passive GIN and 23.74 for passive GAT—and the study does not test statistical significance. The use of extensive per-condition hyperparameter tuning, fixed epoch schedules without early stopping, and a warm-up procedure for passive supervision raises questions about fairness and sensitivity. Finally, the paper does not quantify annotation time, expert agreement, query diversity, training overhead, or performance when corrections are noisy, incomplete, adversarial, or systematically biased. Bottom Line: The paper offers a worthwhile active explanation-supervision mechanism and promising controlled results, but its novelty and practical impact are not yet established beyond small, engineered benchmarks; readers should treat it as an early preprint and require stronger baselines, faithfulness tests, human-cost measurements, and real-world or larger-scale validation before relying on it.

Characterizing Rhetorical Misalignment in Decision-Making with Language Models

Z Cheng, J Chan, S Du, C Tan, Y Guo, H Peng · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a decision-theoretic framework and human-plus-LLM evaluation pipeline for measuring when an LLM’s rhetorical presentation causes decision-makers to choose lower-utility actions despite receiving relevant information. - Why it's important: In high-stakes settings such as clinical decision support, even factually correct model outputs can cause harm if wording induces inappropriate reliance, anchoring, authority effects, or loss aversion. - How it does it: The authors compare rational Bayesian and bias-prompted behavioral decision-makers under natural and controlled language conditions, and conduct a Prolific experiment in which medically trained participants revise answers to USMLE questions after reading model analyses. - The good: Across 939 human annotations and eight model variants, assistance improves mean accuracy from 45.7% to 57.5% but still produces harmful correct-to-incorrect changes, averaging 2.81% and reaching 6.6% for Llama-3.1-Tülu-3-8B-SFT. - The missing: The study does not establish causal attribution of human errors to specific rhetorical features, provide uncertainty estimates or statistical tests, or validate the LLM-simulated behavioral decision-makers against independent human behavioral data. - Read it or not: Researchers studying human-AI decision making and AI safety should read it for the framing and measurement proposal, but practitioners should not treat the simulated disagreement scores as validated clinical-risk estimates.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses a human-AI collaboration problem: language models increasingly present recommendations, explanations, and evidence to people making uncertain decisions, but standard evaluations usually measure model factuality, answer accuracy, or intrinsic cognitive bias rather than whether presentation changes human behavior in harmful ways. The relevant users include clinicians and other decision-makers in high-stakes domains where a correct initial judgment can be overturned by an apparently authoritative or emotionally salient explanation. The specific gap is the absence of a framework that separates the value of information from the effect of its linguistic representation and measures loss relative to a rational-use benchmark. The clinical setting is represented by USMLE-style multiple-choice questions rather than actual patient care. Key Idea The core insight is to define rhetorical misalignment as the utility gap between a rational decision-maker who uses the information conveyed by an AI output and a behavioral decision-maker whose belief updating or utility evaluation is distorted by the output’s language. The paper treats the utterance or rhetorical representation as an independent variable, so two messages containing the same underlying claims can be compared for their effects on decisions. This is a useful conceptual extension of human-AI reliance and Bayesian information-value frameworks, although the empirical operationalization relies on prompted LLM proxies rather than directly observed human utility or cognition. Methodology The human study constructs a text-only dataset of 363 questions aggregated from USMLE Steps 1–3, excluding image-based questions. Participants recruited through Prolific self-report medical training or clinical experience; 162 participants produced 939 question-level annotations. For each assigned question, a participant answers and reports confidence, reads a pre-generated analysis from one of eight models, may revise the answer and confidence, and supplies a rationale for any change. The evaluated models are GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Haiku-4.5, DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-Tülu-3-8B in SFT and DPO variants. The formal model uses binary state and action spaces, a prior over baseline covariates, an optional information covariate, and a payoff function with a safe default and risky action. It defines baseline payoff R∅, rational-information payoff Rℓ, behavioral payoff Rℓ, and rhetorical-misalignment loss Rℓ − Rℓ. The scalable evaluation uses DeepSeek-V3.1 as both a Bayesian-prompted rational decision-maker and a bias-prompted behavioral decision-maker. For controlled comparisons, Gemini-2.5-Pro generates a shared pool of claims, which are decomposed and LLM-rewritten into neutralized statements; model-specific and neutral representations are then supplied to the simulated decision-makers. Critical design choices are: using correct-to-incorrect answer changes as the human harm measure, defining a rational Bayesian counterfactual, and prompting the behavioral simulator with explicit anchoring, availability, confirmation, conservatism, overconfidence, and loss-aversion instructions. The first measure is interpretable, but the paper does not fully justify its aggregation across heterogeneous questions; the Bayesian counterfactual is normative rather than observed; and the neutralization and behavioral prompts are not independently validated as preserving information or reproducing human biases. Key Results In the human experiment, mean participant accuracy rises from 45.7% before model exposure to 57.5% afterward. Participants revise answers in 27.58% of cases on average; the paper reports a mean harmful rate of 2.81% across models, although the table shows model-specific harmful rates from 0.0% for Gemini-2.5-Pro to 6.6% for Llama-3.1-Tülu-3-8B-SFT. GPT-5.1 has 86.7% answer accuracy, a 37.8% human change rate, 25.6% helpful revisions, 2.4% harmful revisions, and +23.2 percentage points net impact. Gemini-2.5-Pro has 93.4% model accuracy and 0.0% harmful revisions; Claude-Haiku-4.5 has 84.5% accuracy and 1.2% harmful revisions; DeepSeek-V3.1 has 85.1% accuracy and 3.7% harmful revisions; Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct has 81.8% accuracy and 2.7% harmful revisions; and Llama-3.1-Tülu-3-8B-SFT has 50.0% accuracy and 6.6% harmful revisions. Authority-related rationales appear in 58.9% of coded cases and are associated with a mean belief change of 0.234, but the coding is interpretive and does not identify a causal mechanism. Model correctness matters but does not determine revision: conditional on initially incorrect human answers, helpful revision is 36.4% when the model is correct versus 17.4% when incorrect; conditional on initially correct answers, harmful revision is 5.6% when the model is correct versus 10.3% when incorrect. In the controlled simulation, rational-versus-behavioral disagreement ranges from 0.8% for Gemini-2.5-Pro to 16.0% for Tülu-3-8B-SFT, with rational accuracy generally exceeding behavioral accuracy; in the naturalistic setting disagreement ranges from 9.9% for GPT-5.1 to 19.3% for Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Smaller models generally show larger controlled gaps, but the family and post-training analyses are heterogeneous: SFT and DPO sometimes widen and sometimes narrow the gap. The strongest empirical result is the repeated observation of harmful human revisions across models, not the claim that particular cognitive biases caused them. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the explicit formulation of language representation as a source of human-AI utility loss and its combination with a human clinical decision experiment and a scalable simulator; the underlying Bayesian decision theory, cognitive-bias concepts, prompting, LLM evaluation, and neutral rewriting are standard components applied in a new measurement setting. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports a human study, a controlled simulation, a naturalistic simulation, model-family comparisons, and a diagnostic bias-prompt validation, but it does not report confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, hypothesis tests, inter-rater reliability statistics, power analysis, or question-level mixed-effects analyses. The human sample is modest and recruited using self-reported medical background; the assignment structure, participant expertise distribution, per-model sample sizes, and balancing across questions are not fully stated in the parsed text. The shared information pool is generated from Gemini-2.5-Pro and neutralized by LLMs, creating a possible benchmark-construction and evaluator-dependence problem: the source model determines the claims, and rewriting may alter factual content or salience. The behavioral simulator is explicitly instructed to exhibit biases, so disagreement may reflect prompt compliance rather than naturally induced cognitive bias. Bias labels for both human rationales and simulated reasoning are also assigned through author- or LLM-mediated coding, with no reported reliability or independent behavioral validation. The paper does not state that code, data, prompts beyond the appendix, model outputs, or trained weights are released; the USMLE-derived dataset may also have redistribution constraints. Baselines are not conventional debiasing, calibrated explanation, neutralization, or human-AI interface baselines, and there is no comparison against explanations deliberately optimized for uncertainty, evidence citation, or calibrated reliance. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a lightweight research-interface component rather than a demonstrated deployed clinical system. Practical: The evaluation pipeline can run on commercially available cloud infrastructure, and the human interface is implemented with Flask and Amazon EC2, but the paper does not provide deployment requirements, latency, or a released artifact. Efficient: The approach requires multiple LLM calls for generation, claim extraction, neutralization, rational simulation, behavioral simulation, and bias annotation; no token, monetary, latency, GPU, or memory comparison is reported. Effective: The human study shows a net accuracy improvement alongside measurable harmful revisions, but it establishes effects on USMLE multiple-choice answers and self-reported rationales, not clinical outcomes, patient safety, or real workflow decisions. Scalable: The simulator increases evaluation throughput relative to human studies, but the paper tests only 363 questions, 60 manually curated bias-validation problems, and the listed model variants; it does not test 10×–100× larger datasets, longer interactions, multimodal inputs, repeated exposure, or institution-scale deployment. The work delivers a research evaluation pipeline and a formal measurement framework; it does not state that it releases a reusable library, CLI, dataset, or deployed clinical tool. Strengths - It identifies a meaningful failure mode distinct from model factuality: a model can provide useful information while its presentation still causes a correct human answer to become incorrect. - The human experiment measures both helpful and harmful changes rather than reporting only aggregate accuracy gains, producing a more decision-relevant safety metric. - The formal decomposition into baseline value, value of information, realized value, and rhetorical value loss gives future work a vocabulary for separating informational errors from presentation effects. - The controlled shared-claim setting is directionally appropriate for isolating language effects, and the comparison across closed-source, open-source, model-size, SFT, and DPO variants reveals that post-training does not produce a uniform rhetorical-alignment trend. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit the empirical evaluation to USMLE-derived clinical questions and acknowledge that these tasks may not represent other domains. They state that the harmful rate is modest and that the study does not measure patient outcomes, economic costs, or institutional impacts. They also acknowledge incomplete coverage of architectures, deployment settings, and prompting strategies, and call for broader domains, improved evaluation protocols, and training methods for rhetorical alignment. The impact statement additionally warns that rhetorical-influence measurements could be misused to optimize persuasion, and that simulation should be treated as a screening tool rather than a substitute for human-subject evaluation. These limitations are directly acknowledged, although their implications for causal interpretation and statistical uncertainty are not fully developed. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper infers cognitive-bias mechanisms from participant rationales and bias-prompted model behavior, but it does not manipulate specific rhetorical features or compare matched messages in a human factorial experiment; therefore anchoring, authority bias, and loss aversion remain plausible interpretations rather than established causal mechanisms. - The human study uses answer correctness on exam questions as a proxy for clinical decision quality. USMLE answer keys provide a clean label, but the setup omits patient preferences, diagnostic uncertainty, time pressure, team interaction, treatment tradeoffs, and consequences of different errors. - The use of Prolific participants with self-reported medical experience does not demonstrate effects on licensed clinicians, and the reported mean of approximately six questions per participant may create substantial participant- and question-level variance that aggregate percentages conceal. - The controlled simulation is not a clean causal test if LLM-generated decomposition and neutralization change claim selection, specificity, ordering, or implied confidence. The paper does not report human or expert verification that the paired representations are semantically and pragmatically equivalent. - The rational and behavioral agents are both instances of DeepSeek-V3.1 with different prompts. Their disagreement can reflect prompt-induced output distributions, instruction-following artifacts, or inconsistent calibration rather than a validated rational-versus-human-behavioral gap. - No confidence intervals, significance tests, seed variability, calibration metrics, or correction for repeated comparisons are reported, making it difficult to determine whether small model differences such as 0.8% versus 1.1% controlled disagreement are reliable. - The paper does not evaluate mitigation methods, despite suggesting uncertainty presentation, alternatives, and critical-comparison interfaces; consequently it diagnoses a risk but does not show how to reduce it. Bottom Line This is a worthwhile conceptual and empirical starting point for researchers evaluating human-AI reliance because the human harmful-revision result is concrete, but its causal claims and LLM-simulation measurements require stronger statistical analysis, expert-participant studies, controlled rhetorical manipulations, and validated mitigation experiments before supporting clinical deployment decisions.

Problem & Motivation: On-policy distillation usually assumes compatible teacher and student tokenizers and relatively similar model families. The paper addresses transfer from a long-context reasoning teacher to shorter-context students, especially when the models use different vocabularies, chat templates, architectures, and context budgets. Naive OPD can evaluate student trajectories under the teacher but then push the student toward long responses that exceed its rollout budget, suppress termination tokens, increase repetition, and destabilize optimization. The practical gap is therefore not only capability transfer, but capability transfer that preserves termination, avoids truncation, and works across heterogeneous tokenization schemes without requiring supervised teacher trajectories. Key Idea: Represent the student rollout as a surface string, re-tokenize that same response with the teacher tokenizer, and transfer teacher log-probabilities only at positions where the teacher and student consume identical text spans with identical boundaries. Unmatched student positions receive no teacher signal beyond a fallback to the student policy, while a KL penalty to the initial student policy constrains policy drift and termination-token advantage masking prevents the teacher from directly discouraging structural stopping decisions. The core insight is that partial, exact text-span alignment can provide sufficient token-level supervision without constructing a many-to-many mapping between incompatible tokenizations. Methodology: Given a conversation, the student applies its own chat template and samples a response using its rollout policy. The response is decoded into a surface string, inserted into the teacher's separately formatted context, and scored by the teacher after teacher-side tokenization. A linear two-pointer scan aligns student and teacher tokens when their cumulative prefixes and current text pieces coincide; partially overlapping pieces are discarded. For aligned positions, the teacher log-probability replaces the student target; for unmatched positions, the target falls back to the student's pre-update log-probability. The resulting fixed advantages are optimized with a PPO-clipped objective, with four policy updates per rollout batch. The paper additionally masks OPD advantages on tokens such as `</think>` and `<|im_end|>`, and adds a student-reference KL regularizer, using coefficient 0.5 for Qwen-series and Intern-S2 models and 1.0 for GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4. The exact full reference-KL objective is not stated in the presented method equations, and the coefficient choices are justified mainly by limited coefficient sweeps rather than a general selection rule. Training uses SU-01, a 30B-A3B teacher, proof data consisting of 63 OPC, 2,948 AoPS, 900 book, and 617 Shuzhimi/Evan Chen problems, 100 rollout iterations, learning rate 1e-6, rollout batch size 64, four responses per prompt, PPO clip 0.2, and maximum distillation lengths of 32K for Qwen models and 6K for GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4. Key Results: On the main table, Qwen3-4B improves from 11.42 to 23.72 ProofBench@4, 47.50 to 64.50 AnswerBench@8, 71.25 to 90.83 AIME25@8, and 23.00 to 35.00 AMOBench@8. Qwen3-30B-A3B improves from 13.80 to 36.47 on ProofBench, 59.13 to 74.46 on AnswerBench, and 88.33 to 93.75 on AIME25. Cross-tokenizer Qwen3.5-35B-A3B improves from 26.78 to 42.39 ProofBench and from 73.16 to 80.15 AnswerBench; Intern-S2-Preview improves from 21.70 to 44.50 ProofBench, 76.03 to 80.10 AnswerBench, and 88.33 to 95.00 AIME25. GLM-4.7-Flash rises from 30.8 to 39.7 ProofBench and 69.6 to 72.0 AnswerBench, while Gemma-4-26B-A4B rises from 25.5 to 34.2 ProofBench but decreases from 68.8 to 67.5 AnswerBench. In a separate Gemini-2.5-Pro-judged ProofBench evaluation, Intern-S2-OPD increases from 34.0 to 55.2, a 21.2-point gain, exceeding the plotted Gemini-2.5-Pro score of 47.2 and GPT-5 score of 39.5, although this comparison uses a different judging setup from the main tables. The OPD-plus-reference-KL ablation on Intern-S2-Preview improves ProofBench from 21.70 to 38.50 and reduces truncation to nearly zero in the shown training curves. Increasing distillation length from 6K to 32K raises Intern-S2 ProofBench from 38.80 to 44.50 and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B ProofBench from 40.07 to 42.39. Scientific transfer is modest but positive: Intern-S2-OPD changes FrontierScience-Olympiad from 60.6 to 60.9, FrontierScience-Research from 1.7 to 5.0, HLE from 19.6 to 20.5, and HiPhO from 38.6 to 41.1. Baselines include the base model, EOPD, and G-OPD only for Intern-S2; these are recent OPD variants, but the study lacks standard supervised-distillation, vanilla OPD, and broader cross-tokenizer baselines. The tested rollout scale is substantial in sequence length but limited in data breadth: 4,528 listed proof problems, 100 rollout iterations, and no reported multi-seed or large-scale production evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The exact-span cross-tokenizer alignment and combination of termination masking with initial-policy KL regularization form the main method contribution, while the observation that naive long-context OPD causes length explosion and repetition is an empirical finding; however, the underlying reverse-KL OPD, PPO updates, and KL trust-region idea are established components rather than new theoretical constructs. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful component studies: direct OPD exposes length and repetition degeneration, special-token masking reduces instability but does not solve length growth, reference KL nearly eliminates truncation in the reported Intern-S2 run, and a coefficient sweep is provided for GLM-4.7. It also compares EOPD and G-OPD and studies data composition, distillation length, teacher choice, tokenizer families, and scientific generalization. However, no error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or independent training seeds are reported. The paper selects the best checkpoint using AIME@4 and AnswerBench@1 while reporting those benchmark families, creating a potential evaluation-selection bias unless the selection and reporting splits are disjoint; this is not clarified. ProofBench relies on model judges—DeepSeek-V4-Flash in the main tables and Gemini-2.5-Pro in the headline figure—and the other benchmarks combine exact verification with GPT-OSS-120B judging, so judge variance and contamination are unresolved. The alignment ratio is high in the plotted cases, roughly 0.90–0.98, but the paper does not provide aggregate ratios by dataset, tokenization pair, or response type. A project-page, code, and models are indicated on the first page, but no actual project URL, repository URL, checkpoint URL, dataset release, or license is stated; the implementation depends on the external Slime and SGLang frameworks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The method can in principle run on commercially available accelerators using existing LLM rollout and training frameworks, but the paper does not report hardware requirements or end-to-end resource use. Efficient: It avoids supervised teacher-trajectory construction and uses a linear alignment scan, but every student rollout still requires teacher scoring and long-context inference, and no wall-clock, GPU-hour, memory, or cost comparison is reported. Effective: The evidence shows large gains on proof and mathematical reasoning benchmarks and small gains on several science benchmarks, but it does not establish robustness on real user workloads, factual reliability of generated proofs, or quality after controlling for output length and truncation. Scalable: The method is tested with 6K and 32K distillation lengths and evaluates responses up to 160K tokens, but there is no experiment at 10×–100× larger data, model, or deployment scale, and the paper only claims rather than demonstrates scalability to substantially larger heterogeneous systems. The work delivers a training method and apparently associated code and model checkpoints, but the release locations and artifact accessibility are not stated explicitly. Strengths: - The shared-surface-string formulation gives a simple, implementable solution to heterogeneous tokenization without requiring an artificial token correspondence or architecture-specific vocabulary projection. - The paper identifies a concrete failure mode—teacher-induced length growth, missing termination, repetition, and truncation—and supplies targeted interventions rather than reporting only final benchmark scores. - Results cover same-tokenizer and cross-tokenizer students across Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Intern-S2, GLM-4.7, and Gemma-4, with gains on both verifiable-answer and natural-language-proof benchmarks. - The length, data-composition, teacher, and reference-KL studies provide evidence that long distillation sequences matter particularly for proof reasoning and that proof-only data can outperform a mixed proof-plus-verifiable-data recipe on ProofBench. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that special-token masking alone does not eliminate length expansion, that larger tokenizer discrepancies make transfer more difficult, and that direct OPD can degenerate into repetition and truncation. It also reports a negative transfer case: Gemma-4-26B-A4B loses 1.3 points on AnswerBench despite gaining 8.7 points on ProofBench. The authors do not provide a dedicated limitations section or quantify the computational cost, seed sensitivity, or failure rate of the proposed method. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central cross-tokenizer objective supervises only exact boundary-and-span matches and falls back to the student distribution elsewhere, but the paper does not compare this choice against soft alignment, byte-level alignment, dynamic mapping, or other cross-tokenizer methods cited in related work. It does not compare against supervised fine-tuning on teacher traces, teacher-generated rejection sampling, standard reverse-KL OPD, or strong non-OPD post-training baselines, making it difficult to isolate the value of SimpleOPD from OPD itself. The headline 55.2 ProofBench result uses a separate judge and appears alongside frontier-model numbers without a controlled re-evaluation of every comparator under identical conditions. Checkpoint selection on AIME and AnswerBench may overstate those reported scores if no held-out selection split exists. The training corpus is small by LLM post-training standards and drawn from public/community sources, yet contamination, train-test overlap, and licensing are not analyzed. The claim that reasoning generalizes out of domain is supported by small gains on three benchmarks and a larger gain on FrontierScience Research, but no task-level error analysis or matched compute comparison establishes that the gains reflect transferable reasoning rather than format, length, or judge effects. Finally, the paper characterizes students as short-context models while allowing 32K distillation and 160K evaluation responses, without clearly documenting each student's actual context limit or the deployment behavior under that limit. Bottom Line: This is a useful and practically motivated OPD recipe with credible evidence that exact text-span alignment plus policy anchoring can transfer proof-oriented behavior across model families, but its novelty is incremental and its headline claims need independent seeds, cost accounting, cleaner checkpoint protocols, and stronger cross-tokenizer and supervised-distillation baselines before it merits high confidence as a general-purpose method.

ARENA: Automated Red-Teaming for Large Audio Language Models

J He, Z Huang, T Jin, Z Sun, C Hong, Y Yu, W Jiang… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ARENA, a closed-loop black-box red-teaming framework that generates text-safe queries and synthesized speech or environmental audio to elicit and detect harmful, audio-grounded behavior in large audio-language models. - Why it's important: Text-only safety tests can miss failures in which benign-looking text becomes harmful only when interpreted jointly with speech or environmental sound, creating an unmeasured deployment risk for voice assistants and multimodal agents. - How it does it: ARENA trains a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-32B controller with reward-weighted supervised fine-tuning and DPO, then uses MD-Judge failure feedback to iteratively revise the query, audio prompt, modality, and waveform realization while reserving Llama Guard 3 for final scoring. - The good: On 520 held-out AdvBench objectives, it reports FDRs of 87.9%, 71.5%, 68.1%, and 75.4% on Audio Flamingo 3, Qwen2-Audio, MiMo-Audio, and GPT-Audio, respectively, substantially exceeding the two static audio-jailbreak baselines. - The missing: The central success metric is determined by a single automated Llama Guard 3 judgment, with no human validation, judge agreement analysis, confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or comparison against stronger adaptive black-box red-team baselines. - Read it or not: Safety researchers and developers of audio-language models should read it for its audio-specific attack formulation and failure taxonomy, while readers seeking validated evidence of real-world safety risk should treat the reported attack rates as preliminary.

Rigor (55), Completeness (60), and Resilience (55) are pulled down by reliance on a single automated judge, absent human validation and uncertainty estimates, narrow adaptive baselines, and unclear compute and selection-budget accounting; the preprint status also warrants caution. Problem & Motivation: The work addresses automated safety auditing for large audio-language models in settings where harmful intent is carried by audio while the accompanying text remains safe in isolation. The affected domain includes voice assistants, accessibility systems, audio-analysis tools, and multimodal agents that combine speech, environmental sound, and language reasoning. Prior automated red-team methods mainly optimize text prompts or visual inputs, and existing audio jailbreak benchmarks provide static test cases rather than target-adaptive generation. The specific gap is the lack of a scalable procedure that jointly handles safe textual framing, audio modality selection, audio recognizability, model refusal behavior, and grounding of the harmful response in the recognized audio content. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat audio-grounded red-teaming as a feedback-controlled generation problem rather than as a fixed prompt-set evaluation: different failure modes reveal which channel must be changed, so a controller can use structured feedback to decide whether to revise the text framing, simplify or replace the audio event, switch between speech and environmental sound, or retry the waveform realization. Methodology: For each harmful objective x, a controller policy generates a structured specification z = (q_p, p_a, m), where q_p is the text-safe query, p_a is a speech transcript or environmental-sound description, and m selects speech or sound rendering. Piper TTS renders speech and TangoFlux renders four-second environmental audio. The target LALM is queried first with a recognition prompt to obtain r_rec and then with q_p to obtain the final response r. The text guard rejects q_p if it is unsafe alone; final success requires Llama Guard 3 to judge q_p safe, r_rec consistent with the intended audio, and r harmful, actionable, and grounded in that audio. Controller training uses 2,000 seed specifications, split into 1,200 speech and 800 environmental-sound cases, which are executed once to create an MD-Judge-labeled log. The first training stage performs reward-weighted SFT on positive records using a shaped reward that adds evidence for disallowed assistance, objective compliance, actionability, grounding, and concrete detail while penalizing generic content, event restatement, and refusal. The second stage applies DPO to higher- versus lower-reward specifications, initialized from the SFT checkpoint, with replay examples to preserve the structured output format. At inference, the controller performs up to K = 30 iterations, conditioning on the prior specification, target response, failure tier, and condensed MD-Judge feedback; environmental-sound attacks can additionally sample multiple waveform variants. The main design decisions—separating MD-Judge from the final evaluator, enforcing text safety before audio execution, and modeling speech versus environmental sound explicitly—are motivated by leakage prevention and audio-recognition failure modes, but the paper does not establish that the particular reward weights, judge prompts, or controller-training choices are optimal. Key Results: On 520 held-out AdvBench objectives, ARENA reports FDR/PSR of 87.9%/100.0% for Audio Flamingo 3, 71.5%/96.3% for Qwen2-Audio, 68.1%/100.0% for MiMo-Audio, and 75.4%/98.5% for GPT-Audio. FDR is the intersection of text-pass and final harmful-grounded-response judgments; the paper reports no human-confirmed harmfulness rate. The baselines are static audio jailbreak sets: AJailBench obtains FDRs of 31.2%, 10.8%, 25.3%, and 24.6%, while JALMBench obtains 12.6%, 11.9%, 10.7%, and 11.3% on the same four targets. These comparisons favor ARENA's adaptive search because neither baseline performs reward-guided refinement. Transfer tests show substantial but incomplete reuse of source attacks: AF3-originated cases achieve 59.7%, 60.0%, and 50.4% ASR on Qwen2-Audio, MiMo-Audio, and GPT-Audio, respectively; diagonal ASR values range from 68.1% to 87.9%. Refinement increases MD-Judge-measured ASR from approximately 23–30% at K = 0 to 88%, 74%, and 68% at K = 30 for AF3, Qwen2-Audio, and MiMo-Audio, with average attempts of 9.2, 9.1, 12.5, and 11.4 for AF3, Qwen2-Audio, MiMo-Audio, and GPT-Audio. Increasing environmental-sound variants from 1 to 16 raises ASR from 70% to 95% on AF3, 59% to 96% on Qwen2-Audio, and 49% to 85% on MiMo-Audio. Category-level ASR is highest in abuse/exploitation and violence/weapons for some targets, while self-harm/substance abuse is comparatively difficult on AF3 and MiMo-Audio. The tests use standard-scale model and benchmark evaluations, not deployment-scale traffic or long-horizon interaction. Novelty Classification: The contribution is primarily a NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: it formalizes two-sided audio-grounded red-teaming and instantiates it with modality-aware generation and failure-aware feedback, although reward-weighted SFT, DPO, black-box iterative search, and automated judging are standard components combined for this audio setting rather than fundamentally new optimization techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a held-out split between the 2,000-case controller-training pool and the 520 AdvBench evaluation objectives, explicitly excluding evaluation prompts, responses, and evaluator labels from training and tuning. It includes comparisons with two static baselines, transferability analysis, refinement-budget and decoding sweeps, waveform-variant ablations, category breakdowns, and failure analysis. However, it reports no ablation isolating reward-weighted SFT from DPO, no comparison with adaptive text-only or adaptive audio baselines, no experiments across random seeds, error bars, significance tests, inter-rater or judge agreement, or human assessment of whether responses are genuinely harmful, actionable, and audio-grounded. The final metric relies on one Llama Guard 3-8B call per retained case, and the search is optimized with MD-Judge, creating possible evaluator-specific artifacts even though MD-Judge and Llama Guard 3 are separated. The paper calls the controller-training data independent, but the seed taxonomy and evaluation objectives both draw from closely related safety categories, so semantic leakage is not fully ruled out. Code is stated to be available on GitHub, but the extracted paper does not provide a repository URL; release status for the 2,000-case dataset, model checkpoint, audio files, judge prompts, and exact evaluation scripts is not stated. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile—the paper evaluates a runnable red-teaming pipeline, although it does not present a deployed auditing service. * Practical: The method can run on commercially available hardware for open-source targets, but it requires a LoRA-tuned Qwen3-32B controller, text-to-speech and text-to-sound generators, multiple target queries, and auxiliary judge calls; the API-based GPT-Audio evaluation additionally depends on vendor access and is not costed. * Efficient: The search averages 9.1–12.5 refinement attempts per objective and permits up to 30 iterations, with additional waveform variants, but the paper gives no wall-clock time, GPU-hours, memory use, API cost, or comparison against the computational cost of static baselines. * Effective: The results show high automated detection rates under the paper's two-sided Llama Guard criterion and identify recognizable failure modes, but they establish effectiveness against a proxy evaluator rather than through independent human confirmation or demonstrated mitigation of real user-facing harm. * Scalable: The method is evaluated on four targets and 520 objectives, but no experiment tests 10×–100× more objectives, models, languages, audio lengths, conversational turns, or waveform variants; scalability beyond this benchmark is claimed rather than measured. The work delivers a red-teaming software framework and controller concept; it states that code is available on GitHub, but no URL or complete artifact inventory is given, and no public dataset or trained controller release is confirmed. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete audio-specific threat model in which text-only moderation passes while joint text-audio interpretation causes harmful compliance, and it operationalizes this with explicit text safety, recognition, grounding, and harmfulness conditions. - The closed-loop controller addresses several distinct bottlenecks—unsafe text framing, refusal, incorrect audio recognition, event restatement, and poor waveform realization—instead of treating audio jailbreaks as fixed prompt templates. - The evaluation spans three locally run LALMs and one API model, and the transfer results show that many discovered cases generalize across targets, supporting the claim that the issue is not limited to one implementation. - The ablations reveal a practically important finding: waveform sampling alone can materially change attack success, with environmental-sound ASR increasing by 25–37 percentage points from one to sixteen variants depending on the target. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper's failure analysis acknowledges target refusals after audio recognition, recognition at the wrong semantic granularity, and near misses that describe risky situations without actionable steps. It also notes that later refinement rounds provide diminishing gains and that target temperature affects measured success. The authors enforce the hard two-sided condition and distinguish the MD-Judge used during search from Llama Guard 3 used for final scoring. They do not provide a dedicated limitations section discussing human validation, evaluator reliability, compute cost, language coverage, or the risk that generated attacks exploit judge behavior rather than genuine safety failures. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unaddressed concern is metric validity: a single automated Llama Guard 3 judgment determines success, while the paper does not report human adjudication, judge calibration, false-positive rates, or sensitivity to alternative safety evaluators. The baseline comparison is narrow and potentially weak because both baselines are static; an adaptive black-box audio baseline, an adaptive text-only baseline with equivalent query budget, and random or sampling-only audio variants are needed to attribute gains to ARENA's controller and feedback loop. The paper also does not report the number of target queries, audio renders, total compute, or monetary cost per successful case, making practical auditing efficiency unclear. The 2,000 seed pool is template-derived and English-only, and the evaluation uses AdvBench objectives with related harmful categories, leaving robustness to naturally phrased user goals, multilingual audio, accents, noisy recordings, longer interactions, and unseen harm taxonomies untested. Finally, the large gains from waveform variants raise a selection-bias issue: retaining the first unsafe response among many generated realizations changes the attack budget and is not compared fairly against equally large-budget baselines. Bottom Line: This is a useful preprint for researchers building audio-language-model safety evaluations because it supplies a clear threat formulation and a reproducible-looking adaptive attack pipeline, but its headline vulnerability rates should not be treated as established real-world failure rates until independent human validation, stronger adaptive baselines, evaluator robustness tests, and full cost reporting are provided.

Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, Haozhe Wang, Tian Xueyun, Zhijing Zhang, Bingnan Li, Shuqi Gu, Kan Ren, Jiaming Liu, Ruihua Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 19 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AVA-Encoder, a hierarchical agentic auto-encoding framework that converts films into text-centered Film Knowledge Graphs and reconstructs them through a fixed video-generation pipeline. - Why it's important: Video agents lack process-level supervision for cinematic planning, while existing video representations are either difficult for agents to edit or too lossy for faithful generation and reconstruction. - How it does it: It combines film-, shot-, and keyframe-level prompting with typed graph relations and two gated textual-gradient loops that separately refine a reusable encoder policy and each input-specific graph. - The good: On 18 held-out clips, AVA-Encoder reports 49.0% overall reconstruction fidelity versus 28.3% for the strongest compared baseline, with gains in all four evaluation directions. - The missing: The evidence relies heavily on judgments from the same proprietary Gemini model family used for video understanding, reward construction, and evaluation, with only six pseudo-training clips and no reported confidence intervals, multiple-seed analysis, or human quality scores for the main benchmark. - Read it or not: Researchers in agentic video generation, structured multimodal representations, and controllable video editing should read it for the representation and evaluation design, but should treat the headline gains as preliminary until independently evaluated with stronger baselines and human studies.
