Problem & Motivation The paper addresses the difficulty of administering conventional tablets to patients with dysphagia, reduced swallowing reflex, nausea, polypharmacy, or limited access to water, with particular attention to children, older adults, psychiatric patients, and patients needing rapid relief. It also addresses formulation problems that limit oral dosage-form performance: balancing porosity against tablet strength, masking bitterness during oral residence, delivering high API doses, improving dissolution of poorly soluble BCS class II and IV drugs, controlling moisture sensitivity, and translating laboratory formulations to scalable manufacturing. The review states that swallowing difficulty affects approximately 26–55% of adults, 50–70% of pediatric populations, and 35–60% of elderly patients, but it does not reconcile the different populations, study designs, or definitions behind these ranges. The claimed gap is not a sharply defined missing result; rather, the paper seeks to consolidate fragmented work across materials, processes, testing, regulation, and clinical use. Key Idea The central insight is that FDT performance is a coupled formulation-and-process design problem: rapid oral disintegration requires water access and porosity, whereas acceptable handling requires mechanical strength, moisture protection, and suitable packaging. The paper further argues that taste masking and solubility enhancement must be integrated into this same design space, using approaches such as coated particles, ion-exchange resinates, cyclodextrin complexes, nanoparticles, amorphous solid dispersions, and lipid carriers. This is a useful organizing principle, but it is a synthesis of established pharmaceutical formulation concepts rather than a new conceptual framework. Methodology This is a narrative literature review covering material and excipient selection, direct compression, lyophilization, spray drying, sublimation, melt and wet granulation, and 3D-printing methods; taste masking by sweeteners/flavors, microencapsulation, ion-exchange resins, cyclodextrins, and adsorption; evaluation of disintegration, dissolution, strength, content uniformity, palatability, and stability; QbD concepts including QTPP, CQAs, CMAs, CPPs, risk assessment, DoE, response-surface methods, and machine learning; nanotechnology platforms; and therapeutic and marketed-product examples. It gives representative process details, such as blending API with excipients before rotary compression for direct compression; freezing aqueous suspensions at approximately −40 to −70°C followed by vacuum sublimation for lyophilization; using volatile camphor or menthol to create porous channels in sublimation; and preparing nanoparticles by media milling, high-pressure homogenization, or precipitation before incorporating them into tablets. It states example objectives and constraints rather than a unified review model: disintegration is generally targeted at 30–60 seconds, dissolution at at least 85% within 15 minutes in selected examples, and hardness or tensile strength is traded against wetting. Critical design decisions—selection of superdisintegrant, choice of manufacturing process, and integration of taste/solubility enhancement—are technically plausible, but their relative merits are not assessed using a consistent evidence framework. The paper does not state databases searched, search dates, screening procedures, study-selection rules, data-extraction methods, or a formal risk-of-bias assessment. Key Results The paper reports findings from cited studies rather than new experiments or a pooled analysis. Representative reported values include crospovidone-associated disintegration times of 15–45 seconds at 2–5% w/w; chitosan-containing meloxicam tablets disintegrating in 21±3 seconds at 4% w/w; several natural-polymer formulations disintegrating in approximately 20–30 seconds; co-processed direct-compression excipients producing 15–30-second disintegration with reported hardness of at least 3 kN; lyophilized tablets disintegrating in 3–10 seconds with stated mechanical strength of 1–2 N; and binder-jet/ZipDose products showing 1–5-second disintegration in the comparison table. The review cites a piroxicam nanoparticle lyophilizate with approximately 220±15 nm particles, 5-second release/disintegration, and enhanced bioavailability; a flurbiprofen formulation with 99.34±1.24% release at 15 minutes and 1.38-fold rat bioavailability versus a conventional tablet; and a nanostructured-lipid-carrier formulation with a reported 2.8-fold preclinical bioavailability improvement. It also cites a valsartan FDT with 28±2-second disintegration and complete release in 20 minutes, and rizatriptan ODT pharmacokinetics with an approximately 1-hour Tmax versus 1.5 hours for a conventional tablet. The main comparison table summarizes direct compression at 15–60 seconds, lyophilization at 3–10 seconds, spray drying at 20–45 seconds, sublimation at 15–40 seconds, melt granulation at 20–50 seconds, FDM printing at 5–30 seconds, and binder-jet printing at 1–5 seconds. These are heterogeneous values from different APIs, formulations, test conditions, and sources, so they do not establish a controlled ranking. Baseline quality is uneven: some cited examples compare with conventional tablets, but the review supplies no standardized cross-study comparator, confidence intervals, pooled effect sizes, or consistent clinical evidence. The tested scale is mostly laboratory or preclinical; commercial examples such as Claritin RediTab, Zyprexa Zydis, and Spritam establish feasibility, not evidence that the reviewed methods generally scale or improve patient outcomes. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: no; NEW METHOD: no; NEW DATASET/benchmark: no; NEW SYSTEM/tool: no; NEW FORMULATION: no; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: only as reported through cited studies; REVIEW/SYNTHESIS: the genuine contribution is a broad narrative compilation of established FDT technologies and recent directions, while the individual technical mechanisms and numerical results are taken from prior publications rather than newly derived or experimentally validated here. Rigor & Reproducibility The review contains no original experiments, preregistered protocol, systematic search flow diagram, study-quality scoring, meta-analysis, uncertainty estimates, or statistical synthesis. It includes no component ablations because it does not evaluate a single proposed formulation; cited primary studies sometimes use factorial designs, Box–Behnken designs, Plackett–Burman screening, or QbD validation, but the review does not consistently report sample sizes, replicate counts, validation errors, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests from those studies. No code, dataset, software package, model weights, or reproducible review database is released or mentioned. The reference list contains apparent metadata and citation-quality problems, including placeholder or malformed DOI strings, duplicated or mismatched references, sources that appear unrelated to the claims they support, and references to future-dated 2026 material in a paper dated July 2026 without a stated retrieval or publication-status convention. Several claims appear insufficiently checked—for example, the text alternates between 30 seconds, 60 seconds, and three minutes as definitions or quality limits; describes some sublingual or buccal products as FDTs without consistently distinguishing dosage-form categories; and cites market-research forecasts as evidence of scientific progress. Because the review does not verify study quality or harmonize test conditions, its quantitative comparisons are vulnerable to selective citation and apples-to-oranges interpretation. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL — the paper synthesizes experimental and commercial evidence but does not itself deploy a system. - Practical: Most direct-compression and granulation approaches can run on commercially available pharmaceutical equipment, while lyophilization, nanoparticle processing, and 3D printing require specialized equipment; the review does not provide validated manufacturing protocols or equipment-specific operating envelopes. - Efficient: Direct compression is presented as low-cost and scalable, whereas lyophilization and binder-jet printing are characterized as very high cost and/or slow throughput; no measured throughput, energy use, yield, cost-per-dose, memory, or compute comparison is provided. - Effective: The evidence supports rapid disintegration and, in selected formulations, improved dissolution or animal bioavailability, but it does not establish consistent improvements in adherence, therapeutic outcomes, or patient safety across populations; the claim that FDTs improve adherence is supported mainly by cited examples and general rationale rather than a synthesized clinical analysis. - Scalable: The review identifies scale-up, moisture stability, continuous manufacturing, and 3D-printing throughput as unresolved issues, but most reported formulations are laboratory-scale and no 10×–100× scale experiment, process-capability study, long-term commercial stability dataset, or validated continuous-production demonstration is presented. The paper stops at narrative review form. It does not deliver a software artifact, formulation dataset, trained model, validated manufacturing tool, or reusable proof technique. Strengths - It covers the full development chain from API and excipient properties through processing, taste, testing, packaging, regulation, and clinical use rather than treating disintegration time as the only endpoint. - It correctly identifies the principal engineering trade-off between rapid water penetration/porosity and mechanical robustness, and links this trade-off to process choices such as direct compression versus lyophilization. - It gives concrete illustrative values and examples, including superdisintegrant concentrations, disintegration times, nanoparticle size, release percentages, and reported preclinical bioavailability ratios. - It highlights clinically relevant constraints that are often underemphasized in formulation reviews, including palatability, pediatric dose appropriateness, moisture exposure, high-dose loading, and the lack of standardized in-vitro oral-cavity/IVIVC methods. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly identify mechanical fragility, high API-dose limitations, taste-masking complexity, hygroscopicity, elevated capital and operating costs, possible oral-cavity instability, scale-up challenges for lyophilization and 3D printing, moisture-sensitive shelf life, incomplete taste masking for high-dose bitter drugs, and the difficulty of developing reliable in-vitro/in-vivo correlations. They also acknowledge that high-dose 3D-printed ODTs such as the approximately 1,000 mg Spritam product are unusual rather than representative. These scope boundaries are useful, but the authors do not acknowledge the absence of a systematic review methodology, the heterogeneity of cited measurements, the uneven source quality, or the uncertainty around several regulatory and market claims. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper calls itself comprehensive and evidence-based but gives no reproducible search strategy, databases, selection criteria, time-window enforcement, or study-quality assessment. - It compares disintegration times, hardness, and costs across technologies without controlling for API dose, formulation composition, tablet geometry, test medium, apparatus, temperature, or measurement protocol. - It does not separate validated clinical evidence from in-vitro studies, animal pharmacokinetics, marketed-product descriptions, and speculative future applications such as AI-driven formulation or point-of-care pharmacogenomic dosing. - Claims of improved adherence, buccal absorption, first-pass avoidance, and faster clinical onset are not supported by a structured review of randomized clinical, pharmacokinetic, or patient-acceptability evidence. - The review does not examine safety and regulatory risks of nanoparticles, residual solvents, novel excipients, pediatric taste systems, dose-content uniformity in 3D printing, or the manufacturing validation burden for personalized products. - Bibliographic inconsistencies and apparent citation mismatches reduce confidence that the cited evidence supports all associated claims; the paper also contains editorial remnants such as references to lectures, courses, students, and unrelated headings. - The proposed QbD and AI/ML directions are described conceptually, but the review does not report predictive performance, external validation, domain-shift robustness, or real-world deployment evidence for formulation models. Bottom Line Read this as a broad introductory orientation to FDT formulation and manufacturing, but do not treat it as a rigorous evidence synthesis or as reliable support for comparative technology, clinical, regulatory, or market conclusions without independently checking the primary sources.

These papers share a focus on making agentic reinforcement learning practical by treating the runtime harness, environment, tools, and execution state as central parts of training rather than optimizing model weights alone. “Agent Lightning v1.0” and “ClawGym II” emphasize framework-level training of opaque or deployment-time harnesses, while “EnvHarness” and “Zetta” adapt environments and recovery mechanisms to generate more useful learning experiences in static and physical settings. “HELIX” extends this direction toward co-evolving models and source-traceable harness portfolios, whereas “Belayer” concentrates on fault tolerance and state-preserving infrastructure for long-horizon training.
